title: Citely Deal Room
pitch: A compliance deal room where the AI agent gathers evidence across contracts and code through five WebMCP verbs — and "confirmed" isn't one of them. Every signature stays human.
about_excerpt: A compliance deal room where the AI agent gathers evidence across contracts and code through five WebMCP verbs — and "confirmed" isn't one of them. Every signature stays human. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Startups that sell data to frontier labs — teleoperation trajectories, first-person video — have to pass three doors before a contract signs: a security questionnaire, a DPA, and a license with warranties the founder personally has to be able to sign. The evidence for those doors lives everywhere: operator contracts on someone's desktop, lineage logging in a GitHub repo, and consent forms that simply don't exist yet. An AI agent is the perfect thing to send out to gather that evidence. It is the worst possible thing to let decide whether a fact is true — because if it's wrong, a founder just signed a false warranty. We wanted to build the version of "agent + compliance" where that line is enforced by the API, not by a prompt asking the model to behave. What it does Citely Deal Room is a case workbench for one business event: Northstar Capture Labs (synthetic) trying to pass a frontier lab's vendor review. Six zones: event card, materials (three states: provided / pending / nonexistent), fact ledger (every fact is a signature — who, when, on what basis), blockers grouped by door and anchored to the counterparty's questionnaire and warranty clauses, an action board, and an escalation record with a hard-stop switch. The page exposes five WebMCP tools . An agent can read the room, propose that a material is pending or nonexistent with evidence, attach evidence to a fact, read blockers, and read frozen briefs. It cannot say provided , cannot confirm a fact, cannot freeze a brief, and cannot clear a hard stop — those are human-only UI actions with signatures. Blockers recompute live as evidence lands; a human freezes the board into a versioned Founder Risk Brief that also downloads as Markdown. Demo: hand the agent the operator agreement PDF and point it at the pipeline repo. It comes back with "agreement exists, no IP-assignment clause," "lineage logging found," "no consent artifacts anywhere" — and the board updates while every proposal stays tagged agent proposed · not confirmed . Flip "Legal claim received" and every propose call is refused with HARD_STOP . How we built it WebMCP : document.modelContext ?? navigator.modelContext feature detection, then registerTool({ name, description, inputSchema, execute }) for each tool. Input schemas use additionalProperties: false with id enums generated from the case file; the state enum is literally ['pending', 'nonexistent'] . Trust model as code : tools and the UI share the same pure state transitions; tools add three guards in order — hard stop → whitelist validation → human-confirmation lock. Every response, success or refusal, carries a verbatim disclaimer and a note to the agent. Rules as data : blocker rules live in room-schema.json ( any_material_not , fact_status_in , all_of ); a different event type is one config file away. Zero backend, zero runtime dependencies : Vite + TypeScript, vanilla DOM built through a textContent -only helper, CSP default-src 'self' , evidence never persisted. package.json dependencies is {} . Tests : 55 tests including the acceptance suite — agent can't set provided ; hard stop refuses writes but allows reads; disclaimer verbatim on every response; zero network (fetch/XHR stubbed to throw + a static source scan); injection text renders as plain text and changes nothing; human confirmations can't be overridden. Challenges we ran into Deciding what the agent must not be able to do was the real design work. We went back and forth on whether "provided" should be proposable and ended up deleting it from the agent's vocabulary entirely: whether a material exists is a client-confirmed fact. Making refusals useful : an agent that gets a bare error just retries. Every refusal explains the rule and tells the agent what to say to the user instead. Prompt injection in documents is the real attack surface for compliance work , so the demo contract carries an injection clause on purpose. Immunity had to come from the tool surface, not from hoping the model resists. Runtime plumbing : agents can't read your desktop; the demo instruction had to change to "read the attached agreement and the pipeline/ directory of the repo." Accomplishments that we're proud of The agent, unprompted, told us it had ignored the contract's "Reviewer Notice" because "it is document content, not your instruction" — and then asked permission before writing to the board. The five-verb surface survived a whole-branch adversarial review: no input reaches confirmed , provided , freeze, or un-hard-stop. A fact the client was about to sign ( every agreement assigns IP ) got stopped by the agent's own evidence — the agent can't confirm, but it can keep a human from confirming something false. What we learned WebMCP changes where the safety boundary lives. With UI-driving agents you write guardrails after the fact; with WebMCP the page's tool schema is the permission model, and the description text is the policy the agent reads at the moment it matters. For anything with liability attached, that's the difference between "please don't" and "you can't." What's next Real deal rooms need accounts, roles, an audit log, and server-side status judgments signed by a person — deliberately out of scope for an open demo. The next step is a second event type (consumer hardware crowdfunding) to prove the "one config file away" claim, and a get_diff tool so an agent can explain what changed between two frozen briefs. title: Full Loop
pitch: Can an agent finish what it started? A WebMCP lifecycle audit that people and their agents fix together.
about_excerpt: Can an agent finish what it started? A WebMCP lifecycle audit that people and their agents fix together. Like Comment Story Updates Audit Corpus Agents Inspiration I run LaunchLoop (launchloop.xyz). We run developer programs like hackathons and accelerators that help companies get builders using their technology, mostly in gaming and AI. We also perform transformations for our clients, getting them ai-ready. And when we have some extra time, we build/incubate our own products, one of them is Methora.io, which is about getting AI-assisted work all the way to done instead of just started. So a WebMCP hackathon was right up our alley. I browsed the public directories of WebMCP-enabled sites to see what people were connecting. What I found was that most sites had tools for searching, pricing, signing up and checking out (the start of the funnel). But very few had tools for cancelling, returning, or closing an account. I couldn't find anyone measuring that, so I built something that does. I don't think WebMCP really works until an agent can do everything a human can on a site. And you can't fix what you can't measure, so hopefully Full Loop helps WebMCP take the next step! What it does Full Loop takes a website's WebMCP tools and sorts them into eight stages of a customer relationship: Discover, Evaluate, Commit, Use, Modify, Reverse, Exit, Support. It shows which stages the site covers and gives it a score. If an agent can commit on a user's behalf (buy, book, sign up) but has no tool to cancel, return or leave, the site is flagged as an open loop. I ran it over the 475 sites in the public webmcp.com directory, about 2,989 tools in total. 148 sites let an agent commit. 144 of those give it no way to undo. No site in the directory has an exit tool. The page also registers eight WebMCP tools of its own, so you can do the audit through an agent in ChatGPT's browser instead of clicking: audit_site and audit_tool_list run the audit and render it on the page find_sites_by_stage , compare_sites and get_corpus_stats answer questions about the directory (for example "which travel sites let you cancel a booking?", which currently returns nothing) draft_missing_tools writes registerTool stubs for the missing stages into an editor on the page set_stub_code lets the agent rewrite a stub in that editor while you edit it too add_review_note lets the agent leave a short note on a stage card Tool calls are logged on the page so you can see what the agent did. How we built it It's a static site: HTML, CSS and plain JavaScript, hosted on GitHub Pages. There's no backend and no AI API. The classification is a set of regular expressions run over tool names and descriptions, checked in a fixed order (Exit and Reverse first, so cancel_order doesn't get caught by the generic order rule). The scoring weights each stage. Stub templates are picked by stage and site category. The tools are registered with document.modelContext.registerTool , with a fallback to navigator.modelContext . Each has a JSON Schema inputSchema and an execute function that updates the DOM and returns JSON in content[0].text . The directory data is a snapshot fetched by a small Node script and committed to the repo, so the site doesn't depend on webmcp.com being up. I tested it in ChatGPT's in-app browser with Codex on GPT-5.6 Sol. Challenges we ran into Word boundaries in regex don't work on snake_case. \bpolicies\b never matched search_shop_policies_and_faqs , so the tool fell through to matching on its description, which mentions "return policy", and it got filed under Reverse. That made a lot of Shopify stores look like they had closed loops when they didn't. Splitting names into words before matching fixed it, and the open-loop rate went from 77% to 97%. Deciding what counts as Reverse also took some thought. Shopify's cancel_cart undoes a cart, not an order, so I put it under Use. The number would have looked better the other way, but it would have been wrong. Accomplishments that we're proud of The 97% figure is reproducible from public data, and as far as I can tell nobody had computed it before. The site works the same whether or not an agent is present. And it has no dependencies, no keys and no server, so there's nothing to break during judging. What we learned With WebMCP the page doesn't need its own model. The agent in the browser supplies the reasoning and the page supplies data and functions. Once I understood that, I stopped trying to add an AI API and the project got simpler. Also, the WebMCP ecosystem right now is mostly acquisition tooling. Sites are giving agents the ability to start things that the same agent can't finish. What's next for Full Loop Full customer flow mapping with green/red lights for which parts are active on WebMCP. I'd also love the audits to be live, and connect to an orchestrator. That way someone can see what is possible with all of the WebMCP sites, while also having a good idea about what is not possible. Also, any site going live on WebMCP should have the full customer journey, so I hope Full Loop becomes integral in ensuring that everyone is setting up WebMCP... THE RIGHT WAY! And I want to bring the lifecycle idea back into Methora, where a job shouldn't count as complete unless it can also be reversed, validated, insured or exited. title: UITester
pitch: AI agent that tests web UIs via WebMCP tool calls, not brittle selectors—catches regressions.
about_excerpt:
AI agent that tests web UIs via WebMCP tool calls, not brittle selectors—catches regressions.

 Inspiration 

 Most "AI test agents" still drive the UI the old way: guess a CSS selector, click, hope it doesn't break on the next redesign. When we saw the emerging WebMCP standard — pages exposing their own actions through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) , with a proper JSON Schema instead of a DOM tree to guess at — it looked like the missing layer for reliable, AI-native UI testing. If a page tells an agent exactly what it can do and what valid input looks like, testing stops being "click and pray" and becomes "call the tool and check the contract." 

 What it does 

 ToolProof is a small Electron "browser" built for one job: point it at any web page and it will test that page through its own tools. 

 
 Load — a target URL opens inside an embedded <webview> , just like a normal browser tab. 
 Discover — it checks the page for a native document.modelContext . If the site doesn't support WebMCP yet, a fallback pass reads the page's own HTML5 form constraints ( pattern , required , min / max , type=email , …) and synthesizes an equivalent modelContext on the fly, so any site can be exercised the same way. 
 Generate scenarios — the discovered tool's JSON Schema is sent to Gemini, which proposes 6–10 realistic test cases: happy path plus boundary and invalid-input cases. If there's no API key, or Gemini fails, a deterministic rule-based generator takes over (missing required fields, out-of-range numbers, regex-violating strings via randexp , invalid enum values) — so the tool never dead-ends. 
 Run — each scenario is executed live, inside the real page, via document.modelContext.executeTool(...) — not simulated clicks. 
 Report — pass/fail is compared against the scenario's expected outcome and shown per-scenario plus a summary. 
 

 A companion demo page implements a real, native document.modelContext.registerTool flow, used to validate the agent against an actual WebMCP-compliant target instead of only the DOM-inference fallback. 

 How we built it 

 
 Electron , with a strict main / preload / renderer split ( contextIsolation: true , no nodeIntegration ) — the renderer never touches Node directly, everything goes through an IPC bridge exposed in preload.js . 
 The target site itself runs in a <webview> , so the agent's "browser" is a real Chromium instance, not a headless stub. 
 A hand-rolled document.modelContext polyfill is injected into pages without native WebMCP support, so the discovery → generate → run pipeline is identical whether the tools are real or inferred. 
 Gemini ( gemini-2.5-flash ) turns a tool's inputSchema into concrete test data; a local, dependency-free rule engine ( scenario-utils.js ) mirrors the same scenario shape as a deterministic fallback. 
 A separate agent-runner (Node + Playwright) explores the same idea headlessly, for CI-style runs outside the Electron shell. 
 

 Challenges we ran into 

 
 IPC serialization : document.modelContext.getTools() can return live objects with circular/non-cloneable references (e.g. a window handle) — Electron's executeJavaScript bridge threw "object could not be cloned" until we normalized every tool down to { name, description, inputSchema } before it crosses the IPC boundary. 
 Timing : tools registered after client-side hydration weren't visible on first check, so discovery needed to poll getTools() for up to ~8s rather than assume readiness on page load. 
 Schema shape drift : some pages return inputSchema as a JSON string rather than an object — discovery normalizes both shapes before generating scenarios. 
 LLM reliability : an LLM won't always return valid JSON or field names that match the schema exactly, so the rule-based generator exists as a hard fallback, not just a nice-to-have. 
 

 What we learned 

 That WebMCP's registerTool / getTools / executeTool contract is a genuinely better testing surface than the DOM — it turns "does the UI still look right" into "does the underlying capability still honor its own contract," which is both more robust to redesigns and closer to what a QA engineer actually cares about.

title: Blnq Studio
pitch: Accessible-by-default web building. Blnq exposes its editor, live preview and WCAG audit to browser agents via WebMCP — so the AI that writes your code also catches its a11y violations.
about_excerpt: Accessible-by-default web building. Blnq exposes its editor, live preview and WCAG audit to browser agents via WebMCP — so the AI that writes your code also catches its a11y violations. Like Comment Story Updates 1 Inspiration I built blnq.studio because front-end work had become a pile of tabs: an editor, a dev server, a browser, DevTools, an accessibility checker, a design spec, and now an AI chat window that can't see any of them. Every one of those handoffs is where quality leaks out — especially accessibility, which is the first thing dropped when you're moving fast and the last thing an AI agent notices, because it can't see what it built. I wanted a single tab where the code, the live preview, the audit and the AI all look at the same thing. WebMCP was the missing piece: it lets the editor tab itself become the tool surface an agent uses, so the loop closes without any extra setup. What it does blnq.studio is a browser-based editor purpose-built for front-end: code, preview, ship — all in one tab. Live multi-file editing — Monaco under the hood, real HTML/CSS/JS files with folders and ES module imports, no build step. The preview updates as you type. Accessibility first — every preview refresh runs the pour engine against WCAG 2.0–2.2 A/AA plus best-practice rules. The A11y panel lists each violation with its impact, a plain-English fix and the exact element. Colour-contrast checks are built into the editor, not bolted on afterwards. Multi-device preview — switch viewports, check every breakpoint, see the FPS overlay, all without leaving the tab. Design systems your AI respects — drop a DESIGN.md at the project root and the editor treats it as the source of truth: colour and font literals that drift from your tokens get flagged, so AI-written CSS stays inside the system instead of inventing new values. Baseline compatibility — a built-in tool tab tells you which features you're using aren't yet widely available across browsers. Collaborate and fork — real-time multi-cursor collaboration over Yjs, forks and merge requests, a community showcase. Ship from the editor — push to GitHub, deploy from the menu, or download the whole project as one self-contained HTML file. AI & MCP, on your terms — AI is optional. When you want it, connect Claude Code (or any MCP client) over the built-in MCP server, use the in-editor chat with your own model, or — new for this challenge — turn on WebMCP and let a browser-native agent drive the tab directly. WebMCP: the editor tab is the tool server Click Start WebMCP and blnq registers 30+ tools with the browser via document.modelContext . No MCP ID, no config file, no separate process. An agent running in the browser can then: Read and edit files by line range or find-and-replace, with undo snapshots and live edits landing in the editor and preview See what it built — blnq_screenshot returns a real PNG, plus element inspection, console errors and viewport switching Audit with blnq_check_preview , which returns JS errors, every WCAG violation with its element HTML and fix hint, and any design-token drift Interact — click, type, press keys, wait for elements — so it can tab through a form or open a modal and re-audit the new state Fix and re-audit until the report is clean The key design decision was that WebMCP isn't a separate integration. blnq has one shared tool registry; the MCP server and the WebMCP endpoint are two thin adapters over it. A tool added to the registry appears in both, and edits behave identically — same validation, same undo, same activity toasts, same prompt history — whichever transport the call came in on. How I built it blnq is an Express + Monaco + Yjs app with a plugin system; the MCP server, AI chat, Baseline and spellcheck tools are all plugins. The accessibility engine runs inside the preview iframe and posts results up to the editor, so the panel a human reads and the result an agent reads come from the same run. WebMCP was around 350 lines: a client module that fetches tool descriptors and calls registerTool() for each (with readOnlyHint annotations and MCP-shaped { content } results including images), and a server endpoint that Zod-validates and runs the shared handler. The endpoint is same-origin only and still requires the tab's random bridge ID; the browser handles user consent on its side. What I learned The accessibility audit turned out to be the most valuable thing blnq can hand an agent. A screenshot tells a model roughly what it built; a WCAG report with the offending element and a fix hint tells it exactly what to change. Structured, model-readable audit output beat any amount of prompt engineering. And WebMCP inverts the usual relationship: the page stops being something an agent scrapes and becomes something it calls . Once you have a decent tool registry, the browser becomes the integration layer for free. What's next Structured JSON from blnq_check_preview so agents can diff violations between audits A blnq_fix_a11y tool that applies remedies for common rule classes automatically Focus-order and keyboard-navigation audits driven by key-press sequences Ship the Chrome origin-trial token on blnq.studio so WebMCP works without flags Share a collaboration session with an agent so humans and AI can work on the same project live Built With ai css framework-free html javascript Try it out blnq.studio Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by David Yarham Like Share this project: Updates David Yarham posted an update — Aug 26, 2026 04:58 PM EDT I dont have a youtube or any video of Blnq, it is a live site and no need Log in or sign up for Devpost to join the conversation. title: Open Racer Racing Line Editor
pitch: An open-source racing line editor that lets AI agents create track layouts through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: An open-source racing line editor that lets AI agents create track layouts through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Racing Line 3D View Codex using WebMCP Inspiration I built the first version of the racing line editor about six years ago. I wanted a tool to prepare for karting and learn unfamiliar tracks. I studied onboard videos and drew every braking point, apex, and acceleration zone by hand. I kept wondering whether an AI could help me. Last year, I returned to the project and added a 3D WebGL view. Claude and Codex helped me bring it back to life. The editor was also recognized in the 2025 Google Maps Platform Awards. What it does The racing line editor lets you draw and edit racing lines on a satellite map. Points can represent braking, acceleration, or transition. Lines can be saved locally and viewed in 3D. In the demo, Codex reads an existing full-circuit line. Two shorter layouts are missing. Through WebMCP, it reads the circuit, the reference line, and the editor guidance. It then creates both missing layouts directly in the editor. How I built it For this challenge, I separated the editor from the older Open Racer application and rebuilt it as a standalone open-source app. It uses Vite, React 19, JavaScript, Google Maps Platform, and Paper.js. Lines are stored locally with IndexedDB and can be exported as JSON. There is no backend or sign-in. The WebMCP tools use the same editor state as the visible controls. Agents can inspect the track, read line-creation guidance, edit points, undo changes, and save or load lines. I use Vitest for unit tests, Playwright for browser tests, and GitHub Pages for deployment. The hardest part A racing line is more than coordinates. Point order matters. The line must stay on the drivable surface, and one circuit can contain several layouts. The challenge was giving the agent enough context while keeping every change visible and understandable to the user. What I learned Structured WebMCP actions reduce guessing. They make agent changes more predictable and easier to verify. title: 3DStreet: Agent-Built Urban Planning Visuals via WebMCP
pitch: Describe an urban street project and watch an AI agent build it in 3D: real locations, elevation, Google 3D Tiles maps via 20+ WebMCP tools in the 3DStreet urban design editor.
about_excerpt: Describe an urban street project and watch an AI agent build it in 3D: real locations, elevation, Google 3D Tiles maps via 20+ WebMCP tools in the 3DStreet urban design editor. Like Comment Story Updates Starter prompt First response, pretty good but missing a lane Add the second lane Geolocate it to San Francisco Inspiration 3DStreet is an existing open-source 3D street-design tool used by planners, advocates, and students to reimagine real streets: add a bike lane, widen a sidewalk, see it in context on Google's photorealistic 3D Tiles. The hardest part has never been the rendering. It's the dozens of small edits between "what if this street were safer?" and a picture you can bring to a city council meeting. WebMCP collapses that gap: the browser agent you already have becomes the operator of a professional design tool, in your own signed-in tab, with you watching every move. What it does Open 3dstreet.app in ChatGPT's in-app browser (or Chrome 149+) and the page registers 26 WebMCP tools with document.modelContext . No extension, no relay, no setup. Then just talk: "Make a street with two drive lanes, protected bike lanes, and wide sidewalks with street trees" : the agent composes a managed street segment by segment. Each segment type carries the same presets a human gets from the sidebar (surface, markings, vehicles, pedestrians), so a "bus lane" comes with buses and BUS stencils instead of a grey slab. "Set the location to 4th & King in San Francisco" : server-side elevation lookup anchors the scene into Google's 3D Tiles. getGeoContext then gives the agent a machine-readable bridge between scene coordinates and lat/lon, including the compass bearing of the street's centerline and both endpoints, so it can align a design with the real road. "Take a plan-view snapshot" : the tool orients a north-up top-down camera and returns an image content block plus camera metadata (tilt, north-up, ground extent), so the agent sees its own work and can self-correct. Every mutation goes through the editor's command system: fully undoable, visible live in a transcript panel ( webmcp · managedStreetCreate …), and gated by a one-click Read-only toggle. The first tool call of a session dismisses the welcome modal and opens the Console tab, so the human always sees the agent at work. Read tools ( getScene , getSessionInfo , listMixins , listSegmentPresets ) let the agent orient itself before acting, and creation tools wait for the street to actually mount and report back what rendered, so "created" is backed by geometry rather than a hopeful return value. How we built it One registry, three LLM consumers. 3DStreet already had a tool registry feeding an in-editor assistant and an MCP relay for desktop AI apps. During the submission period we added a third transport: a React hook that feature-detects document.modelContext and registers every tool via registerTool({ name, description, inputSchema, execute }) , funneling execution through one shared executor so WebMCP, the relay, and the in-editor chat behave identically. We registered Chrome origin-trial tokens for our domains, so stock Chrome 149–156 needs no flag . Then we iterated through four rounds of live testing with an OpenAI WebMCP agent, treating every failure as a tool-surface bug compiled by Sol 5.6, then reviewed and fixed with Fable 5.1: Round 1: safety rails. Destructive tools are fenced to the user-editable scene subtree (an agent can't delete the camera rig); component names are validated against A-Frame's registry so hallucinated writes fail loudly; every error is written for the model . Round 2: grounding. The agent couldn't tell which side of the street was north, put a bus model in the stencil painter (sideways buses), and reported success for content that never rendered. We added getGeoContext , north-up plan snapshots with camera metadata, schema validation for every street field with the valid values listed in the error, per-type segment presets, and post-create readback. Round 3: guidance. The agent built synthetic buildings on top of the real Google 3D Tiles ones, then verified from street level. Fix: tool descriptions now lead with the geo rule, plan view is the default verification snapshot in geo scenes, and each mutating result ends with a nextStep nudge. Round 4: persistence and payload. Agent-built scenes vanished on reload, and a full-res PNG snapshot was 2.5 MB of base64. Added saveScene / loadScene , an unsaved-edits nudge, a 1280 px JPEG snapshot, and the build version in getSessionInfo so an agent can tell when it's hitting a stale deploy. Challenges we ran into Auth inside agent browsers. Our first runs hit unreliable third-party sign-in popups in embedded agentic browsers, so we shipped a demo carve-out: geospatial anchoring works signed-out for California locations (server-enforced bounding box + expiry). By round 2, sign-in was working in ChatGPT's browser, so we removed the warning but kept the carve-out so judges can try the demo with zero friction. Spec drift mid-trial. navigator.modelContext became document.modelContext in Chrome 150; bulk provideContext gave way to per-tool registerTool . We support both generations with feature detection. Testing a consumer that barely exists. Few agents call WebMCP tools yet, so we built a headless-Chromium harness that shims modelContext , registers the real page, and round-trips every tool, including verifying that the read-only gate and scene-containment guards refuse correctly. The agent believes the tool. When a create call returned "ok" for a segment that silently dropped a field, the agent moved on. Readback and validation errors turned out to matter more than any new capability. Image data transfer. It was not possible during our testing to use the output images generated from 3DStreet to be used as input images for ChatGPT AI Image Modification (whether through the compliant WebMCP protocol, or download, or DOM manipulation). I gave up debugging this and figured it's a work in progress on OpenAI MCP Client side to be able to use web outputs as model inputs. EDIT: finally got it working, sort of, it downloaded it to the file system and then read it back to do further AI image renders. What we learned Tool descriptions are the prompt . WebMCP has no system-prompt channel, so every description, error string, and nextStep line is agent UX. Three of our four testing rounds shipped mostly copy and defaults, not code. And an agent driving the user's own session, with undo and a visible transcript, is a fundamentally better trust model than headless automation: the human sees, and can reverse, everything. We had to add a lot of commands that are different types of state and documentation like geo location status / objects available / street segments available / etc. What's next A more general getInstructions orientation tool, auto-reopening the last scene on a bare URL so a returning agent picks up where it left off, a fetchable snapshot link for the human, and the same tool surface via Gemini in Chrome the day it consumes WebMCP. It still doesn't know how to place streets in the correct orientation. We'll need to leverage existing OSM street paths / nodes for that. If existing, explain what you updated 3DStreet is an existing open-source street-design editor. All WebMCP functionality was built during the submission period: the document.modelContext.registerTool integration exposing 26 tools ( src/editor/lib/mcp/useWebMCP.js , docs/webmcp.md ), origin-trial tokens, the WebMCP status bar and live transcript UI, agent-safety guards on scene commands, and an anonymous geospatial demo mode for agent browsers. Four rounds of live agent testing then added geospatial grounding tools ( getGeoContext , north-up plan snapshots), segment presets and schema validation, post-create readback, guidance-first tool copy, and saveScene / loadScene persistence. See PRs #1931, #1936, #1938, #1939, and #1944. Testing instructions No account needed. Open https://3dstreet.app in ChatGPT's in-app browser or Chrome 149+. The chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing flag is NOT required on this domain because origin-trial tokens are live. The first tool call opens the Console tab in the right panel automatically. title: Duz UI
pitch: An agent-capable component system for the WebMCP era.
about_excerpt: An agent-capable component system for the WebMCP era. Like Comment Story Updates 1 Home page Inspiration I started Duz UI because I kept thinking about what websites will look like when AI agents become normal users of the web. Right now, agents often have to look at the DOM, guess what an element does, and simulate clicks or typing. It works, but it feels backwards. The application already knows that something is a dialog, a select, a table, or a form field. The agent should be able to use that information directly. When I saw WebMCP, I really liked the idea of websites exposing structured tools to agents. But I also realized that manually writing WebMCP tools for every page and every component would become repetitive very quickly. That made me think about shadcn/ui. Developers already build most of their app from reusable components, so what if the component itself could support both humans and agents? That became the idea behind Duz UI: One interface. Two users: humans and agents. What it does Duz UI is a shadcn-compatible React component system with built-in WebMCP support. The components still work like normal UI components for humans, but they also expose structured capabilities that an AI agent can understand and call. If you already have a shadcn project, you can run: npx duz-ui migrate --overwrite Duz UI upgrades supported shadcn components in place. You do not need to change your imports or rewrite all your existing component usage. After migration, an agent can do things like select tabs, fill inputs, choose values from selects, open dialogs, toggle checkboxes, control tables, and read information directly from the UI. There are also a few CLI commands: npx duz-ui init npx duz-ui add <component> npx duz-ui migrate npx duz-ui doctor doctor checks whether the integration looks correct and points out problems without automatically changing anything. Duz UI currently supports both Radix UI and Base UI. Developers can also build their own custom components on top of the same capability system instead of being limited to the built-in ones. The documentation site also uses Duz UI itself. The docs, component pages, playground, and demo are running the same components and runtime that developers actually install. How I built it I built Duz UI as a TypeScript monorepo with three main parts: the component registry, the CLI, and the documentation/gallery site. The runtime is split into a few layers: React Component ↓ Capability ↓ Capability Registry ↓ WebMCP Adapter ↓ document.modelContext The React component still owns the actual state. A capability describes what an agent is allowed to read or do with that component. The registry tracks the capabilities that currently exist on the page, and the WebMCP adapter exposes them to the browser as tools. One thing I cared about a lot was avoiding a second copy of the UI state. Duz UI always reads from the real React component state instead of maintaining a separate "agent state" that could get out of sync. I also intentionally avoided using DOM automation as a fallback. If Duz UI does not know how to perform something semantically, it refuses the request instead of randomly trying to click or type into the page. For existing shadcn projects, I built the migration CLI using TypeScript and ts-morph . The migration system tries to recognize known shadcn component implementations. If it knows that the component is safe to replace, it upgrades it. If the source has been modified and Duz UI cannot confidently recognize it, it leaves the file alone unless the developer explicitly uses --overwrite . The registry supports both Radix UI and Base UI implementations, while keeping the agent-facing behavior as similar as possible. The gallery is built with React, React Router, Vite, Tailwind CSS, and Cloudflare Workers. I also added tests for the runtime, WebMCP tool behavior, CLI migration, component behavior, and parity between Radix UI and Base UI. Challenges I ran into The hardest part was probably migration. shadcn is different from a normal component library because the developer owns the source code after installing a component. They might change styles, imports, props, or even the component structure. Because of that, I could not just say "if the file is called dialog.tsx , replace it." I ended up making migration conservative. If Duz UI cannot prove that a component looks like a known shadcn implementation, it does not touch it by default. Another challenge was state synchronization. At first, it is tempting to keep some extra state for the agent because it makes the integration easier. But then React and the agent can disagree about what actually happened. For example, an agent might request a new value, but a controlled React component could reject that value. Duz UI needs to report the value the component actually ended up with, not just what the agent asked for. WebMCP itself was also an interesting challenge because it is still evolving. While testing with Chrome, I ran into differences between the current browser behavior and the specification, including how tool inputs are passed to executeTool . I ended up handling that difference inside the WebMCP adapter so the rest of the project does not need to care about it. Supporting both Radix UI and Base UI also took more work than I expected. They solve similar UI problems, but their APIs are not always the same. I had to make sure that the WebMCP-facing semantics stayed consistent even when the underlying implementation was different. Another important challenge was deciding what should not be automatic. Just because an agent can press a button does not mean it should automatically understand the business meaning behind it. For more important actions, Duz UI lets the developer explicitly expose the action instead of guessing based on the button text. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I am probably most proud that Duz UI can take an existing shadcn application and make it agent-capable without forcing the developer to redesign the whole application around AI. The existing React code can stay mostly the same. I also like that the project became more than just a small WebMCP demo. It now has a real CLI, a shadcn-compatible registry, migration support, Radix UI and Base UI support, custom component support, a diagnostics command, a live playground, documentation, and automated tests. Another thing I am proud of is that the documentation site does not use a special demo-only implementation. The gallery is generated from the same registry and installed using the same CLI path that real users get. So the thing I show in the demo is actually the thing developers can install. What I learned The biggest thing I learned is that agent interaction on the web is really a semantics problem. A UI component already knows a lot about itself. A select already knows its options. A table already knows its rows and columns. A tab system already knows which tab is active. A dialog already knows whether it is open. It does not make much sense to throw all of that away and then ask an AI agent to rediscover it from the DOM. I also learned that giving an agent access to a UI needs clear boundaries. Not everything in application state should automatically be readable, and not every action should automatically become callable. Another big lesson was that adoption matters. Even if the WebMCP architecture is good, developers probably will not use it if they have to rewrite their application to get started. That is why migration and compatibility with the existing shadcn workflow became such a big part of Duz UI. And because WebMCP is still changing, I learned that it is really useful to keep browser-specific behavior isolated behind one adapter instead of spreading it through the entire codebase. What's next for Duz UI The next step is supporting more agent-native components and improving the existing ones. I also want migration to understand more shadcn versions and more real-world customized components, so developers can adopt Duz UI with less manual work. I want to improve custom capability support too. Developers can already build custom components with the Duz UI runtime, but I would like the tool layer to become more extensible as well. As WebMCP continues to evolve, I also want to add more real-browser compatibility tests and keep the project working across changes in the API. Long term, I want agent support to feel like a normal capability of a component system, not something every application has to build from scratch. title: ThreatTriage WebMCP
pitch: Human-visible, agent-ready defensive cyber triage that lets people and browser agents safely analyze suspicious messages, organize incidents, and build response plans with WebMCP.
about_excerpt:
Human-visible, agent-ready defensive cyber triage that lets people and browser agents safely analyze suspicious messages, organize incidents, and build response plans with WebMCP.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 Security incidents are a bad place for an AI browser agent to guess. Suspicious messages can contain unsafe links, urgent language, credential requests, and untrusted instructions, while many schools, nonprofits, and public-service teams may not have a dedicated security operations center. 

 ThreatTriage explores a safer agent-native pattern: the website explicitly exposes defensive capabilities through WebMCP while keeping every result visible to the human operator. 

 What it does 

 ThreatTriage is a privacy-first defensive cybersecurity workflow where a person and a browser agent can collaborate on suspicious-message triage. 

 It can: 

 
 analyze suspicious SMS, email, or chat messages; 
 create a local incident case; 
 build a defensive response plan; 
 draft an unsent cybersecurity awareness notice; 
 list local incident cases; and 
 mark a case as reviewed. 
 

 Instead of forcing an agent to inspect the page and guess which controls to click, ThreatTriage exposes six bounded WebMCP tools with structured JSON schemas. 

 Every agent action is also reflected in the same visible interface used by the human and recorded in the Agent Activity panel. 

 How we built it 

 ThreatTriage is a dependency-free static web application built with HTML5, CSS, vanilla JavaScript, browser localStorage, and GitHub Pages. 

 The WebMCP implementation uses the imperative API on document.modelContext . 

 Six tools are registered through await document.modelContext.registerTool(...) : 

 
 analyze_suspicious_message 
 create_incident_case 
 build_response_plan 
 draft_awareness_notice 
 list_incident_cases 
 mark_case_reviewed 
 

 Each tool has a clear description, constrained input schema, execution handler, and relevant safety annotations such as readOnlyHint and untrustedContentHint . 

 The WebMCP handlers reuse the same application functions as the manual interface. This means agent actions do not happen in a hidden automation layer—the user immediately sees the resulting analysis, incident case, response plan, notice, or status change. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The biggest challenge was designing tools that were useful without becoming overly broad. 

 Cybersecurity workflows involve untrusted content, so ThreatTriage needed strong boundaries. It never opens suspicious links, sends messages, changes external accounts, or produces offensive cybersecurity functionality. 

 Another challenge was keeping agent activity understandable to the human. We solved this by updating the normal page UI after each WebMCP action and adding a visible Agent Activity log. 

 We also deliberately avoided backend dependencies and external APIs so the challenge demo would remain reproducible and privacy-conscious. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We built a complete end-to-end WebMCP workflow with six structured tools. 

 Agent actions update the same human-visible workspace instead of operating through a separate hidden automation path. 

 The MVP requires no backend or API key, stores demo data locally in the browser, and maintains defensive-only safety boundaries. 

 The application is publicly deployed, open source, and successfully tested with Chrome's WebMCP tooling. 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP works best when websites expose domain-level intentions instead of low-level UI operations. 

 A tool such as build_response_plan is more reliable and understandable than asking an agent to locate several controls and simulate a sequence of clicks. 

 We also learned that agent-native UX should remain human-native UX. Structured tools become easier to trust when their effects are immediately visible to the person using the application. 

 What's next 

 Future versions could add optional encrypted persistence, organization-specific incident playbooks, role-based workflows, exportable incident summaries, stronger defensive scoring, and integrations with authorized IT or security channels. 

 Consequential external actions would still require explicit human approval. 

 Privacy and safety 

 ThreatTriage is defensive-only. 

 The current MVP has no backend and no API key. Demo message and incident data remain in browser localStorage. The app never opens URLs found in suspicious messages and does not provide malware, exploitation, credential-harvesting, persistence, or unauthorized-access functionality. 

 Risk scoring is an educational heuristic and is not intended to replace a professional security investigation.

title: Bouquet Studio
pitch: Turn your wishes into a bouquet you can see, shape, and confidently order.
about_excerpt: Turn your wishes into a bouquet you can see, shape, and confidently order. Like 1 Comment Story Updates A better way to choose flowers One shared editing system Using WebMCP to Inspect and Improve Bouquets From idea to order Inspiration I do not know much about flowers. Whenever I buy a bouquet, I run into the same questions: What flowers do I want? How should they be arranged? What style am I looking for? I usually cannot answer those questions in floral terms. What I do know is who the bouquet is for, why I am giving it, and how I want it to feel. An agent can translate those intentions into flower choices, but a text recommendation only solves half the problem. I still need to see the flowers together, react to them, and shape the design until it feels right. A generated image can provide inspiration, but it is disconnected from the products I can actually buy and difficult to revise precisely. Bouquet Studio started with a simple idea: let people describe the feeling instead of naming the flowers, then let the person and agent shape the actual bouquet together . Why WebMCP is the right fit Most online flower shops are designed for human eyes. Online flower shops contain the information an agent needs, but that information is often scattered across product pages, FAQs, announcements, and checkout. An agent can navigate those interfaces, but it has to repeatedly interpret pages, images, and UI state like a human would. WebMCP gives the agent a direct way to understand and operate the same flower shop: Task-level actions . Instead of opening products and applying filters one by one, the agent can search for bouquets matching the customer’s complete request, inspect their contents, customize them, and continue toward ordering. Direct bouquet-editing tools . When the customer wants to change a bouquet, the agent can add, remove, replace, move, resize, and reorder flowers; change wrapping; undo changes; save and restore versions; and request rendered images or diagnostics when it needs to inspect the result. Without these tools, an agent would have to repeatedly analyze screenshots, estimate click or drag coordinates, and determine whether visual actions succeeded. The agent can receive the shop’s full context on demand . On a customer-facing website, useful information naturally lives in different places, which makes sense for people browsing step by step, but an agent must first discover and combine those details. Through WebMCP, the shop can provide the information the agent needs together, rather than forcing it to discover and combine information scattered throughout the website. This makes flower shopping a strong WebMCP use case: product knowledge, multi-step actions, and visual decisions all need to work together. WebMCP lets the agent access the right context and tools while keeping the customer in control of the visual decisions . How does it create a better experience? Start with intent, not expertise . People can describe the recipient, occasion, mood, budget, or simply how they want the bouquet to feel. The agent translates those cues into suitable products or a first arrangement without requiring the user to know flower names. React instead of specify . It is often easier to recognize what feels right than to describe it from scratch. Users can look at a visible bouquet and say “warmer,” “less formal,” or “more delicate,” then watch the agent adjust the actual flowers, composition, and wrapping. Explore without pressure . Users can try different directions, compare alternatives, ask questions, and undo changes without asking a florist to prepare version after version or starting over. Turn uncertainty into confidence . The final bouquet is something the user has actually seen and shaped, not a black-box recommendation, and it can be ordered directly. What can people and agents do together now that was difficult before? Previously, an agent could recommend flowers, generate an inspiration image, or navigate a flower shop. The customer still had to bridge the gap between that recommendation and a real, orderable bouquet. Bouquet Studio turns that handoff into a shared workflow: A customer can say: “A longtime teammate is leaving for a new role. I want the bouquet to feel grateful and optimistic, but still professional.” The agent can turn that intent into several options using flowers that are actually available , each with different flowers, colors, wrapping, and composition. From there, the agent and customer work on the same live bouquet . The agent can make changes directly in the editor, while the customer sees those changes immediately and can refine them visually. Human and agent edits share the same state, undo/redo history, and saved versions. The agent contributes structured reasoning: which flowers are available, where they are positioned, what is hidden, which elements overlap, and where the composition may feel empty . The customer contributes the judgment that matters most: does this bouquet feel right for this person and this moment? Once the design feels right, it continues into checkout. There is no need to recreate the recommendation or search for real flowers that resemble an AI-generated image. The new capability is the end-to-end collaboration loop itself . Intent, reasoning, visual editing, and purchasing remain connected instead of becoming separate handoffs. How We implemented WebMCP We built the human-facing editor first, then added WebMCP by testing it with fresh agents that had no prior knowledge of Bouquet Studio. We observed where they struggled and refined the tools around those problems. Agent feedback shaped the workflow . Early tests showed that undo and redo were critical: an agent could revise its latest change, while a person could reverse an agent’s action directly instead of explaining the correction in chat. Human and agent edits now share the same bouquet state, edit history, and saved versions. Guidance appears where decisions happen . Agents initially produced horizontal rows, excessive symmetry, repeated colors, and wrapping that competed with the bouquet. We added concise arranging guidance directly to the tools used to choose flowers, position them, and style the wrapping. Agents can inspect what they created . They can request the rendered bouquet, a color map showing flowers, greenery, and empty space, and a visibility report identifying hidden blooms and overlapping flower IDs. This combines an overall visual impression with specific information the agent can act on. Predictable corrections became reliable actions . When agents repeatedly positioned flowers too far outside the wrapping, we added a fitting action that handles the geometry automatically and leaves the agent to focus on flower choice, composition, and mood. Together, these decisions turned WebMCP from a collection of tools into an iterative collaboration between the customer, the agent, and the website. The agent handles intent and creative exploration, the product handles reliable constraints, and the customer remains in control of what ultimately feels right. title: Blindfold
pitch: Analyse a file your AI could never read — without showing it a single row. A million rows in the tab. 27 KB to the agent. Zero rows disclosed.
about_excerpt: Analyse a file your AI could never read — without showing it a single row. A million rows in the tab. 27 KB to the agent. Zero rows disclosed. Like 1 Comment Story Updates ChatGPT asked for this chart and got back zero bytes of data. It never saw a salary. Asked for the highest salary in Engineering it refuses: a maximum is one person's exact pay. It offers a percentile instead. Once the data is loaded the page revokes its own network access, and the browser refuses all five ways out. The exact text the agent received: department medians and cohort sizes. Search it for a name and there is none. 98.9 MB read into the tab, 2.2 KB released to the agent, zero raw rows. Analyse a file your AI could never read — without showing it a single row. A million rows in the tab. 27 KB to the agent. Zero rows disclosed. Live: https://beeeeen.github.io/blindfold/ · Source: https://github.com/Beeeeen/blindfold The four things the rules ask the description to explain Answered directly, before the narrative sections below. Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP Because the guarantee depends on where the code runs . A server-side MCP would have to hold the data in order to analyse it — the privacy claim would be a promise about someone's backend. In-page, the rows sit in memory the agent has no way to address, while the agent still directs the whole analysis. Take WebMCP away and this project does not degrade into a worse version of itself. It stops existing. How it creates a better user experience You can point an agent at a 99 MB spreadsheet and have an answer in seconds, without either of the two things that normally stop you: the context window and the upload. When the guard refuses, the refusal arrives with a legal alternative — "use p25, median or p75" — so the agent corrects itself on the next turn instead of dead-ending. And the page keeps a receipt: every byte that crossed to the agent, verbatim, searchable, exportable. What people and agents can do together that was difficult or impossible before Three things, in increasing order of how much WebMCP is doing: Analyse a file larger than any context window, without sampling. A million rows is ~26 million tokens. The agent answers questions about all of it because it never reads any of it. Delegate authority over data you are not willing to disclose. You can now hand an agent the controls to a payroll file while it stays structurally unable to read a row. Delegation and disclosure used to be the same act. Have an agent show you something it never saw itself. render_chart takes aggregates and a shape, draws on the human's screen, and returns one sentence saying it is up and that nothing came back with it. The person gets the picture; the model gets zero bytes of data. A server-side agent cannot show you anything without first holding it. How we implemented WebMCP document.modelContext.registerTool() (with a navigator.modelContext fallback for hosts still on the pre-150 Chromium location), eight tools, no SQL. The parts that took real work: Re-registered per dataset , so tool descriptions name that file's actual columns and tiers rather than describing a generic shape. Withdrawal by AbortSignal . Chrome 152 ships no unregisterTool , so aborting the previous batch is the only way to replace a toolset without colliding with names already registered. Refusals as return values, not exceptions , each carrying a reason and a legal alternative. A write tool that returns nothing. render_chart mutates the page and discloses zero bytes. Inspiration Every real dataset hits two walls at once, and they are usually treated as separate problems. The first is size. A 99 MB spreadsheet is roughly 26 million tokens. No model reads that, so people paste a sample and get an answer about the sample. The second is disclosure. Uploading the whole file to answer one question means handing over every name and salary in it, which is why most organisations ban it outright. The realisation that started this project is that both walls have the same door. If the agent never reads the rows, the file can be any size and nothing has to be disclosed — those stop being two features and become one consequence of the same design. WebMCP is what makes it reachable: the tool executes inside the page, so the data can sit in memory the agent has no way to address while the agent still directs the work. That is not a convenience. It is a different trust model, and it only became available when tools started running in the browser. What it does Blindfold is a data workbench you drop a spreadsheet into. It reads the file into DuckDB-WASM inside your tab — no server, no upload — and exposes eight WebMCP tools to whatever agent is attached. The agent can compute almost anything: aggregates, distributions, correlations, cohort comparisons with effect sizes. It can draw charts on your screen. What it cannot do is see a row. The page revokes its own network access. A counter reading zero is the page marking its own homework, so once the engine boots Blindfold injects a CSP taking away its own ability to reach the network — connect-src 'none' , form-action 'none' , img-src data: . From then on the browser refuses fetch, XHR, WebSocket, sendBeacon and tracking pixels. There is a button that attempts all five so you can watch them fail, and you can read the policy out of document.head yourself. There is no SQL tool. Deliberately. Free-form SQL can't be proven non-disclosive without a parser and a lot of hope. The agent fills in narrow structured specs and the page compiles them to queries it controls. A leak should be impossible to express , not merely refused afterwards. Columns are graded before the agent hears about them. Direct identifiers ( full_name , email , employee_id ) are sealed : not groupable, not filterable, never returned. Personal measurements ( base_salary ) are aggregate-only. Every grade is one click to override, and changing one re-registers the entire toolset with new descriptions. k-anonymity, enforced. Any group covering fewer than five people is suppressed before it becomes a return value. compare_groups is stricter: both cohorts must independently clear k, because a "gap" computed over two people is just those two salaries with extra steps. Refusals teach. min / max on a salary is blocked — a maximum is one real person's pay — and the refusal tells the agent to use p25/median/p75 instead, so it recovers on the next turn rather than giving up. A ledger, on screen. Bytes into the page versus bytes released to the agent, values spent against a disclosure budget, calls refused, groups suppressed. A transcript, not a summary. Every call is stored with the exact text that went back, character for character. Search it for a name and there is none. Measured on a million rows — 99 MB, about 26 million tokens of text: Read and classified 3.2 s Median salary by department 0.07 s Pay gap by level, both cohorts k-checked 0.11 s Salary histogram by level 0.11 s Tenure vs pay, per department 0.04 s Bonus by level × region × department 0.09 s Sent to the agent 27 KB, about 6,800 tokens Raw rows sent to the agent 0 Pushed further on the same machine: 5,000,000 rows (502 MB) answers in 0.42s, and 10,000,000 rows — a full gigabyte, about 264 million tokens — still answers every query in under a second, releasing 7 KB. The disclosure ratio there is 1 : 37,369. One byte reached the agent for every 3,799 that did not, and on the way it found a real seeded result: a gender pay gap of about 3% at IC1–IC3 that widens to 12–14% from IC4 upward. The model never saw a salary. That 27 KB is five questions' worth. Ask fewer and it is a couple of kilobytes; ask a hundred and it climbs, which is exactly why there is a disclosure budget rather than only a per-query check. The number that does not move is the one underneath it: zero rows, at any question count. How we built it Vite, TypeScript, no framework, no backend. DuckDB-WASM is the query engine; Observable Plot draws. Tools register through document.modelContext.registerTool() , with a fallback to navigator.modelContext so the page works in ChatGPT's built-in browser and in Chrome 149+ behind the testing flag. Three WebMCP details did most of the work: Tools are registered per dataset, not once at load. Descriptions name the actual columns and their tiers, so the agent reads what it may ask for instead of discovering it by trial. Loading a second file unregisters the first file's tools. render_chart is a one-way mirror. The agent supplies aggregates and a shape; the chart appears on the human's screen; the return value is a sentence confirming it, carrying zero bytes of data. A server-side agent cannot show a person something without first holding it. This one can — that asymmetry is only available in-page. Refusals are return values, not exceptions. Each carries the reason and a legal alternative, which turns the guard into something the agent can navigate rather than something it fights. T

video_transcript_excerpt: A million people's salaries. Ninety-nine megabytes — twenty-six million tokens. No AI can read a file this size. And you would never paste it into one anyway. So watch one analyse it anyway, without ever seeing a single row. Every column is graded before the agent is told the file exists. Name, email, employee ID — sealed. It cannot group by them, filter on them, or ever receive them. The grading is a heuristic — column names and how unique the values are — so sometimes it will be wrong. One click overrules it. Watch what happens when I seal a column the agent was just using: every tool is withdrawn and re-registered, the descriptions rewritten around the new grading, and the query that worked a moment ago is refused. Eight WebMCP tools, and notice what is missing: there is no run_sql. The agent cannot write a query at all. It fills in a form, and the page compiles it. The same eight tools appear in ChatGPT and in Chrome behind the flag. This is the standard, not one app. So I ask ChatGPT where pay is least equitable. It reads the schema, compares the cohorts level by level, and draws me the chart. It asked for that chart, I can see it, and what came back to the agent was zero bytes of data. It has still never seen a salary. Ask for the highest salary in a team, and it refuses. A maximum is not a statistic — it is one person's exact pay, copied out of the file. And the refusal tells the agent what to ask instead, so it recovers on the next turn. But a counter reading zero is just this page marking its own homework. So the page revokes its own network access. Watch me try to leak the data on purpose. Fetch. XHR. WebSocket. Beacon. Tracking pixel. Chrome refuses all five. And this is every byte the agent actually received. Not a summary — the literal text. Search it for a name, and there is none. Ninety-nine megabytes in. Kilobytes out. Zero rows. And it holds: ten million rows, a full gigabyte, every query still under a second. Blindfold — analyse a file your AI could never read.

title: Ilma: Weather Agents Can Trust
pitch: Ilma turns weather into agent decisions: calibrated probabilities, forecast stability, a decide-by date, stake-weighted calls, branchable scenarios. All with a verified accuracy record.
about_excerpt: Ilma turns weather into agent decisions: calibrated probabilities, forecast stability, a decide-by date, stake-weighted calls, branchable scenarios. All with a verified accuracy record. Like Comment Story Updates 1 Inspiration Agents plan trips, deliveries and events, and they read a weather forecast as a fact. Six models disagree about Saturday, and every weather tool hides that. Ilma shows the agent how much to trust the forecast right now, with proof, and lets the human and the agent work on the same page. What it does ilma.io is a live multi-model forecast site that is also a WebMCP server. It registers 19 tools on document.modelContext . The human's gesture is agent-visible state. Drag across the chart, click two hours, or tap a day: the picked window goes into every tool description (the tools are re-registered on each change) and into every result. assess_plan with no arguments assesses what the human selected. get_current_view resolves "here" and "that weekend". The agent works on the page, not only in the chat. mark_hours paints its reasoning onto the human's chart. select_window makes the same gesture the human makes. set_plan writes a plan card both parties edit; human-edited lines survive a rewrite and come back flagged. share_plan returns one link that reopens place, plan, highlights and selection for another person or another agent. snapshot_chart returns a PNG of what the human sees. The human stays in control. Ilma, a small avatar, narrates each tool call. An activity log lists every action in plain words with Undo on the newest change of each kind. Read-only tools carry readOnlyHint ; anything the human typed carries untrustedContentHint , so a plan card cannot prompt-inject the agent. The numbers are earned. get_probability , get_rain_probability , get_stability and when_to_decide come from a pre-registered benchmark that has snapshotted every major forecast source every five hours since July and scores them nightly against real stations. why_trust_this returns the verification record itself: matched pairs, confidence intervals, p-values against Foreca, the Finnish Meteorological Institute and Google. Event presets (sauna, sailing, hike, wedding, drone, paint, harvest) give agents semantics instead of thresholds. How we built it One tool table in the page. It registers on the open standard, re-registers when page state changes, and also drives the site's own chat agent (GPT-5.6 Luna), so three doorways share one toolset. The forecast blend and the verification pipeline run on a VPS (Python, FastAPI, SQLite, 25M+ forecast rows, 32 cities in 5 countries). The site is static on Vercel. Challenges WebMCP has no "push state" call, so page state travels in descriptions and results, with re-registration through an AbortSignal. Calibration had to come before tools: probabilities are verified frequencies, not model output. Judges may test in browsers without native WebMCP, so every surface feature-detects and fails closed. Accomplishments The blend beats Foreca, FMI and the best single model over days 1 to 7, each Holm-significant, and the site's headline claim is gated on that significance and recomputed nightly. If we stop being better, the site stops saying so. title: Pixel Art Tutor
pitch: Create and edit pixel art with a hands-on agent assistant by your side.
about_excerpt: Create and edit pixel art with a hands-on agent assistant by your side. Like Comment Story Updates GIF About Pixel art is a staple for game development, but players hate AI slop and today's image generation models still struggle getting pixel art to be "pixel perfect". We wanted to fix that by enabling users and agents to collaborate and create art in a more traditionally-accepted sense. What it does Pixel Art Tutor is a WebMCP-powered studio for creating pixel art (sprites, animations, characters, and tilesets). WebMCP is a strong fit because it gives agents structured access to canvas content that would otherwise be invisible to them. Agents can read sprites as compact ASCII grids, critique artwork, paint individual pixels, fill regions, transform sprites, manage palettes, create animation frames, and build tilemaps. Humans can draw, guide, request edits, and refine the work in the same canvas. With shared rooms via PartyKit, collaborators see edits and agent activity live (making human-agent co-creation possible where traditional browser automation would be unreliable or impossible). How it was built The app is made with React, TypeScript, Vite, Zustand, and PartySocket/PartyServer for real-time collaboration. On startup, the app registers ~43 imperative WebMCP tools through document.modelContext.registerTool , plus a declarative tool for creating sprites. All agent actions use the same store actions as the human UI, so edits remain visible, undoable, and synchronized. The app also includes a built-in critique engine, animation timeline, palette tools, tilemap editing, and game-engine exports. Unexpected challenges The biggest challenge was translating a visual canvas into a useful agent interface. We needed compact representations that agents could understand, precise tools for pixel-level changes, and safeguards so human edits, agent actions, undo history, and room synchronization stayed consistent. What's next for Pixel Art Tutor Next, we want to improve multi-agent collaboration, add stronger room permissions and conflict handling, expand the tutoring system, support more creative workflows, and make it easier to publish and share collaborative pixel-art projects.
