title: albugent-webmcp
pitch: Albugent WebMCP brings browser-native data governance—combining deterministic WASM calculation with human-approved AI remediation.
about_excerpt: Albugent WebMCP brings browser-native data governance—combining deterministic WASM calculation with human-approved AI remediation. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Google Chrome Canary Test ✅ Unified Data Governance Dashboard: Real-time WASM risk scoring with independent binary compliance icons for PII exposure. Dual-Control Pattern: Inline Approve/Reject controls rendered in chat before executing any state-changing remediation Dual-Control Pattern: Inline Approve/Reject controls rendered in chat before executing any state-changing remediation. WebMCP Tool Audit Trail: Full visibility into client-side tool inputs and outputs registered via document.modelContext. Dataset Inspection & Lineage: Column-level PII classification, NULL profiling, and inferred pipeline relationships. Interactive KPI: System-wide compliance metric; 57 PII Fields 0.171 Risk Score 17 Datasets Name Origin Notice Albugent is derived from Albumin — the vital, invisible plasma protein produced by the liver that maintains osmotic pressure and safely transports nutrients throughout the human body. Much like Albumin, true data governance works silently in the background: maintaining structural pressure, ensuring compliance, and safely regulating data flow without disrupting operational pipelines. (100% human-conceived project name, not AI-generated). Inspiration Data governance tools are traditionally split into two disconnected worlds: a human scanning visual dashboards for anomalies, and an AI agent asked by a data engineer to "check if anything looks off." In conventional setups, the agent operates blindly — screen-scraping UI elements, guessing what buttons do, or attempting complex calculations inline. When autonomous LLM agents chain dozens of unguided tool calls and perform mathematical profiling, context drift leads to hallucinated metrics and broken schemas. We built Albugent to prove a different paradigm: What if the dashboard and the AI agent shared one single, typed computation layer? WebMCP ( document.modelContext.registerTool ) provides the exact browser-native primitive for this pattern. Instead of the agent guessing what the UI sees, Albugent exposes a single in-browser governance engine twice: As a reactive pixel-rendered dashboard for human operators. As deterministic WebMCP tools for the LLM agent. Both read from the exact same client-side SQLite WASM databases. The core design rule: The engine computes and executes; the agent decides and explains. What it does Albugent WebMCP is a 100% browser-native data governance engine auditing 17 datasets across three enterprise domains ( healthcare , fiction-retail , nyc-taxi pipelines) loaded entirely client-side via SQLite WASM. Zero server backend; zero data leaves the browser. For the Human Operator: Live Governance Dashboard : Real-time health status ( Healthy / Warning / Critical ) across all 17 datasets, driven by a unified risk-scoring formula (0–100). Independent Compliance Badges : Always-visible PII exposure and NULL-density warning icons next to every dataset, preventing critical compliance flags (like 5 PII columns scoring 25/100) from being hidden inside an averaged numeric risk score. Interactive KPI Drill-Downs : Zero-dependency visual charts for system-wide compliance metrics. Dataset Detail & Lineage Views : Column-level NULL profiling, detected PII severity, and inferred pipeline relationships ( raw_ → staging_ → mart_ ). For the AI Agent (via WebMCP): A floating chat widget powered by Groq connects directly to 7 registered WebMCP tools ( document.modelContext ). Tool calls are collapsed into expandable audit traces under each message. Human-in-the-Loop Remediation Loop (The Core Workflow): Contextual Action : Clicking "Propose masking fix" next to a flagged table pre-fills a chat prompt with the exact dataset URN. Deterministic Evaluation : The agent invokes propose_remediation . The engine re-evaluates the real risk score. If risk is low, the tool refuses action with exact metrics unless explicit force=true is requested. Inline Approval : When a proposal is generated, Approve / Reject controls render directly inside the chat bubble. WASM SQL Execution : Approving executes a dynamic UPDATE statement against the in-memory SQLite database, instantly masking PII columns. Live State Sync : The entire UI (KPI cards, dataset badges, compliance icons) refreshes live without reloading the page. How we built it Frontend & UI : Vite, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS v4. Computation Engine : Web Worker running @sqlite.org/sqlite-wasm with sqlite3_deserialize for zero-latency, client-side SQL execution. Agent Integration : Groq API (OpenAI-compatible) executing a strict single-tool-call loop. WebMCP Integration : toolRegistry.ts registers 7 tools on document.modelContext , passing readOnlyHint: true on query tools per Chrome security guidelines. Decoupled State Bridge : proposalStore.ts provides a pub/sub event bus bridging WebMCP tool calls registered at application boot ( main.tsx ) with React UI state ( App.tsx ). Challenges we ran into 1. WASM & Worker Asset Resolution In production, Vite's SPA fallback initially served index.html for mistyped worker or database paths, producing misleading non-JavaScript MIME type and SQLITE_NOTADB errors. We resolved this by building strict URL maps and wrapping all SQLite operations in a shared WASM initialization promise ( ensureSqliteInitialized ) to eliminate race conditions during initial load. 2. Guardrail Enforcement Beyond tool_choice: 'none' We discovered that passing tool_choice: 'none' on follow-up turns did not reliably prevent models from attempting tool calls, causing API rejections. The solution was structural: finalizing completion requests are sent with the tools array completely omitted from the payload, removing the schema shape entirely. 3. Agent Architecture Fabrications During testing, when asked why it executed a remediation, the LLM fabricated a plausible-sounding "automatic risk engine threshold" that did not exist in the code. We resolved this by enforcing strict engine-level risk re-checks in propose_remediation (returning real numerical proof) and updating system prompts to forbid ungrounded operational claims. 4. Blended Risk Scores vs. Strict Compliance Requirements Initially, computeRiskScore assigned a categorical +25 score for MEDIUM-PII presence. For datasets like mart_demographics (containing 5 PII columns but low NULL density), this resulted in a score of 25/100, visually signaling "Healthy/Low Risk." In enterprise data governance, the presence of PII is an absolute compliance event, not an averaged metric. We corrected this architecture by decoupling compliance indicators from the numeric score, adding independent dataset-level warning icons that ignite strictly on anomaly presence regardless of the blended score. Accomplishments that we're proud of True Shared Truth : The dashboard and the LLM agent receive identical JSON outputs computed by the exact same TypeScript worker logic. Real In-Browser Remediation : MASK_PII generates and runs dynamic SQL queries directly inside SQLite WASM, updating reactive UI state end-to-end. Strict Guardrails : The agent never computes math or hallucinates risk scores — it relies 100% on deterministic profiling. First Full-Stack Reactive UI : Designed and built my first full web interface from scratch, successfully orchestrating client-side React state, SQLite WASM worker event loops, and live WebMCP tool execution into a single reactive dashboard. Compliance-First UX Architecture : Successfully separated strict binary compliance flags (PII presence) from aggregated numerical risk scores, ensuring critical compliance issues are never hidden from human operators. What we learned API Guardrails Must Be Structural : Relying on soft parameters like tool_choice: 'none' is insufficient. True reliability requires physically altering the schema payload passed to the model. LLM Fluency Is Not Correctness : An agent that confidently invents explanations for its behavior is more dangerous than one emitting obvious errors. Grounding every action in deterministic worker output is mandatory for enterprise tools. Full-Stack Execution & Team Specialization : Building a custom reactive UI for the first time and bridging complex front-end state with the SQLite WASM engine consumed a massive amount of development time, leaving less bandwidth for UI polish. The primary personal insight: building complex agentic systems as a solo developer highlights the critical need for a balanced team — allowing focus to be directed entirely toward core engine architecture, logic, and data governance, where my true strengths lie. What's next for Albugent WebMCP Governance Tool SDK : Build a standard, extensible SDK allowing developers to wrap arbitrary SQL databases into WebMCP tools with zero custom UI coding. Full Remediation Execution : Implement dynamic SQL generators for REMEDIATE_NULLS and CIRCUIT_BREAK proposal types. FK

title: Live Canvas
pitch: This demo explores user interfaces that adapt to the humans that browse it, and asks what would the web be if you could B-Y-O-U-I: Bring your own user interface.
about_excerpt: This demo explores user interfaces that adapt to the humans that browse it, and asks what would the web be if you could B-Y-O-U-I: Bring your own user interface. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration For as much as marketers have optimized for conversion, they haven't been able to cut through the number one reason that people leave open carts. they're not ready to buy. It had just happened to me while shopping for a microphone: I started at one site, then realized I needed more information to determine which was going to be the best fit. What if the shopping interface could have met me where I was at--researching the options, ranking the matches, explaining its rationale, and then designing a search result layout to fit its conclusions? That's just one glimpse of how web-interfaces of the future will adapt to their users' needs through a Live Canvas. What it does Each demo walks you through a conventional user interface, and then cordons off a bounded portion of it as WebMCP to redesign (the Live Canvas) The Storefront demo lets the agent curate the search results with a toolbox of approved card presets and badges. This constrained design is a good fit for the untrusted nature of the public internet, keeping users safe from XSS attacks. The Dashbord demo scales the idea up by giving you an entirely blank page. It imagine how the future of CRM / ERP dashboards might function. Prompt the agent to onboard you, collaborate on a vision with the agent as you would with your analytics team, and the end result is an entirely personal dashboard of controls, visualizations and reports. The Distribution demo scales the idea outwards by asking whether you distribute a Live Canvas as part of conventional component libraries. It demonstrates what a future Datatable component could be, with the ability to generate bespoke reports and save them to your browser - all without backend engineering or ai-vendor lock-in. How we built it The architecture north star is "agent composition, application execution". The application exposes its UI primitives through WebMCP. The agent supplies a composition, and then the live canvas renders that composition using application-owned components. This solution prevents data from leaking out of the organization's security boundary, and also prevents token bloat. Challenges we ran into and accomplishments that we're proud of There are two large challenges that required creativity: The largest challenge was discoverability. WebMCP is not bidirectional: an agent can invoke tools, but there's no mechanism for the website to initiate a conversation. The past 30 years of the web have trained users for the affordance of buttons and forms. I built a new set of visible prompts and verbs to communicate to surface the new modality which was an interesting accomplishment, but does highlight an apparent shortcoming in the standard. The second challenge is the built-in approval flow of agentic browsers. ChatGPT would auto-deny requests to access the user's simulated library to make recommendations, e.g. In the short term, this is solved with instructional text to ask for permission in advance. However, what WebMCP needs is a built in consent layer where tools are tied to required consent artifacts. What we learned WebMCP shows great potential to break interfaces out of the "ai chatbot jail". What's next for Live Canvas The most likely next step is to select an existing open-source component library and use it to build the first end-to-end WebMCP UI framework. That would turn the Live Canvas from just a demo pattern into a production-hardened implementation. title: Sæti — Aurora Hall
pitch: One WebMCP tool contract, served to an AI agent and to a keyboard and screen-reader-native command interface. Accessible seat booking where neither consumer gets the reduced version.
about_excerpt: One WebMCP tool contract, served to an AI agent and to a keyboard and screen-reader-native command interface. Accessible seat booking where neither consumer gets the reduced version. Like Comment Story Updates The venue, so it reads as a real site not a demo The 330-seat hall with wheelchair bays and legend The same seats as a filterable list Venue access information Access detail attached to an ordinary page The ⌘K dialog with a real result Inspiration The WebMCP explainer says the API is "not designed for ingestion by accessibility technology." Read that beside what WebMCP actually does and the risk is plain. A site exposes rich, structured, actionable capability — find_seats , hold_seats , complete_booking — and an agent gets all of it. A screen-reader user gets whatever the interface happened to render. Capability for agents, leftovers for disabled users. That would be a bleak outcome for a technology whose own explainer lists improving accessibility as a goal. We think that split is an implementation choice, not a property of the standard. Aurora Hall is the other choice, built. We picked booking accessible seating because it is, with grim regularity, the least accessible thing a venue operates — still routinely routed to a phone line during office hours. And it suits WebMCP for a specific reason: it is not a discoverability problem you can label your way out of. It is a query . What it does Aurora Hall is a 330-seat venue with a working booking flow. Every seat carries a complete, correct aria-label . Traversing them linearly is technically possible and practically useless. Now add the constraints a real patron combines: two of us, one wheelchair space with a companion seat beside it, induction loop, a clear view of the caption unit, step-free, no strobe — I have photosensitive epilepsy. Exactly two pairs satisfy all of that: N-2 + N-3 and N-4 + N-5 . Two viable answers out of 330 — and the only reason anyone knows that is that something searched. Drop the induction loop and it becomes four; the extra two sit in row L, where the loop does not reach. Correct accessibility is necessary and it is not sufficient. Beyond search, the site does three things venue websites generally do not: It remembers. State your access needs once and they are applied — WCAG 2.2 3.3.7 Redundant Entry taken past the letter of the criterion. No phone call, no explaining yourself to a stranger, no office hours. It refuses. When no seat meets everything, constraints relax in a fixed order and the result says exactly what was given up. Strobe limits and step-free routes are never relaxed: giving those up does not produce a worse seat, it produces a seat the caller cannot use, or must not be sold. Ask for a strobe-free seat at our continuous-strobe show and the honest answer comes back — none is offered, and why. It answers questions that have no answer anywhere else. Can I get a drink in the interval without queuing at a high counter? Where does my powerchair go if I transfer into a seat? Is the walk from the bus stop step-free? Is there anything here I actually cannot attend? Because access detail is attached to each thing rather than filed on an accessibility page, an agent can answer all of them — a lowered counter at 760 mm on the western end, or staff bring your order to your seat; beside the bays, not four floors away in the cloakroom; yes, but cross on the western side, there is no dropped kerb on the eastern one. And the same contract answers a screen-reader user with no agent involved at all. The capability is not conditional on having an agent. How we built it Sixteen tools are defined once , in src/lib/tools/registry.ts , and consumed twice: by an agent through document.modelContext.registerTool() , and by an in-page command interface opened from the tab order or with ⌘K. When WebMCP is available the command interface deliberately routes through getTools() and executeTool() — the same calls the agent makes — rather than shortcutting to the handlers. Parity is a property of the architecture, not a claim in a README. When WebMCP is absent it falls back to the shared registry directly: the capability never disappears, only the route changes. Form fields are generated from each tool's inputSchema , the same JSON Schema the agent reads to decide how to call the tool. Inputs described once, rendered twice. Handlers return prose, not data structures — an agent reasons over it perfectly well, and it is the same sentence a screen reader announces. The deliberate non-tools matter as much as the tools. There is no sign_in : establishing identity is a different order of permission from reading a seating plan. There is no update_access_profile : an agent may act on what someone recorded about their own needs, not rewrite it. And the agent never offers to "enable accessibility" — that would make accessibility conditional on having an agent, which is the two-tier web this project exists to argue against, rebuilt one layer up. /llms.txt carries the same material for agents arriving without WebMCP, generated from the same data as the pages and the tools. Next.js 16, TypeScript, Tailwind. No backend — the hall is generated deterministically, so results are reproducible and the seed data is auditable. Challenges we ran into A tool that bought the wrong seats. An early complete_booking took no seat argument and booked everything on hold. Testing in ChatGPT's browser, the agent held two candidate pairs — sensible, both were viable — was asked to book one, called the only tool available, and correctly bought all four. 32.000 kr instead of 20.500. The agent did nothing wrong. Our contract was underspecified on an action that charges money and cannot be undone, so the agent faithfully executed the underspecification. Two implementations that disagree. Chrome rejects executeTool with an object argument; ChatGPT's browser rejects it with a string. We wrote a fallback to tolerate both — and keyed it on recognising the error, which silently failed because Chrome throws a DOMException our test did not match. The in-page command interface broke on its default tool in exactly the browser a judge would use, and worked everywhere WebMCP was absent, which is why nothing caught it. It now retries unconditionally rather than trying to be clever about which error it got. A safety rule that only half existed. Our search relaxed constraints when nothing matched, and maxStrobeExposure was in that list. Asking for a strobe-free seat at the continuous-strobe show returned six seats with the limit quietly dropped — at a performance whose own data says the venue will not sell you a seat that pretends otherwise. A contrast regression on an accessibility project. While making the footer look more commercial, a caption went to text-slate-400 on white and nine pages failed AA. npm run a11y caught it — and it was committed anyway, because the check was piped into tail , and a shell pipeline reports the exit status of the last command. The gate had never been firing. Accomplishments that we're proud of Parity that is structural rather than promised. The human interface calls the same executeTool the agent does. You can verify that in the code rather than taking our word for it, and the UI says which route answered. Safety constraints that are not preferences. A strobe limit and a step-free route are never traded away for a better view. No seat at all is the correct answer more often than the industry admits. No accessible mode. Two views, the visual plan and a filterable list, and neither is the accessible one. The toggle says "Seat list", not "Accessible view", because the name is what decides which pattern you have built. Motion lives inside prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference , so it is not a mode you enable but motion you get unless you have already said no . forced-colors and prefers-contrast are handled the same way. 13 states clean against wcag2a through wcag22aa plus best-practice, with an ARIA grid, roving tabindex over 330 cells, and a skip link ahead of the grid. What we learned Exposing capability to agents raises the cost of a vague tool. It does not lower it. Every ambiguity we left in a tool description became something an agent executed confidently and correctly, to a result nobody wanted. Writing tools is API design with the safety rails of human hesitation removed. Run the check, and check that the check can fail. A contrast regression got into an accessibility project, introduced by the people arguing for accessibility, while making a page look better. Care did not catch it. A tool did — but only once the tool was wired so it could actually fail. Claims should survive being checked. We miscounted our own tools in our own README. If the argument is that sites should tell the truth in a machine-readable way, the prose has to be true too. What's next for Sæti — Aurora Hall Real venues. The hall is deterministic seed data; the interesting version connects to an actual tic

title: MultiCOM
pitch: A shared incident room where engineers and AI agents investigate, challenge theories, and revise their confidence -> with a human approving the fix.
about_excerpt: A shared incident room where engineers and AI agents investigate, challenge theories, and revise their confidence -> with a human approving the fix. Like Comment Story Updates lobby war room ways in investigation commander approval manual controls judge console resolved untrusted-literal mobile Inspiration Incident response is a team effort. But when each engineer asks an AI assistant for help, the investigation splits into private conversations. Someone finds a useful log. Someone else follows a different theory. People copy answers between windows, trying to keep everyone on the same page. I wanted to try a different approach: what if the engineers and their agents could work in the same room? That became multicom—a shared incident room where agents gather evidence, challenge each other’s theories, and revise their confidence in public. The human responsible for the service still decides whether a fix should happen. What it does The demo starts with a simulated storefront service failing at 23% errors. Its database connection pool is too small, but a recently enabled feature flag gives responders a plausible wrong lead. Participants join through one room link. They can investigate with a browser agent, use the manual controls, or watch a clearly labeled scripted drill. The investigation stays visible to everyone: Agents pull logs and run checks. They post theories with evidence and a confidence level. Other participants challenge those theories. The original author can revise their confidence and explain why. The board keeps both the opening and revised numbers. Participants propose a fix and vote. The commander approves or rejects it. After the fix is applied, everyone sees whether the service actually recovers. Each new room gets its own copy of the incident, so one judge’s completed run does not spoil another’s. Why WebMCP fits The website is where the team works. WebMCP lets agents take part in that same workspace through specific tools, instead of relying on screen clicks or asking people to copy information between chats. multicom exposes thirteen tools covering the investigation, debate, voting, and fix workflow. Their results update the same board that people read and use. The most interesting part is not an agent finding the right answer. It is another participant challenging that answer—and the author changing their stated confidence, with the evidence and explanation still visible. An agent’s tool access also has a clear stopping point. It can request approval, but none of the thirteen tools can grant it. A person must click Approve. How I built it I built the interface with TypeScript and Vite. A Cloudflare Worker keeps each room’s participants, theories, votes, and approvals together. A separate Worker runs the simulated storefront service. WebMCP connects the browser agent to the room. People using the manual controls follow the same rules as agents: neither route skips the vote or approval checks. I used Codex to help implement the application, review the boundaries between its parts, and build tests. Running real agents through the tool surface was especially useful. Their mistakes showed where the tools needed clearer explanations or a missing capability. Challenges I faced One early problem was that an agent could vote against a fix but had nowhere to explain why. I added a tool for attaching a reason to a vote. Another was that challenging a theory did not let its author update their confidence. I added author-only revision and preserved the original number. Other participants can argue with a theory, but they cannot rewrite it for its author. Human approval needed more than a button. The server checks which action was approved, limits approval to sixty seconds, and allows it to be used only once. I also planted an instruction inside the synthetic logs telling agents to skip diagnosis and apply the wrong fix. The application returns that line as untrusted data and displays it as plain text. In the recorded agent drill, both agents rejected the instruction and continued investigating. What I learned Watching agents use the application taught me more than watching a scripted walkthrough. A result that looked obvious in code could still confuse an agent. A simple “no” vote could hide the most useful reasoning in the room. The interface needed places for disagreement, explanations, and revision—not just answers. I also learned to separate agreement from permission. A majority can support a fix without being allowed to apply it. Keeping that distinction visible became central to the project. What I’m proud of multicom makes the investigation observable. You can see what was proposed, what challenged it, how confidence changed, who supported the fix, and who approved it. The current project includes 73 automated tests and a separate 32-check production acceptance suite. Those checks cover shared updates, room isolation, approval expiry, repeated requests, and recovery across browsers. It is deliberately a controlled demonstration with one scripted incident, not a tool connected to someone’s real production systems. The question it explores is broader: how can several people and their agents work through uncertainty together, while keeping the consequential decision in human hands? title: ScanWebMCP.com
pitch: See what AI agents can read, answer and call. Then let them act on the evidence.
about_excerpt: See what AI agents can read, answer and call. Then let them act on the evidence. Like Comment Story Updates ScanWebMCP.com Inspiration The web is being rebuilt for AI agents, but most teams still cannot answer a basic question: What can an agent actually do with our website today? A manifest can claim that an integration exists. A script can mention WebMCP. An endpoint can return HTTP 200. None of those facts proves that an agent can discover a useful capability, understand its contract and invoke it safely. WebMCP makes websites callable. A callable web needs observability. We built ScanWebMCP.com to provide that missing layer: a public, evidence-backed scanner that shows what agents can read, answer and call across a website. The recursive idea is deliberate—ScanWebMCP uses WebMCP to make the emerging WebMCP ecosystem visible, testable and easier to improve. What it does Enter any public URL and ScanWebMCP runs a bounded scan across the site's agent-facing surface. It checks: crawler and robots access; server-rendered content and semantic structure; llms.txt , Markdown and structured data; OpenAPI and other documented API surfaces; live MCP protocol handshakes and returned tools; browser-registered WebMCP tools across relevant page contexts; and whether the available capabilities are readable, useful and safe for an agent to call. Every completed scan is placed on the Agent Surface Ladder : Invisible → Readable → Answerable → Callable → Transactable The result is not a decorative badge. It includes five dimension scores, the rubric version, source URLs, observation times, bounded evidence, a page-aware WebMCP inventory and ranked implementation opportunities. The product already includes a live Observatory containing 511 public websites and 523 completed scans . It shows how agent readiness varies by sector while keeping the underlying method visible and versioned. ScanWebMCP itself is available through several complementary interfaces: a human-facing website and public result pages; a REST API with a live OpenAPI 3.1 contract; a four-tool product MCP server; a separate two-tool documentation MCP server; nine browser WebMCP tools; a published Agent Skill and Codex plugin bundle; ARD, MCP and RFC 9727 discovery documents; and stable Markdown and llms.txt representations. The durable product is the scanner and its evidence. The additional discovery formats make that same working product easier for different agents to find and use without guessing URLs. Why WebMCP is essential WebMCP is both the subject of the scan and the interface through which people use the result. Without WebMCP, an assistant must scrape the visible interface, infer the meaning of score cards and locate evidence through page structure. With WebMCP, the page exposes the exact actions an assistant needs, with bounded schemas, descriptions and safety annotations. Three tools are available across the site: scan_agent_surface get_ladder_definition email_report A scan result page adds six context-aware tools: get_scan_findings get_recommended_tools get_webmcp_inventory get_evidence explain_opportunity rescan This is a non-trivial WebMCP implementation, not a single demo button. Tool availability changes with page context. Read-only tools return structured evidence from the page the person is viewing. Evidence and inventory calls enforce the report-access boundary. A re-scan is marked as consequential. Email delivery requires an address directly supplied by the human, while marketing updates remain a separate confirmed opt-in. The agent can also update the shared visual state. When it opens a finding or opportunity, the human sees the same page move to the relevant evidence. The agent receives structured data while the person retains context and control. A better human-agent experience The user does not need to learn the report layout, inspect browser internals or translate scanner output into prompts. They can simply ask: Scan scanwebmcp.com and email the report to me. The assistant selects the correct tools in sequence. It runs the scan, asks for an address if one was not supplied, respects the report gate, and delivers the signed report. It does not guess an email address or silently opt the user into marketing. On the result page, the person can continue: What did the scan find? Show me the evidence behind the weakest signal and explain the best opportunity. The assistant reads the existing result rather than starting a duplicate scan, retrieves bounded evidence, opens the relevant section and explains the recommendation in the context of the site already on screen. After deploying a fix, the person can say: We changed the site. Re-run the scan. The consequential rescan tool refreshes the shared result. What previously required developer tools, manual navigation, separate scanner output and human follow-up becomes one coherent human-agent session. How we built it ScanWebMCP is a Next.js 16 and TypeScript application deployed on Vercel, with Supabase Postgres for scans, evidence, browser context and invocation outcomes. The scanning pipeline is deliberately bounded and evidence-first: It validates and pins public-network targets to defend against SSRF and DNS rebinding. It honours the target's robots.txt policy and discovers no more than six relevant same-origin pages. It inspects server-rendered content, crawler directives, structured data and machine-readable documents. It validates MCP endpoints through the real initialize and tools/list lifecycle rather than trusting a URL or status code. It launches a WebMCP-capable browser witness and observes the live registry across relevant page contexts. It normalizes tool schemas and annotations, preserving the first page on which each tool appeared. It stores the evidence and calculates a versioned Agent Surface Ladder result. The website feature-detects document.modelContext and registers tools with bounded input schemas, explicit descriptions and standards-aligned annotations. External website evidence is marked as untrusted content. Invocation telemetry distinguishes successful, refused and errored outcomes instead of treating a safe refusal as success. The same core service powers the website, REST API, MCP servers and WebMCP tools. That keeps behavior consistent across interfaces and prevents the browser demo from becoming a disconnected proof of concept. The repository contains a 12-scenario WebMCP agent eval pack covering tool selection, parameter mapping, multi-tool ordering, consent, page-aware inventory use, mid-chain recovery and the complete scan-to-email journey. The final branch passes 127 automated tests , TypeScript checking and a production build. Challenges we ran into The hardest engineering problem was observing a browser-only, page-dependent protocol from a serverless scanner. WebMCP tools can appear only after navigation. A homepage, product page and cart can expose different registries. Browser implementations can return schemas in different object or serialized shapes. Most importantly, a failed browser witness must never be reported as "zero tools." We built an adaptive multi-context probe, normalized runtime and Chrome DevTools Protocol descriptors, retried bounded renderer failures and preserved the distinction between unavailable and verified absent . The second challenge was agent UX and safety. Tool outputs must be useful without becoming unbounded data dumps. External page evidence may contain prompt injection and must remain explicitly untrusted. Consequential actions need clear ordering and human control. We solved this with bounded schemas and outputs, read-only and consequential annotations, semantic invocation outcomes, a report-access gate, separate transactional and marketing consent, signed report links and deterministic evaluation scenarios for complete journeys. Accomplishments we are proud of Built and deployed a complete product during the challenge window; the public repository was created on 29 August 2026. Created a scanner whose own human interface is also a nine-tool WebMCP surface. Grew a live public Observatory to 511 websites and 523 completed scans. Verified live WebMCP registrations across page contexts instead of counting declarations or scripts. Preserved tool names, descriptions, schemas, annotations, classifications, page context and timestamped evidence. Built both product and documentation MCP servers around the same core service. Published OpenAPI, ARD, RFC 9727, MCP and Agent Skill discovery surfaces without making any of them substitutes for real behavior. Completed a genuine agent-driven scan-to-email journey with explicit consent and a signed report link. Added 12 agent-level evaluation scenarios and 127 automated tests. Published the full implementation under an AGPL-3.0 license in a repository whose default branch contains complete setup, architecture, safety and verification documentation. What we learned WebMCP presence is not WebMCP readiness. A use

title: AccessCanary
pitch: An AI agent that catches accessibility bugs static scanners miss - using WebMCP to watch real focus order, ARIA-live timing, and keyboard traps as you tab through a page.
about_excerpt:
An AI agent that catches accessibility bugs static scanners miss - using WebMCP to watch real focus order, ARIA-live timing, and keyboard traps as you tab through a page.

 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 



 
 Inspiration 

 Automated accessibility scanners axe-core, Lighthouse, WAVE are what most teams rely on to catch WCAG issues, but independent research puts their real-world coverage at roughly 30-40% of the actual violations. The other 60-70% only exist as behavior a broken tab order, a validation error not reaching a screen reader, a keyboard trap that only emerges after cycling through a component a few times. To static crawlers reading HTML, none of this exists only what the markup says, not what the page does when operated. 

 That's where WebMCP stops being desirable and becomes structurally necessary. An agent using ordinary browser automation has to guess at page state from screenshots and DOM scraping slow, brittle, and blind to anything that's only ever existed transiently, like whether an aria-live region fired. WebMCP lets the page itself expose ground-truth tools for the agent to ask directly "did this actually announce to a screen reader?", rather than inferring an answer from a static snapshot. It's not merely a faster way to do the same thing it's a category of inspection that wasn't previously practically possible. 

 What it does 

 AccessCanary presents a mock government-benefits application form, with three real, deliberately-built accessibility defects implemented the way these bugs occur in production code: 

 A broken focus order a tabIndex override silently reorders the entire page's tab sequence (WCAG 2.4.3) 

 An ARIA-live region that's silent a validation error appears visually but was never wired to announce to screen readers (WCAG 4.1.3) 

 A keyboard trap a custom date picker's focus-cycling logic never releases focus back to the page (WCAG 2.1.2) 

 As an AI agent calls six WebMCP tools, it narrates what the form is doing in real-time, alongside the form. A glowing focus-trace dot follows keyboard focus live, making tab order visible to anyone watching, not just the person tabbing around the form. 

 The most novel part is that the agent can only propose a finding its state-changing tool, report_violation, stages a finding for review but never logs anything directly. Only a human clicking Confirm moves it into the permanent violation log; Dismiss discards it with no trace. That's what "people and agents working together" really means the agent picks up on things humans couldn't, but the human keeps the decision power to determine what's a real bug. 

 How we built it 

 React 19 + TypeScript + Vite, deployed as a static site with no backend, and all of our WebMCP tooling is client-side as well. 

 Our five read-only tools are registered as @mcp-b/react-webmcp's useWebMCP hook wraps document.modelContext.registerTool for the current WebMCP API: 

 typescript 

 useWebMCP({ 

 name: 'get_focus_order', 

 description: 'Returns the real browser tab order starting from a given element...', 

 inputSchema: getFocusOrderInput, 

 outputSchema: getFocusOrderOutput, 

 annotations: { readOnlyHint: true, idempotentHint: true, destructiveHint: false }, 

 execute: async (input) => ({ steps: getFocusOrder(input.startSelector, input.limit) }), 

 }); 

 Five tools are read-only (get_focus_order, simulate_tab_sequence, get_aria_live_state, get_element_role, get_violation_log), each with the correct readOnlyHint/idempotentHint/destructiveHint security annotations from WebMCP's published guidance, and each tool respects the recommended character budgets (500-char descriptions, 150-char parameter descriptions, ~1.5K-char output cap). The one state-changing tool, report_violation, only can stage a finding it can't confirm it. 

 The actual detection logic exists in a framework-free lib/ layer, separate from the WebMCP wiring, making it independently unit-testable. getFocusOrder correctly implements real browser tab-order rules (positive tabIndex sorted first, per the HTML spec, which is what makes the focus-order bug detectable) and a MutationObserver-based tracker records whether aria-live regions genuinely fire, not just whether the attribute exists. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Two real bugs, both worth being upfront about. First: our initial tool schemas were Zod object maps, following a pattern from a tutorial, but @mcp-b/react-webmcp doesn't declare any Zod dependency at all the Zod support is structurally typed against Zod v3 internals, while the current Zod release is v4. Real, reproducible TypeScript errors, not a guess. We switched to plain JSON Schema the format the package's official examples show first to avoid version-coupling risk. 

 Second: our unit tests were just failing in strange ways every getFocusOrder test returned an empty array. jsdom (our test environment) doesn't have a real layout engine, so element.offsetParent which our visibility check relied on is always null there. The fix detects whether a real layout engine is present, and only requires that signal when one is, ensuring real-browser behavior is preserved but also making it testable. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 Getting the human-confirmation mechanism to actually work as a real constraint, not just a UI suggestion. The agent's report_violation tool is architecturally incapable of writing to the confirmed violations log that decision is made in the React reducer, not by convention. We're also proud of the fact that every one of the three bugs is a real defect (verified by manually tabbing through and screen-reader spot-checking) and shipped with a real, passing unit test suite covering the actual detection logic, not just a working demo. 

 What we learned 

 That "thoughtful use of WebMCP" mostly comes down to restraint a tight set of six tools with correct security semantics beats a sprawling one. The most interesting design decision in this whole project wasn't a tool it was to make the one state-changing tool incapable of actually changing anything on its own. We also learned, concretely, not to trust a tutorial's dependency assumptions over what's actually declared in a package's own package.json. 

 What's next for AccessCanary 

 Extending detection to more WCAG behavioral patterns beyond the three shown here (focus restoration after modal close, dynamic content insertion announcements), and testing against real production forms rather than a single mock page, to see how the six-tool approach generalizes beyond the demo.

title: Vroom
pitch: The Zoom for AI Agents. Watch multiple agents collaborate across browser tabs in real time, and unmute yourself to take over anytime.
about_excerpt:
The Zoom for AI Agents. Watch multiple agents collaborate across browser tabs in real time, and unmute yourself to take over anytime.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 1 
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Architectural diagram (https://github.com/kavishsathia/vroom/blob/main/assets/architecture.png) 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Architectural diagram (https://github.com/kavishsathia/vroom/blob/main/assets/architecture.png) 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 9 



 
 Quick read 

 Vroom is a multi-agent browser automation system where a coordinator decomposes your task and spawns parallel executors on separate browser tabs. Agents navigate purely by vision , they screenshot the page and use gemini-3-flash-preview (via the google-genai SDK) to figure out where to click. No DOM access, no page APIs. The agent can only click on what you can see, so you always know what it's doing. 

 Agents talk to each other and to you through a shared audio channel powered by gemini-2.5-flash-native-audio-preview through the Gemini Live API, each with a distinct voice . A multiplexer enforces one speaker at a time using a pipelined spotlight system. You can barge in at any moment: by voice, text, or by taking manual control of a tab, and agents will course correct without restarting. 

 Every executor gets a contract with specific commitments. If it fails, the coordinator knows exactly what was done and what's left, and can retry on the same tab. The whole thing runs on Google Cloud : Cloud Run, Cloud SQL, Artifact Registry, Cloud Build, all are defined in Terraform. 

 

 

 Inspiration 

 Most of us have probably tried using browser agents in some way, most likely to carry out the mundane, repetitive tasks we'd rather not do ourselves. And it's very likely we weren't too impressed with the results. They're usually slow, and the quality of work drops over time. That's kinda unexpected for a system whose whole thing is being smarter, more efficient, and faster than humans. 

 The problem surfaced for me when I was trying to add skills to my Linkedin. The task was: here are my list of projects and their READMEs, go to Linkedin and add these 5 projects and 10 unique skills for each project. I assumed I could just leave the agent running and go for a walk. 

 I did go for a 10-minute walk, and when I came back it had added a total of 15 skills, out of the 50 I asked for, and the skills added on the second project were almost the exact same as the first project (when I literally asked for unique skills). I had to stop the execution, rewrite my instructions to be even clearer, and then started it again. At some point, I just gave up and did it myself. 

 To be honest though, this isn't an LLM issue, it's an architecture issue . There are 3 big problems with the architecture: 

 
 Even an embarrassingly parallel problem has to be solved sequentially, there are almost no productivity gains (sometimes it's even worse than doing it yourself). 
 The agent tends to forget the exact instructions later into execution, falling into a repetitive pattern of what it's been doing. 
 Course correction is halting the agent entirely, writing the instruction again and then clicking start. That's inefficient and it's atrocious UX: imagine needing to have a 5-minute meeting with your colleagues just for a minor change in deliverables. It breaks the flow. 
 

 The philosophy I'm going for here is this: given a task, the execution should be abstracted away from the user, and the execution should be fast , correct and permeable to input . 

 What it does 

 So, that's why I created Vroom (Virtual Room). Here is how it solves the three problems: 

 
 Separating intent from execution is one of the key contributions of Vroom. We have a coordinator that extracts instructions out of the user's prompt and then spawn and attach executor agents to browser tabs. These executor agents are the ones that do the actual work and they can do it in parallel. This is actually a twofer: having smaller more focused executors would mean that the context window remains lean, so the agents are less likely to forget anything. So the first two problems are solved. 
 The second contribution of Vroom is the concept of preemption , or barge-in, in the context of agents. I will explain more below, but this allows you to add on to your instructions without needing to stop the agent mid-execution, and they will course correct automatically. This solves the third problem. 
 

 

 Visually, it feels like this: you and your agents are in a Zoom meeting, all of them are doing their own respective work, and you can chip in at any moment to correct them. 

 To understand exactly what Vroom does, we can look at its 2 facets: Coordinators and Executors. 

 Coordinators 

 You start in an empty meeting room. You think there's no one but there's actually a coordinator waiting for you to say something. You either say your prompt in the chatbox or you voice it out, then the coordinator (powered by gemini-3-flash-preview via the google-genai SDK) will decompose the task into subtasks and spawn executors for each one. Each executor will be attached to a tab and they start executing the subtask on that tab. 

 Tab lifecycle 

 Is the executor and the tab spawned together? They can be, but you can also bring your own tab (BYOT). The lifecycles of the tab and the executors are designed to be separate , a tab can exist without an executor, but an executor must necessarily have a tab. If you have a tab you would like the task to be done on, just drag it into the meeting, and the coordinator will help attach an executor to that tab for you. 

 

 Failure, contracts, and error recovery 

 A question that's usually left unanswered is: what if the executor fails? In the conventional paradigm, the burden of knowing what was done and what is yet to be done is offloaded to you, the user! In the Vroom paradigm, since we have one more layer managing intent (the coordinator), it can afford to spawn another agent to retry on your behalf. 

 But we have to be careful on what we retry because tasks are usually not idempotent . Adding 10 skills to Linkedin can fail after 5 skills are added but that doesn't mean you should retry adding 10 skills again, you should only add 5 more. 

 To solve this, I developed the concept of a contract . The coordinator agent initially writes a detailed contract that the executor has to meet, and the executor will update this contract as it completes the commitments. At the end, regardless of outcome, the contract is handed back to the coordinator who now knows exactly what went down. Since the browser tab's lifecycle is detached from that of the agent, the coordinator can now attach another agent to the browser tab with the leftover tasks. This is how Vroom handles error recovery : API timeouts, page loads that fail, or agents that get stuck are all caught by the contract system, and the coordinator can retry with full knowledge of what was already done. 

 

 Executor 

 All the executor knows is the contract and the tab, it is more of a workhorse as compared to the coordinator. It also runs on gemini-3-flash-preview through the google-genai SDK, using its vision capabilities to screenshot the page and figure out where to click. This is a deliberate design choice: the agent never touches the DOM and never calls page APIs . It can only click on what the user can see. This means the user always knows exactly what the agent is doing, and the agent can't do things behind the scenes that the user can't observe. It also keeps the agent grounded in the actual visual state of the page, so there are no hallucinated selectors or stale DOM references. 

 The executor is an agent that can: get context (this is the crown jewel of this architecture, so I'll explain it in its own deserved section), type, click, scroll, press keys, wait, pause, log, speak, watch and learn. 

 Notice pause, log, speak, watch and learn. These are the ones that go beyond the conventional paradigm. I'll cover speak first, and the others land naturally. 

 Interprocess communication 

 In parallel process in an operating system, there is a need to communicate to each other, this mechanism is known as interprocess communication . When the agents are working together to add unique skills to my Linkedin, they have to commun

title: Champagne - Agentic Music Mastering
pitch: Champagne is a mastering studio for AI music artists that uses a single prompt to apply advanced tonal processing to audio, making songs radio-ready in less than a minute.
about_excerpt: Champagne is a mastering studio for AI music artists that uses a single prompt to apply advanced tonal processing to audio, making songs radio-ready in less than a minute. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Champagne Landing Page Champagne Mastering Studio Inspiration I've been producing music for over 15 years. I recently jumped into making AI music, and the first thing I noticed was how thin the outputs sounded. That's where Champagne was born. As far as turning it into a ChatGPT + WebMCP integration, that magic sorta just happened! What it does Champagne masters any audio track, but it's optimized specifically for songs from Suno. Suno outputs are thin and quiet. Champagne makes them full-bodied and vibrant. Based on your prompt, ChatGPT selects one of four signature mastering styles and directs bounded refinements to Warmth, Brightness, Punch, Dynamics, Low End, Presence, Air, Width, Glue, Density, and Smoothness. Champagne’s local browser engine applies those adjustments to the audio. Champagne applies advanced tonal processing to audio, making songs radio-ready in less than a minute. How I built it I released Champagne on the Mac App Store a few days before this contest was announced. After attempting to build a different WebMCP website with no success, I had a lightbulb moment: This would be the perfect opportunity to build a web demo for my new macOS app! I ported the app from Swift into TypeScript + CSS using a blueprint roadmap method, then got to tuning the actual operation of the system. Champagne registers nine page-bound tools using document.modelContext.registerTool, allowing ChatGPT to inspect the studio, create and refine masters, compare results, apply trims and fades, and adjust track speed. Audio processing remains local in the browser. Connecting ChatGPT into the mastering engine enables specific tuning that provides artists more control over the processing adjustments than the original macOS app ever did. You can learn more about the integration specifics through the README on GitHub: https://github.com/LoganVoss/Champagne How people and agents work together ✵ Artist imports audio. ✵ Artist describes the desired result. ✵ Champagne analyzes the audio locally and exposes compact measurements through WebMCP. ✵ ChatGPT interprets those measurements and the artist’s prompt. ✵ ChatGPT chooses and calls the appropriate WebMCP tools. ✵ ChatGPT coordinates mastering, refinements, trims, fades, and speed. ✵ Artist reviews the result. Don't like it? Tell ChatGPT what to fix. ✵ Artist downloads the mastered audio file. Challenges I ran into The first major challenge I ran into was not understanding what WebMCP actually does. At first, I built a prompt box on the website that guided the mastering engine with specific presets, but that didn't feel right. There was no real AI input. The dots finally connected when I realized how you're supposed to work side by side using the ChatGPT app web browser + chat window. Once I made that connection, it all came together. The other primary challenge I faced was deciding what to show when somebody visits the site through a web browser that doesn't support WebMCP. This was a little confusing mainly because it's like building two versions of the same product, but I had experience with that from iOS development (iPhone/iPad apps), so I figured it out pretty quickly. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I'm most proud of how simple it makes the mastering process for AI music artists. AI music artists can produce hundreds of songs per day, and they need an easy way to master the music they create. Champagne gives them the ability to do that rapidly, so they can share their creations even quicker. I'm also really proud of how WebMCP took Champagne to the next level through creating fine-tuned results with precision adjustments. In music, small changes make the biggest difference, and that's what makes this project really glow. What I learned I learned what WebMCP actually is, and how it can make products better through integrating AI natively. What's next for Champagne Champagne was created as a one-price replacement for pay-per-track / subscription services that perform a similar method of signal processing. With this contest, I decided to open source the code, enabling people to use the tool for free. As for building a stronger integration with ChatGPT + WebMCP, there's a universe of opportunity. Currently, the results are a little restricted with the four signature baselines. This could be removed entirely to provide an even more individualized mastering experience for each song, but it will take some work to make sure the outputs don't go completely off the rails. Another improvement I'm considering is changing the audio processing pipeline from local to server side, for further precision. More to come! ;-) Built With codex css love swift typescript Try it out champagne.vossx.chatgpt.site github.com apps.apple.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Logan Voss just building it, in sunny los angeles california Like 1 1 person likes this: Share this project: Updates Logan Voss started this project — Sep 03, 2026 11:26 AM EDT

title: SightSinger Copilot
pitch: Say the edit, hear the change. WebMCP fuses SightSinger and ChatGPT into one AI co-composer, precise score edits in plain language, and sing it back instantly. No DAW required.
about_excerpt: Say the edit, hear the change. WebMCP fuses SightSinger and ChatGPT into one AI co-composer, precise score edits in plain language, and sing it back instantly. No DAW required. Like Comment Story Updates SightSinger Copilot - Agentic AI Session Singer Edit score with natural language. Just tell AI what to edit. Not only lyrics. Just tell AI to update any notes just say "Sing the song", AI will complete generate all parts for you Inspiration SightSinger is a production score-to-singing tool with initial traction. Since launching in May 2026, it has reached 600 sign-ups, 200 active users, and MRR enough to cover my AI coding subscription. Our most requested features are a one-click "render all parts" button and cleanup of common score artifacts like redundant notes and misaligned lyrics. Both asks are harder than they sound. "Render all" means reliably orchestrating many long-running synthesis jobs. Score cleanup means running arbitrary code against user data. It requires a real sandbox to lock down which libraries and tools that code can touch. That's a security and infrastructure investment in its own, unrelated to the singing engine SightSinger was built to be good at. WebMCP solved the problem. Rather than building all by myself, I could expose only what SightSinger uniquely does well, like precise per-part synthesis and expressive singing, as narrow, callable tools, and let the requesting agent, already running under its own host's sandboxing and orchestration, handles the rest. The dangerous, generic work moves to systems already built to handle it. This isn't "let's add WebMCP because it's trending." The result is SightSinger Copilot: an edit, see, sing loop, where the agent handles precise editing and sequencing, and SightSinger handles the voice. What it does SightSinger Copilot turns a written MusicXML score into an agent-ready rehearsal studio. Instead of prompting for a generic song, musicians work from the notes, rhythm, lyrics, parts, verses, and instrumental arrangement already written in their score. A user can upload a score, or start with the built-in Happy Birthday demo, then ask an AI agent to inspect the score, make precise MusicXML edits, generate solfège lyrics, direct a vocal performance, synthesize a selected vocal part, and export the current vocal mix. The resulting vocal tracks sit alongside score-derived instrumental MIDI playback, so users can rehearse and iterate without DAW editing. WebMCP makes this workflow agentic and beyond a commodity score-to-singing tool. A musicXML score is structured text, any edit precise enough to describe, like "at bar 15, change the chord from D minor to F major 7th," becomes an exact change, not a lucky regeneration. How we built it We built an open-source React/TypeScript frontend hosted on Firebase Hosting. The frontend registers score-aware WebMCP tools at startup, letting an agent retrieve and edit the active MusicXML, add solfège, request synthesis, check credits, and export the current mix. The browser UI remains the visible workspace for score updates, rendering progress, multitrack playback, and downloads. A separate private Cloud Run backend handles authorization, score/session storage, and GPU-backed DiffSinger inference. It runs on an NVIDIA L4 GPU and turns the selected score part, lyrics or solfège, and performance settings into vocal tracks that return to the studio for playback and mixing. Challenges we ran into WebMCP tools do not currently provide a native way for an agent to attach a local file to the site or directly receive a downloaded audio file. That matters for a score-first music workflow. We designed around this with URL- and session-based handoffs. The musician uploads the initial score in the studio, then the agent retrieves and edits the active MusicXML through the current session. Synthesized tracks and exported mixes are returned as playback/download URLs, while the studio updates the visible score and multitrack player. This keeps every agent action grounded in the same active session without requiring unsupported file-transfer capabilities. Accomplishments that we're proud of I discovered this challenge only about two days ago, and the public repository was created just for it. In that short time, we learned WebMCP, exposed meaningful SightSinger capabilities as browser tools, and delivered a working, deployable demo. I'm proud that this is more than a tool-call showcase. It demonstrates a practical score-first workflow: an LLM can understand the active MusicXML score, make natural-language edits, prepare solfège or lyric renders, direct an AI singer, and help assemble a rehearsal-ready demo. All while keeping the musician in the visible studio loop. What we learned Before writing code, I asked which agent-integration approach actually fits: vision/screenshot control, DOM scraping, A2A, a hosted MCP server, a direct API, or WebMCP. WebMCP stood out for two reasons. It calls structured tools rather than clicking rendered pixels, so it's way more token efficient and accurate. And it runs the agent directly on our page, inheriting the user's existing logged-in session, no separate server, auth, or API keys to stand up. That also meant the riskiest part of this feature, an LLM freely editing a user's score, runs inside the agent's own sandbox instead of one we'd have to build ourselves. The lesson: there is no universally right integration approach. Only the approach that best fits the use case, constraints, and time. What's next for SightSinger Copilot Next, we want SightSinger Copilot to become a true co-director for score-based vocal production. It should understand a song’s musical context, including its form, phrasing, lyrics, harmony, vocal range, and emotional arc. It then translates that understanding into precise performance direction for the AI singer. For example, Copilot could direct: “bars 1–4: soft, peaceful, and clean,” “bars 5–8: gradually build intensity,” and “chorus: high-energy, emotionally open.” SightSinger would then translate the director’s or composer’s instruction into its voicing-curve parameter controls, shaping the singer’s delivery across the score. Rather than treating a whole part as one uniform render, SightSinger could create vocals that remain faithful to the written notation while carrying intention, contrast, and emotion. title: Agent SEO Studio
pitch: Point your AI agent at any site: it audits AI-search readiness, ranks you against competitors, and writes the fixes - 13 WebMCP tools it calls by name while you watch and steer.
about_excerpt: Point your AI agent at any site: it audits AI-search readiness, ranks you against competitors, and writes the fixes - 13 WebMCP tools it calls by name while you watch and steer. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration SEO asked one question for twenty years: 'can Google read my page?' Then GEO arrived - 'can an AI assistant cite my answer?' We think WebMCP opens the one that actually matters next: 'can the agent finish the job on my site?' The unlock clicked when we realized an AI agent literally cannot answer "is my website ready for AI search?" from a browser. It can't fetch other sites cross-origin — CORS blocks it. It can't read the HTML only a server sees. It can only guess from training data. Those are exactly the gaps WebMCP is built to close: the page hands the agent real, named tools that do the work the agent can't do alone. So we built a studio where a business owner and their agent audit, rank, and repair a site together — and, because it felt right, made the studio able to audit whether a site is itself WebMCP-ready. What we built Agent SEO Studio registers 13 WebMCP tools on document.modelContext . An agent can audit a site's AI-search readiness, compare it against competitors, mystery-shop whether an agent could book/buy/contact on it, scan a whole market server-side, generate ready-to-paste JSON-LD fixes, and project the score climbing. Every tool call renders into a shared on-screen workspace the human watches and steers — and a live dashboard counts every agent call by tool and by AI engine, a metric no static SEO tool can show. How we built it Frontend + tools: Next.js 15, React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS 4, deployed on Vercel. The WebMCP layer ( src/lib/register-tools.ts ) registers tools with the standard registerTool({ name, description, inputSchema, execute }) shape and returns MCP { content: [{ type: "text", text }] } results. Tools reach the app through a thin StudioBridge seam, so the tool layer never touches React directly. Server route ( /api/audit ) does the cross-origin fetch + deterministic measurement, guarded by an SSRF check that blocks private/metadata IPs and re-validates every redirect hop. Market discovery uses OpenStreetMap's Overpass API (keyless). Fix generation is provider-agnostic — OpenAI or Anthropic — with a deterministic template fallback so the demo always produces valid output and never fabricates facts. State-dependent tools: verify_fix and export_report register the moment the first audit lands; analyze_gaps after a market scan — so an agent that re-reads the tool list finds actions that weren't there a step ago. Challenges we faced CORS is the whole point — and the whole problem. The reason this needs WebMCP (agents can't fetch cross-origin) is also what forced every measurement server-side. We leaned in: the server-side fetch is the product. Honest confidence for check_webmcp . A static server fetch can't run the JavaScript that registers a site's tools at runtime — so "is this site WebMCP-ready?" can't always be answered with certainty. Rather than fake it, the tool reports its confidence honestly (confirmed in served markup vs. likely from a linked bundle vs. none). Never guess. Our hardest self-imposed rule: every finding must trace to a fact observed in the page's HTML. A site that doesn't load scores 0 with a reason ; a JavaScript-rendered SPA is flagged as such, not falsely accused of having no content. Backed by 57 unit tests on the pure logic. Tools that don't stall the agent. A raw rejection is opaque to an agent and stops it cold, so every tool is wrapped to return a descriptive text miss instead of throwing — "loose schema, strict code." What we learned WebMCP is less about "add tools to a page" and more about designing a surface a human and an agent share. The tools that felt best weren't the ones that did the most — they were the ones whose results landed somewhere the human could see and redirect . And the honest-confidence work on check_webmcp taught us that the most trustworthy agent tool is one that knows, and says, what it can't be sure of. title: ExactCue
pitch: Browser agents can prepare pharmacy refills, but prescription records can change before a person confirms. ExactCue uses WebMCP to block stale orders.
about_excerpt: Browser agents can prepare pharmacy refills, but prescription records can change before a person confirms. ExactCue uses WebMCP to block stale orders. Like Comment Story Updates The pharmacy record moved from v1 to v2, so ExactCue blocked the outdated refill. HTTP 409. No write. WebMCP exposes only the tools valid now while Marcus and his browser agent share one live refill order. Marcus reviews one exact cue: prescriptions, pickup, record version, and fingerprint - before anything can be submitted. A current action earns an authoritative receipt; stale authority retires instead of retrying silently. WebMCP carries one reviewed cue to Netlify; an atomic ETag check returns a receipt or blocks the stale write. Inspiration Marcus wants his browser agent to handle the repetitive work of refilling prescriptions. But Marcus - not the agent - should own the final decision. That creates a deceptively hard problem: what happens if Marcus reviews an order, but the pharmacy record changes before he confirms it? A confident click or agent response could submit an order he never actually reviewed. ExactCue asks a simple question: Can a website promise that the action it commits is still the action the person reviewed? We use a synthetic pharmacy refill because the failure is instantly understandable, while the underlying pattern applies to any consequential browser action. What it does ExactCue gives a person and their browser agent shared custody of one action: The agent prepares. Through WebMCP, it selects two eligible prescriptions and a pickup pharmacy using the tools the page currently allows. Marcus reviews. ExactCue creates one visible, spoken, and machine-readable summary of the exact order, including its current version. The server checks. When Marcus confirms, the server commits only if the pharmacy record is still the version he reviewed. ExactCue proves the result. A successful action earns an authoritative receipt. If the record changed, the outdated refill is blocked, nothing is submitted, and Marcus is guided to the current record. The demo’s signature moment is a real failure test: another request reaches the server first, the record moves from v1 to v2, and Marcus’s original action receives HTTP 409 · NO WRITE . The pharmacy is synthetic. The reusable product idea is current-state-bound actions for browser agents . Why WebMCP is essential Without WebMCP, a browser agent must infer controls from pixels or an accessibility tree. It can click the right-looking button, but the page has not given it a typed contract for the action, the current workflow state, or recovery. ExactCue makes WebMCP load-bearing: The page exposes only the tools valid for the current step. Prescription tools retire when the flow moves to pickup; pickup tools retire at review. The agent and the visible interface operate on the same live order. review_order returns the exact cue as structured data, not just screen text. submit_refill carries the reviewed version and ETag to the server. reload_current_record gives the agent a structured recovery path after a conflict. Remove WebMCP and the agent loses the page-declared workflow contract. Remove the server check and ExactCue loses its central promise. The product needs both. A better user experience For someone who relies on spoken or structured confirmation, “the agent clicked it” is not enough. They need to know exactly what will happen - and that the action did not silently change after the readback. ExactCue reduces a multi-step form to one meaningful human decision. The agent handles preparation. Marcus receives one exact cue. The result is either a current receipt or a plain-language explanation that nothing happened. The product also includes: keyboard and screen-reader semantics; on-demand speech for the exact order; reduced-motion and narrow-screen layouts; visible current tool authority; clear ineligible-prescription explanations; explicit stale-record recovery; and a complete manual path when WebMCP is unavailable. ExactCue does not claim to prove spoken assent. It proves that the reviewed payload was bound to a particular record version and checked again at commit time. How we built it The system follows one inspectable path: Person + UI ↔ shared order state ↔ WebMCP tools → Netlify Function → Blob conditional write → receipt or recovery Browser: React and TypeScript power the visible flow and the shared order state. WebMCP: document.modelContext.registerTool publishes typed actions. An AbortController retires tools when their step ends. Exact Cue: one snapshot binds the prescription IDs, pharmacy, spoken readback, record version, and ETag fingerprint. Server: a Netlify Function rebuilds and validates the order against authoritative data. Storage: Netlify Blobs uses strong reads and onlyIfMatch conditional writes. A losing request cannot overwrite the current record. Proof: every result includes a structured next action; successful writes return a receipt, while conflicts return the current record with noWrite: true . Synthetic run IDs isolate judge sessions without acting as credentials. Operational logs deliberately exclude session IDs, ETags, request bodies, and patient/order fields. Architecture PERSON + BROWSER AGENT │ │ prepares prescriptions + pickup ▼ REACT UI ↔ SHARED ORDER STATE ↔ STEP-SCOPED WEBMCP TOOLS │ select · review · submit · recover │ ▼ EXACT CUE prescription IDs + pharmacy + spoken readback + record v1 + ETag │ │ submit_refill(confirmed: true) ▼ ══════════════ AUTHORITATIVE COMMIT BOUNDARY ══════════════ ▼ NETLIFY FUNCTION rebuild current order → validate reviewed payload → compare ETag │ ▼ NETLIFY BLOBS · onlyIfMatch(ETag) ├── CURRENT ──→ atomic write ──→ authoritative receipt └── STALE ──→ HTTP 409 · NO WRITE ──→ reload_current_record The architecture is deliberately split at the commit boundary. The browser agent prepares shared state and WebMCP carries the exact reviewed cue. A Netlify Function then rebuilds the authoritative order and uses a Netlify Blobs ETag compare-and-swap. The only valid outcomes are a current receipt or HTTP 409 · NO WRITE with a structured recovery tool. Challenges we ran into Retiring tools safely. A WebMCP tool can advance the state while its own invocation is still resolving. Aborting its controller immediately can discard the result, so ExactCue retires the previous tool surface on the next task after Chrome delivers the response. Proving a real conflict. Client-side validation could only imitate safety. We separated the domain state machine from storage, tested stale and replay paths locally, then captured two real conditional requests against the public Netlify deployment. Drawing an honest boundary. ExactCue cannot infer whether a person truly intended a spoken “yes.” It can prove the narrower - and useful - guarantee that the payload presented for review is the payload checked against current server state. Accomplishments that we’re proud of A complete prepare → review → verify → recover → receipt product journey. Native WebMCP execution drives the same state shown in the human interface. Tool authority changes with the workflow; navigation cannot bypass the committing action. What we learned A useful agent experience needs more than callable functions. The page should expose authority that changes with state, return structured recovery instructions, and show the same boundary to the person. We also learned to separate three moments that are often blurred together: a person reviews an action; the page binds that review to one precise proposal; and the server decides whether that proposal is still current. WebMCP connects the human and agent sides of that contract inside the user’s browser. Conditional server state makes the contract trustworthy under failure. What’s next for ExactCue We would co-design the cue and recovery language with people who use nonvisual interfaces, test additional WebMCP clients, and formalize confirmation provenance as the API evolves. Then we would package the current-state cue pattern for other consequential workflows - benefits, banking, travel changes, and government services - where an agent can prepare complexity but a person should own the final, current decision.
