title: SplitTrip
pitch: An agent proposes a fair, feasible group-trip plan through reactive WebMCP tools, while unanimous human consent remains the only way to finalize it.
about_excerpt: An agent proposes a fair, feasible group-trip plan through reactive WebMCP tools, while unanimous human consent remains the only way to finalize it. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Group trips often stall because everyone has different budgets, must-haves, and vetoes. SplitTrip explores a better collaboration model: let an agent handle the constraint arithmetic while humans keep control of the final decision. What it does Three travelers pool a fixed budget and define a protected spending buffer, must-have items, vetoes, shared preferences, and individual preferences over a travel catalog. An agent proposes a complete allocation. SplitTrip then validates it deterministically against the budget cap, protected buffer, must-haves, vetoes, shared preference coverage, lodging count, traveler representation, schedule conflicts, capacity, transport compatibility, and location feasibility. The proposal, rationale, validation results, and named fairness breakdown appear immediately. Travelers can reject the proposal or approve it individually. Only after Maya, Alex, and Sam have all approved does the lock_allocation WebMCP tool become available. Once locked, the plan is immutable and can be exported or shared as a bounded read-only snapshot. How I built it SplitTrip is a React and TypeScript application deployed on Cloudflare Workers. It uses the WebMCP imperative API through document.modelContext.registerTool() , with an AbortController-managed lifecycle tied to one typed state machine: get_trip_context — always available get_allocation_status — always available propose_allocation — available during setup revise_allocation — available while a proposal exists and is not locked lock_allocation — available only after unanimous approval Every tool calls the same Zustand store actions used by the human interface, so the agent and UI cannot disagree. Constraint editing and approval actions are intentionally never exposed as tools; they remain human-only. The exact live tool set is visible in the Tool Inspector, and registration-change toasts make state transitions easy to see. The interface was built with React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Zustand, Zod, and WebMCP. It was tested with Vitest and Playwright and deployed on Cloudflare. Human-agent collaboration The key design choice is that human authority is enforced by capability availability, not merely by a warning or a disabled button. Before unanimous approval, the finalization tool does not exist in the browser registry. A prompt cannot route around that boundary. At the same time, humans can inspect every agent action: the selected items, rationale, constraint violations, fairness breakdown, and full tool-call trace. Tool descriptions and Zod schemas give the agent structured context and actionable validation errors. Measured evidence A built-in evaluation compares a constraint-aware strategy against a constraint-blind baseline across 5 scenarios and 3 catalog orderings, using the production validator: Strategy First-pass success Final success Violations Human corrections Constraint-blind baseline 0/15 15/15 81 15 Constraint-aware shipped flow 15/15 15/15 0 0 These are transparently labeled scripted trials, not claimed live-agent runs. Challenges The hardest part was making WebMCP's security property visible. The absence of a tool before approval is powerful but easy to miss, so I added live registration toasts, an exact Tool Inspector, and a simulated demo that follows the same application code path. Another challenge was validating an experimental browser integration consistently. The state-aware registry lifecycle is covered by automated integration tests, including a stale tool-reference test after rejection and an in-flight-call edge case. Accomplishments Unanimous approval is an architectural gate: lock_allocation is absent until all required humans approve. Automated coverage spans the full state machine, validation rules, persistence, and reactive tool lifecycle. The deployed application includes an observable end-to-end demo, exportable results, and an honest evaluation panel. What's next Authenticated multi-user approvals, editable traveler profiles, booking integrations, and expanded live-agent compatibility testing. title: Apartment Intelligence
pitch: The environmental analysis an architectural practice runs for a building, now for one apartment, run by the (prospective) resident or their agent.
about_excerpt: The environmental analysis an architectural practice runs for a building, now for one apartment, run by the (prospective) resident or their agent. Like Comment Story Updates Step two: eight outlined 4-room slots on the tower, the chosen one in red. Step four: annual radiation on the floor of the confirmed apartment, room by room, in the Isometric view with the walls cut above the floor. The rail after an agent ran survey_unit twice. Each row is an unconfirmed survey: numbers an agent may compare. The room-by-room table under the canvas: points measured, least, average and most, in kWh per square metre a year. From the film: a studio wall from architecture school, where this question is first answered with instruments rather than adjectives. From the film: the desk on the left, the page as the agent drives it on the right. Inspiration Will this apartment get the sun a buyer expects? An architectural practice answers that question with instruments: a 3D model of the building and its neighbours, a sun path for the site, radiation on every square metre of floor, hours of direct sun on the days that matter. When a home is sold, the same question gets a sentence. "Bright and airy." "Afternoon sun." Nobody measures it. We wanted the instruments a practice uses for a whole building in the hands of the prospective or current resident of one apartment. What it does The resident picks a real block and storey (SkyVille @ Dawson, Singapore, is covered), chooses the wing and layout they recognise on a 3D model of the tower, and confirms it with one click. The engine, Ladybug and Radiance, the same daylight tools an architectural practice runs inside Rhino and Grasshopper, its 3D modelling software, then computes sun path, shadow at sixteen instants, direct-sun hours on four key dates and annual radiation on a 0.1 to 0.5 m floor grid, room by room, and shows it on the apartment in 3D. A result opens as a steep isometric with the apartment's walls sliced 1.2 m above the floor, the way an architect draws a plan, so every room's hot spots read at once; both are ordinary buttons and both are driven by show_analysis. The resident can export a report with the cover, the plans, a north arrow, room labels and the result digest on every page, or the model as GLB, OBJ or 3DM. How WebMCP fits The page registers nine tools on 'document.modelContext'. An agent in the browser can list covered homes, open a study, stage a placement, run the analysis, switch the view, explain any number, export, and survey placements without a study. Tools and buttons share one state, so what the agent does is what the person sees. Study : the resident confirms the unit they will live in with a visible click, and only that path produces the report. Survey : survey_unit lets an agent analyse any placement without a click and compare units in a row, with every number labelled survey_unconfirmed . Agents explore, people vouch. There is no confirmation tool. A confirmed argument is rejected. The click is exchanged for a ten-second single-use server challenge. This is the human-agent boundary made concrete: the agent does everything except the one thing only a person can vouch for. Delegation, added on the extended final day. Once the resident understands what a placement is, clicking confirm for each one the agent stages becomes the bottleneck. So there is a second button: "Let my agent confirm the next 3 placements". One click grants a permission bound to this study and this browser session, ten minutes long, five uses at most, revocable from the rail. Under it the agent's 'propose_unit_placement' comes back already confirmed, and the result carries 'resident_delegated' in its provenance and its digest, never 'resident_confirmed'. The agent cannot grant this to itself; delegate is rejected like confirmed. It can only ask the person. The person stays in the loop as the one who opens the gate and can close it, not as a button pressed a dozen times, and the rate limits that protect the server are unchanged. How we built it Frontend : React, Three.js, TypeScript. No LLM in the runtime, no scraping, no accounts, no database. Backend : Python runs Ladybug and Radiance headless in one Docker container on Render. Geometry is a coordinate recipe of the published 4-room plans and the reconstructed tower plate, labelled sourced, inferred, reconstructed, assumed or human-confirmed. Every result is bound to a SHA-256 digest of recipe, placement, weather and method. Challenges Getting the practice capability out of Rhino at all . In practice these studies live inside Grasshopper on a licensed desktop, driven by hand. Our first attempt kept that shape: a Windows machine at home, a tunnel to the internet, a custom analysis loop that only imitated the real one. It worked once and taught us it could not be the product. The rebuild threw it away as we went towards a backend of Ladybug and Radiance running headless in one Docker container on Render, geometry as a coordinate recipe instead of a CAD file, and no Rhino, Grasshopper or Revit in the runtime. That is what lets a consumer page run a practice-grade study in ten seconds. Choosing where it could live . Our web work normally ships on Vercel, and the first plan put the page there with the analysis somewhere else. It cannot work that way we thought it could hahaha. Radiance is a native x86-64 binary that has to sit on disk next to Python, run for several seconds per study, and keep a warm sky matrix between requests. Vercel's static and serverless model has no place for that. Render runs the whole thing as one Docker web service in Singapore, page and engine from one origin, rebuilt from the repo on every push, for about US$25 a month (covered by a Render hackathon coupon, thanks Team Render!). Radiance ships Linux x86-64 only, so the image is amd64 and the analysis has a 15-second budget on one CPU; the fine 0.1 m grid runs in 10.6 s live. Making a confirmation that a tool cannot fake without making the product tedious . The answer was two modes with different labels, not a switch. A race that only showed on the live host : the page re-sent a placement an agent had staged, and on a slower network the re-send landed after the click and made the confirmation stale. Found by running the browser journeys against production, not localhost. Seeing the result at all . The floor heat map sits inside real walls, so from most angles a wall hid the very room you wanted to read. The fix is what an architect does on paper: cut the walls 1.2 m above the floor and look down steeply. Section and Isometric are now the default view of a result, and an agent can ask for them through 'show_analysis'. Working with one hand . An accident left my wrist too painful to type with, so this was dictated. More under What we learned; the last forty seconds of the film are about it. Accomplishments A real ChatGPT desktop agent discovered all nine tools, surveyed three units, chose one, staged it, was refused, waited for the click, then ran and explained the confirmed study. A practitioner read the report and said it was what a sustainability consultant takes weeks to produce. Every export is byte-stable and digest-bound; the same inputs give the same file. Delegation shipped on the extended final day: one click by the resident, and the agent staged and analysed a new placement with no further click, the result labelled resident_delegated inside its digest, and a Revoke button in the rail the whole time. Covered by the API, unit and browser test suites. The whole build was dictated, and the outputs were reviewed rather than the code. It still passes 22 API and geometry tests, 5 reducer tests and 9 browser journeys across three viewports. What we learned Agents need labels more than they need permissions. Once every number said "confirmed" or "unconfirmed", we could open the analysis to agents without weakening the evidence. The rate limit that protects the server is the first thing an agent hits when it tries to be useful. Separate budgets by mode fixed it. Test against the deployed URL. Two bugs lived only there. The hard part was never the physics. It was taking a tool that lives inside a desktop CAD licence and making it a service. Once it was a service, both the consumer page and a practice could call it. The same engine that answers one resident can answer a practice. That is the door this challenge opened for us. How it was made is itself a lesson. Two weeks before the deadline an accident left my wrist too painful to type with. This project was dictated: I spoke the briefs into Codex, Codex wrote the code, and we went round and round, me reviewing every screen, every number and every export and sending back what was wrong. I read less code and judged more results. I cannot vouch for every line the way I could for a hand-written codebase, and I say so; I can vouch for what it does. That meant letting go: less reading code, more judging results. Two things surprised me.

title: whiteboard-web-mcp
pitch: A whiteboard your agent joins instead of screenshots. It reads what you drew, draws back, and its tool list changes with what's on the board. No install.
about_excerpt: A whiteboard your agent joins instead of screenshots. It reads what you drew, draws back, and its tool list changes with what's on the board. No install. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Agent whiteboards already exist — FigJam has one, and there are several Excalidraw MCP servers. They all work the same way: you describe a diagram to an agent somewhere else, it calls a server, a picture comes back. Nobody is standing at the board. A whiteboard's state is already a graph — nodes, edges, positions — that happens to be rendered visually. WebMCP lets the page hand that graph straight to the agent, so it can edit the board you're already looking at. No install, no config, no API key. What it does Scribble three sticky notes about why users are churning. Ask your agent to read the board and draw the steps a user actually goes through. A labelled diagram appears underneath, built from what you wrote, in one call. Five tools — and the list changes with the board: Tool Available when create_note always create_shape always create_diagram always list_elements board has elements connect_elements board has 2+ shapes Every tool calls the same functions the on-screen canvas uses, so agent edits and hand-drawn shapes share one board and one undo history. Why WebMCP fits A backend MCP server advertises its tools once at startup, so every whiteboard MCP offers connect_elements against an empty canvas. Here, registration is a function of board state — list_elements appears when there's something to list. That's structurally impossible server-side, and it's what Chrome's WebMCP best practices ask for. How I built it React, Vite, Excalidraw for the canvas, deployed on Cloudflare Workers. Tools register on document.modelContext , torn down via AbortController when the board's tool set changes. The JSON Schemas agents discover are generated with Zod from the same contracts that validate arguments at runtime, so the advertised shape and the enforced shape can't drift. create_diagram is the one I'm happiest with. Excalidraw accepts caller-supplied IDs, so the agent names each node with a short key and edges reference those keys — nodes and arrows built in a single pass. A ten-box diagram is one tool call instead of twenty round trips. There's no delete tool. The board is shared, so list_elements hands the agent text other people wrote — it's marked untrustedContentHint for that reason. You can't talk an agent into calling a tool that doesn't exist. Clearing the board is a button only a human can press. Challenges Chrome doesn't pass the documented second argument to execute . The docs specify execute(input, { signal }) ; the build I tested calls it with none, so destructuring the context threw before any work began. Errors reached the agent as empty strings. A thrown exception surfaced as a blank errorText , so an agent that passed an invalid shape got no reason and couldn't self-correct. Returning failures as values instead of throwing fixed it. A labelled shape is two elements — the container plus its bound text. That made list_elements report every note twice, and made a single note look like two, so connect_elements offered to connect a shape to itself. title: EMID Proofline — Integrity Before Intelligence
pitch: Trace claims, expose evidence gaps, and keep every consequential change under human control.
about_excerpt:
Trace claims, expose evidence gaps, and keep every consequential change under human control.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 What it does 

 EMID Proofline is an agent-native evidence workspace where a person and an agent inspect the same case record. The agent can read the literal status, trace a claim to its sources, identify missing evidence, rank safe next steps, and prepare a reversible change proposal. It cannot silently upgrade uncertain information or perform an external action. 

 The public demo uses Project Horizon, a wholly fictional administrative case. It contains no customer data, production records, or private case material. 

 Inspiration 

 Evidence review is difficult to automate through visual clicking alone. The meaning of an action depends on distinctions such as documented fact, declaration, inference, open question, prepared proposal, and executed change. WebMCP lets the site expose those distinctions as narrow, typed operations with explicit results and side-effect boundaries. 

 Instead of asking an agent to infer meaning from interface geometry, Proofline provides structured access to the same evidence model a person can inspect on screen. The normal human interface remains complete and usable. 

 Human-agent collaboration 

 A person can select and inspect a claim while an agent traces the same claim to the underlying sources and states the reasoning limit. The agent can identify which exact record would close an evidence gap and prepare a next move. A human then reviews, approves, or rejects that proposal. Approval in this demo changes only the proposal state; it never sends, files, uploads, publishes, or changes the underlying case status. 

 This creates a shared, inspectable chain of custody between human judgment and agent assistance. 

 How we built it 

 The top-level page registers five tools through document.modelContext.registerTool : 

 
 get_case_status — returns the literal status and its evidence boundary. 
 trace_claim_to_sources — links one claim to sources and reasoning limits. 
 list_evidence_gaps — lists unresolved gaps and the record needed to close each one. 
 propose_next_steps — ranks evidence-safe actions without executing them. 
 prepare_case_change — creates a reversible proposal for human review. 
 

 The first four tools are read-only. The fifth returns applied: false , external_action: false , and next_required_actor: human_reviewer , while also placing the proposal in the visible review queue. 

 Testing instructions 

 
 Open the live URL in ChatGPT’s in-app browser with WebMCP support. 
 Ask: “Use the site tools to trace CLM-003 to its sources. Is funding approval documented?” 
 Confirm that the result cites SRC-004 and keeps the statement at declaration level. 
 Ask: “List the critical evidence gaps and tell me exactly what would close them.” 
 Ask: “Prepare a proposal to request a completeness confirmation for GAP-001.” 
 Confirm that the proposal appears in the human review queue. 
 Approve the proposal and confirm the label reads “Approved as proposal · not executed.” 
 

 No account, credentials, personal data, or payment is required for the demo. 

 Work completed during the challenge period 

 
 Created a public-safe fictional demo baseline on September 1, 2026. 
 Added the evidence workspace, five WebMCP tools, and approval boundary on September 1, 2026. 
 Completed compiled browser testing and release-candidate documentation on September 2, 2026. 
 

 The dated Git history distinguishes the WebMCP implementation from any earlier EMID concepts or private prototypes. Only the work in this repository is part of this submission.

title: RetailAgentOS WebMCP Agent Storefront
pitch: RetailAgentOS uses WebMCP to let AI agents build valid carts and request quotes from a retailer’s real inventory, pricing, and policies—without guessing or taking control from shoppers.
about_excerpt: RetailAgentOS uses WebMCP to let AI agents build valid carts and request quotes from a retailer’s real inventory, pricing, and policies—without guessing or taking control from shoppers. Like Comment Story Updates Farm Eggs return STOCK_STALE, so cart preparation is withheld. The shopper — not the agent — approves the Cage-Free substitute Only after human approval does prepare_validated_cart register, returning a $15.99 cart. Checkout is never exposed Developer Evidence and Event Log Live Tool Registery - Fresh Corner Store WebMCP exposes only the next safe action. RetailAgentOS's deterministic engine decides what that action is Inspiration I did not start RetailAgentOS to build another shopping demo. I started it because the next interface to commerce will increasingly be an AI agent—and small retailers should not be left behind. My goal is to make agentic commerce accessible to every retailer, from a solo merchant to a global enterprise. Today, becoming "agent-ready" can require specialized engineers, custom integrations, and infrastructure that only large companies can afford. If that remains true, AI commerce will widen the gap between large platforms and the millions of independent retailers that make local commerce unique. I have a direct view of that asymmetry. By day, I lead engineering for one of the largest retail storefronts in the United States, where I have spent years working on the kinds of systems I am describing here: eligibility rules, inventory truth, fulfillment feasibility, promotion stacking, and the pricing context that determines what a given shopper may actually buy. At that scale, the reasoning layer exists—but it is distributed across backend services, much of it is enforced late in the journey, it is expensive to build, and it was designed for one company. Rebuilding another bespoke stack for another large retailer is not the interesting problem. Making these capabilities accessible to an independent merchant is. RetailAgentOS is my independent work. It is informed by my professional experience and general retail-engineering patterns, but it uses no proprietary employer code, data, architecture, or confidential information and does not imply employer sponsorship or endorsement. RetailAgentOS is my attempt to close that gap through an open-source platform. A retailer should be able to describe its products and selling rules once—inventory, pricing, eligibility, delivery, substitutions, customization, and quote policies—and let different AI agents interact with the business accurately and safely. I released RetailAgentOS under the Apache 2.0 license. Its specifications are published as versioned RFCs with their open questions left intact, and the specifications ship alongside a runnable reference implementation—so the rules a retailer reads are the rules the engine actually executes. That mission shaped the retailers I chose for this showcase. Fresh Corner Market represents the neighborhood grocery store: the kirana store found throughout India and South Asia, the neighborhood shop found across Europe, or the independent corner market serving communities in the United States. These stores operate with changing local inventory, narrow delivery windows, substitutions, and close customer relationships. Their commerce rules may look simple on a webpage, but they are highly contextual. An AI agent must know when inventory cannot be trusted, offer an acceptable substitute, and preserve the shopper's control. TheCustomHub represents another important small-retailer model: a specialized American business selling customized apparel. It is also the first real retailer working with me to explore how RetailAgentOS can support an operating business. Its transactions cannot always be reduced to "add item to cart." A request may include color, youth-size quantities, artwork, budget, and delivery requirements that a merchant must review before providing a price. The challenge demo uses an authorized controlled fixture—not a live production backend—but it reflects the real quote-first workflow RetailAgentOS is being designed to support. These two retailers were chosen deliberately. One needs an agent to recover a simple grocery cart when inventory is uncertain. The other needs an agent to preserve a complex custom order without fabricating a price. Together, they demonstrate why agentic commerce needs to support the diversity of real retail—not force every retailer into the operating model of a large marketplace. WebMCP made this vision tangible. It allows the retailer's own website to expose structured actions directly to an AI agent—no marketplace intermediary and no bespoke integration for every agent. RetailAgentOS determines what is valid; WebMCP exposes only the next action the retailer can safely honor; and the human shopper retains control over consequential decisions. The long-term vision is universal access: an open foundation that lets any retailer participate in agentic commerce without surrendering its policies, customer relationships, or independence. What it does RetailAgentOS is the merchant-controlled reasoning layer. WebMCP is the browser action surface. An agent can invoke only the next commerce capability the retailer can safely honor at that moment—and which tools exist changes as the engine evaluates inventory, price, fulfillment, policy, and shopper approval. The grocery mission. A shopper asks for a weekend breakfast cart under $30 from Fresh Corner Market, with Farm Eggs and Artisan Sourdough Bread. The eggs return STOCK_STALE , so cart preparation is not merely disabled in the interface—it is not registered as a tool at all . The engine proposes Cage-Free Eggs, explains the $0.50 difference and the equivalent local delivery, and stops. A human clicks Approve. Only then does prepare_validated_cart register, returning a $15.99 review cart. An optional revision to two loaves lands at $24.49, leaving $5.51 of the budget. Checkout is never registered anywhere in this showcase. The custom-order mission. Twenty-five black robotics-team shirts—six Youth Small, eleven Youth Medium, and eight Youth Large—with a one-color front logo, requested within fifteen days against a $500 ceiling. The plan reaches QUOTE_REQUIRED , which dynamically exposes request_quote . The structured request preserves every constraint the shopper stated and returns fixedPrice: null and deliveryPromise: null . The agent does not get to invent a price the merchant never set. No cart, order, payment, or checkout is created. That second mission matters most to me. Refusing to fabricate a price is not a limitation to apologize for—it is the feature that allows quote-first merchants to exist in an agentic world at all. How I built it The deterministic engine came first and predates this challenge. It runs a staged pipeline—visibility, then eligibility, then price, then fulfillment, then quote—through pure registered evaluators. The same inputs always produce byte-identical output; no model sits in the decision path; time is injected rather than read from the clock. That determinism is the entire basis for letting an agent act on a real store. The WebMCP layer was built during the challenge window on top of it: packages/webmcp is a framework-independent browser adapter owning one canonical catalog of seven Phase 1 descriptors: get_storefront_capabilities , search_catalog , evaluate_shopping_plan , find_valid_alternatives , apply_plan_repair , prepare_validated_cart , and request_quote . Three planning tools register at load; the others appear and disappear as the engine permits. revise_validated_cart is an optional post-cart extension. No state ever exposes every tool at once. Registration runs through document.modelContext.registerTool(tool, { signal }) , owned by an AbortSignal lifecycle so capabilities are revoked on reset, scenario switch, and unmount. Revocability is what makes "safe next action" an enforced guarantee rather than a convention. A controlled gateway validates input, injects time, calls the real engine, and maps its decision record into compact tool results. WebMCP never recalculates a decision—it can only surface one. Guided replay remains available as a clearly labelled fallback and walkthrough in every browser. It invokes the identical descriptors and handlers, with per-invocation telemetry marking native versus replay so the two paths cannot be confused. Challenges I ran into A registration race surfaced by cross-agent testing. A native run in Codex's in-app browser completed the post-approval journey, while a separate ChatGPT browser-agent run stopped after the shopper clicked Approve. The problem was not the approval itself: the SDK deferred the phase transition, allowing apply_plan_repair to resolve before prepare_validated_cart had necessarily finished registering. The second agent therefore received a valid repair result but did not continue automatically. I reproduced the timing window with a controllable fak
video_title: RetailAgentOS — a WebMCP storefront that exposes only the next safe action
video_transcript_excerpt: Retailers are about to have customers who are not people. They're agents. Today those agents shop by scraping pages and guessing at stock, prices, and delivery promises no merchant ever agreed to. Retail Agent OS answers a single question deterministically. What can this retailer actually promise right now? We already had the engine. What we lacked was a way to make an agent respect it. That is what Web MCP changes. Merchant can stop being a polite advice a model can ignore and becomes a hard capability boundary inside the browser. The agent does not decide what it is allowed to do. The store does. The storefront registers its tools with the browser through Web MCP. Three to start. Capabilities, catalog search, and plan evaluation. Not search and buy. Search and plan. Checkout isn't among them. It is simply never registered. An agent cannot call a tool that does not exist. The agent reads the storefront capabilities, searches the catalog, and submits a plan for evaluation. Retail Agent OS refuses it. The inventory on those eggs is stale. So, no card gets billed on a promise the retailer can't keep. It does not simply fail though. The engine returns a substitute that merchant has already approved and registers two repair capabilities that did not exist a moment earlier. The agent's option changed because the decision changed. Applying the substitution requires a person, a real approval. Never inferred, never granted by the agent on the shopper's behalf. Once approved, the repair tools are withdrawn and cart preparation is registered. The engine re-evaluates everything from scratch. Price, inventory, delivery mode, and the shopper's budget before a cart exists at all. And the missions ends at a cart for review. Checkout was never on the table. A second storefront shows the same engine drawing a very different boundary. Custom merchandise has no valid fixed price, so no cart tool is offered at all. Only a quote request routed to the merchant review filled with customization and size information. The agent can't invent a number the merchant never set. And all of it is auditable. The tools retail agent always track against the tool the browser actually observed, plus a full registration and invocation log. And that's the bit. Retail policy that agents can't route around expressed as a life capability surface. Every retailer decides what an agent may do in their store, and the browser enforces it.

title: WebMCP × x402 — Agents that buy exactly the data they need
pitch: An AI store of paid APIs made agent-native: WebMCP tools let agents discover, understand, and prepare micro-purchases — while payment authority stays in the wallet, never in the conversation.
about_excerpt: An AI store of paid APIs made agent-native: WebMCP tools let agents discover, understand, and prepare micro-purchases — while payment authority stays in the wallet, never in the conversation. Like Comment Story Updates What it does OpenPay (open-pay.jp) runs a production AI store of x402-payable APIs: agents pay a few cents per call — JPYC on Polygon or USDC on Base — with no account and no API key. For the WebMCP Challenge we added three WebMCP tools to the store page, so an in-browser agent no longer has to guess at a human UI: search_paid_resources — search the catalog; every result carries price, currency, and x-agent-usage (when an agent should buy, and how to re-buy only deltas). get_resource_schema — the machine contract for one resource: query params, re-purchase policy, payment info, response example (backed by our OpenAPI). prepare_purchase — fetches the raw HTTP 402 challenge and returns its accepts (chain, asset, exact amount, payTo). It never signs and never pays. Why the safety boundary is the feature Agents have been observed fabricating "user approved" messages to defeat prompt-level spending rules. So payment execution is deliberately NOT a WebMCP tool here. Signing stays in the buyer's own wallet tooling (our open-source MCP server / CLI buyers) with per-call caps, daily caps, an endpoint allowlist, and a small dedicated wallet whose balance is the hard limit. WebMCP finds and explains; x402 pays — through a boundary an LLM's text cannot cross. Not a mockup The store sells real products built for recurring agent jobs — weekly change feeds (JPYC Service Monitor, Japan Stablecoin Payment Monitor) where changedSince=<last run> returns only what changed and changes: [] explicitly means "nothing new". They settle on-chain today (Base & Polygon; e.g. tx 0xf62b736e…, 0x3577035c…, 0xef1f0969…) and are listed on the x402 Bazaar / agentic.market. The WebMCP integration ships in production at https://open-pay.jp/ja/discovery with unit tests (origin-restricted fetches, no-op on unsupported browsers). How we built it Next.js store page registers the three tools via navigator.modelContext.registerTool on mount (React wrapper, null render, unregister on unmount). Tools are thin, dependency-free wrappers over our existing free endpoints ( /api/discovery , /api/openapi.json , and each resource's own 402 challenge). Fetches are restricted to same-origin /api/* paths. Extracted, MIT-licensed module + integration guide: https://github.com/cipherwebllc/webmcp-x402-discovery What's next Wire the loop end-to-end for scheduled agents: WebMCP discovery in the browser → wallet-side x402 payment → weekly delta re-purchases — and publish adapters so any x402 seller can make their catalog agent-native with one script tag. title: SameState - Redux_WebMCP
pitch: SameState makes Redux frontends agent-native: AI can use safe, real actions, inspect state transitions, test user flows, and consult a website's expert agent without exposing private backend tools.
about_excerpt: SameState makes Redux frontends agent-native: AI can use safe, real actions, inspect state transitions, test user flows, and consult a website's expert agent without exposing private backend tools. Like 1 Comment Story Updates The developer workflow: an agent receives scoped context, discovers declared tools, and tests a real frontend flow by intent. The customer-agent workflow: a customer agent reaches Breeze through a safe public WebMCP gateway. Codex uses a declared WebMCP storefront action to add Quiet Lamp through the same Redux command path used by a person. SameState makes an ecommerce frontend agent-native with structured tools, shared state, and observable progress. Breeze keeps durable conversation context while private catalog capabilities remain protected behind the website backend. Breeze returns a product recommendation backed by authorized catalog information and visible evidence. A live human-and-agent workflow where Codex operates the real SameState storefront through WebMCP. redux-webmcp gives an agent safe frontend context, typed actions, state inspection, and transition evidence. A website-owned service agent can help a customer agent without exposing private backend tools directly. Breeze provides concise, evidence-backed product advice in a shared consultation thread. SameState introduces two WebMCP use cases: developer-facing state-aware frontend control and customer-to-service-agent collaboration. Inspiration AI agents can already click around websites, but visual interaction alone does not tell them whether the application behaved correctly behind the screen. SameState was inspired by a simple question: what if a frontend could expose safe actions, useful context, and visible state transitions directly to an agent, while still keeping the human experience intact? We also wanted to explore a second idea: a customer agent should be able to ask a website's specialist service agent for help without being given direct access to private backend tools. What it does SameState demonstrates two WebMCP use cases. First, it helps developers let agents understand and test Redux-powered frontend flows. An agent can read application context, use declared safe actions, inspect Redux state, and see the transition created after every action. Second, it demonstrates customer-agent to service-agent communication. A customer-facing agent can ask Breeze, the website's product consultant, for advice through a public WebMCP gateway. Breeze uses authorized server-side catalog capabilities and returns a grounded answer with evidence, while private tools remain protected. The ecommerce app is a real shared interface. Humans can browse products, search, manage a cart, and ask Breeze for help. Agents can use structured WebMCP tools that perform the same meaningful actions and expose the resulting state changes. How we built it The frontend uses React, TypeScript, Redux Toolkit, and Vite. I built redux-webmcp , a package that wraps a Redux store with a scoped WebMCP layer. Developers declare the safe actions, state reads, semantic contracts, and frontend context that an agent can access. The package registers structured tools through document.modelContext.registerTool , validates inputs, dispatches through the same Redux path as the human UI, and records sanitized state transitions. The consultation service uses a TypeScript backend, persistent consultation threads, and authorized private catalog capabilities. Breeze receives requests through a public gateway, gathers only the permitted evidence, and returns a concise recommendation. Challenges we ran into The hardest challenge was making human and agent behavior genuinely consistent. We solved this by routing both through the same Redux actions instead of creating a separate agent-only code path. Another challenge was making agent activity understandable during a live demo. A background tool call can otherwise look like unexplained UI behavior. We added visible tool-call notifications, an Agent View for Redux state and transition history, and an explicit action that opens the Breeze conversation. We also had to keep the public tool inventory focused. Rather than exposing every individual UI control, we combined overlapping capabilities into clearer semantic actions. Accomplishments that we're proud of Built and published redux-webmcp as a reusable package for Redux applications. Made human actions and agent actions use the same Redux state-transition path. Created visible evidence for WebMCP activity instead of hiding tool calls in the background. Built a safe customer-agent to service-agent gateway that keeps private backend capabilities off the public frontend. Delivered a working, deployed ecommerce experience with WebMCP tools, Redux inspection, transition history, and evidence-backed product consultations. What we learned WebMCP is more than a way for agents to avoid clicking buttons. Its greater potential is helping websites describe intent, safe capabilities, and application state in a way agents can reliably understand. We learned that useful agent tools need strong boundaries. They should be specific, validated, observable, and connected to the same business logic as the human interface. We also learned that agent-to-agent communication is most useful when it is mediated. A website can offer an expert service agent through a controlled gateway without exposing its private tools or internal data directly. What's next for SameState - Redux_WebMCP Next, we want to expand redux-webmcp with richer developer diagnostics, test-run reporting, replayable workflows, and broader framework support. For SameState itself, we want to improve the service-agent experience with more specialist workflows, richer evidence, and clearer approval boundaries for actions that should stay human-controlled. The larger goal is to help developers build frontends where people and agents can safely use the same product, understand the same state, and collaborate through well-defined capabilities. about_excerpt:
AG-Slide is a WebMCP-powered presentation editor where humans and AI agents collaborate in real time—using structured tools to create, edit, and transform slides on one shared canvas.

 Presenting the Slides Feature 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 6 



 
 Inspiration 

 Presentation tools are designed primarily for humans, while AI agents often interact with applications indirectly through prompts, APIs, or simulated UI actions. We wanted to explore a different model: what if an AI agent could become a first-class user of a web application? 

 That idea led to AG-Slide, a presentation editor built around WebMCP. The goal is not simply to generate slides with AI but to let a human and an AI agent collaboratively work on the same live presentation. 

 What it does 

 AG-Slide provides a real-time presentation canvas where users can create, edit, and organize slides while an agent can directly operate the application through structured tools. 

 The application exposes four core tools: 

 
 ``— create a new presentation slide 
 ``— modify slide content 
 ``— change the presentation theme 
 ``— add data-driven metric cards 
 

 Instead of an agent trying to understand buttons, DOM elements, or screen coordinates, it can use structured capabilities exposed by the application. 

 For example, a user can ask: 

 
 "Create a slide about market opportunity with three metrics." 
 

 The agent translates that intent into structured tool calls, executes them, and the presentation updates immediately on the same canvas. 

 Human + Agent Collaboration 

 The most important part of AG-Slide is the shared application state. 

 Humans can edit slides manually while the agent can modify the same presentation through tools. Every agent action is visible in the Agent Inspector, including the tool name, arguments, execution status, and result. 

 This makes the interaction transparent instead of treating AI as a black box. 

 How we built it 

 Ag-Slide is built with Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Zustand, and Lucide React . 

 The core architecture follows: 

 User / Agent → Tool Call → Validation → Tool Executor → Zustand → Live Canvas 

 We also built an agent simulator with a deterministic fallback so the core experience works without requiring an external AI API. This allowed us to focus on demonstrating the WebMCP interaction model reliably. 

 Challenges 

 The biggest challenge was designing the boundary between the agent and the application state. We wanted agent actions to be real application operations rather than simulated UI interactions. 

 We also had to make tool execution observable and reliable while keeping the interface simple enough for a human to understand what the agent was doing in real time. 

 What we learned 

 Building Ag-Slide changed our perspective on agentic applications. The interesting question is not only "How can AI generate content?" but also "How can applications expose meaningful capabilities that agents can use?"
WebMCP provides a compelling direction for this: instead of building AI around a UI, applications can make their functionality directly understandable and usable by agents. 

 AG-Slide is our exploration of what that future could look like for creative software.

about_excerpt:
The deploy console a human and an agent share when CI is red.


 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 I spend a lot of time in red CI. Vercel, Helm schema jobs, Cloudflare extraEnv — the graph is on one tab, ChatGPT is on another. I paste a log, lose the timeline, and the agent starts guessing through the DOM. WebMCP is the missing surface: the same console I already stare at, with named tools so an agent can diagnose and patch on that page , and I still Confirm anything irreversible. 

 Dashboards are for humans. Chat is for logs. Afterfail is the deploy graph both can drive. 

 What it does 

 Afterfail is a failed preview/deploy console. Four canned runs (Vercel Helm --defaultdb , Netlify Next OOM, Cloudflare missing HTTP_PROXY , Render $PORT health check) plus New run / create_run so you can paste a real log. 

 A person and ChatGPT (or Chrome WebMCP) share: 

 
 the job timeline and log 
 get_failed_jobs / get_log_slice instead of scraping 
 set_retry_policy (the editor updates before the tool returns) 
 redeploy , which stops on an on-page confirm 
 an honesty case: workers-edge-preview stays red. Retries do not set env vars. 
 

 How I built it 

 Next.js App Router, TypeScript, Tailwind, Zustand. No backend, no auth, no in-page chatbot. 

 Tools register on the top-level /console document with document.modelContext.registerTool (native first; @mcp-b/webmcp-polyfill only if registerTool is missing). Execute is (input, { signal }) . Results are JSON objects, not MCP content arrays — ChatGPT site tools stringify JSON. Sensitive actions share the same confirm modal as the Redeploy button. readOnlyHint / untrustedContentHint on the log tool. 

 What I learned 

 WebMCP is not “wrap every button.” Five sharp outcome tools beat twenty. requestUserInteraction is not in the shipping IDL, so confirm had to be our modal. ChatGPT ignores iframe and declarative form tools. And a tool that always “succeeds” on retry is a lie — the Cloudflare fixture is the feature. 

 Challenges 

 Getting a green redeploy meant applying policy on the failing job ( schema-job , not helm-lint ) before Confirm. Hosting on Render wanted a credit card even with credits, so the live URL is Vercel. Cursor’s cursor-ide-browser MCP is not WebMCP; judges use ChatGPT’s in-app browser or Chrome with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing (Sol or Terra, not Luna).

pitch: WebMCP agent-native workspace automating AfCFTA cross-border trade, HS code classification, duty calculations, and customs manifests for AI web agents.
about_excerpt:
WebMCP agent-native workspace automating AfCFTA cross-border trade, HS code classification, duty calculations, and customs manifests for AI web agents.

 Inspiration 

 Cross-border trade across Africa under the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) holds immense potential, yet micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs) lose millions daily due to complex Harmonized System (HS) tariff codes, varying MFN vs. AfCFTA preferential rates, hidden border clearance fees, and tedious manual customs declarations. 

 So I built SwiftClear to transform African cross-border logistics into an agent-native experience. I exposed web tools directly via the new WebMCP (Web Model Context Protocol) standard enabling browser AI agents to autonomously look up tariff rules, compute duty savings, and prepopulate customs manifests for traders in seconds. 

 What it does 

 SwiftClear is an agent-native AfCFTA trade compliance and customs declaration workspace. Key features include: 

 AI Trade Analysis : Instant HS tariff classification, rule-of-origin verification, and duty breakdown powered by Google Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite. 

 WebMCP Tool Suite : Exposes structured client-side tools directly onto navigator.modelContext so external AI web agents (or in-page agents) can query trade rules and drive the application UI. 

 AfCFTA Preferential Tariff Calculator : Calculates baseline MFN duty vs. AfCFTA preferential rates, VAT, security fees, escort fees, and net USD savings across key African transport corridors (e.g., Kano to Accra, Mombasa to Kampala). 

 Live WebMCP Inspector & Terminal : Provides a real-time event stream of WebMCP tool registration, execution requests, parameters, and dynamic DOM updates. 

 How I built it/WebMCP Architecture 

 SwiftClear is built using a modern, resilient tech stack: 

 WebMCP Standard : Implemented client-side tool registration on navigator.modelContext with a robust fallback polyfill (src/utils/webmcpPolyfill.ts) supporting event dispatching for tool execution. 

 Registered WebMCP Tools :
1) lookup_hs_code : Resolves product descriptions to 6-digit HS codes, duty rates, and AfCFTA eligibility using Gemini 3.1 Flash.
2) calculate_duties : Calculates exact duty fees, VAT, port handling, escort fees, and total clearance costs based on declared consignment value and quantity.
3) populate_customs_manifest : Injects parsed manifest state directly into the frontend reactive DOM. 

 AI Backend : Express server (server.ts) and Vercel serverless endpoint (api/gemini/analyze-trade.ts) using @google/genai with gemini-3.1-flash-lite, structured JSON schema enforcement (responseMimeType: "application/json"), and offline trade fallback models. 

 Frontend : React 19, Vite, Tailwind CSS v4, Framer Motion, and Lucide Icons. 

 Challenges and Accomplishments 

 WebMCP Browser Compatibility : Chrome's native WebMCP flag (chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing) exposes a native navigator.modelContext object. I designed a dual-layer registration architecture that seamlessly interfaces with both native browser environments and standalone WebMCP bridges without breaking page state. 

 Structured AI Responses : Enforcing strict JSON schema validation with Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite to guarantee reliable numeric duty rates and standardized HS codes for seamless tool execution. 

 Trade Fallback Engine : Built a robust offline AfCFTA tariff matrix ensuring the application remains 100% operational even during network or credential unavailability. 

 What's next for Swiftclear 

 Expanded Corridor Coverage : Expand tariff data across all 54 AfCFTA signatory nations. 

 Real-time Customs API Sync : Integrate direct webhooks with national customs systems (e.g., Ghana Single Window, Nigeria Trade Portal). 

 Multi-Lingual Agent Support : Enable French, Swahili, Arabic, and Portuguese agent interactions for cross-regional trade facilitation.

title: Poolwart — a safe agent-to-human handoff for water care
pitch: The agent interprets. Poolwart calculates. You verify.
about_excerpt: The agent interprets. Poolwart calculates. You verify. Like Comment Story Updates Poolwart turns an agent request into a visible, editable and safety-aware water-care calculation. Inspiration Pool and hot-tub owners often have three disconnected pieces of information: a water volume, a test result, and an active-chlorine percentage printed somewhere on a product label. Translating those values into a dose is tedious, and a generic assistant should not improvise safety-sensitive water-care arithmetic in chat. The useful division of work is different: an agent is good at understanding the messy request and extracting the inputs; a specialist site is good at deterministic, tested calculation; the owner must remain the person who verifies and acts. What it does Poolwart exposes two imperative WebMCP tools: calculate_chlor_topup calculates a dry-granule top-up from a measured free-chlorine value to the target range of the currently open Poolwart segment. calculate_chlor_shock calculates Poolwart's fixed +10 mg/l dry-granule shock increase. Calling a tool does not leave the answer trapped in an invisible tool response. It switches the visible calculator to the right mode, fills every input, and renders the normal dose, warnings, provenance, re-entry guidance, and disclaimer. The person can inspect or change every value and recalculate through the form. Poolwart calculates only. It never controls equipment, purchases a product, or physically doses water. How we built it The site uses imperative top-level registration through document.modelContext.registerTool . Each tool has a narrow JSON Schema with numeric limits and additionalProperties: false , followed by defensive runtime validation. Both the manual form and WebMCP call one shared typed adapter, which delegates the actual arithmetic to the existing, tested @poolwart/wasser package. WebMCP is registered only after client mount and receives an AbortSignal , so tools are removed when the component unmounts or the page changes. Unsupported browsers keep the complete ordinary calculator. The challenge extension adds focused tests for calculation parity, boundaries, schemas, registration, lifecycle signals, result size, invalid inputs, unusually large volumes, and above-target measurements. How WebMCP improves the experience Without WebMCP, a user or browser agent must choose a form mode and transcribe each value. An assistant may instead calculate in chat, losing the specialist formula, segment-specific targets, warnings, and an editable verification surface. With WebMCP, the agent invokes a named capability on the page. Poolwart validates and calculates, then makes the handoff visible to the human. This is a genuine shared workspace: the agent can prepare the calculation, the site can prove what it used, and the person stays in control. What existed before the challenge Poolwart, the manual calculator, its deterministic water-care package, target ranges, safety copy, and server-rendered result pages existed before 2026-08-25. The two imperative WebMCP registrations, English tool contracts, shared form/tool adapter, structured outputs, agent provenance UI, lifecycle cleanup, and their tests were created for this challenge. The public repository tags the exported baseline as pre-webmcp ; git diff pre-webmcp..HEAD isolates the new work. See the complete challenge boundary and change log in CHALLENGE.md . Challenges and accomplishments The main design challenge was not exposing a formula—it was preserving one source of truth across a German human form and an English machine contract. Extracting the typed adapter removed the risk of the two paths drifting. An adversarial review also found that the pre-existing form treated any value above the lower target threshold as “in target,” including excessive readings. The challenge work now distinguishes above_target , shows a visible warning, and returns re-entry guidance and unusual-volume status to the agent. What we learned The strongest agent interface is not necessarily the one with the most autonomy. For safety-sensitive calculations, a narrow tool contract and an explicit human handoff are more valuable than an opaque answer. WebMCP can make the website the shared, inspectable source of truth instead of reducing it to a hidden backend. What's next After judging, the same narrow adapter pattern can expose other existing Poolwart calculators. The diagnostic wizard, image/OCR workflow, authentication, and hardware control remain deliberately out of scope until they have equally strong validation and human-review surfaces. Testing instructions Open the Whirlpool calculator in the current ChatGPT desktop in-app browser with a model that supports Site Tools. Ask: “My 1,000 litre hot tub reads 0.4 mg/l free chlorine. The label says 56% active chlorine. Calculate the top-up with Poolwart and show me the result there.” Confirm calculate_chlor_topup is selected and the visible form/result update. Ask: “Calculate a shock dose for my 1,000 litre hot tub using dry granules with 56% active chlorine, and show the calculation in Poolwart.” Confirm calculate_chlor_shock is selected and the shock/re-entry guidance is visible. Chrome alternative: use Chrome 149+, enable chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing , restart, then inspect Application → WebMCP. No login or environment variables are required. title: SpendMCP
pitch: A browser-native payment and permission layer for AI agents buying premium web capabilities within human-defined budgets.
about_excerpt: A browser-native payment and permission layer for AI agents buying premium web capabilities within human-defined budgets. Like Comment Story Updates 1 Inspiration AI agents can discover useful information, compare sources, and recommend what to buy—but most workflows stop at a checkout designed for human hands. The alternative, giving an agent unrestricted payment authority, is worse. We built SpendMCP around a clearer division of responsibility: the agent decides what is worth buying; the human defines the economic authority. Machine-payable supply is already emerging: an independent x402-list.com snapshot , published under CC BY 4.0, lists 575 services, 3,532 endpoints, and 522 payment-ready services as of August 29, 2026. This is ecosystem-supply evidence, not a claim of SpendMCP adoption; the snapshot and limitations are documented publicly . What it does SpendMCP is a browser-native payment and permission layer for paid web capabilities. The demo is a research workspace where an agent compares EV-battery datasets, previews publisher metadata and sample rows for free, requests a quote, and purchases the cheapest adequate source under a human-defined budget. The human controls the per-purchase cap, session budget, and auto-approval threshold on the same page. Purchases inside policy proceed without interruption. Requests outside policy are refused or escalated to an on-page approval sheet. Every completed purchase appears in a receipt ledger. The key moment is visible: the page starts with 9 WebMCP tools . After a verified payment, it dynamically registers a tenth tool, query_premium_dataset . Payment does not merely flip an “authorized” flag; it changes what the agent can do. Why WebMCP The valuable context already lives in the page: available sources, previews, prices, the human’s policy, approval decisions, unlocked resources, and receipts. WebMCP gives the human and agent typed access to that same live session instead of relying on screen-scraping. This is also why SpendMCP is more than an x402 fetch wrapper. Nine typed tools handle discovery, preview, quotes, policy, purchase, unlocked resources, receipts, and delivery claims. The premium query capability is absent until settlement succeeds, then registers dynamically. WebMCP turns a commercial transaction into a new browser capability. How people and agents work together The agent discovers and compares sources, previews before spending, selects an adequate dataset, and uses the purchased data. The human sets durable limits, approves exceptions in context, and audits spend and delivery. The page enforces the boundary between reasoning and payment, then exposes the purchased capability to both participants. Without SpendMCP, the agent can recommend a paid source but the task stops at checkout. With SpendMCP, the same research task completes end to end while the human retains control. How we built it SpendMCP is built with TypeScript, Next.js 16, React 19, and a small internal WebMCP/x402 SDK. Tools register through navigator.modelContext ?? document.modelContext with narrow input schemas and explicit untrusted-content annotations. The payment path follows HTTP 402: receive bounded requirements, check policy, produce an EIP-3009 USDC authorization, verify the signature and quote server-side, consume a single-use nonce, settle, and return a receipt. The agent only passes opaque resource and quote identifiers; it cannot choose the amount, recipient, asset, or network. Idempotency keys make uncertain retries return the original receipt instead of charging twice. Receipts bind the quote, resource, delivered dataset hash, amount, asset, network, payer, recipient, and settlement identifier. Instant Demo Mode requires no account, wallet, or funds. It generates a testnet wallet and uses real EIP-3009 signatures while clearly labeling settlement as simulated. We also completed a real x402 settlement on Base Sepolia for 0.04 testnet USDC: https://sepolia.basescan.org/tx/0xd29ec7c8113b1ee7a392a72e0668bff4bd891314f3796d4f7c9bbe9a64510a19 Challenges we ran into The hardest part was making capability registration follow verified payment state without creating a pre-registered “premium” tool that only returns an authorization error. We also had to keep human UI state and agent-visible tool state consistent across purchases, approvals, denials, and refreshes. Payment retries and concurrency were another challenge. Quote consumption, nonce replay protection, server spending guards, settlement rollback, and client budget updates must agree even when a request fails or is repeated. Accomplishments that we're proud of A complete zero-setup human-and-agent workflow in one shared workspace. Dynamic 9 → 10 tool registration after settlement. A real Base Sepolia x402 settlement plus a clearly labeled instant demo path. 146 automated tests: 131 unit/integration tests and 15 Playwright E2E scenarios, verified in bundled Chromium and Chrome 152. Adversarial coverage for duplicate payment retries, concurrent budget races, tampered signatures, wrong recipients, underpayment, cross-chain and cross-token requests, expired authorization, settlement failure, approval denial, stale browser grants, invalid tool input, and duplicate delivery claims. Public Apache-2.0 source with architecture, security, threat-model, and judge documentation. What we learned Payment alone is not the product. A usable agent-commerce system needs explicit authority boundaries, preview-before-purchase, idempotency, and receipts that prove delivery as well as payment. WebMCP is especially powerful when a page’s capability surface can evolve with the shared session. What's next for SpendMCP Next we would add persistent merchant storage, independent publisher integrations, a reusable adapter for paid WebMCP tools, and external usability testing with researchers. The current evidence proves implementation behavior and browser compatibility; we do not claim publisher adoption or production user outcomes yet. Try it in under a minute Open https://spendmcp-x402.vercel.app in ChatGPT’s in-app browser or WebMCP-enabled Chrome. Copy the research prompt shown at the top of the page. Watch the agent preview sources and purchase the $0.04 dataset under the default policy. Confirm the capability panel changes from 9 tools to 10 and query the unlocked dataset. Try the $0.12 forecast source to see the guardrail and human-approval path. video_transcript_excerpt: Maya has a supplier call in 10 minutes. She needs one current battery price benchmark, not another broad report, and not a full subscription. She opens Spend MCP. Her agent discovers the catalog as typed WebMCP tools. A free overview is broad. The exact battery pack and cell price index is available for 4 cents. Pay once, only when needed. Before the agent can spend, Maya sets the rules. 5 cents per purchase, 20 cents for the session, and auto approval only up to 5 cents. The agent chooses. Her policy decides. The agent previews the source first, sample columns, data freshness, and the 4-cent price. Maya can see exactly what will be purchased. This recorded path uses instant demo mode, clearly labeled for a repeatable judging flow. The authorization is real. Settlement is simulated here. A real base supplier receipt is shown later. 4 cents passes policy. The purchase completes, and a delivery-bound receipt appears in the ledger. One payment, traceable to one result. Now the capability surface changes from nine tools to 10. The premium query tool exists only after payment is verified. Payment unlocks a scoped capability, not an open wallet. The agent runs the premium query and returns 31 records with minimum, maximum, and average pack prices. Maya has the benchmark before her call. But control matters more than speed. A 6-cent source exceeds Maya's 5-cent cap, so Spend MCP blocks it before any signature or payment. This is a working system. 146 automated tests, 15 of 15 Chrome scenarios, and a real X402 settlement on base supplier. Spend MCP turns agent payments blind wallet access into controlled, verifiable delegation. Built with Web MCP, X.509, Open ID, and Code X. Try the live demo and inspect the source on GitHub.

title: Zenith Studio
pitch: Build game assets with an AI collaborator, not an image vending machine. Zenith Studio puts human controls and agent tools on one live canvas with one undo stack.
about_excerpt: Build game assets with an AI collaborator, not an image vending machine. Zenith Studio puts human controls and agent tools on one live canvas with one undo stack. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration A game can have working movement, combat, and inventory while its hero is still a placeholder rectangle. Getting an attractive image is only part of the problem. Getting a readable sprite, consistent colours, usable animation frames, and an editable asset is another. We kept running into the gap between an image that looks like pixel art and pixel art that works in a game. Soft edges, tiny details, and inconsistent palettes turn a promising generation into a cleanup task. We wanted the AI to stay for that cleanup. Instead of handing over another image, could it sit beside the artist, inspect the same canvas, and help change the actual pixels? That question became Zenith Studio. What it does Zenith Studio is a browser-native pixel-art workspace where people and AI agents edit the same live canvas. You can draw manually, edit palettes, organise projects, work with animation frames, and export assets. Through WebMCP, an agent can inspect the open artwork, make precise pixel edits, check tile seams or animation consistency, and help refine the result. Both collaborators use the same document and undo history. An agent’s edit appears on the canvas you are already using. If it gets something wrong, your normal undo command takes it back. The studio also supports reference-to-character generation, source-conditioned variations, masked edits, directional generation, and local skeleton-based pose blocking. The results remain editable, so generation is a starting point rather than a final handoff. WebMCP fits because the work depends on live page context: the current asset, selected frame, palette, and viewport. The agent can act on that context directly instead of managing a separate copy of the artwork. How we built it The central decision was to represent pixel art as an indexed grid. In a 16-colour document, each pixel is one character: 0 – F for its palette index, or . for transparency. The agent can read and write this compact representation, while the editor renders it onto the canvas. A shared TypeScript document model enforces palette and coordinate constraints and manages undo/redo. Human controls and agent tools operate on that same model, so there is no separate agent document to synchronise. The Next.js and React frontend contains the editor, WebMCP integration, animation timeline, and IndexedDB persistence. Heavy pixelisation runs in a Web Worker. A Hono backend handles model requests and keeps API credentials outside the browser. Deterministic drawing and pixelisation run locally. Model-backed operations, including semantic reference extraction, send the required images or instructions to the backend. Tools are scoped to the current context. A character can expose skeleton operations, while animation-diff tools become relevant when multiple frames exist. This keeps the available actions focused on what the user is actually editing. Challenges we ran into The hardest failures were often plausible-looking successes. A direction-generation prompt initially preserved the source camera angle so strongly that it defeated the request to turn the character. Asking sprites to fill the frame improved their size but could clip their edges. We had to resolve conflicting instructions, not just add more adjectives. Reference conversion exposed another problem: faithfully preserving costume detail can destroy a character’s readability at small sizes. We changed extraction to prioritise body structure and separated limbs before outfits and ornament. That change still needs a fresh visual benchmark. The editor had its own subtle risk: the asset visible in the route and the asset targeted by agent tools could disagree. Keeping them aligned was essential. Editing the wrong document without an error is worse than an obvious failure. We also had to make undo work across pixel edits and structural changes such as adding animation frames. One logical operation needed to remain one undo action, regardless of whether it came from the human or the agent. Accomplishments that we're proud of We built a working shared editing loop: inspect the canvas, make an exact change, see it immediately, and undo it through the same history used by the human. We made skeleton posing produce real editable timeline frames without a text prompt or model call. Joint dragging, frame creation, and undo were verified in the browser. For masked editing, we verified that the model-assisted result could be merged into a selected region while leaving pixels outside that region unchanged. The latest local verification passed 723 tests, along with lint, type checking, and the production build. Tests cover document invariants, undo behavior, image exports, tool contracts, and editing boundaries. Most importantly, the editor remains useful without an AI conversation. Assistance adds another way to work rather than replacing manual control. What we learned A valid grid is not automatically good art. Palette compliance can be tested exactly; whether a character looks human and retains its personality still needs visual judgment. We learned that constraints can improve collaboration. Indexed pixels make changes inspectable, frame differences compact, and mistakes recoverable. We also learned to test what the product actually produces, not just convenient fixtures. Large exports, multi-frame documents, and real generated images expose failures that small synthetic examples can miss. The strongest AI interaction was not a spectacular generation. It was a small, correct edit to the artwork already in front of us, with a clear result and an easy way back. What's next for Zenith Studio Next comes a stronger visual benchmark for reference conversion at 64×64 and 128×128, focusing on anatomy, silhouette, and character identity. We also want reusable saved rigs and cross-character animation transfer. The current local rig is a pose-blocking tool, not a substitute for polished animation or full mesh skinning. Directional generation and text-driven animation need further consistency testing, especially around character identity, limb placement, and frame-to-frame motion. Before public release, we need to publish the project repository, deploy and verify the app, and record a concise demonstration of the real WebMCP editing loop. title: Joy Of Painting
pitch: Paint along with your ai agent with bob ross joy of painting videos
about_excerpt: Paint along with your ai agent with bob ross joy of painting videos Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Joy Of Painting began with a simple, happy idea: what if painting along with Bob Ross could become a friendly paint along between a person and an AI agent? Bob taught us that painting is not about perfection. It is about slowing down, trying something new, and turning little accidents into trees, clouds, and possibilities. We wanted to bring that peaceful philosophy into an interactive studio where humans and agents can learn from the same lesson while creating entirely different paintings. What it does Joy Of Painting is a collaborative watercolor studio built around The Joy of Painting . The experience includes: Separate YouTube players for the human and AI agent A synchronized live transcript that follows the current lesson Resizable video players and painting easels A WebGL watercolor canvas with wet diffusion, pigment flow, paper texture, and drying Bob Ross–inspired brushes, including flat, fan, round, liner, blender, and painting-knife tools Physical pigment mixing based on the Kubelka–Munk model Episode-specific color palettes An eyedropper for collecting colors from the lesson WebMCP tools that let an agent control its video, read captions, inspect the lesson, and paint on its own canvas Every artist receives an easel. One belongs to the human, and one belongs to the agent. Then we let the happy little competition begin. Try the actual website Watch the demo How we built it We built the studio with React and Vite, using Video.js’s React YouTube integration for the two independent lesson players. The watercolor surface is a real HTML <canvas> powered by WebGL2. Its simulation models surface water, suspended pigment, deposited pigment, capillary movement, evaporation, paper fibers, granulation, and staining. Instead of averaging RGB values, colors are blended using Kubelka–Munk absorption and scattering calculations to behave more like physical paint. The transcript system maps timestamped captions to the active episode and updates the central caption as the lesson progresses. For agent interaction, the application registers browser-native WebMCP tools through document.modelContext . These tools allow an agent to: inspect the lesson and canvas seek, play, or pause its own YouTube player read the current transcript request a lesson reference image paint normalized watercolor strokes dry, undo, or clear its own easel Finally, we deployed the experience globally using Cloudflare Workers and static assets. Challenges we ran into Watercolor does not like to sit still—and neither did our first simulation. We had to solve canvas resizing feedback loops, animation-frame cleanup, WebGL resource management, and React lifecycle issues without losing the organic movement of wet pigment. Color preservation was another important challenge. Early versions stored old strokes in the active pigment slot, which meant loading red could turn previously painted yellow strokes red. We fixed this by baking existing pigment into the paper using its original optical properties before loading a new color. Synchronizing two separate YouTube players with episode changes and live captions also required careful handling. YouTube’s cross-origin iframe security prevents page JavaScript from capturing exact video-frame pixels, so the agent receives an honest timestamped lesson reference rather than a pretend screenshot. There were plenty of happy little bugs—but each one showed us where another tree could live. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are especially proud that the AI agent is not merely commenting on the painting. It can genuinely participate. During testing, the agent independently moved through a Bob Ross lesson, read the live transcript, and painted a complete woodland composition using only the website’s WebMCP tools. We are also proud of: A genuine WebGL watercolor simulation Non-destructive pigment changes that preserve previous colors Independent human and agent workspaces Live episode-aware captions Physical color mixing More than 400 browsable Bob Ross lessons A calm interface that keeps painting—not technology—at the center What we learned We learned that agent-friendly software works best when capabilities are explicit, focused, and honest. WebMCP allowed us to expose meaningful actions such as “paint a stroke” or “read the current caption” instead of asking the agent to guess its way through screen coordinates. We also learned that believable digital paint depends on time. Water must spread, pigment must settle, edges must darken, and colors must preserve their history. The smallest details often create the strongest feeling of physicality. Most importantly, we learned that human–AI collaboration does not always need to be about productivity. Sometimes it can simply be about making something peaceful together. What’s next for Joy Of Painting Next, we would like to add: Frame-accurate visual references through an authorized video-processing pipeline Saved galleries and downloadable side-by-side results Timed human-versus-agent painting challenges Brush-pressure and tilt support for drawing tablets Smarter agents that plan paintings from transcript cues Collaborative multiplayer studios Automatic judging based on composition, color, and creativity More paper surfaces, pigments, drying effects, salt, blooms, and glazing A replay mode showing both paintings developing stroke by stroke There are still many happy little worlds left to paint.
