title: Desksembly
pitch: An agent-ready desk, assembled in front of you.
about_excerpt: An agent-ready desk, assembled in front of you. Like Comment Story Updates Problem Buying a complete desk setup is a multi-product decision disguised as unrelated product pages. Shoppers must compare categories, resolve exact variants, track budget and availability, remember their choices, and reproduce the final decision in a cart. A generic browser agent can imitate clicks, but it has no reliable contract for non-DOM state inside a visual workspace and can overwrite a choice made while it was planning. Solution Desksembly gives the shopper and their browser agent one shared, directly manipulable miniature desk world. The experience starts with a human-locked orange lamp and a natural-language request for a cozy US work-from-home setup under $350. The browser agent reads the current scene, composes Shopify-native discovery with Desksembly's site-owned WebMCP tools, validates exact product IDs, and stages the proposal through visible parcels. The shopper can inspect, drag, move, lock, unlock, or remove products through either the 3D canvas or its equivalent accessible list. When the shopper changes the constraints to a 90 cm desk, a $300 budget, and US availability, a stale agent call is rejected. After refreshing, the agent preserves the locked keyboard and all unaffected IDs, returns only the conflicting plant, and stages one replacement. Before any cart consequence, Desksembly produces an exact, versioned review. Approval is digest-bound, expiring, and single-use. Partial cart outcomes remain partial and block checkout. Why WebMCP Desksembly demonstrates an open interaction model where the human owns taste, spatial corrections, locks, and approval; the agent owns repetitive discovery, validation, and precise execution; the website owns state correctness and consequential-action boundaries; and commerce facts never come from model output. The defining WebMCP moment is a browser agent operating a non-DOM 3D world, surviving a concurrent human edit through optimistic versioning, and composing site-owned capabilities without scraping buttons or embedding a store-specific chatbot. Human + Agent Collaboration The shopper can manually reshape the desk and lock products they want to keep. The agent works from the same versioned scene, stages visible proposals, and must refresh after a human edit instead of silently overwriting it. The final cart action happens only after an exact human review and one-time approval. Implementation Desksembly exposes five focused site-owned WebMCP tools alongside Shopify-native tools: deskbuilder.get_scene deskbuilder.preview_plan deskbuilder.stage_plan deskbuilder.move_product deskbuilder.get_review Tool inputs use strict Zod schemas, and every scene mutation carries an expected version. Next.js and Shopify Hydrogen provide SSR, typed Storefront queries, ShopifyScripts, native WebMCP, Standard Actions, and request routing. Zustand supplies fresh synchronous state reads. React Three Fiber and Three.js render the world; GSAP owns cancellable transactions; Motion renders the activity ribbon. Key Features Five focused deskbuilder.* tools alongside Shopify-native tools Retryable STALE_SCENE failures and exact scene versioning Cancellable parcel arrival, opening, reveal, and placement Accessible product list plus keyboard and manual controls Visible human-owned product locks Constraint shock that preserves exact unaffected IDs Reduced-motion replay with the same five-item result SHA-256 proposal/review digests and one-time approval Partial deterministic cart truth and disabled-checkout disclosure Manual and deterministic fallback when WebMCP is unavailable AI and Codex The deployed application hosts no model API. It relies on a compatible browser agent to interpret free-form requests and compose Shopify's native tools with Desksembly's WebMCP tools. AI output is never trusted as price, availability, cart, or checkout truth. OpenAI Codex supported WebMCP and Shopify research, product planning, architecture review, implementation, debugging, automated testing, browser verification, deployment, evidence capture, repository publication, and submission preparation. Testing Open the live app in ChatGPT's in-app browser or Chrome with WebMCP enabled. Confirm the Shopify tool family plus exactly five deskbuilder.* tools. Run the deterministic replay, lock the QuietType keyboard, apply the 90 cm / $300 / US constraint shock, and prepare the exact review. The final deterministic cart flow demonstrates accepted-only receipts, single-use approval, preservation of an unrelated line, and explicitly unavailable Shopify Checkout. Verified matrix: 30 Vitest tests, 10 integration tests, 5 Playwright journeys, and 10 prompt-family evals. A clean public clone passed npm ci , typecheck, and production build. No credentials are required. Links Live app: https://devp-one.vercel.app Public repository: https://github.com/ashish921998/desksembly-webmcp Demo video: https://youtu.be/p8wuwpKSj_g Known Limitations No participant Shopify development store was available. The desk catalog and final scene cart are clearly labeled deterministic data. mock.shop separately proves native tool coexistence and the cart gate, but not exact desk-scene carting. Shopify Checkout remains disabled. The scene uses primitive geometry, and scene state is session-only. title: AegisDesk
pitch: AegisDesk is a human-in-the-loop AML investigation workspace that helps financial institutions detect, investigate, and resolve compliance alerts faster.
about_excerpt:
AegisDesk is a human-in-the-loop AML investigation workspace that helps financial institutions detect, investigate, and resolve compliance alerts faster.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 



 
 What inspired me
I built AegisDesk after seeing how fragmented AML compliance workflows really are. Financial crime investigators often juggle multiple disconnected systems—alert queues in one tool, transaction data in another, document requests over email, and audit trails buried in logs. This fragmentation slows investigations, creates gaps in auditability, and forces analysts to piece together context manually. 

 At the same time, I became interested in WebMCP and human-in-the-loop automation. The idea of giving AI agents structured tools while keeping humans in control of sensitive decisions felt like the right fit for compliance work, where accountability and explainability matter more than raw automation speed. 

 AegisDesk is my attempt to bring those two ideas together: a single workspace for AML investigations that uses explainable, human-controlled automation instead of black-box decisioning. 

 What I learned
Building AegisDesk taught me several things: 

 Human-in-the-loop is non-negotiable in compliance. Automation can handle repetitive tasks, but high-risk decisions—like escalating a case, approving a transaction, or filing a report—must remain under explicit human control. WebMCP's confirmation gate pattern (gateDecision before mutating actions) became central to the design. 

 Auditability is a feature, not an afterthought. Every action in AegisDesk is written to an append-only activity log, with a real-time activity rail for investigators to see what's happening. This wasn't just about compliance requirements; it also made debugging and collaboration easier during development. 

 Edge-native architecture can work for serious workloads. Running the entire backend on Cloudflare Workers—with D1 for structured data, R2 for documents, and Durable Objects for real-time activity streaming—proved that you don't need a traditional cloud stack to build production-grade compliance tooling. 

 Explainability beats cleverness. Investigators need to understand why a tool returned certain results. Simple, transparent screening tools with clear inputs and outputs are more useful than complex models that can't be interrogated. 

 How I built it
AegisDesk is built as a single Cloudflare Worker serving both the API and SPA: 

 Backend: Hono app on Cloudflare Workers, with 10 WebMCP tool endpoints for case management, screening, document handling, rules, and activity. All mutating actions pass through a confirmation gate before execution. 

 Data layer: D1 (aegisdesk-db) for cases and rules, R2 (aegisdesk-docs) for document storage, and a Durable Object (ActivityRoom) for real-time activity streaming and replay. 

 Frontend: React/TypeScript SPA with components for the case queue, case detail modals, rules management, and an activity rail that shows live updates via WebSocket. 

 Audit trail: An append-only activity log (worker/src/activity-log.ts) captures every action and fans out to the Durable Object for real-time broadcasting. 

 Optional integrations: Alpaca (for trading data) and Notion (for external audit pages) are wired in but designed to cleanly skip if credentials aren't configured. 

 The development workflow used wrangler dev for local testing and iterative fixes, with each verified change reflected in the bundle hash. A live demo is deployed at https://aegisdesk-api.otemaach.workers.dev . 

 Challenges I faced
Balancing automation and control. Early versions leaned too far toward automation. I had to pull back and add explicit confirmation gates for sensitive actions, even when it made workflows slightly slower. The trade-off was worth it for compliance use cases. 

 Real-time activity without complexity. Getting WebSocket handshakes, Durable Object connections, and activity replay to work reliably on the edge took several iterations. The final design uses a simple /ws endpoint and a single ActivityRoom DO per session. 

 Fragmented data problem. AML investigations inherently involve multiple data sources. Instead of trying to unify everything, I focused on making the workspace a control plane where investigators can trigger screening, request documents, and add notes while maintaining a single audit trail. 

 Deploy vs. source drift. The deployed Worker version fell behind the local source during development (proven by bundle-hash mismatch). This highlighted the need for a more disciplined deploy process before demos or submissions. 

 Testing sensitive flows. Some flows (like approve/reject final submit) were intentionally blocked on live demo data, so I relied on integration tests and local wrangler dev to verify the correct code paths without risking real compliance actions. 

 AegisDesk is still evolving, but it's proven that you can build a secure, auditable, human-in-the-loop AML workspace on edge infrastructure—and that compliance teams benefit more from explainable tools than from opaque automation

title: Agent Zen Garden
pitch: Agent Zen Garden is a WebMCP playground where AI agents design websites through real browser tools. An agent chooses a layout, writes the CSS, and publishes a live design humans can review and refine.
about_excerpt:
Agent Zen Garden is a WebMCP playground where AI agents design websites through real browser tools. An agent chooses a layout, writes the CSS, and publishes a live design humans can review and refine.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Agent Zen Garden designs page 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Agent Zen Garden homepage 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Agent Zen Garden designs page 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Agent Zen Garden homepage 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Agent Zen Garden designs page 
 
 1 2 3 



 
 Inspiration 

 I kept coming back to the original CSS Zen Garden: one structure, many possible designs. WebMCP made me wonder what that idea would feel like if the designer were an AI agent operating inside the browser. 

 The result is Agent Zen Garden, a place where agents can make visual decisions, write the page, and leave something a human can actually browse and react to. 

 What it does 

 Agent Zen Garden gives browser agents a structured design workflow: 

 
 Browse available layouts 
 Select a layout and name the design 
 Inspect its editable slots 
 Change styles, copy, fonts, and images 
 Navigate to a live preview 
 Save and share the result 
 

 Every design gets its own persistent workspace and public share URL. Humans can browse the design catalog and compare what different agents created. 

 How we built it 

 The project is a small Node.js and Express application with SQLite for session metadata and filesystem-backed workspaces for each design’s HTML and CSS. 

 The landing page registers tools through the native WebMCP imperative API when the browser supports it. The same tools are also available through HTTP endpoints, with a compatibility manifest at /.well-known/mcp.json. 

 The tool flow is intentionally explicit: list layouts, select one, examine it, then mutate the design. Each mutation reloads the preview so the agent can see its work in the browser. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The biggest challenge was understanding the boundary between a website that exposes tools and an actual browser agent that can call them. WebMCP support is still new, and browser configuration can make a working tool appear unavailable. 

 We also had to make the experience reliable when an agent makes several changes in sequence. Persistent sessions, isolated workspaces, share URLs, and clear tool responses became important very quickly. 

 A final challenge was designing tools that leave room for creative decisions without making the agent guess at the page structure. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We built a working WebMCP design sandbox rather than a static demo or code generator. 

 An agent can start from a layout, make several visual changes, navigate to the live result, name the design, and leave it behind for someone else to view. The designs survive server restarts, and the human-readable catalog makes the output visible even without an agent connected. 

 We’re also proud that the project supports both native WebMCP and a practical HTTP fallback while the browser ecosystem is still developing. 

 What we learned 

 The most useful tools are not necessarily the most powerful ones. Small, well-described operations such as examine_layout, set_style, and set_copy gave the agent enough structure to make meaningful decisions without hiding the work inside one giant function. 

 We learned that the human-facing result matters just as much as the agent interaction. A design needs a visible preview, a name, attribution, and a way to return to it later. 

 Most importantly, WebMCP feels less like adding chat to a website and more like giving an agent a role inside an existing workflow. 

 What's next for Agent Zen Garden 

 The next step is to make the garden more collaborative: version history, side-by-side comparisons, better attribution, and clearer human feedback tools. 

 We also want to add more expressive layout primitives, improve image and font handling, and let agents refine an existing design instead of always starting from a template. 

 Longer term, Agent Zen Garden could become a shared gallery of agent-made interfaces—a place to see not just what agents can code, but what they choose to make.

title: Interleave
pitch: Catch delayed agent actions before they overwrite a person's work.
about_excerpt: Catch delayed agent actions before they overwrite a person's work. Like Comment Story Updates The Plane workbench reproduces a stale agent write and shows the exact rule, expected value, and actual value. Inspiration WebMCP lets an agent take useful actions inside a website. But the person does not stop using the app while the agent works. That creates a quiet and dangerous race: an agent reads the current state and starts a slow task. The person makes a newer change. The delayed agent action then finishes with old information and overwrites the person's work. Every request can still report success, so normal logs may never explain what went wrong. We built Interleave to catch that moment, explain it clearly, and turn it into a test that prevents the same bug from returning. What it does Interleave records one shared session across the agent, the person, and the application. It captures the pending tool call, meaningful human edits, state revisions, and the final write on one ordered timeline. When a rule is broken, Interleave shows: the exact product rule that failed; what the final value should have been; what value was actually written; which state revision the agent started from; and which newer revision existed when the delayed work finished. The developer can then replay the same recording, compare the current behavior with a proposed fix, remove every unnecessary step, and export a deterministic regression test. Our flagship demo uses public issue makeplane/plane#9674. Plane queues a metadata crawler. A person saves a newer title while that crawler is waiting. The delayed worker later writes an older title over the human edit. Interleave witnesses the overwrite, reduces it to three required actions, and replays the same recording against a revision guard that preserves the person's work. The workbench also includes reservation and TodoMVC adapters to show that the recorder is reusable across different application models. Why WebMCP is essential Interleave is built around a real WebMCP interaction, not a chatbot wrapped around a dashboard. The Plane demo exposes nine native tools while idle. The agent can read the incident, start the delayed update, replay a recording, compare implementations, reduce a failure, and export proof. While the crawler is pending, the tool surface changes to five controls that match the application's live state: read, save newer metadata, hold, complete, or cancel. The slow tool returns a real pending promise. While that promise is unresolved, the person can keep using the visible application. That shared moment is the core experience: WebMCP gives the agent a clear semantic action, while Interleave observes how that action interleaves with human work. We use document.modelContext.registerTool directly. There is no WebMCP polyfill and no reconstructed agent transcript. Tools have clear names, input descriptions, state-aware availability, AbortSignal cleanup, and compact evidence receipts. Large recordings, tests, and patches stay behind explicit downloads instead of filling the agent's context. A better experience for people and agents Without Interleave, a person can watch a correct edit disappear and have no explanation. With Interleave, the app can show exactly which delayed action caused the loss, what should have happened, and whether a guard fixes it. This also changes what developers can do. A hard-to-reproduce session becomes a small, repeatable test. A person can continue working while an agent performs a slow task, and both can verify that the latest human intent survived. How we built it The application uses Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, and native WebMCP. The reusable @interleave/recorder package has no runtime dependencies and no React dependency. Each integration supplies four things: a focused state reader, meaningful human actions, a correctness rule, and replay behavior. The recorder handles calls, results, errors, cancellation, timestamps, before-and-after state, immutable snapshots, redaction hooks, interruption, and bounded history. The Plane integration is pinned to public commit da1a7ab. We traced the issue from the API handler to the queued worker, built a deterministic local model, prepared a compare-and-set patch, and added focused worker and endpoint contract tests. The fixture never contacts a live Plane deployment or user data. Challenges we ran into Keeping the race real An animated log would look convincing but prove very little. We had to keep one actual tool promise pending while a real human edit changed the same state, then record the delayed completion at the correct checkpoint. Changing tools without cancelling the active call The available WebMCP tools need to change while work is pending. Re-registering too early can clean up and abort the call being recorded. Interleave waits for the active call to settle before replacing the tool surface. Recording meaning instead of noise Raw DOM mutation streams are large and fragile. Interleave records semantic actions such as edit_metadata and add_todo, so the person's intent survives in the evidence even when the stale write erases it from the screen. Reducing an asynchronous failure Reduction must rerun each candidate against fresh state. Interleave removes one command at a time and keeps it removed only when the same rule still fails. Accomplishments we are proud of A complete native WebMCP acceptance run in the browser: dispatch, real human click, delayed overwrite, replay, comparison, reduction, and export. A three-command minimal reproduction for a documented open-source bug. A proposed Plane patch with all 37 tests passing in the two affected upstream modules, including 13 new cases. A 50-test Interleave release gate covering the recorder, all three adapters, replay, reduction, exports, and the state-aware WebMCP surface. A dependency-free recorder package that another WebMCP application can install and adapt. What we learned WebMCP can be more than a way for agents to click fewer buttons. It gives web applications a structured boundary where agent intent, human intent, and application state can be observed together. We also learned that correctness rules must stay close to the product. Interleave provides the recording and proof system, while each application defines what must be preserved. What is next for Interleave Next we want to publish the recorder to npm, add adapters for editors and collaborative work tools, connect recordings to CI, and make browser-level regressions exportable to more test runners. We also want to take the Plane patch through upstream review and use that process to improve Interleave's contribution workflow.  Inspiration 

 I've always envied things I couldn't do well yet, like writing novels, and drawing. My hands are super stiff... 

 I've actually built relatively things before this challenge . I built a ai novel writer called "inkmarshal" simply because I want to write a novel for fun but my writing is bad, and I thought someone like me may interest in it. I built an image generate application call "lunerylab" as well for the same reason. 

 So combination of both easily come through my head. Plus my son is deep into
picture books — Dog Man gets read until the spine gives out — and I believe he will have fun by making one for himself. 

 So basically I prefer to use ai to achieve something with ai that I couldn't do well yet (still have chance and time who knows) 

 What it does 

 Apertale is a site for making cool interactive books. Its powered by WebMCP which make agent using our site creator tools. There are beautiful samples for you to read, and hopefully bring audience's interest. 

 Then you make your own. Give it a prompt, some photos, or both, and your ChatGPT
starts building pages inside the book you're looking at. Drag something it just placed. Or tell it to undo one thing, and it removes exactly that. Then one link to share it to anyone. 

 How I built it 

 I vibe coded it, serious vibe coding strategy. 

 Design first, because I'm super picky about UI/UX — probably 70–80% of my time went
there. Real comps in Figma and Codex (Production Design plugin) before any app
code existed. 

 I choose three.js for the book, because I prefer 3d and I used it a lot for making 3d game demo for fun. 

 I published it on gptsite, it is so convenient at this stage. I would love to host it on a domain if it scale. 

 Challenges I ran into 

 It has to be the images generation usage control and time consumption for this. A picture book eats art and one page at a time was too slow and too expensive. What I landed on: four pages per frame, then sliced apart. A quarter of the generations, and pages drawn together actually look like they belong together. 

 Also image bytes. WebMCP passes data, not files, so I made that handoff visible instead of pretending it happened. 

 Accomplishments that I'm proud of 

 The overall aesthetic, the whole feel of it. It is a project I would put out and show to anyone at any time. 

 Also the Agent Sketching feature too. You can mark up what you want changed and have the sketch actually change from that mark. That one came out better than I expected. 

 And most importantly, it works. Not a video, not a mockup. Open the link, read a book, make one with your agent, publish it. 

 What I learned 

 That the bottleneck was never the coding. It was knowing exactly what I wanted.
Every time I was vague with the AI I got something vague back, and every time I
could describe the thing precisely — this page turns like this, this reveals like
that — it came out right. 

 What's next for Apertale 

 Better asset handoff, cut down time usage. And I am also considering animations. Then background tasks.

title: LaunchMate
pitch: An AI-powered WebMCP business planner that turns an idea into a product, price, launch plan, and marketing kit—with humans making the final decisions.
about_excerpt:
An AI-powered WebMCP business planner that turns an idea into a product, price, launch plan, and marketing kit—with humans making the final decisions.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 




 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 




 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 6 



 
 Inspiration 

 We wanted to build a simple way for people with a digital business idea to move from an idea to an actionable launch plan without needing to figure out every step themselves. 

 The idea for LaunchMate came from the challenge of turning a simple business goal into practical decisions: What product should I create? How much should I charge? How should I launch it? And how should I market it? 

 We wanted to demonstrate how a human and an AI agent could work together, with the human making the important decisions while the AI handles structured tasks through WebMCP tools. 

 What it does 

 LaunchMate turns a business goal into a structured digital-product launch workflow: 

 Goal → Product → Price → Launch → Marketing 

 A user first enters a business goal, such as wanting to sell a digital product to students. 

 LaunchMate then provides: 

 
 Three digital product ideas 
 A selected product 
 A suggested price based on cost and margin 
 A 7-day launch plan 
 An AI-generated marketing kit 
 

 The marketing kit includes: 

 
 Target customer 
 Value proposition 
 Product description 
 Marketing headline ideas 
 Social media ideas 
 Call to action 
 

 The application also shows agent activity so users can see the actions performed during the workflow. 

 How we built it 

 LaunchMate was built as a lightweight web application using HTML, CSS and JavaScript. 

 The application uses WebMCP tools as structured actions that an AI agent can discover and invoke. 

 We created five WebMCP tools: 

 
 set_business_goal 
 suggest_product 
 calculate_price 
 build_launch_plan 
 generate_marketing_kit 
 

 The AI agent coordinates these tools in sequence. The application maintains the workflow state and renders the results back into the user interface. 

 The project was also published as a public GitHub repository and configured for GitHub Pages deployment. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 One of the biggest challenges was making the AI-generated results reliably flow between the different stages of the workflow. 

 In particular, the marketing stage required careful handling of structured WebMCP responses. The application needed to correctly map the returned data into the user interface while also providing fallback behavior when a tool response was incomplete. 

 Another challenge was coordinating the human and agent actions. The user should be able to select a product while the agent can continue the workflow using the selected product. 

 We also spent time testing the complete workflow from the initial business goal through product selection, pricing, launch planning and marketing generation. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We are proud that LaunchMate demonstrates a complete human-and-AI workflow rather than simply generating text. 

 The project connects multiple structured WebMCP tools into one workflow and makes the individual agent actions visible to the user. 

 We are also proud of building a working end-to-end prototype that can take a simple business goal and turn it into a concrete launch plan. 

 What we learned 

 We learned that building an AI agent workflow requires more than generating good text. 

 Reliable structured data, tool schemas, state management, error handling and UI rendering are all important parts of the experience. 

 We also learned how WebMCP tools can provide a structured interface between an AI agent and a web application, allowing the agent to perform specific actions instead of relying only on unstructured responses. 

 Most importantly, we learned that a good human-AI workflow should give the human control over important decisions while allowing the agent to handle repetitive and structured tasks. 

 What's next for LaunchMate 

 The current version focuses on the core web experience. 

 Next, we would like to expand LaunchMate with: 

 
 A more complete digital-product creation workflow 
 Real payment and checkout integration 
 Product landing-page generation 
 More detailed marketing campaigns 
 Analytics and sales tracking 
 Additional AI-powered business tools 
 A mobile application 
 A fully deployed production version 
 

 Our long-term goal is to turn LaunchMate into a practical AI business-launch assistant that helps people go from an initial idea to a real digital product and launch.

title: Nusantara Weather - WebMCP Agent Weather

about_excerpt:
A human + agent weather experience for Indonesia

Ask the app what you want to know in natural language, and let a WebMCP-capable agent turn that intent into live weather actions on the page.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 1 
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 Indonesia is a country of thousands of islands, diverse climates, and rapidly changing weather conditions. Yet checking the weather often still means opening multiple apps, searching for a city, interpreting forecast charts, and deciding what the information actually means for a trip or daily activity. 

 We wanted to explore a different experience: what if people could simply tell a weather agent what they need, and the agent could understand their intent, find the relevant weather information, and take action for them? 

 That idea became Nusantara Weather - WebMCP Agent Weather . 

 The project was inspired by the emerging WebMCP vision of a web where humans and AI agents can interact through real, useful tools. Instead of building another static weather dashboard, we wanted to create a weather interface that acts as a bridge between human intent and structured weather actions . 

 A user should not need to know which forecast API to call or which data points matter. They should be able to say: 

 
 “Find the safest dry window to travel in Bandung this afternoon.” 
 

 And the application should understand the request, gather the relevant weather data, analyze it, and present a useful answer. 

 What it does 

 Nusantara Weather combines a beautiful weather dashboard with an agent-ready WebMCP interface . 

 Users can explore weather across Indonesia by selecting a city or searching for a city through the Find a city interface. The main dashboard highlights five major cities for a clean and focused experience, while typing into the search bar reveals additional Indonesian cities as suggestions. 

 The application can also understand natural-language weather requests through WebMCP tools. 

 For example: 

 
 “Find the next dry window in Jakarta.” 

 “Compare Bandung and Surabaya for rain today.” 

 “What is the safest time to travel in Bali this afternoon?” 
 

 The agent can use registered WebMCP tools to retrieve weather information, compare locations, identify upcoming rain windows, and follow the user's intent. 

 The project includes tools such as: 

 
 get_indonesia_weather — retrieves current and forecast weather for a selected Indonesian city. 
 compare_indonesia_weather — compares weather conditions between cities. 
 find_next_rain_window — identifies upcoming periods with higher or lower rain probability. 
 follow_weather_prompt — interprets a natural-language request and drives the application according to the user's intent. 
 

 The key idea is that the user describes the goal, while the agent handles the interaction with the web application . 

 How we built it 

 We built Nusantara Weather as a lightweight web application with a strong focus on progressive enhancement and agent interoperability. 

 The frontend provides: 

 
 A modern weather dashboard 
 Indonesia-focused city search 
 Top-city recommendations 
 Forecast and rain information 
 Natural-language prompt interaction 
 Agent activity and decision feedback 
 Responsive UI for different screen sizes 
 

 For weather data, the application uses live forecast information from Open-Meteo. 

 For the agent layer, we implemented the WebMCP Imperative API using the required tool registration pattern: 
 await document . modelContext . registerTool ( { 
 name : "get_indonesia_weather" , 
 description : "Get weather conditions and forecast for an Indonesian city." , 
 inputSchema : { 
 type : "object" , 
 properties : { 
 city : { 
 type : "string" , 
 description : "Indonesian city name" 
 } 
 } , 
 required : [ "city" ] 
 } , 
 execute : async ( input ) = > { 
 // Fetch weather data
 // Update application state
 // Return structured weather information
 } 
 } ) ; 
 
 This means the application is not only designed for humans clicking buttons. It exposes structured capabilities that an AI agent can discover and execute. 

 The architecture follows a simple flow: 

 Human prompt → Agent intent → WebMCP tool → Weather data → Decision → UI update 

 We also designed the application with progressive enhancement in mind. The weather website remains usable as a normal website, while WebMCP-enabled environments can interact with the same application through agent-accessible tools. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 One of the biggest challenges was designing an interface that works well for both humans and agents. 

 Traditional web interfaces are usually built around clicks, buttons, forms, and navigation. Agents need something more structured: clearly defined tools, predictable inputs, meaningful descriptions, and structured outputs. 

 Another challenge was handling natural-language intent. 

 A request such as: 

 
 “When should I leave for Bandung if I want to avoid rain?” 
 

 doesn't directly map to a single API call. The system has to translate the user's goal into a sequence of actions: 

 
 Identify the destination. 
 Understand the requested time period. 
 Retrieve forecast data. 
 Evaluate rain conditions. 
 Determine the most suitable window. 
 Present the result in a human-friendly way. 
 

 We also wanted the interface to stay visually simple even though the application supports a large number of Indonesian cities. Instead of showing every city immediately, the frontend focuses on five major cities and reveals additional cities dynamically through search suggestions. 

 Finally, WebMCP is an evolving part of the web platform, so we had to think carefully about compatibility and progressive enhancement rather than assuming every browser has the same capabilities. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We are proud that Nusantara Weather is more than a weather visualization. 

 It demonstrates how a web application can become agent-interactable without sacrificing the human experience . 

 Some highlights we are especially proud of: 

 
 We implemented real WebMCP tool registration with document.modelContext.registerTool() . 
 We created multiple purpose-built weather tools instead of exposing one generic API endpoint. 
 We added a natural-language follow_weather_prompt workflow that connects user intent to application behavior. 
 We created an Indonesia-focused city dataset with coverage across major regions and islands. 
 We designed the city search so the interface stays clean while still supporting many locations. 
 We built the product around decisions and actions rather than simply showing raw forecast numbers. 
 We created a polished visual identity for the project, including a custom Indonesia weather favicon. 
 

 Most importantly, we believe the project demonstrates a compelling direction for the open web: 

 websites that are understandable not only to humans, but also to intelligent agents. 

 What we learned 

 We learned that building an agent-friendly web application requires a different way of thinking about product design. 

 It is not enough to expose data. The application needs to expose capabilities . 

 A useful agent tool should answer questions like: 

 
 What does this tool do? 
 What input does it expect? 
 What result will it return? 
 Can the action change application state? 
 Is the result meaningful enough for an agent to reason about? 
 

 We also learned that natural-language interfaces work best when the underlying system is structured and predictable. 

 The prompt may be unstructured, but the execution should not be. 

 That led us to a design principle we will continue using: 

 Unstructured human intent in, structured actions out. 

 Finally, we learned that great agent experiences should not replace good human interfaces. The strongest experience is one where humans can interact directly while agents can use the exact same web capabilities programmatically. 

 What's next for Nusantara Weather - WebMCP Agent Weather 

 Nusantara Weather is only the beginning. 

 Our next step is to make the agent significantly more capable of understanding real-world context. 

 We want users to eventually be able to ask things like: 

 
 “I have a flight from Jakarta to Bali tomorrow. When is the safest time to leave for the airport?” 
 

 or: 

 
 “I'm planning an outdoor event in Bandung this weekend. Find the best day and explain why.” 
 

 From there, Nusantara Weather could combine weather with additional web capabilities such as: 

 
 Traffic and travel conditions 
 Flight and transportation information 
 Local ev

title: WebMCP Computer
pitch: An operating system that lives inside the browser, with WebMCP as its native control layer. A full computer built for agents as first-class citizens.
about_excerpt: An operating system that lives inside the browser, with WebMCP as its native control layer. A full computer built for agents as first-class citizens. Like 3 Comment Story Updates One machine, two users: WebMCP Computer Press any key—or call any tool—to wake the machine A real remote Browser, live Tool Monitor, Terminal, and agent-made app—one desktop A computer built for agents as first-class citizens. Instead of imitating humans with screenshots, mouse coordinates, and typing, agents control the machine directly through WebMCP - while the human watches and intervenes through the same desktop. Inspiration We wanted to see what a computer would look like if agents didn’t have to use it like humans. Instead of looking at screenshots, moving a mouse, and typing into interfaces, the agent gets direct access to the computer through WebMCP. Files, apps, windows, processes, settings, and the terminal are all tools it can call. The whole thing runs inside one browser tab. You see the same desktop as the agent, watch what it’s doing, and can take over at any point. Run agent-generated code without giving the agent access to your computer. Watch what it does and jump in whenever you want. The demo in 30 seconds Ask the agent to create a small website. Watch Files, Terminal, and Preview update in real time. The new page registers its own site_* tools. The agent calls those tools through the computer that created the page. That is WebMCP inside WebMCP : tools appear when an app opens or a page is served, then disappear cleanly when it closes. Why WebMCP WebMCP gives a page a structured way to describe what an agent can do: named tools, JSON schemas, descriptions, and safety annotations. WebMCP Computer treats that surface like a syscall table. Instead of exposing one form, it exposes the operating system— app_open , fs_write , term_exec , window_move , settings_set , ps , kill , and dozens more. For normal computer operations, the agent needs no screenshot and no coordinate. Every action is typed, bounded, and visible. What humans and agents can do together Build in a fresh machine. Edit files, run shell commands, serve a folder, and preview the result without touching the host computer. Share one live workspace. Human and agent use the same files, windows, processes, and terminal. See every action. An agent cursor moves to the affected window, activity toasts name the verb, terminal rows are tinted, and Tool Monitor records the call. Operate the real web. The Browser app drives a shared remote Chrome and can discover and call another site's WebMCP tools. Opt into real Linux. The cloud kernel adds a temporary container with Git, Node.js, and Python, streaming command output into the visible Terminal. Publish from the machine. An agent can publish a text-only site and hand the human a public URL and QR code. How we built it WebMCP layer: @nekuda/webmcp-sdk , with strict schemas and ask/act/transact annotations. Kernel: a pure-TypeScript Zustand store for processes, windows, settings, and the shared event stream. Local shell: just-bash with core utilities, awk , and jq ; network and language runtimes stay in the opt-in cloud container. Filesystem: ZenFS on OPFS with reload-safe session restore. Preview: a virtual in-tab server that runs pages in opaque sandboxed frames and bridges their dynamic tools to the host registry. Browser and cloud: capability-scoped Cloudflare Workers for remote Chrome, temporary Linux workspaces, and publishing. The UI is React 18, Vite, strict TypeScript, and hand-written CSS—no UI kit. The current build is covered by 339 unit tests and 27 native-Chrome end-to-end tests . Tool vocabulary Domain Tools Apps and windows app_open app_close app_list window_focus window_move window_resize Filesystem fs_read fs_write fs_edit fs_list fs_search fs_mkdir fs_delete fs_move Terminal and processes term_exec term_read term_state term_history ps kill System sys_status os_manual os_search settings_get settings_set screensaver_wake Browser (remote Chrome) browser_open browser_goto browser_click browser_type browser_read browser_screenshot browser_site_tools browser_site_call Cloud (opt-in) cloud_exec os_publish Agent-made apps ui_open Per-app, while the window is open editor_open_file files_reveal notes_append notes_preview notes_stick preview_get_console preview_get_url preview_reload Dynamic, from served pages site_* (registered by the page itself; capped at 16 per Preview) Challenges and lessons The hardest problem was tool lifecycle. Tools must register only while their window exists; a generated page must be isolated yet still able to publish safe tools; and local, browser, and cloud state must remain understandable to both users. We learned that WebMCP works best when it is more than an automation layer: it can be the computer's native interface. Try it Launch WebMCP Computer in ChatGPT's in-app browser or Chrome with WebMCP enabled. Wake the desktop, then ask: Create a small website, serve it, and interact with its WebMCP tools. View the source . about_excerpt:
ProtocolOS turns complex research protocols into agent-ready workflows, helping researchers and AI coordinate participants, assessments, visits, and study tasks efficiently.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 Research protocols define exactly what must happen, yet daily operations are often split across documents, spreadsheets, calendars, and task systems. Coordinators spend valuable time reconciling those sources to answer a deceptively simple question: what does this subject need next? ProtocolOS began with the idea that a protocol should be an operational workflow that people and browser agents can understand together—not just a static document. 

 What it does 

 ProtocolOS turns research protocols into shared, agent-ready workflows. It organizes multiple synthetic studies, subjects, stages, visits, assessments, samples, tasks, and completion criteria in one polished workspace. 

 Coordinators can: 

 
 See today's priorities across multiple studies 
 Understand a subject's current stage, visit, and outstanding work 
 Build and publish a visual protocol workflow 
 Generate a visit checklist from the published workflow 
 Complete tasks while keeping related records synchronized 
 Check whether a subject is ready to advance, with explicit reasons when advancement is blocked 
 

 All demo records are fictional and use generic IDs such as SUB001. ProtocolOS contains no real protected health information. 

 How WebMCP creates real utility 

 Without WebMCP, an agent would have to infer operational state from pixels and page text. That is fragile when a missed assessment, sample, or sign-off can change whether a visit is complete. 

 ProtocolOS registers fourteen imperative tools through document.modelContext.registerTool(). They cover portfolio summaries, priorities, workflow inspection and publishing, subject status, assessments, visits, samples, missing tasks, readiness, checklist creation, task completion, and guarded stage advancement. 

 Read operations are marked read-only. Mutations are explicit and update the same React state shown to the coordinator. Every response includes structured results, synthetic-data indicators, workflow provenance, and a compact technical receipt. 

 Human and agent collaboration 

 A coordinator can ask, “What does SUB001 need today?” The agent retrieves the current stage and visit, incomplete tasks, assessments, sample requirements, and next action. It can create the checklist and complete an approved item. The visible workspace updates immediately, and the activity trail records who changed what and when. 

 Crucially, the model does not decide whether a subject advances. ProtocolOS evaluates the published completion gates and returns a clear allowed-or-blocked decision with the exact remaining requirements. The workflow remains the source of truth while the agent accelerates coordination. 

 How we built it 

 ProtocolOS is a responsive React and TypeScript application styled with Tailwind CSS and hosted with OpenAI Sites. Synthetic seed data powers a multi-study dashboard, subject records, a visual workflow builder, visit checklists, activity history, and an agent workspace. WebMCP actions are registered directly in the live page so a compatible browser agent can use the product's own operational contract. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The hardest part was making agent actions and visible UI state feel like one system instead of a chat demo layered on top of a dashboard. We also had to model advancement safely: status checks must be useful and read-only, while actual transitions remain explicit, auditable, and governed by published rules. 

 Designing a workflow builder that stays flexible across study types was another challenge. We avoided study-specific terminology and made stages, visits, requirements, and gates configurable. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We built a polished multi-study workspace where fourteen WebMCP actions operate on the same state people see. The challenge demo shows retrieval, checklist creation, synchronized completion, audit history, and a guarded workflow decision in under three minutes. 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP is most compelling when tools represent meaningful domain actions rather than page-navigation shortcuts. Clear schemas, workflow provenance, read/write separation, and visible state synchronization make an agent experience more trustworthy and useful. 

 Judge demo 

 
 Ask: What does SUB001 need today? 
 Ask: Create SUB001's visit checklist. 
 Ask: Mark task T-001-3 complete for SUB001. 
 Ask: Can SUB001 advance to the next stage? 
 

 The final check is intentionally blocked and explains the remaining tasks, assessment, and samples. If the demo has already been used, choose Reset challenge demo in the Agent workspace. 

 What's next for ProtocolOS 

 Next, ProtocolOS can add protocol import, reusable workflow templates, role-based approvals, integrations with validated research systems, and configurable audit exports—while preserving the same human-visible, workflow-governed approach.

title: Aimily Context Review
pitch: From agent signal to governed collection truth: Context Graph diffs, exact-hash human approval, signed receipts and undo for fashion teams.
about_excerpt: From agent signal to governed collection truth: Context Graph diffs, exact-hash human approval, signed receipts and undo for fashion teams. Like Comment Story Updates Mobile signal: fitting-image evidence becomes the same governed revision workflow. Approved brief: human approval unlocks a buyer-ready, hash-bound artifact. Applied preview: a verified receipt preserves production_data_changed: false and exposes undo. Context ready: WebMCP reads signed collection state before any revision exists. Review required: exact diff, confidence and artifact hash await human approval. Native discovery: Chrome 151 sees the live document.modelContext tool inventory. Native recovery: the complete apply and undo receipt chain remains verifiable. A meeting should not silently mutate a collection Fashion decisions arrive as messy human context: a buyer meeting, a fitting image, a voice note, or a direct instruction. Personal agents are good at carrying that context, but giving an agent direct mutation authority over collection truth creates a trust problem. Aimily Context Review turns the signal into a governed revision instead. A personal agent enters the live workspace through WebMCP. Aimily resolves an exact before-and-after diff, maps downstream consequences through a Context Graph, separates explicit evidence from deterministic consequences and labelled inference, and preserves bounded alternatives. Nothing changes until a human approves the exact SHA-256 artifact hash. After approval, a buyer-ready brief becomes available. The agent can apply only that approved artifact to an isolated preview. Every transition creates a chained receipt that the server verifies across seven invariants: hash, link, artifact, sequence, policy, chronology and identity. Undo restores the preview without erasing the decision record. The agent brings the signal. Aimily owns truth, policy and recovery. WebMCP is the doorway. What people and agents can now do together The agent reads the current collection context. It drafts connected intent-level changes across creative direction, materials, pricing and calendar. Aimily resolves values, rationale, evidence and confidence. The Context Graph exposes affected areas, uncertainty and unselected alternatives. A human approves the exact artifact hash in the interface. Approval is never agent-callable. The approved brief and apply intent appear only after approval. Apply changes only the signed Challenge preview, never production collection data. The receipt chain proves what happened and undo remains available. The WebMCP tool inventory changes with the governed lifecycle. Context starts with three tools. Impact inspection appears only after a draft. The approved brief and apply appear only after exact-hash approval. Apply disappears after use and undo appears. The authority boundary is visible in the interface and generated from the same tool objects registered with the browser. Why WebMCP is essential This is not a chatbot beside the product. WebMCP gives the personal agent narrow, page-scoped access to the same signed collection state the human is reviewing. The page uses document.modelContext.registerTool() to expose typed intent tools. Read operations use readOnlyHint: true ; draft, apply and undo use false . Every source-bearing tool uses untrustedContentHint: true . Inputs use strict JSON Schema, results are structured, cancellation propagates with AbortSignal , and every result states the next valid action and whether production data changed. The tools never read the DOM and never interpret screenshots. They call a same-origin server boundary backed by the shared deterministic collection-revision domain. How we built it Next.js 16, React 19 and TypeScript. Seven page-scoped WebMCP intent tools with dynamic registration and abortable lifetimes. HMAC-signed HttpOnly session and signed state pointer. Same-origin enforcement, per-IP rate limiting and strict Zod validation. Exact-hash approval, stale-state, replay and cross-session protections. SHA-256 chained receipts verified before each new state token is signed. A shared pure domain for revision, Context Graph impact and approved brief generation across UI, WebMCP and tests. A separate Vercel project with a deployment-only signing secret and no canonical Aimily credential. A public sample collection and isolated preview. No Supabase or production data path exists in the Challenge package. Challenges we ran into The hardest problem was not registering tools. It was making authority legible and enforceable across a lifecycle. A stale agent handle must not retain authority after the state changes. A human approval must bind to an exact artifact rather than a conversational summary. A valid token from one session must fail in another. Rejected attacks must not corrupt the valid state. Receipt history must remain trustworthy through apply and undo. The visible authority list must never drift from the native browser inventory. We addressed those risks with dynamic registration, server-side policy, exact-hash approval, session-bound signed state, seven receipt invariants and an acceptance runner that compares the visible governance rail with the browser's native tools at every stage. Evidence, not claims 37 focused Challenge tests pass. A 16-control production red-team passes origin, schema, session, tampering, prompt-like evidence, approval order, artifact hash, replay, cross-session isolation and the complete approval, apply and undo receipt chain. Chrome 151 natively discovers and invokes the full lifecycle on public HTTPS. ChatGPT's in-app browser independently proved native context read, governed draft, dynamic registration, stale-handle rejection, readback and impact inspection. Desktop and mobile runs preserve three chained receipts, seven valid integrity checks and production_data_changed: false . The public repository passes a clean install, dependency audit, focused tests and production build in protected GitHub Actions. Existing product and Challenge-period work Aimily existed before the Challenge. Its private product architecture and full collection-creation system are not being entered as newly built work. The Challenge-specific extension was built after submissions opened on 25 August 2026, with dated work beginning on 27 August. It includes the isolated signed sandbox, document.modelContext adapter, page-scoped intent tools, dynamic authority, exact-hash human approval policy, Context Graph review, receipt-chain verification, native Chrome and ChatGPT evidence, adversarial evals, public evaluation repository and the 75-second film. The public AGPL-3.0 repository contains only the narrow standalone evaluation package and the shared deterministic revision subset it needs. It contains no canonical Aimily history, commercial pricing, billing, public landing, mobile application, production credential, production data, or canonical remote MCP implementation. What we learned The most useful agent is not always the one with the most power. Trust grows when the product can show exactly what the agent knows, what it inferred, what changed, who approved it, and how to recover. WebMCP is strongest when it does not bypass product governance. It lets the agent enter the product's real decision boundary while the application remains the system of record. What's next The Challenge package is intentionally a public beta sandbox. The next product step is to bring the same governed signal-to-revision pattern into authorized signed-in collection workspaces, while keeping WebMCP as a doorway into Aimily rather than turning it into the product core. title: Smart Link
pitch: The link management platform where AI agents handle geo-targeting, \nA/B testing, and bot protection — so marketers just describe what \nthey want and get a production-ready tracking link in seconds.
about_excerpt:
The link management platform where AI agents handle geo-targeting, 
A/B testing, and bot protection — so marketers just describe what 
they want and get a production-ready tracking link in seconds.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Link Analytics: Granular details showing device types, referrers, and geolocations for short links. 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Bio Page Builder: Interface allowing users to design and customize landing pages with custom links and themes. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 User Dashboard: Main interface displaying real-time link clicks, total redirects, and traffic analytics.

 Link Creator: Simple and fast interface to generate new short links with custom routing parameters.

 1 2 3 4 5 



 
 Inspiration 

 Content creators, influencers, and small business owners spend hundreds of dollars 
monthly on tools like ClickMagick, Voluum, and Linktree — just to manage links and 
track who clicks them. We wanted to build one platform that replaces all of them, 
and takes it a step further by letting AI agents do the complex marketing setup work 
on behalf of the user. 

 What it does 

 Smart Link is a link management and bio page platform with full WebMCP agent support. 

 Users can create short links, build bio landing pages, track real-time analytics 
by country and device, run A/B tests to find the best-performing URL, and protect 
their links from bot traffic automatically. 

 What makes Smart Link unique is its agent-native design. When opened in ChatGPT's 
in-app browser, the platform exposes three WebMCP tools that AI agents can use: 

 
 create_marketing_link: Creates a fully-configured tracking link in one step — 
with geo-targeting rules (route Saudi users to an Arabic page, French users to 
a French page), device routing (mobile vs desktop), UTM tracking parameters, 
A/B testing between multiple URLs, and bot protection. A task that would normally 
take a marketer 15 minutes across multiple tools now takes one sentence. 
 get_link_analytics: Retrieves total clicks, human vs bot breakdown, top countries, 
device types, and A/B test results for any link by short code. 
 shorten_url: Instantly shortens any URL without requiring an account. 
 

 How we built it 

 The platform is built with a full-stack architecture using React, Tailwind CSS, 
and Vite on the frontend, deployed on Vercel. The backend runs on Node.js with 
Express.js, MongoDB Atlas for persistence, and Redis for caching and rate limiting, 
deployed on Fly.io. We use Brevo for email campaigns and Lemon Squeezy for 
subscription billing. 

 For WebMCP, we registered the three agent tools directly in the HTML using 
document.modelContext.registerTool(). We built a dedicated public API endpoint 
that AI agents call to create links with full marketing configuration. When a 
logged-in user opens the site in ChatGPT's browser, their session token is read 
automatically so created links appear in their personal dashboard. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The biggest technical challenge was achieving sub-150ms redirect speeds while 
simultaneously recording click analytics and running bot detection in real time. 
We solved this by caching redirect targets in Redis and processing analytics 
asynchronously in the background. 

 For WebMCP, the challenge was designing a public API that exposes advanced features 
like geo-targeting and A/B testing to AI agents, while preventing abuse through 
strict rate limiting and Google Safe Browsing URL safety checks on every request. 

 Accomplishments that we are proud of 

 Smart Link is a live production application with 41 registered users and over 
1,800 tracked clicks — built and running before this hackathon. We are proud of 
the sub-150ms redirect performance and being one of the first link management 
platforms to expose agent-native WebMCP tools, allowing marketers to set up 
complex geo-targeted, bot-protected campaigns through a single natural language 
conversation. 

 What we learned 

 We learned how to design APIs that serve both humans and AI agents — with clear 
parameter descriptions, meaningful error messages, and structured responses that 
agents can reason about. We also deepened our understanding of Redis caching 
strategies for high-traffic systems. 

 What's next for Smart Link 

 We plan to add create_bio_page and run_ab_test as new WebMCP tools, letting agents 
build full landing pages and launch experiments without touching the UI. We also 
plan to add AI-powered UTM suggestions and integrate Facebook Pixel and Google Tag 
Manager firing directly through the agent tools.

title: Dream Realm WebMCP
pitch: An AI-native playable creator world where humans and AI agents participate together in gameplay and creation.
about_excerpt: An AI-native playable creator world where humans and AI agents participate together in gameplay and creation. Like Comment Story Updates One-line positioning Dream Realm is an AI-native playable creator world where humans and AI agents can participate together in gameplay and creation. Inspiration and product idea Most agent integrations sit beside an experience: they explain a game, fill a form, or automate a separate dashboard. Dream Realm explores a more interesting possibility. A human and an AI agent share one living creator world, see the same mission state, and contribute to the same result. The broader Dream Realm concept includes Dance, Music, and Fashion creator rooms. This challenge submission deliberately focuses on one reliable end-to-end Dance loop so judges can experience the complete human-agent relationship rather than a wide but fragile demo. Dream Realm itself is pre-existing work. Its IP, Naya, HUB, creator-world concept, playable browser foundation, original missions, performance renderer, human video export, Tower response, and return flow were not created during this challenge. The challenge work is the meaningful WebMCP extension that lets an agent participate in that existing live world through structured, validated actions. Why Dream Realm is a strong WebMCP use case Dream Realm combines real-time game state, sequential mission rules, creative choices, visible consequences, and a human-controlled media export. Those are difficult for a general agent to operate reliably by guessing at buttons or interpreting screenshots. WebMCP gives the live site a small, explicit vocabulary for collaboration: read the current state, start a route, restore a Dance signal, resolve Murk's doubt, compose Naya's performance, prepare the output, update Trending Tower, and return to the HUB. The tools do not create a parallel simulation. They operate the same state and controller used by the visible mouse/touch interface, so every agent action is immediately visible to the person and every human action changes what the agent reads next. How WebMCP improves the player experience The player keeps agency over the parts that should feel personal and consent-driven. They activate the portal, can play every interaction normally, and retain visible control of recording and downloading the final WebM video. An agent can help interpret the current mission, submit structured signal choices, preserve a chosen creative combination, and move the shared experience forward without brittle UI automation. This creates a cooperative rhythm: A person enters Dream Realm and chooses a Gateway Mission or Direct Creator route. The agent reads the live state and valid next actions. Human and agent repair Noiz corruption and resolve Murk's doubt in the same mission. They choose Naya's outfit, scene, movement, and effect together. The agent prepares the exact performance while the person explicitly records/downloads the video. The shared output updates Trending Tower and changes the HUB. What people and agents can now do together Before WebMCP, an agent would have to infer screen state, locate transient controls, and imitate clicks. That is slow, fragile, and disconnected from the game's meaning. With WebMCP, the agent understands named game actions and validated transitions while the player watches the same world react. The result is not “AI plays the game for you.” It is a mixed-initiative creator loop: the agent can assist with stateful gameplay and composition, while the human keeps control of entry, interpretation, media recording, download, and final creative judgment. How WebMCP was implemented The pre-existing browser slice was meaningfully extended during the challenge with a thin shared controller, window.DreamRealmChallenge , over the existing application state and functions. Eight tools are registered with document.modelContext.registerTool() : get_dream_realm_state start_dream_realm_route submit_dance_signal resolve_murk_doubt set_creator_choices prepare_performance send_output_to_tower return_to_hub Each tool has a narrow JSON schema and validates both input and current game state. The read tool never mutates. Mutating tools reject invalid transitions with explicit error codes. The adapter uses feature detection, so browsers without WebMCP continue to run the ordinary mouse, touch, and keyboard experience. No tool fakes DOM clicks, and no second game state is maintained. The final Naya performance is rendered from the selected outfit, background, movement, mission result, and outcome effect. Recording and download remain a visible human action using MediaRecorder . Sending the finished output to Trending Tower is blocked until that human-controlled recording exists. Pre-existing versus challenge-added PRE-EXISTING: Dream Realm IP and visual identity; Naya and the other original characters; the Option C HUB; the playable creator/game concept; private-access entrance; Gateway and Direct Creator routes; Dance gameplay; Murk/Noiz logic; creator selections; Naya performance rendering; human MediaRecorder export; Tower response; unlock; HUB return; and the original mouse/touch/keyboard browser foundation. BUILT / MEANINGFULLY EXTENDED DURING THE WEBMCP CHALLENGE: the shared DreamRealmChallenge controller over the existing state; eight document.modelContext.registerTool() registrations; JSON schemas; structured agent actions; read-only and mutating-tool boundaries; input and transition validation; explicit error codes; agent participation across Gateway, Creator, Naya performance preparation, Tower, and HUB; preservation of the human recording/download boundary; the minimal public challenge build and deployment; public WebMCP testing; debugging and challenge-specific stability fixes; and provenance/licensing/test documentation. Where existing Dream Realm code was changed, those changes were made only to expose and stabilize the shared controller and WebMCP flow; they do not represent the underlying Dream Realm product as newly created. BASELINE.md records pre-August-25 source timestamps and checksums, while the dated Git history begins with the untouched baseline and then separates controller, tools, tests, fixes, and release documentation. Broader Dream Realm context The submitted experience is intentionally one complete browser vertical slice: Gateway Mission → creator choices → Naya performance → Tower response → HUB. It demonstrates a shared human-agent world architecture, not the full scope of Dream Realm. PRE-EXISTING DREAM REALM: Dance, Music, and Fashion are the first creator-world spaces explored in Dream Realm. This challenge demo uses Dance as the complete WebMCP vertical slice. The broader world is designed to expand into additional interactive spaces such as puzzles, shops and commerce, sports, story missions, and social experiences. Dream Realm also has a separate Unreal Engine 5 immersive proof exploring the world beyond the browser. CHALLENGE-ADDED WEBMCP WORK: This submission proves the human-agent interaction model inside the browser. WebMCP operates the same live state and visible experience used by the player. WebMCP is not currently implemented natively inside the Unreal proof. FUTURE PRODUCT VISION: Future Unreal and 3D experiences may extend this interaction philosophy to richer character, NPC, and world interactions. This is future direction, not functionality claimed or demonstrated in the current submission. Built with HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Canvas, MediaRecorder, Web Audio, and WebMCP Site tools. title: AINumbers
pitch: Browser-native, verifiable fintech tools and OpenChainGraph workflows that AI agents can call through MCP. Private and serverless by default.
about_excerpt:
Browser-native, verifiable fintech tools and OpenChainGraph workflows that AI agents can call through MCP. Private and serverless by default.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 



 
 Inspiration 

 AI agents are increasingly asked to help with consequential financial and compliance work, but a fluent answer is not enough. A user, reviewer, or auditor needs to be able to inspect the inputs, reproduce the calculation, and verify the result independently. 

 AINumbers brings that standard to browser-native fintech tooling. It makes deterministic tools usable by people in a web page and by agents through the same underlying computation. 

 What it does 

 AINumbers is an open-source suite of browser-native fintech tools and OpenChainGraph workflows. The tools cover payments, AML/KYC, risk, regulatory compliance, tokenization, and more. 

 Each OpenChainGraph workflow produces a reproducible SHA-256 execution hash over canonical inputs and outputs. That gives an agent's result a verifiable receipt rather than asking users to trust a black box. 

 For this WebMCP submission, AINumbers exposes browser tools to agents through WebMCP while preserving the ordinary human-facing form. The same computation powers both paths, so a person and an agent receive the same structured result and the same receipt. 

 How we built it 

 The site is built as self-contained HTML and JavaScript tools with no account requirement and no data transmission after page load. Calculations run locally in the browser using deterministic logic and WebCrypto hashing. 

 We added WebMCP registration using the current document.modelContext API, with a fallback to the earlier navigator.modelContext surface. Browsers without WebMCP retain the same normal web experience. 

 The project also offers an MCP server for agent integrations and publishes its source code, manifests, schemas, and OpenChainGraph specification publicly. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 WebMCP is a draft browser API, and its surface moved during implementation. A registration pattern that had previously worked through navigator.modelContext no longer registered tools in current Chrome. 

 We diagnosed the issue with a small probe tool, updated registration to prefer document.modelContext , preserved a compatibility fallback, and documented the complete debugging session so others can reproduce it. 

 What we learned 

 Agent tooling is more trustworthy when it is not a separate, opaque path. A shared human-and-agent computation path, structured output, and independently verifiable receipt make it easier to test, inspect, and rely on agent-assisted work. 

 What's next 

 We will continue expanding WebMCP coverage across AINumbers tools, keep compatibility checks current as the draft API evolves, and make verifiable browser-native tools easier for agents and humans to use together.
