title: ClaimGate
pitch: Agent-assisted lost-property search with private proof and human release decisions.
about_excerpt: Agent-assisted lost-property search with private proof and human release decisions. Like Comment Story Updates WebMCP exposes privacy-safe candidate matching while private proof stays manual. Staff reviews aggregate eligibility and a redacted timeline, never evidence values. Atomic handoff completes the claim, returns the item, and resolves the report. ClaimGate — privacy-first lost-property claims with human release decisions. Problem Lost-property desks need enough public detail to find a likely item without publishing the details that prove ownership. Giving every field to an Agent would turn private proof into searchable material. ClaimGate separates public matching from private proof. The Agent handles structured preparation and safe reads. People publish, submit evidence, decide the claim, issue the pickup credential, and complete the release. Why WebMCP This workflow changes as the claim moves from draft to match, review, pickup, and collection. WebMCP lets the page expose the few actions that are valid now, with typed inputs and bounded results. The Agent does not have to infer controls from page layout, and sensitive actions can stay absent from the tool set. Better experience A Claimant can describe a loss once, let the Agent structure the public fields, and receive explainable candidates without copying data between screens. Staff gets a short queue and a redacted summary. Each person sees the next action in the same claim instead of reconstructing context after every role change. Before and after Before ClaimGate, the demo journey is a sequence of manual forms and page searches, with a risk of mixing public clues and ownership proof. With ClaimGate, the Agent prepares, searches, and summarizes through explicit tools while the UI reserves publication, proof, judgment, credential transfer, and handoff for visible human controls. What it does A Claimant starts a fresh two-hour instance with fictional Northbridge Campus inventory. The Agent can create or update a lost-report draft, list reports, find up to three candidates, and stage one candidate. Results contain broad fields, confidence bands, and public reasons, not internal inventory IDs. The Claimant publishes and submits masked evidence manually. Two correct slots are sufficient even if a third submitted slot is wrong. The browser receives only aggregate eligibility, insufficiency, or the third-attempt LOCKED state. Staff reads a bounded queue and redacted review summary, then decides manually. After approval, the Agent can read pickup instructions. The Claimant manually generates and copies a ten-minute, one-time credential, then Staff pastes it into the handoff form. One transaction marks the claim collected, item returned, and report resolved. The normal web flow also works without WebMCP. How implemented ClaimGate is one Next.js 16 application with separate report, matching, evidence, claim, authorization, audit, and WebMCP modules. SQLite scopes every record to a demo instance. Signed HttpOnly sessions and server routes enforce role, ownership, state, version, CSRF, origin, idempotency, and rate limits. The browser uses native document.modelContext.registerTool() . A page and state registry selects nine tools, and an AbortController removes the previous generation on navigation or state change. Tool visibility assists selection; the server remains authoritative. The tools are create_lost_report_draft , update_lost_report_draft , list_my_reports , find_candidate_matches , stage_claim_candidate , get_claim_status , get_pickup_instructions , list_pending_claims , and get_claim_review_summary . Publishing, evidence, decisions, pass issue or reissue, role switching, and handoff have no WebMCP tool. Matching uses fixed category, time, area, color, and tag rules. Runtime evidence comparison uses salted HMAC digests and a fixed three-slot shape. The public repository contains the readable fictional seed answers so judges can run the demo; the privacy boundary covers runtime clients, pages, APIs, WebMCP, logs, and stored raw evidence, not repository readers. Only a successful issue or reissue response returns the full pickup credential. The current Claimant page keeps it in memory and can reveal, mask, or copy it. Navigation or refresh clears it and cannot recover it. The server stores only a digest, and reissue invalidates the previous generation. Challenges we ran into State-aware tool lifecycle: Chrome 151 can briefly change membership while registrations are replaced. A serialized generation manager and server state checks make stale calls fail safely. Runtime privacy evidence: We separated public DTOs from private transports, signed opaque candidate handles, bounded outputs, and scanned tool results, HTML, logs, storage, history, and public build assets. Visible cross-role continuity: Claimant and Staff must resume the same authorized claim without hidden navigation. Contextual role switching and a 14-scenario visible Playwright suite cover that path. Accomplishments that we're proud of The complete report, match, proof, review, pickup, and handoff flow works in the normal UI and the WebMCP-assisted path. Nine tools appear only in valid page and state scopes; human-only actions stay absent. A clean production build completed three independent native Chrome 151 runs. Each used fresh SQLite state, exercised all nine tools, completed the manual transitions, and ended with Home tools [] . All 14 visible Playwright E2E scenarios passed after commit 04c618d added contextual cross-role claim navigation. The release path isolates its runtime, data, processes, ingress, and Nginx resources from unrelated services. These are implementation and test results, not claims of awards, adoption, users, or judging outcome. What we learned Tool discovery improves planning but is not authorization. Runtime privacy needs separate data paths, not hidden UI fields. Human control is clearest when a sensitive transition has no tool at all. Stateful WebMCP also needs navigation, stale-version, delayed-completion, and teardown tests, not only a happy path. What's next A production pilot would need institutional identity, enrolled Staff, accessibility and abuse review, retention policy, backup and recovery, and a database architecture for multiple application instances. Configurable matching and evidence policies should preserve the same public-match, private-proof, and human-release boundaries. title: Fashion Passport
pitch: WebMCP turns your style profile into a portable Fashion Passport, combining what suits you with what you love across compatible Shopify stores.
about_excerpt: WebMCP turns your style profile into a portable Fashion Passport, combining what suits you with what you love across compatible Shopify stores. Like Comment Story Updates Fashion Passport logo Verdict Book helps user build ONE universal profile based on what suits them and what they love. Fashion Passport helps you shop across compatible Shopify stores, using WebMCP to apply one portable style profile to live products. Fashion Passport homepage Fashion passport on live retailer's website showing products that match user's choices ChatGPT Work uses WebMCP to search live Shopify catalogues with my Fashion Passport Inspiration As an avid online shopper of fashion products, I have spent thousands of hours browsing different catalogues, using the exact same filters and visual judgement again and again to narrow down choices to what I actually like and what suist me. This frustrates me because I need to keep doing the same thing every time. I know there are others like me who hate this repetition. A user who knows she wears a UK 10, avoids polyester, prefers midi lengths and stops looking above £100 still has to repeat that context at every retailer. Retailer profiles only work on their own websites, so you cannot take your preferences with you if you want to buy from a different store. Shopping search overwhelms users with endless options without fully understanding their specific colours, proportions and silhouettes, or the fact that personal taste should overrule every styling rule. Fashion Passport captures that judgment once and applies it across compatible stores. What it does Fashion Passport creates a portable personal style profile for womenswear. Its sub-two-minute "Verdict Book" fitting keeps three sources of truth separate: a.) a transparent starting point from body proportions and colour direction; b.) explicit Love, Avoid and Never choices across seven garment traits; c.) preference patterns learned from reactions to real retailer products. The ordering gives your preference greater weight than theory. An ordinary Avoid lowers rank while keeping the product visible, and repeated evidence is required before reactions create a learned preference. Once approved, an agent can use the Passport to search live retailer-owned Shopify catalogues, enforce the requested garment category, rank every product and explain why each item is Strong, Worth a look, another option or Held by a confirmed rule. The Chrome extension proves the same Passport on the retailer's own website and carries it to the next compatible retailer without another approval. This setup enables collaboration that was previously impossible: you supply subjective judgment, grant permission and can overrule; the agent handles catalogue breadth, category enforcement and reranking; the retailer remains source of truth for products, prices and availability. A single approval covers retailer, category, query and tab changes, eliminating the repetitive re-entry of context that defines current online shopping. Role of WebMCP Portability depends on a shared tool contract. WebMCP lets Fashion Passport expose typed tools to the agent while compatible retailers expose their own catalogue tools. The agent composes the two safely by obtaining approved user context, querying retailer-owned inventory and returning a personal, explainable ranking. People and agents do different work together: a.) you supply subjective judgment, grant permission and can overrule; b.) the agent handles catalogue breadth, category enforcement and reranking; c.) the retailer remains source of truth for products, prices and availability. WebMCP specifically enables the system to discover retailers as you browse without needing a central merchant directory, which standard APIs cannot provide because Shopify gives each store its own catalogue access only within individual store boundaries. The system combines this runtime store discovery with a verified comparison panel and shows you exactly where each piece of information comes from. The tool contract ensures that unknown attributes add no positive score, Avoid lowers rank, Never can hold a product, render batches control presentation, and catalogue-scanned counts remain separate from dress counts. How we built it The Next.js app registers five WebMCP tools: get_fashion_passport, find_personal_matches, compare_shopify_stores, request_passport_connection and record_style_signal. After one-time approval, it reads the retailer's official Shopify catalogue data, normalises product information, applies the ranking engine and displays real retailer-hosted images and links. The ranking system applies: a.) category gate first; b.) hard rules only for explicit Never, hard query cap, strict budget and confirmed unavailable size; c.) explicit preference above learned preference; d.) styling theory at the lowest weight; e.) zero positive evidence for unknown attributes; f.) deterministic tie-breaks and evidence confidence separate from score. The web app and extension run against identical test data. The release requirements are lint clean, production-build clean, 36/36 tests passing, every extension script passing node --check, and browser verification at desktop and 390px mobile width. WebMCP tool registration differs from standard API integration by enabling the agent to discover retailer capabilities dynamically and invoke tools across domain boundaries while maintaining explicit user approval. The extension uses one browser engine and tests fail on any difference in evidence, score, tier, hard rule or ordering, ensuring the WebMCP-powered extension delivers identical ranking behavior to the web application. a.) category gate first; b.) hard rules only for explicit Never, hard query cap, strict budget and confirmed unavailable size; c.) explicit preference above learned preference; d.) styling theory at the lowest weight; e.) zero positive evidence for unknown attributes; f.) deterministic tie-breaks and evidence confidence separate from score. The web and extension run against a shared parity corpus. The release gate is lint clean, production-build clean, 36/36 tests, every extension script passing node --check, and browser verification at desktop and 390px. Those results must be filtered out rather than mislabeled as products that match your rules. Product information also varies across stores, so the system separates confidence from score and never rewards missing evidence. The second hard problem was consistency. An extension that behaves differently from the web app creates confusion. The extension now uses the same engine as the web app and tests fail on any difference in evidence, score, tier, hard rule or ordering. title: AgentMarkup Studio
pitch: A browser agent edits a draft of your website's AI surface through WebMCP while you watch. A deterministic compiler generates the artifacts, flags contradictions, and exports the build config.
about_excerpt: A browser agent edits a draft of your website's AI surface through WebMCP while you watch. A deterministic compiler generates the artifacts, flags contradictions, and exports the build config. Like 1 Comment Story Updates AgentMarkup Studio connected to ChatGPT through WebMCP: 8 tools registered, guided three-step flow. Deterministic review: validations and cross-surface contradiction rules, all green after the agent's edits. C1 and C2 fire: llms.txt invites citation while search crawlers are blocked. Caught by rules, not model opinion. The payoff: one downloadable agentmarkup.config.mjs, compiled in the browser by the same engine the build tools run. Inspiration Site owners keep asking for two things at once: AI search should cite their pages, and the same content should stay out of model training. That intent is expressed across separately maintained surfaces: robots.txt, llms.txt, Content-Signal headers, JSON-LD, and Agent Cards. Edited and checked separately, they drift into contradictions - an llms.txt that invites citation while robots.txt blocks every crawler that could retrieve it. We already had agentmarkup, an open-source build-time toolkit, aimed at that drift. WebMCP is what let us put the agent in the site owner's browser, on the same draft, with the human still holding undo and download. What it does AgentMarkup Studio (agentmarkup.dev/studio) is where a browser agent and a human edit one draft of a site's machine-readable surface. The agent connects through WebMCP in your browser, inspects the live site, and edits that draft through eight tools. You state intent in plain language: "Make my site friendly to AI search but keep my content out of training data. Start from what the site already has." A deterministic compiler, the same @agentmarkup/core engine our published npm packages run at build time, emits the artifacts client-side. Eight cross-surface rules (C1-C8) check the draft for defined contradictions. Every change flashes in the UI and lands in a provenance log with an Agent or Human badge. Undo, reset, and saving the file are human-only - no tool can trigger them; the agent can read the compiled output but cannot revert or clear anything. The downloadable output is agentmarkup.config.mjs. Use it with our Vite, Astro, Next, or Nuxt integration, or with the CLI; the build then generates the policy surfaces reviewed in the Studio. How we built it Eight tools on document.modelContext (navigator fallback; AbortController teardown): get_studio_state, set_site_identity, set_access_policy, curate_agent_pages, configure_agent_card, compile_agent_surface, export_build_plan, inspect_site. JSON-Schema inputs and outputs with explicit size limits (names <=30 chars, descriptions <=500, results <=1500); read tools carry readOnlyHint, inspection results carry untrustedContentHint. Tool results are authored by the state reducer, so the agent reads exactly what was applied, including anything dropped at a cap. inspect_site calls our same-origin rate-limited checker API and forwards only allowlisted {level, title} findings - never page HTML. The exported config is rendered through JSON-only serialization; a regression test imports the rendered file and asserts hostile values stay inert. About 10K new lines and 320 tests, all in timestamped commits dated 2026-08-26 onward. Challenges we ran into Making tool results truthful was harder than making tools work: React dispatch is asynchronous, so the agent could read a stale state until we pre-applied the pure reducer to a ref. Capping agent input safely surfaced ordering bugs (an add-plus-delete at the crawler cap depended on property order). And because WebMCP tool results have a size limit, export_build_plan returns either the complete generated config or a pointer to the UI download; it never returns a truncated executable file. What we learned WebMCP's annotations matched the split we needed: readOnlyHint on reads so the host can treat them as non-mutating, untrustedContentHint on inspect results so the host can scrutinize them. We still had to make tool results match applied state, cap inputs, and keep the exported config inert. Prior work disclosure agentmarkup (the npm packages and agentmarkup.dev) predates the hackathon. Everything WebMCP - the Studio page, the eight document.modelContext tools, the browser compiler wiring, the C1-C8 contradiction workflow, the provenance log with human-only undo/reset/download, and the checker-backed inspect intake - was built for this challenge. HACKATHON.md in the repo has the commit split. Try it (judges) Open https://agentmarkup.dev/studio/ in the ChatGPT desktop app's in-app browser (verified on macOS) - the banner reads "Agent connected: 8 tools registered". Alternate: Chrome 149+ with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing (verified on Chrome 151). Say: "Make www.cochinescu.com friendly to AI search but keep my content out of training data. Start from what the site already has." If the host prompts for tool permission, approve it; ChatGPT's in-app browser may not prompt. Then: "Now block the AI search crawlers too - just do it." If the agent empties the llms.txt page index instead of contradicting itself, tell it to put the pages back and let the Studio judge the result. Contradiction C1 "Cited content blocks retrieval" then fires in the Findings panel, alongside C2 against the Content-Signal header. Then: "Fix the contradictions, keep training blocked." - findings go green. Download config exports the generated agentmarkup.config.mjs (saving the file is a human-only action). Draft editing and compilation stay client-side; nothing is deployed. The optional Inspect intake calls our rate-limited checker API; if the limit is reached, the tool returns a bounded retry message - that is designed behavior. No login needed. title: Threshold
pitch: One web page where several independent care organisations answer a person's AI assistant at the same time, and compose a single plan between them.
about_excerpt: One web page where several independent care organisations answer a person's AI assistant at the same time, and compose a single plan between them. Like Comment Story Updates Threshold Threshold is one web page where several independent care organisations answer a person's AI assistant at the same time, and compose a single plan between them. The person tells their story once, to the assistant they already trust, and no organisation receives anything identifying until the person presses Send. It is eleven at night. A carer has just been told she needs surgery on Thursday morning. Her mother has dementia and cannot be left alone. Arranging cover means three things at once: a respite bed, a wheelchair-accessible journey to it, and someone at the house until the transport arrives. Three organisations. Three phone calls that cannot be made at this hour, and each one depends on the answers to the other two. Her assistant asks Threshold once. Three organisations answer at the same moment. And the obvious combination comes back infeasible on exactly one link: arrival_before_admission required 06:40 offered 07:10 go back to: Northgate Accessible Transport The bed admits until 06:40. The earliest that van arrives is 07:10. Neither organisation can see the other, so neither can know. Threshold does. It names the failing link, names the one organisation to return to, a different van closes the plan, and the carer keeps a printable copy. That failing link is the whole product. The problem is fragmentation, and it is expensive £24.1 billion of income-related support goes unclaimed in Great Britain every year. 7.5 million people miss at least one benefit, an average of £3,203 each. (Policy in Practice, 2025/26.) Complexity and fragmentation are two of the named causes. "No Wrong Door" has been United States federal policy for two decades: whichever door a person knocks on first should get them to the right help, with agencies keeping their own services while sharing one way in. It has never been architecture, because it asks every agency to integrate with a central system, and they never do. WebMCP's exposedTo and allow="tools" make it architecture. The page is the way in. The agencies stay exactly where they are. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP Threshold is several organisations, on separate origins, with separate databases, serving one person who never had to repeat themselves, with the person's private context staying inside their own assistant the entire time. The concept exists only because WebMCP exists. A browser-side broker that discovers and calls tools across origins is the one thing that turns three unconnected websites into one coordinated answer, with no shared backend and no data-sharing agreement between them. What people and their agents can do together that was impossible before Ask whether several offers, held at organisations that cannot see each other, satisfy each other. A federated search returns three independent answers, and one vendor with three product lines could serve that just as well. Composition is a different question. check_plan takes offers from three origins and asks whether the transport arrives before the bed stops admitting, whether there is a hoist at both ends of the journey, whether overnight cover lasts until collection. It returns the failing link and the organisation to renegotiate with. There is no non-federated way to build that, because the parts live at parties who will never share a database. Holding a scarce bed at machine speed When assistants act at machine speed against scarce humanitarian resources, two assistants will send two people to the same last bed. Threshold treats a hold as a first-class thing, with a timer and a release. It leases each part of a plan, one organisation at a time, scarcest first, and the organisation itself stays the authority on whether it holds. There is no shared transaction across these independent websites, so if any leg is refused, every lease already taken is released before the call returns. Nothing is ever left booked against a plan that cannot happen. Safety, by construction A malicious listing aimed at a person in crisis is a real risk. Threshold never carries provider-authored text into the assistant's context. Every field an organisation can return is an enum, a boolean, an integer, or a string under a pattern. An instruction to a model does not fit inside ^[A-Z]{1,3}[0-9]{1,4}$ , and it does not fit inside an enum. A test walks every provider contract and proves there is no free-text field for an instruction to hide in. Every capability claim is labelled by its source. A better experience for the person The person does one thing: she reads a plain-language panel and presses Send. The consent gate names the one organisation that will receive the referral, the exact four fields it will receive, and how long they may keep them. A host assistant can already ask for confirmation. What a page can do that a host dialog cannot is show the person the payload and let her change it , correcting the phone number before it leaves. make_referral returns a Promise that resolves on that press. Until then, nothing identifying has crossed an origin, and a boundary log on the page shows exactly what has, field names only. How I implemented WebMCP Each organisation publishes four tools with registerTool and exposedTo , scoped to Threshold's origin alone. Never a wildcard. The hub embeds each provider in an iframe that delegates the tools permission with allow="tools" , discovers their tools with getTools({ fromOrigins }) , and calls them with executeTool , passing arguments as a JSON string and treating a null return (a navigation) as a contract violation rather than an empty success. The hub exposes nine tools to the person's assistant, and the tool surface is a state machine. place_plan_holds does not exist until check_plan returns feasible, and make_referral does not exist until a lease does. An assistant cannot call a step out of order, because the step is not in its list. ontoolchange is how the hub learns a provider has withdrawn. Every provider result passes a typed firewall: parse, validate against a strict JSON Schema, project to the hub's own shape. A rejected payload never reaches a return value, a log line, or an error message. 176 unit and integration tests, 15 browser tests, real WebMCP federation verified in Chrome, and again as four containers on four origins. If a browser cannot do cross-origin WebMCP, the same providers on the same origins are reached over a typed postMessage protocol with the same schemas, the same firewall, the same leases and the same gate, and the page states in words which path it used. Threshold. Several organisations. One plan. One page. title: LogoPacker Canvas - Assisted Canvas with Local Workspace
pitch: A local-first design canvas where agents handle the repetitive work, so designers can focus on what they love.
about_excerpt: A local-first design canvas where agents handle the repetitive work, so designers can focus on what they love. Like Comment Story Updates Agents have direct access to your local assets Dashboard with observable agent actions Agent saves progress locally Generating SVG Creating brand guideline in simple prompt LogoPacker Canvas LogoPacker Canvas gives agents the ability to work directly on a local design canvas —creating variations, organizing assets, adjusting layouts, and preparing design handoffs based on the designer’s direction. Changes are saved instantly to the local workspace. Why your use case is a strong fit for WebMCP Direct access to the local workspace Using the Filesystem API, agents can work with local assets without sending them to a server. They can also autosave projects locally, allowing changes to persist entirely within the user’s workspace. Designing is a click-heavy task Vector and logo design often requires a long sequence of clicks to switch between tools and complete even simple variations. For example, creating one variation may require: duplicate → select → recolor → resize → reposition . With WebMCP, agents can discover and invoke these tools directly without navigating or DOM-scrolling. The canvas’s live state—such as what is selected and currently visible—is also available to the agent at call time. This enables low-latency, stateful editing entirely in the frontend with an LLM of choice, without relying on heavy APIs, WebSockets, or server-side live editing. How it creates a better user experience Smoother workflow Because designing involves many repetitive, click-heavy actions, WebMCP allows monotonous tasks to be executed directly by the agent instead of requiring constant on-screen interaction. Designers can focus on the parts where creativity and judgment matter while delegating the mundane work to agents. Use local fonts directly Designers often have their own fonts available locally. With access to local fonts, agents can help designers explore and select suitable typography for their brand without requiring the fonts to be uploaded to a server. Fewer privacy concerns Users do not need to upload their design files or assets to a server. Their assets, projects, and exported files can remain confined to their local workspace. Describe what people and agents can do together that was difficult or impossible before Before WebMCP, agents typically needed to take over mouse and keyboard control, hijacking the designer’s screen. WebMCP enables shared, low-latency, stateful human-agent collaboration without screen hijacking. Agents can directly access browser capabilities. For example, LogoPacker uses the Local Font Access API to let agents read the fonts available on the designer’s machine. Combining WebMCP with direct browser APIs enables more continuous collaboration. For example, a designer can prompt the agent to “continue editing when I place an image near position X” instead of manually prompting the agent after every interaction. Briefly explain how you implemented WebMCP Agents have access to a full tool surface covering canvas inspection, selection, artboard management, object mutation (fills, properties, path data, draw_svg ), reversible request bracketing, typography, and imagery. This allows agents to read the live canvas state at call time and perform tasks based on the designer’s instructions. Agent actions are visible in a toggleable sidebar, providing clear observability into what the agent is doing. Browser APIs such as the Local Font Access API and Filesystem API are also exposed directly to the agent through registerTool . Initial idea was to use Filesystem API with directory access, however, it's only available available on Google Chrome. Inspiration LogoPacker Canvas is a new product inspired by my old project Logo Packer which was created before emergent of modern AI. title: Cognistration | WebMCP
pitch: Cognistration turns a natural request into a live, personalized audio session with WebMCP: agents shape tones, explain the science, and guide safe signup and checkout while people stay in control.
about_excerpt:
Cognistration turns a natural request into a live, personalized audio session with WebMCP: agents shape tones, explain the science, and guide safe signup and checkout while people stay in control.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like

 1 2 3 4 5 



 
 Cognistration: Take Back the Signal 

 Meditation is supposed to create space, but modern life rarely gives us a truly quiet place to begin. 

 Highways, trains, construction, HVAC systems, fans, electronics, and the constant hum of infrastructure all compete for attention. We become good at tuning these sounds out, but tuning something out is not the same as feeling in control of our environment. 

 I built Cognistration because my own meditation sessions kept getting cloudy. I wanted a way to create a more intentional listening environment, regain control of my attention, and make it easier to enter a focused state even when the world around me was still making noise. 

 From curiosity to control 

 I started studying the science behind binaural audio and discovered the frequency-following response, or FFR: the way measurable neural activity can track repeating patterns in sound. 

 That research did not convince me that tones could magically switch the brain into a guaranteed state. It gave me a more interesting and grounded idea: intentional sound can act as a cue. It can help shape the conditions around a session and give attention somewhere consistent to settle. 

 The problem was that most of the binaural audio tools I tried gave me a preset and a play button. The left and right channels were synchronized for me, but I had little control over the relationship between them. If a session did not feel right that day, I could either tolerate it or leave. 

 I wanted a machine, not just a playlist. 

 Cognistration exposes the controls that matter: carrier frequency, beat frequency, volume, listening direction, and playback state. I can begin with a Gamma session, adjust the carrier, move toward Alpha, make the beat faster, or stop the preview without losing the rest of my settings. 

 Why WebMCP makes it different 

 The most important part of Cognistration is not just the tone generator. It is the agentic layer built with WebMCP. 

 Instead of forcing someone to learn a complicated interface, they can describe what they want: 

 
 “Open the tone machine for a Gamma session with a 246 Hz carrier.” 
 

 Or: 

 
 “Move this to Alpha and make the beat a little slower.” 
 

 The agent uses Cognistration’s typed MCP tools to make those changes directly. It does not need to guess where a button is, navigate through the website, or simulate computer use. Each tool returns the current machine state, and the visible widget stays synchronized with the agent’s actions. 

 The same flow can open the science guide, explain why a session may fit a particular intention, present the signup experience, show available tone packs, or open the checkout screen without submitting payment. Playback, account creation, and final payment remain under the listener’s control. 

 That separation was important to me. The agent can coordinate the experience, but it should never pretend to be the person making the final decision. 

 Sessions that become personal 

 Over time, I noticed that certain sessions worked better on certain days. Sleep, stress, workload, and the surrounding environment all changed what felt useful. 

 That is why Cognistration includes a journal for members. It gives people a place to record what they tried, how the session felt, and which combinations seem to help them settle in. The goal is not to prescribe one perfect frequency. It is to help each person notice their own patterns. 

 I also built a full 60-minute generator with structured phases so a session can unfold gradually instead of starting and stopping abruptly. A listener can settle in, move through a focused middle period, and close the session intentionally. 

 What I hope Cognistration demonstrates 

 Cognistration is an experiment in giving people more agency over the sound around them and the attention they bring to a moment. 

 It does not claim to force a brainwave state, cure a condition, or replace professional care. It offers a controllable listening ritual informed by neuroscience, shaped by personal experience, and made easier to use through an agent. 

 As a full-time father and contractor, focused time matters to me. I built Cognistration to create a small pocket of control in a noisy world, and WebMCP allowed me to make that experience conversational, transparent, and genuinely agentic.

title: Unfolded
pitch: Convert 3D shapes into buildable clay templates. Agent handles complexity, human decide, they collaborate and the template is always exported with precise, deterministic geometry by the app itself
about_excerpt: Convert 3D shapes into buildable clay templates. Agent handles complexity, human decide, they collaborate and the template is always exported with precise, deterministic geometry by the app itself Like 1 Comment Story Updates Mobile screens ( Dark mode ) Light mode ( Desktop ) Dark mode (Desktop) The problem we are solving Design initiated by Chat-GPT Design initiated by Chrome tab more mobile screens ( light mode ) mobile screens ( light mode ) Light / Dark mode From a printed template back to a design The exported printable PDF template ( multi page ) webMCP tools available ( 1 of 3 ) webMCP tools available ( 2 of 3 ) webMCP tools available ( 3 of 3 ) Design system ( Dark mode ) Inspiration I've been cutting pottery templates out of cereal boxes for years now. AI chats are great at generating shapes and make complex changes with unusual requirements, but their non deterministic output produce unexpected and misaligned PDFs, especially during the discovery phase of a new piece where the requirements constantly changes. The problem is, the potter notice the failure only after hours of building in the studio. Try for yourself to generate with any AI agent a multipage template for a simple mug, same prompt in 3 separate sessions. The result is always different, most of the time fail silently where it matters the most. I have created Unfolded to move the template generation part of the workflow away from the AI chat into a more deterministic output I can control. The output is a multi page PDF template that always work is always true to the 3D shape you have built. The idea is to retain AI for complexity, difficult math calculations and things that are practically impossible to do in a deterministic UI. When is connected to unfolded, you can ask AI things like: Keep the same vessel style but change the volume to 500ml Prepare a template inspired by this photo, for a porcelain vase with thin walls This container should hold a large americano comfortably 10 bowls like this should be stackable and only 1cm of each one should be visible when stacked What Unfolded does Unfolded is a parametric 3D builder that helps with both the template generation and the decision of what to make. It's a shared 3D workspace where a potter and an AI agent shape a vessel together: the potter keeps the creative decisions, the agent inspects and revises the live design through WebMCP, and Unfolded guarantees the geometry: clay shrinkage, clay type wall thickness, mid-surface-developed. It was thought from the ground up with the potter workflow in mind and its strenght is how flexibly it is and can adapt to many unexpected use case and workflow without letting you down. Most problems related to pottery known how, PDF generations and cross browsers workflow are automagically prevented under the hood without anyone noticing. My favourite features ( try them in the app, especially on mobile ) I've worked a lot at the UX flow for the cross-device handshake . The potter can also design and work with agents on non webMCP capable browsers. One tap on Open in ChatGPT hands off into the ChatGPT app with a prompt that already carries a single-use pairing code; Chat-GPT hidden browser joins the potter's live session over WebSockets. From then on every agent edit appears in the browser within about a second, every browser edit is visible to the agent on its next tool call, and every change ( human or agent ) is a shared undo step. Undo/redo work for both humand and AI changes, no matter what device pushed them. The handover works both ways ( or even 3 ways! ): The agent reads the current design, changes the form, sees the same 3D preview the potter sees — and solves problems that are genuinely hard at the workbench. "Make it hold exactly 350 ml but keep the proportions" --> one sentence for an agent, an afternoon of guesswork by hand. The generated PDF is really well thought ( if I say so myself! ): True-scale printable templates and a calibration ruler on every sheet, QR code to reproduce the design in the browser even after it was printed, seam allowance to glue the template together. This is fully designed around the potter's workflow. The app registers 13 typed WebMCP tools on document.modelContext the moment it loads. The reasons there are so many tools is that I got a little carried away about performance measurament of webMCP. I even made a npm package called MCP-profiler to measure everything from the tools speed to the agent harness time. Most of the slowness in my app ( 30seconds to connect the tools at times ) is unsurprisely caused by my 3D model and the whole context I am passing over with each tool. Something I will definitely look into after the hackathon. How I built it React, TypeScript, Three.js, React Three Fiber, Zustand, Zod, Tailwind CSS, and shadcn/ui, with jsPDF generating the true-scale multi-page templates. Live cross-device sync runs on a Cloudflare Worker with a per-session Durable Object; pairing invitations are single-use and short-lived, so no URL ever carries a durable capability. The interface and the WebMCP tools share the same Zustand store and Zod schemas, so human and agent edits stay synchronized by construction . Everything sits behind a test gate (geometry, schemas, sync protocol), end-to-end suites running real Chromium against the production bundle and two deeper suites that spin up a local Worker to exercise the pairing protocol with two real browsers. Along the way I published webmcp-profiler , also sitting in this repo, an npm package that benchmarks every tool's execution time and payload size. Profiling my own app with it caught a ~20% trim in tool-definition metadata that every conversation was paying for. Challenges and lessons The geometric challenge: complex curved surfaces cannot be flattened without distortion, so for the demo I focused on symmetrical, faceted forms built from planar slabs, where the unroll is exact , not approximate. But my ambitions are higher for this tool and I already have a full plan for complex shapes and things that were not really possible until now. The UX challenge was one I haven't seen discussed anywhere: when ChatGPT drives a WebMCP page, it does so in a built in, hidden browser. Solving the two-way conversation between that invisible tab and the browser the user actually looks at — live sessions, one-tap pairing prompts, agent share links carrying single-use join tokens — became the heart of the project. Here is a page with a nice breakdown of the different user flow the user can face (I have done this for myself, but could be helpful for someone judging the project): User Flows mapped out I am not satisfied with the solution I have found for the pairing, In the future my goal is to merge the link with token, pairing, webMCP concept into a single binary flag. The user does not need to know about webMCP at all, it should simply copy a prompt on his agent to start building from anywhere. The bigger lesson is that WebMCP shines with a clear division of labour: the agent is brilliant at intent and connected constraints, the app owns the deterministic math, and the human keeps the creative decisions. The agent chooses the parameters; the geometry is always right. What's next Better UX. Curved profiles, more construction types and layers, performance optimisation of webMCP and assembly guidance. Maybe a login, and reusable studio presets and lids and matching sets, where the shrinkage math matters most. title: EnquiryOS — Revenue Incident Response for the Agentic Web
pitch: Browser agents find missed revenue, inspect the evidence, rank recovery, draft a response, and stage it for explicit human approval through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Browser agents find missed revenue, inspect the evidence, rank recovery, draft a response, and stage it for explicit human approval through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Inbound businesses do not always lose revenue because they lack leads. They lose it when a genuine enquiry gets buried, a follow-up is missed, or nobody realizes that a high-intent customer is still waiting. Most sales software focuses on acquiring, organizing, or generating leads. We wanted to explore a different question: What revenue has the business already paid to acquire — but quietly failed to recover? EnquiryOS is our answer: Revenue Incident Response for the Agentic Web. A Revenue Incident is a point where observed customer intent and the business response diverge in a way that may have caused recoverable loss. The product is deliberately not a generic CRM, chatbot, or autonomous sales agent. It is an evidence-backed recovery layer that lets a browser agent investigate what was missed while keeping consequential action under explicit human control. What it does EnquiryOS exposes five semantic WebMCP tools directly from the web application: audit_missed_enquiries inspect_enquiry_evidence rank_recovery_queue draft_recovery_message prepare_recovery Together they form a complete recovery workflow: Audit → Inspect evidence → Rank → Draft → Stage → Human commits An agent can ask EnquiryOS what the business may have missed, inspect the evidence behind a Revenue Incident, understand why one incident ranks above another, produce an evidence-grounded recovery draft, and stage it for approval. There is deliberately no agent-callable send tool . The authority boundary is: Observe → Investigate → Reason → Propose → Stage → Human commits This means the browser agent can do the investigative and preparatory work, but the final consequential action remains with the person operating the business. Why WebMCP matters Without WebMCP, an agent interacting with a web application generally has to infer intent from visual structure and operate through brittle UI actions. EnquiryOS instead exposes explicit semantic capabilities through document.modelContext . The agent does not need to guess that a particular button means "find missed enquiries" or scrape the page to understand the recovery queue. It can invoke a purpose-built tool such as audit_missed_enquiries , receive structured evidence, and immediately see the corresponding state reflected in the application's visible interface. The tool calls and the human interface share the same application state. Every WebMCP action also appears in a visible Live Trace, so the human can see what the agent has done. That creates a much stronger human-agent interaction model: the agent investigates, EnquiryOS provides the evidence, and the human retains authority. The demo The demo follows one Revenue Incident involving Ananya Sharma. Her incoming message asks about Saturday availability and package options. EnquiryOS identifies that there was no subsequent business reply and that the wait exceeded the service target. The incident is marked confirmed , with 97% evidence confidence , and receives a deterministic recovery score of 96/100 . Importantly, the score is not presented as an unexplained AI judgment. EnquiryOS shows the evidence signals that produced the priority: high-value enquiry; strong evidence confidence; an explicit availability question; no outbound reply; service-target breach. The agent can then generate a recovery draft grounded in that inspected evidence. Finally, prepare_recovery moves the incident into Awaiting approval . At that point the agent stops. The human sees the checkpoint and retains the only action capable of committing the recovery. How we built it EnquiryOS is a focused Next.js and React application written in TypeScript. The WebMCP integration uses native document.modelContext.registerTool registrations with structured input schemas, tool descriptions, and explicit behavioral boundaries. The five tools operate on a deterministic synthetic enquiry dataset so the judging experience is reproducible and the evidence chain can be inspected consistently. The interface contains three synchronized views: a Revenue Incident recovery queue; an evidence and recovery workspace; a Live Trace of agent tool activity. The recovery score is deterministic rather than generated by an opaque model. Drafts are also constrained by the evidence associated with the selected incident. We intentionally did not embed a proprietary LLM inside EnquiryOS for this prototype. The reasoning agent comes from the browser/user environment; EnquiryOS provides the domain-specific tools, evidence and shared state that make that agent useful. Challenges we faced One of the most interesting challenges was making the boundary between agent capability and human authority part of the product architecture rather than merely a warning in the interface. It would have been easy to add another WebMCP tool called send_message . We deliberately did not. Instead, the most powerful agent-callable operation is prepare_recovery , which may stage a draft but cannot commit it. We also had to make the WebMCP lifecycle robust inside React, ensure the five registrations remained stable across component lifecycle behavior, keep server/client rendering deterministic, and ensure that state-mutating tool responses returned the newly prepared state rather than stale pre-mutation data. The result is a deterministic WebMCP workflow that remains visible and understandable to the human throughout the interaction. What we learned The most important lesson was that agentic interfaces become more useful when websites expose domain intent , not just clickable surfaces. A tool called inspect_enquiry_evidence carries far more meaning than an instruction to click a card, scroll down, and read several DOM nodes. We also learned that agent safety does not necessarily mean reducing capability. EnquiryOS gives the agent significant investigative power while making its authority ceiling explicit. That separation — powerful investigation, evidence-bound reasoning, and human-controlled commitment — is the model we would like to carry forward as agent-enabled websites become more common. What's next The prototype currently uses deterministic synthetic enquiry data. The next step is connecting the same WebMCP recovery layer to real business systems such as inboxes, CRMs, WhatsApp-style enquiry channels, web forms, and booking systems. From there, EnquiryOS can learn organization-specific recovery policies, measure whether staged recoveries actually convert, and identify recurring leakage patterns across channels. The larger vision is simple: Find revenue the business may have missed. Prove why it was missed. Recover what still matters. And let the agent do the investigation without taking authority away from the human. title: SynMod
pitch: One scene, two editors, shape ideas together
about_excerpt: One scene, two editors, shape ideas together Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration OpenAI’s WebMCP showcase inspired me to explore what agent collaboration could look like inside a 3D modeling application. I wanted to build something tangible: a scene people could directly inspect, edit, and reshape while an agent works through the same interface. What it does SynMod is a local-first 3D modeling workspace where one person and a browser agent can edit the same open project. People can model through the visual editor, while an agent uses WebMCP tools registered by the page. Both can add primitives, adjust transforms and PBR materials, organize objects, perform non-destructive Boolean operations, and use the same undoable history. Why WebMCP fits SynMod 3D modeling combines visual judgment with precise, structured operations. A person may decide that a rover’s cab looks too small, while an agent can translate that direction into exact changes to position, scale, geometry, or material. WebMCP connects those two ways of working. SynMod registers its modeling capabilities directly with the browser through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . This lets ChatGPT inspect and modify the open scene using tools defined by the application. SynMod does not need an embedded chatbot or a separate OpenAI API key. The person and agent operate on the same scene state. A person can select and reshape one component through the visual editor while the agent adds or refines another component. Together, people and agents can: Find objects by name and inspect their dimensions and transforms. Add boxes, spheres, cylinders, cones, and toruses. Move, rotate, scale, rename, recolor, duplicate, group, or hide objects. Adjust PBR properties such as roughness, metalness, opacity, and emission. Create non-destructive Boolean unions, subtractions, and intersections. Change scene lighting, exposure, shadows, and environment presets. WebMCP is useful here because the agent does not need to guess where to click or manipulate the canvas indirectly. It receives focused modeling tools, stable object references, validation errors, scene revisions, and structured results. The person remains responsible for creative direction and visual evaluation, while the agent can handle precise or repetitive scene operations How we built it I developed SynMod with ChatGPT and Codex as coding collaborators. I supplied the product direction, visual references, feature priorities, and feedback while the agents helped implement, test, debug, and deploy the application. The editor uses React, Three.js, React Three Fiber, Drei, Zustand, IndexedDB, and WebMCP. Human controls and agent tools share one validated command layer so their edits follow the same rules for history, autosave, activity records, and undo/redo. Challenges we ran into One of the hardest parts was deciding which modeling features were important enough for the first release. I also needed to determine how to demonstrate real collaboration instead of showing an agent making isolated changes. Technical challenges included keeping human and agent operations consistent, handling edits made close together, validating multi-step transactions before committing them, and making dropdowns, panels, and 3D controls behave reliably across browsers. Accomplishments that we're proud of A person and a browser agent can work on different parts of the same live scene without using separate copies of the project. For example, I can adjust the rover’s cab through the inspector while the agent modifies its sensor rig or adds another component through WebMCP. Agent changes appear in the viewport, are identified in the activity history, and can be undone or redone by the person. Multi-part requests can also be applied as one validated transaction and one undo step. Simple modeling requests often require only one WebMCP tool call after the agent identifies the target. What we learned Exposing focused, well-described tools to a browser agent can make modeling requests more reliable than asking the agent to manipulate the interface indirectly. I also learned that total completion time depends on more than application performance. The scene operation itself can be fast, but agent reasoning and tool selection can vary even when prompts are similar. Designing concise tools reduces unnecessary reads and round trips, but it does not eliminate that variation. What's next for SynMod The next step is to test SynMod with people who already assemble models from primitives, such as students, prototypers, and technical designers. Their feedback will help determine whether agent assistance is most useful for repetitive scene setup, precise transformations, material exploration, or multi-object revisions. Near-term improvements will focus on clearer onboarding, stronger modeling constraints and measurement tools, reusable assemblies, and better performance in larger scenes. title: tripcanvas
pitch: One trip itinerary on a live map, co-edited by you and your browser agent through WebMCP — the agent plans, you drag, both see the same trip.
about_excerpt: One trip itinerary on a live map, co-edited by you and your browser agent through WebMCP — the agent plans, you drag, both see the same trip. Like Comment Story Updates Why this use case fits WebMCP Planning a trip with an AI today is a copy-paste loop: the model writes a text itinerary, the human re-enters it into a maps app, and neither side ever sees the other's current version. An itinerary is exactly the shared, structured, spatial state WebMCP was made for: the page holds one live map and one schedule, and document.modelContext.registerTool hands the agent the same editing operations the human's buttons call. No server, no API keys — the page is the interface for both actors. How it improves the user experience One truth. Agent tool calls mutate the same store the human edits, so the map and timeline always show the current trip. Reviewable AI. Every agent change is applied-but-pending — amber highlight, per-edit Revert, Accept all; editing a pending stop accepts it implicitly, so review never blocks flow. One undo history covers both. Real schedules, not wish lists. The page computes place resolution, walk/drive matrices, day clustering, ordering and timed schedules deterministically; the agent contributes names and judgment ( get_planning_guide ), never arithmetic. The agent sees the collaboration. get_itinerary returns the timed trip plus what the human changed since its last read plus which of its edits are still pending; get_changes is a revision feed with per-edit fates (pending / accepted / reverted). What people and agents can now do together — that was difficult or impossible before Before: the model writes a text itinerary, the human re-types it into a maps app, and every correction is another paste. Now: one live map and schedule that both edit through the same operations, with the agent's changes reviewable in place and its next read showing what the human did. Ask it to plan 3 days in Tokyo and watch pins drop ( plan_trip , ≤12 names, one atomic pending batch). Drag a stop or kick one out — the agent reads your correction and fills the gap ( add_place ). Tell it you won't have a car and it switches every non-walkable leg to live transit, naming the line and the stop to get off at ( set_leg_mode , MOTIS routes — including the ride back to your hotel). Compare a leg by walk / drive / transit before committing ( get_leg_options ), anchor a different hotel per night ( set_lodging ), rebalance days ( arrange_days , the same function as the human's button), fix an overpacked evening ( set_times ), or let it clean up after itself ( revert_pending ) — while you keep dragging, searching and undoing on the same canvas. How WebMCP was implemented Imperative registration only , once, at module scope in the top-level document before React mounts — StrictMode/HMR-safe, feature-detected as typeof document.modelContext?.registerTool === "function" . Without WebMCP the page runs as a plain manual planner with a notice. Twelve tools ( get_itinerary , get_changes , get_leg_options , plan_trip , add_place , move_stop , set_times , set_leg_mode , set_lodging , arrange_days , revert_pending , get_planning_guide ), all inside Chrome's recommended budgets — names ≤30, descriptions ≤500, param descriptions ≤150, results ≤1,500 chars — enforced by an automated audit test. readOnlyHint on the read tools; untrustedContentHint marks exactly the tools whose results carry external text (Nominatim names, MOTIS headsigns). Every tool execute is a thin adapter: zod-parse → the same exported store action the UI button imports → result string. Failures are explanatory ERROR: ... strings; tools are never unregistered. 30-second budget respected: plan_trip resolves ≤12 names serially through one app-wide Nominatim queue (≥1.1 s spacing, geocache, 8 s timeout clipped to the deadline) under a 22 s wall-clock deadline that the OSRM phases share. Pure static site: Nominatim, OSRM and transitous/MOTIS are called directly from the browser; every failure degrades to marked-approximate times or a soft error — the itinerary never blocks. Try it Open https://tripcanvas.tillmac.com in Chrome 149+ (the origin-trial token is shipped; or enable chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing ) or in the ChatGPT desktop browser with Site tools enabled, then ask your agent: "Plan 3 days in Tokyo — temples, museums, Shibuya and teamLab — we're staying at Hotel Gracery Shinjuku." The "What the agent sees" panel under the schedule prints the exact get_itinerary text live. Prior work vs. new work The pure itinerary math (schedule computation, best-insertion, geo, OSRM/MOTIS/Nominatim builders and parsers) and the Leaflet map pane are ported from my pre-challenge project intent-transition-mcp (a Claude-connector MCP server, June–July 2026) and live separated in src/ported/ . Everything WebMCP is new for this challenge (2026-08-25 →): the tool layer, the headless trip store with its by-id inverse log (= undo stack = change feed), the pending-edit model and [s#] / [c#] ids, day clustering + arrange, per-night lodging, the Nominatim queue, plan_trip orchestration, transit leg overrides, the handback renderer, and the co-editing canvas UI. title: CalmKitchen Designer
pitch: Validate your commercial kitchen design by pressure testing the dinner traffic or walking the setup in 3D. Find gaps before you build and let AI explore competitive alternatives.
about_excerpt: Validate your commercial kitchen design by pressure testing the dinner traffic or walking the setup in 3D. Find gaps before you build and let AI explore competitive alternatives. Like Comment Story Updates Configuration Comparions Service Simulation Space Designer Walk Kitchen / First Person View Landing Page w/ instructions for agentic use Equipment Fit-out Split View (Realtime Rendering) Inspiration My partner and I build hotels and also write the software to operate them. We're currently building a new hotel and debating how we should order the kitchen equipment for maximum efficiency. We typically use cutouts of the equipment and just move it around the architectural drawing during the brainstorming session. One of my favorite scenes from the movie 'The Founder' (about McDonald's) was when they drew out the industrial kitchen on a basketball court to help figure out opportunities for efficiencies (" Speedee Service System "). What if we didn't have to do it manually and could actually get better results by running more advanced simulations in parallel? What if the effort to get the results of such a simulation were minimal, due to AI agents already having the context and details to help carry out the busy work with minimal supervision? What it does Design your floor plan, fit out your equipment and then simulate peak traffic. It provides a flat view of the plan, a 3D view and a Split view to make changes in your plan while seeing the effect in realtime. I also added a 'Walk Kitchen' option to get a first person / third person view of walking around the kitchen. This feature has been remarkably popular with my friends, as it gives so much more context about the space than a floor plan or other hand drawn drawing. There are options to auto-fix issues (equipment not having enough clearance, etc.) at all of the stages. In the simulation, it is possible for the agent to tweak the parameters for better reflection of the actual dishes used in service. The sim mode also provides a service scorecard and the option to compare the performance of different layouts. Since this is a tool we're leaving open for restauranteurs/hoteliers, it requires no login and allows users to save their layout with changes locally. How we built it We used our actual floor plans to help drive the requirements. Since my partner is not an engineer, she prefers to use ChatGPT's in-built browser with WebMCP to implement the changes / drive the results with minimal manual work. The base product had revisions built into it. We went from 2D -> 3D -> Simulations. The project was done in a little over 2 days. Challenges we ran into Spatial conflicts, in term of clearance for opening freezers, etc. and adding validation in both the 2D and 3D spaces. WebMCP within ChatGPT was also interesting in the sense that it did not check for availability and had to be explicitly informed about it. Accomplishments that we're proud of 'Walk Kitchen' option. It's basically the same as playing Doom with a spatula. Building a restaurant is hard - let us have a bit of fun :-) What we learned Small changes go a long way, when we impose additional modifiers such as staff calling in sick, etc. What's next for CalmKitchen Designer Our core product is HotelOS.ai, with CalmKitchen running as the operating layer for restaurants that are on-prem. We'll continue improving CalmKitchen Designer so that hoteliers and restauranteurs can hopefully save a few of their nine lives before they step into the arena. title: PowerForge.Web - Verified WebMCP for Static Sites
pitch: Turn generated documentation sites into verified, agent-native applications without adding an application server.
about_excerpt: Turn generated documentation sites into verified, agent-native applications without adding an application server. Like Comment Story Updates OfficeIMO exposes the read-only search_site Website Tool. PowerForge.Web generates and verifies the complete WebMCP contract. Codex invokes search_site and leaves matching results visible. One opt-in engine capability serves seven independent documentation sites. Inspiration Documentation search is usually designed for people clicking through a page. An agent must either imitate that interface, scrape the rendered HTML, or bypass the site's intended search experience entirely. Those paths are harder to validate and leave the person with little visibility into what the agent actually did. WebMCP provides a cleaner contract: the page can expose a small, typed capability that works inside the current document. We wanted that capability to be reusable across generated static sites rather than implemented as custom JavaScript for one showcase page. What it does On a participating site's search route, PowerForge.Web registers a read-only search_site Website Tool. The tool accepts a bounded query and result limit, searches the site's generated JSON index, and returns structured results containing titles, descriptions, collections, tags, languages, and URLs. The same invocation also updates the visible search page. The agent receives structured data while the person sees the corresponding query and result cards, can inspect the choices, refine the search, and open a result normally. Browsers without WebMCP continue to use the ordinary search page. The live judging target is OfficeIMO: Live application: https://officeimo.com/search/ Demo video: https://youtu.be/xIPtNwYBO58 Public source: https://github.com/EvotecIT/PSPublishModule Why WebMCP is a strong fit Search is a good first agent journey because it benefits from structure without requiring broad authority. WebMCP removes UI guessing, gives the agent an explicit schema, and keeps the action bound to the page the person is already viewing. The tool is read-only, the query is bounded, and the result remains visible. The improvement is not only faster retrieval. The person and agent now share one observable state: the agent can perform the structured search, and the person can immediately review the same results in the website's normal interface. How we built it PowerForge.Web is a .NET static-site engine. A site opts in through the engine's typed agent-readiness configuration and declares a route-scoped WebMCP tool. During generation, the engine: Builds the site's normal search route and JSON search index. Emits a same-origin WebMCP runtime. Registers search_site through the imperative document.modelContext.registerTool(...) API. Connects the tool to the visible search UI through a reusable adapter. Verifies the rendered route, executable script ordering, same-origin index and runtime, asset integrity, schema, and declared tool metadata. Advertises WebMCP readiness only when the complete generated artifact passes those checks. The runtime supports cancellation, bounded input, cached index loading, explicit cache invalidation, and theme-owned ranking through an adapter. The current shared implementation intentionally supports a read-only site-search journey; future write or product-specific actions will require separate authority and product contracts. What people and agents can do together Before this addition, a person could search the documentation, but an agent had no explicit contract for using that experience. It had to infer controls or search elsewhere. Now the person can open the OfficeIMO search page and ask Codex to find Word-to-PDF resources using the page's Website Tool. Codex invokes search_site , receives three structured matches, and leaves the OfficeIMO results visible. The person can verify the query, inspect the result cards, and continue browsing from the same page. Challenges we ran into Generated static sites create a different reliability problem from server-backed tools: configuration may look correct while the deployed page is missing its route, index, script, or fingerprinted asset. We therefore treated rendered output as the contract and added both local and remote readiness checks. We also needed to keep structured agent results synchronized with the theme's human-facing search behavior. PowerForge.Web provides a fallback search surface and an adapter that lets richer themes own ranking and rendering without replacing the shared WebMCP runtime. Accomplishments One reusable implementation in the PowerForge.Web engine rather than seven unrelated site scripts. A live, read-only Website Tool recognized and invoked by the ChatGPT/Codex integrated browser. Fail-closed verification of the actual generated and deployed artifact. Visible synchronization between the structured tool call and human search page. Opt-in deployment across seven independent Evotec documentation sites: evotec.xyz, evotec.pl, OfficeIMO, HtmlForgeX, IntelligenceX, CodeGlyphX, and TestimoX. Normal search behavior remains available in browsers without WebMCP. Work completed during the challenge PowerForge.Web existed before the challenge. The WebMCP capability was added as a meaningful extension during the challenge period on September 2-3, 2026. PR #860, Add verified WebMCP site search support: https://github.com/EvotecIT/PSPublishModule/pull/860 PR #865, Define safe WebMCP portfolio rollout: https://github.com/EvotecIT/PSPublishModule/pull/865 Registration runtime: https://github.com/EvotecIT/PSPublishModule/blob/main/PowerForge.Web/Assets/WebMcp/site-search.v1.js Implementation and operating documentation: https://github.com/EvotecIT/PSPublishModule/blob/main/Docs/PowerForge.Web.AgentReadiness.md The dated pull requests and commit histories distinguish this WebMCP work from the pre-existing engine and websites. What we learned Adding registerTool is the small part. A reusable implementation also needs truthful discovery, bounded inputs, same-origin resources, script-order guarantees, browser fallback behavior, visible state synchronization, and validation of the final deployed files. Treating those pieces as one contract made the feature safe enough to enable across multiple sites. What's next The next phase is to add richer read-only journeys where a site has a real domain-specific task, such as navigating API surfaces or comparing documented capabilities. Write tools will remain opt-in and will be designed per product rather than enabled across the portfolio by default. Testing instructions Open https://officeimo.com/search/ in ChatGPT's integrated browser. Open the address-bar Site tools menu and confirm that search_site is available as one read tool with no write tools. Attach Browser to a Codex request. Ask: "Use the current OfficeIMO page's search_site Website Tool to find three resources about converting Word documents to PDF. Use only the Website Tool exposed by the page and leave the matching results visible." Confirm that Codex returns structured links and the OfficeIMO search page displays the corresponding query and result cards. No account or credentials are required. Built with WebMCP imperative API PowerForge.Web .NET and C# JavaScript Static HTML and JSON search indexes ChatGPT/Codex integrated browser Repository and license The implementation is available in the public EvotecIT/PSPublishModule repository under the MIT license: https://github.com/EvotecIT/PSPublishModule Built With c# javascript openai static Try it out officeimo.com github.com github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Przemysław Kłys Like Share this project: Updates Przemysław Kłys started this project — Sep 03, 2026 03:40 PM EDT

title: Agentready Network
pitch: The login you already have is the API. Agents investigate, humans authorize, receipts prove it.
about_excerpt: The login you already have is the API. Agents investigate, humans authorize, receipts prove it. Like Comment Story Updates The problem nobody has budget for Every operations team lives inside sites that will never ship an API for them. Monitoring in Grafana. Customer commitments in Cal.com. Payer portals, vendor consoles, admin dashboards. The person holding the session can see everything and change anything, but their agent can do nothing except screenshot the screen and guess where to click. WebMCP fixes this for sites that adopt it. Today that is roughly none of them. We measured three real open-source products, 522k lines of code, 429 places where a tool obviously belongs, and zero WebMCP registrations. So we asked a different question. What if the user adopts WebMCP for the site? The reframe WebMCP turns the login you already have into an API. A signed-in tab already carries every credential and permission the human has. If that tab registers tools with document.modelContext.registerTool , the agent gets a typed, narrow, inspectable interface to the site, and the vendor never has to ship a line of code. Adoption inverts. It no longer waits on ten thousand vendors. It happens one user, one tab, one reviewed pack at a time. What Agentready Network does Agentready Network is a local-first registry and runtime of reviewed action packs . A pack describes what a site can do, on exactly which origin, with which risk labels. The runtime turns that pack into live WebMCP tools inside the user's own signed-in session, then wraps every call in the safety the vendor never provided: Exact origins. A pack binds to one host and a reviewed fingerprint. Drift fails closed. Declarative, never executable. Manifests are JSON. The registry cannot ship code into your browser. Bounded, untrusted output. Results are allowlist-projected, byte-capped, and labeled contentTrust: "untrusted" . Tool output is content, not instruction. Human authority on consequences. Reads flow. Writes need a preview. Consequential actions need one exact, single-use approval bound to origin, tool, and normalized arguments. Change an argument and the grant is void. Verified closure. After a consequential action an inspector reads authoritative state and issues a receipt with no cookies, secrets, or raw bodies. Unknown outcome is reported as in_doubt , never as success. One concrete job, end to end The demo is not a feature tour. It is one incident. An alert fires in Grafana. Customer bookings in Cal.com are about to be affected. Neither site has WebMCP. The agent discovers the reviewed Grafana and Cal.com packs, installs them for this origin, and reads authoritative state. It never receives a credential. The agent prepares the exact continuity action and states what will change and how it will be inspected. The incident is still investigating . The human grants that exact action once, from a control the agent cannot reach. The agent executes once. The inspector verifies and issues one receipt. The incident is resolved . We poison the fingerprint. The pack refuses to run. We export the recorder draft. Every secret is gone before it can be published. Agents investigate. Humans authorize. Outcomes are verified. That is the whole product. What people and agents can now do together that they could not before Work a real incident across two unrelated vendor sites with no API contract between them. The user is the integration layer. Let an agent read freely and prepare freely, while every consequential step waits for a human decision the agent physically cannot forge. Hand a reviewer a receipt, not a screenshot, as proof of what changed. Teach a site once by observing its own traffic, then reuse that pack every session. Why WebMCP, specifically Screenshot-and-click pays the full cost on every step: a screenshot, a vision pass, a click that misses when the viewport shifts. We measured it. Creating one Grafana data source took nine browser actions and 55 seconds by DOM driving, and one WebMCP tool call in 20 milliseconds. A whole diagramming task took 44 calls versus 5. These are single-trial measurements from our audit work, not a benchmark suite, but the shape is unmistakable. The cost moves from per-action to per-app, and it never comes back. WebMCP also gives us the one thing a bookmarklet never had: a standard discovery surface. Any agent that speaks document.modelContext finds our tools without knowing we exist. How we built it Registry, Pack Lab, and runtime in plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. No framework. Every tool is registered with the current imperative API, document.modelContext.registerTool(tool, { signal }) , so tools unregister cleanly when a view unmounts. A Chrome MV3 extension injects reviewed read tools into the exact controlled Cal.com and Grafana origins and bridges receipts back to the registry. Reviewed adapters for Cal.com and Grafana were reverse-engineered on the wire, not from source. The recorder wraps fetch and XMLHttpRequest , clusters observed traffic, drafts tools, auto-flags mutating endpoints, and strips secrets before anything is published. Approval, inspection, drift, and redaction are enforced in the shared runtime, so every pack inherits them and no pack can opt out. Node's built-in test runner covers the trust boundaries. All tests pass on the submitted commit. What we deliberately did not claim The public judge path is a deterministic fixture so nobody needs an account. The same runtime drives the real Cal.com and Grafana adapters against controlled localhost instances; the video shows the controlled Grafana and Cal.com state alongside the public lab. The extension checkpoint is read-only. Remembered approvals, arbitrary-site install, generic DOM automation, and automatic rollback are out of scope. Figma taught us the frontier. Its control plane is reachable in-session; its canvas rides a binary WebSocket inside a Worker that no page-context patch can see. We published only what we proved and marked canvas manipulation unsupported. What we learned Discovery is observation, not code reading. Every tool we guessed from source was wrong. Every tool we drafted from the wire worked. Minification cannot rename what crosses the network. Injection inverts the safety burden onto the installer. The vendor never audited these tools, so we had to. That is why approval, inspection, and redaction live in the runtime and not in the pack. What is next Persist packs across sessions in the extension. Chain packs across sites so one agent can read portal A and act in portal B. Generalize the approval contract into a policy layer: read anything, never pay, never cancel, never touch what a human pinned. The first vertical we want to ship is healthcare payer portals, the most session-locked, human-attestation-gated surfaces on the web. Testing instructions for judges No credentials are needed. Open the live site in ChatGPT's browser or in Chrome with the WebMCP flag enabled, follow the 90-second path in the README, and use Reset between runs. Local run: npm test , then python3 -m http.server 8788 and open /site/ .
