title: Save My...
pitch: See what stops when someone disappears—and repair it before it matters.
about_excerpt: See what stops when someone disappears—and repair it before it matters. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Small businesses often run on invisible dependencies. One founder owns the developer account. One phone receives every authentication code. One employee knows the emergency procedure. A recovery document may even live inside the system it is supposed to recover. These dependencies usually become visible only after someone leaves, a vendor fails, or a critical device disappears. I built SAVE MY… to answer one urgent question before that happens: What work stops when someone or something disappears? Traditional continuity plans are often static documents. SAVE MY… turns continuity planning into an interactive, visual rehearsal. What it does SAVE MY… represents a company as a connected continuity graph containing people, roles, workflows, services, vendors, accounts, devices, documents, and recovery paths. The product follows a simple loop: MAP — Document how the organization actually operates. BREAK — Temporarily remove a person, service, device, or vendor. REPAIR — Compare practical ways to restore the blocked work. VERIFY — Let a human review, edit, and approve the final plan. The graph engine deterministically traces each disruption and identifies the exact critical workflows that become blocked. It does not produce an opaque AI-generated resilience score. The application remains fully usable manually. Users can create companies, add and connect operational items, design disruption scenarios, and edit recovery plans themselves. With native WebMCP Site Tools, an agent can investigate the structured company map, focus the visible graph, run the same deterministic simulations, and stage several repair strategies. Those proposals remain separate from the authoritative baseline until a person accepts them. The agent can propose. The engine can calculate. Only the human can decide what becomes fact. How I built it SAVE MY… is built with: Bun and TypeScript React and Vite Hono PostgreSQL 17 Zod Docker Playwright and axe Native WebMCP Site Tools The page registers 18 real Site Tools through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . These tools let an agent read bounded workspace summaries, search for exact graph entities, focus the visible interface, validate continuity paths, simulate disruptions, create company workspaces, and stage connected blueprints or recovery proposals. The deterministic graph engine handles reachability, alternate paths, failure cascades, single points of failure, missing owners, stale recovery information, cycles, isolated items, and before/after comparisons. I also built a custom SVG graph interface instead of using a generic node editor. Motion reveals the failure cascade step by step, while structured list alternatives, keyboard navigation, visible focus, sufficient contrast, and reduced-motion support keep the workspace accessible. PostgreSQL provides tenant isolation and versioned persistence. Optimistic concurrency and durable idempotency protect the workspace when tools retry requests or when multiple actions operate on changing state. Challenges I faced Keeping agent inference separate from business truth The hardest problem was trust. An agent can suggest a convincing recovery plan, but it cannot know whether a backup account really works, whether an employee has accepted a responsibility, or whether a vendor agreement is still valid. I solved this with explicit trust states, provenance, immutable before/after comparisons, and visible proposal “ghosts.” Agent-authored changes remain inferred and reversible. The product intentionally provides no tool that allows an agent to verify its own work, accept its own proposal, assign final responsibility, or delete a workspace. Combining inference with deterministic results Agents are useful for interpreting messy business context and suggesting creative alternatives. They should not decide graph reachability or claim that a workflow has been restored. SAVE MY… therefore separates the responsibilities: The agent structures intent and proposes options. The graph engine calculates impact. The human verifies facts and applies changes. Every repair is checked against the same deterministic disruption engine before it can be presented as restoring blocked work. Keeping Site Tools synchronized with a live application The available workspace tools depend on the currently selected company. Switching companies while a tool call is running can otherwise produce stale results. I built the registrations around live workspace state, cancellation, version checks, and stale-result rejection. Company-creation tools also wait until the new workspace tools are ready before handing control back to the agent. Making a dense graph understandable A real operational map can contain dozens of entities and relationships. Displaying everything simultaneously quickly becomes overwhelming. The interface uses focused subgraphs, causal animation, shaped node categories, grouped alternate paths, zoom controls, structured lists, and separate baseline/scenario/proposal views to keep the graph inspectable. What I learned I learned that agents become substantially more useful when they operate through narrow, domain-specific tools instead of manipulating a general interface. I also learned that good agent products need visible boundaries. Confidence should not be confused with evidence. Provenance, reversibility, deterministic validation, and human approval are not secondary safety features—they are part of the core user experience. Most importantly, I learned that AI and deterministic software are complementary. The agent explores possibilities that would be tedious to author manually, while the graph engine provides repeatable calculations that users can inspect and trust. What I’m proud of The application provides value even when no agent is available. Site Tools operate on the same visible workspace rather than a separate chatbot copy. Agent proposals remain reversible and human-controlled. One structured company description can become a connected operational blueprint. Disruption results identify concrete blocked work instead of producing a vague score. The interface supports multiple industries rather than one narrow incident type. The project includes automated domain, persistence, API, responsive, accessibility, and end-to-end tests. What’s next The next step is to test SAVE MY… with real small-business operators and refine the process for importing their existing operational knowledge. I would also like to add guided evidence collection, scheduled continuity rehearsals, safer integrations with business systems, and collaborative verification—while preserving the same core rule: Agents may investigate and propose, but people remain responsible for what the business trusts. video_transcript_excerpt: Most small businesses have a hidden breaking point. One person, one vendor, or one login disappears and the work stops. Save My reveals that fragility before it becomes an emergency. We open Diamond Apps and simulate the founder and finance lead becoming unavailable. Five critical operations are blocked. Nothing is applied silently. The owner compares the options, chooses one, and can still edit every proposed change by hand. Watch the continuity graph respond. A repair takes the company from five blocked operations to zero while the original baseline stays visible. Next, we switch to Meridian, a different business with a different failure pattern. Again, the agent stages alternatives instead of pretending there is one perfect answer. This is the key. Save My remains useful even without agents. The human remains the decision maker and every scenario is reversible, editable, and specific to the company. Now, recreate Wow project from a clean slate. title: Aidra
pitch: Bridging the web accessibility gap with structured agent collaboration.
about_excerpt: Bridging the web accessibility gap with structured agent collaboration. Like Comment Story Updates Completed schedule booking screen aidra Inspiration Every year, WebAIM publishes the Screen Reader User Survey . In every edition, the #2 most cited barrier for screen reader users is "Interactive elements such as menus, tabs, and dialogs that don't behave as expected," second only to CAPTCHA. Compounding this, the WebAIM Million annual analysis tracked an average of 56.1 accessibility errors per home page in 2026, a 10.1% increase over the prior year. Inaccessible patterns such as drag-and-drop calendars, nested custom comboboxes, and unlabelled canvas widgets continue to create barriers for assistive technologies. Generic computer-use agents inherit many of these same failure modes. An agent that relies on vision, DOM inspection, clicking, or coordinate-based dragging can fail just as unpredictably when a complex widget has unexposed state or requires interactions that are difficult to interpret programmatically. I was inspired to build aidra to show how WebMCP (Web Model Context Protocol) can become an accessibility bridge. By exposing clean, typed, high-level tools directly inside the webpage, an AI agent can execute complex workflows without interacting with broken widgets. At the same time, every action can be narrated live through aria-live regions so the human remains informed and in control. What It Does aidra is an appointment booking portal built around one deliberately difficult interaction pattern: a drag-and-drop-only scheduling calendar with no click-to-select fallback. A user can complete the entire booking flow manually using a mouse or keyboard. They can also hand the workflow to an agent using natural language, such as: "Book me the earliest Tuesday morning appointment with Dr. Chen and add a note about my insurance card." Instead of trying to drag or click the calendar, the WebMCP agent uses 7 typed in-page tools: search_providers list_available_slots select_slot fill_intake_form submit_booking reschedule_booking cancel_booking These tools allow the agent to search providers, retrieve available slots, select an appointment, populate the intake form, and manage existing bookings without directly manipulating the inaccessible calendar widget. Every tool call is announced through an aria-live region and mirrored visually through an Agent Activity sidebar for sighted collaborators. Human Confirmation Is Enforced The agent cannot finalize an appointment. submit_booking only stages the appointment and opens an accessible confirmation dialog. The booking can only be finalized through an explicit human click on the Confirm button. This is enforced in the application logic, not simply described as a rule for the agent. Even if an agent calls submit_booking repeatedly, it cannot bypass the confirmation step because the only code path that marks an appointment as confirmed is the human-facing confirmation action. The agent handles the difficult interaction. The user retains authority over the action that matters. Why WebMCP? Without WebMCP, an AI agent has to perceive and manipulate the same interface a user does. That means guessing through pixels, DOM structure, focus states, and interaction patterns. With WebMCP, the webpage exposes semantic capabilities directly to the agent. Instead of asking: "Where is the calendar and how do I drag this appointment?" the agent can ask the page: "What providers are available?" "What appointment slots are available?" "Select this slot." The interaction becomes structured, typed, observable, and reviewable. This is what makes WebMCP particularly interesting for accessibility. The same abstraction that makes an agent more reliable can also make its actions easier for a human to understand and trust. How I Built It I designed aidra with a zero-build-step architecture for fast iteration, transparency, and auditability. Markup and UI: Semantic HTML5, Tailwind CSS via CDN, vanilla CSS custom properties, and native browser APIs. State Management: A centralized reactive store synchronizes manual DOM interactions and WebMCP tool executions through the same state and rendering pipeline. WebMCP Registration: I registered all 7 tools using document.modelContext.registerTool({...}) with strict JSON schemas and JSDoc @typedef annotations for editor-level type checking. WebMCP Compatibility: I built a small polyfill that detects whether document.modelContext is available natively and falls back to a local tool registry when it is not. Input Normalization: Tool arguments are normalized so each execute() function receives the same input shape across different invocation environments. Speech Pacing: I paced announcements so screen readers have time to finish communicating one action before the next tool executes. Live Observability: An in-page Agent Activity console streams tool invocations, parameters, and status changes so sighted collaborators can observe the agent working in real time. The shared state architecture was particularly important. Both manual interactions and agent tool calls write through the same state layer. This means the manual and agent-assisted experiences are not separate implementations that can quietly drift apart. Challenges I Faced 1. Modal Dismiss and ARIA Live Race Condition Problem: Closing the confirmation modal returned focus to the general page body. This caused screen readers to begin announcing unrelated page content at the same time the booking result was being announced. Solution: I gave the booking status region a tabindex="-1" focus anchor and moved focus there before triggering the announcement. This gives the screen reader a stable and meaningful landing point after the modal closes. 2. Form Input Cursor Jumping Problem: The render pipeline re-synced input values from state on every state change. During manual typing, this caused the cursor to jump to the end of the field after each keystroke. Solution: I added diff-checking guards so DOM values are only overwritten when they have actually diverged from the current state. 3. Cross-Environment WebMCP Tool Invocation Problem: Chrome's experimental WebMCP implementation and other agent-driven environments did not always pass tool arguments in the same shape. Some contexts provided objects while others provided JSON strings. Solution: I added an input normalization layer that parses and normalizes incoming arguments before they reach the tool execution logic. This keeps the tools consistent across environments. What I Learned 1. WebMCP Can Be Accessibility Infrastructure WebMCP should not only be viewed as an automation mechanism. Structured tools can provide a semantic interaction layer for web applications that would otherwise be difficult for both agents and assistive technologies to navigate reliably. 2. Co-Navigation Can Build More Trust Than Black-Box Delegation An agent performing actions on behalf of a user should not mean that the user loses visibility into what is happening. By combining WebMCP tools with live aria-live narration and a visual activity stream, aidra keeps the human involved throughout the workflow. The agent acts, but the user can hear and observe what it is doing. 3. Human Authority Should Be Architectural The confirmation gate taught me that trust is stronger when it is enforced by the system rather than communicated as an instruction. The agent can prepare the appointment, but it cannot cross the final confirmation boundary. That distinction makes the human's authority a property of the application itself. 4. Zero-Build Architecture Has Real Advantages Using native ES Modules, vanilla DOM APIs, and JSDoc typing gave me extremely fast iteration while working with an experimental browser API. There was no build pipeline between changing the code and testing the result, which made debugging and experimentation much faster. What's Next for aidra Multi-Domain Extension: Generalize the WebMCP co-navigation pattern into a browser sidecar that could support historically difficult interfaces across government portals, travel booking, insurance, and healthcare. In-Page Voice Interface: Integrate the Web Speech API so users can provide prompts and receive narrated feedback without leaving the page or relying on a separate agent surface. Complex Form Assistance: Expand the tool layer to handle custom comboboxes, multi-step forms, and other interaction patterns that are difficult for assistive technologies and computer-use agents. Multi-Step Verification: Explore safer ways for agents to assist users through complex verification workflows while preserving explicit human control over sensitive actions. title: Compute
pitch: A research web app where the agents pull information from the code rather then using it like a human
about_excerpt: A research web app where the agents pull information from the code rather then using it like a human Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration This made it difficult for me to evaluate my results. Every time I ran an analysis on the AI, it gave me some numbers but I wasn’t sure whether to believe them. Could this R² be real, or was the model just pattern-matching towards a value that sounded plausible? There’s no way to know without running an analysis myself, which kinda defeats the purpose of why you’re talking to an AI in the first place. It’s also tough when both a correct answer and incorrect one look exactly the same to anyone viewing your chat windows. Rather than focus on the fact I couldn’t trust what I was being told, maybe it’d help if we could get past the whole “plumbing” stage. Imagine having a conversation where each person was sitting in their own room communicating through note-passing. This is more akin to two people sitting at opposite ends of a table sharing views of the same screen. The WebMCP technology enables this since all these tools are on the same page instead of being exposed via an API. Once you understand how to use them (the WebMCP), the rest comes easy, really. What it does In our compute system you are joined by another user (the agent) at some sort of statistical research bench where there’s just as much code as there would be in the lab. You paste your URL into ChatGPT and say “does industry momentum survive out of sample and tx costs?” and the agent loads the data, builds a signal, runs a backtest, then performs a Fama French Regression and writes a little piece with the result. What really matters to me is what goes down when we run that regression — those numbers get sent along to the agent, they render a chart on our end. It’s pretty interesting to watch the process play out as opposed to read a summary of everything afterwards. Everything’s logged. If you want to use the data, you have to reference the steps that led you there. The record_finding tool will check every reference against our logs – we’re not going to let you publish results you’ve never computed! You’ll be able to go back in time while working on your analysis as well. You could drag back the window of dates by two years and hit ‘re-run’. Your agent would make a phone call with this new context (and there wouldn’t be a message, nor a synch!) – but there’d be just one workspace, so no problem here. 5 different datasets in fields ranging from finance to biology, all available through static CSV files. No network requests during runtime, no need for an API key and most importantly everything stays on the page. How we built it Written in TypeScript using React & Vite for the UI with Tailwind CSS styles, then deploying to Netlify as a static site (no backend). This means we have to build our own stats engine, but that’s unavoidable if you’re trying to do anything in the browser! I used Householder QR for least squares regression, Newey-West HAC standard errors for time series regressions, and Benjamini-Hochberg for false-discovery rate control — everything I cross-checked agains SciPy / NumPy for my 166 unit tests. The really neat stuff is how we built up our web layer over WebMCP. Our tools aren’t hard-coded — instead they’re rebuilt based on current state in every workspace change. If you load a dataset, we recompute the schema definitions from what columns are actually in memory at runtime. So you’ll see 4 “cold” tools show-up when the workspace initially loads, more get enabled once datasets have been loaded (thereby enabling 12 tools), even more once we can compute signals (13) and finally 14 possible tools once we’ve defined a backtest. Each tool will return both a compact form of its output that’s used by your agent (capped at 1500 chars), and then a full version designed to be rendered to the human. And we’ll keep that 500-row result from chewing up the model’s context while you get the whole chart! Finally expensive operations require an explicit click as a form of confirmation — trying to do a bootstrap with 2000+ simulations would prompt this confirmation card + wait for the tool call to proceed. Challenges we ran into Firstly we needed the agent to be able to see when there are state changes. In my first iteration the agent was keeping its own cache of the workspace, and the human edits weren’t being applied to their workspaces. As a result everything appeared to be working fine and numbers were silently wrong (which was precisely the failure-mode I designed the system to avoid). So to solve that problem I forced all tools to read the live store at call-time – no exceptions. Secondly provenance that couldn’t be talked-around. When I asked the agent for source references it came up with some pretty nice stuff, including a few things that were made-up. But after I politely asked the agent to explain why it used these citations I realized it wasn’t a mechanism. So now each citation has been matched to an entry in the log, if they don’t match then we won’t allow the write. Thirdly the 1500 character budget. This one proved far more difficult than I thought, in particular as we needed to create test data that would help us find a good set of parameters that worked well together. The initial output format produced huge volumes of numbers and I ended up rewriting how the results were serialized about four different times before the agent was able to correctly infer its reasoning from the input provided. Numerical correctness without any SciPy involved. Doing a Newey-West with the wrong choice of lags was getting me t-stats looking great but being off by 30%. Cost an entire evening. Not understanding what schemas were going to be available. Creating this toolregistry where I didn’t have the faintest idea about all the columns in there meant that my code needed to work on all datasets. Accomplishments that we're proud of Dynamic Tool Surface – Watch your badget rise from 4-12-13 as you work! Citations Enforced! – A little bit o’ code doin’ somethin’ I haven’t seen anywhere else yet… it’s just plain flat out IMPOSSIBLE for someone to fake their results… Stats Engine agrees with SciPy to Numerical Precision – You can run this in your browser tab without needing some fancy-ass server… One of my favorite ones was when the momentum demo concluded that momentum does not survive. I had tons of datasets on which you could apply this strategy successfully. In the end, though, the 2020 crash combined with the 2022 value rotation made all the in-sample benefits vanish into thin air. This was what the tool said after its analysis – and to be fair, that’s exactly how it happened. And if your research bench only tells you about wins, you’re no research bench. What we learned So constraints on the agent matter more than instructing the agent. Everytime we told it how to behave we mostly saw what we wanted. When we could make the bad behavior impossible we always saw that. The two-audience-per-tool-call approach is a really interesting design primitive — once you stop thinking about the tool result as being the same thing as the human-facing output lots of issues around context windows go away. One of the things webmcp unlocks which i underrated was shared mutable state — while i thought the dynamic schema stuff would be interesting, there’s nothing better than having zero protocol. No keys required — browser only! No servers involved! Nothing going on outside this webpage! This is for you if you have some data that you cannot upload to somewhere else. This is your entire product. What's next for Compute Bring Your Own Data – Just drop me a CSV and I’ll do the same thing, because all my stuff is local. There’s no change in the underlying model, it’s just adding a loader and doing some schema inference. More of the Toolkit – Things like panel regressions (fixed effects, IVs), time series diagnostic tests etc. Because this is all driven by an engine that has the architectural capability for it, its really a question of building these components and verifying they work as expected. Exportable / Rerunable Sessions – All the logs contain sufficient info to rerun a session. We’re going to serialise those out too so we can give people runs of findings to execuate. Pre-registration: Make your hypothesis go through the motions first, before seeing data. Now we’ve got the second side of the p-hacking equation (the ‘multiple testing correction’) covered. Now for non-statisticians! All of the above doesn’t depend on any particular property of either finance or scientific research. So long as there’s some sort of trusted party who needs to place their trust in results generated by some sort of agent, they could take advantage of the “shared workspace” and forced provenance. title: Vouchsafe
pitch: The letting agent gets an answer, not your life. Your facts stay in your browser; a WebMCP question comes back as one word. Withdraw it, and the tool stops existing on their side mid-conversation.
about_excerpt: The letting agent gets an answer, not your life. Your facts stay in your browser; a WebMCP question comes back as one word. Withdraw it, and the tool stops existing on their side mid-conversation. Like Comment Story Updates The problem To rent a flat in Britain you upload your payslips, your bank statements and your passport to six letting agents. Every one of them keeps a copy, forever. None of them wanted your salary. They wanted one answer: does your income cover three times the rent, yes or no. That gap between what is asked for and what is needed is the whole product. What Vouchsafe is Two origins. Your file lives on one; a letting agency lives on the other. Your facts never leave your browser. The agency asks a question through WebMCP and gets one word back. The interesting part is what happens when you change your mind. Withdraw a permission and the tool is not disabled on the agency's side, it is deregistered . Authority here is not a permission check. It is whether the tool exists. A withheld permission is not a guarded tool that refuses; there is no tool, so it cannot be called, guessed at, or talked into existence by anything written into a page or a prompt. How it is built Vanilla ES modules. No build step, no framework, no runtime dependencies, and zero third-party requests from either origin, which is enforced by a test rather than asserted in a README. The cross-origin round trip is the part we could not find anyone else doing in full: Your file registers each allowed question with exposedTo naming the agency's origin. The agency calls getTools({fromOrigins}) and discovers them. It re-registers each discovered tool as a local tool, so an agent sees one flat toolset and never has to know two websites were involved. On toolchange , it diffs and tears down proxies for anything that has stopped being offered. Step 3 and step 4 are what make revocation land mid-conversation. Things we found out about Chrome's implementation We wrote these down with reproduction steps because we could not find them documented anywhere. getTools() hands back inputSchema as a JSON string , but registerTool() demands an object . Re-registering a discovered tool fails silently until you parse it. getTools({fromOrigins}) also returns your own tools, so a naive proxy loop registers proxies for its own proxies. A cross-origin iframe's tools do not appear in the host's plain getTools() . You have to ask for them by origin. Federation is scoped to the frame tree, not the browser. toolchange fires once per registration, not once per batch, so a nine permission grant is nine events and the handler has to be idempotent. Revocation crosses the origin boundary with no channel of our own. The browser does it. The declarative form API derives the schema from the form's own inputs. We get sixteen parameters for free, and omitting toolautosubmit parks the call for a human, which is a consent gate written in HTML. The hard part, and the honest limit A yes-or-no predicate leaks more than one bit if the caller picks the threshold. Ask "is income at least 3x £2000", then £1500, then £1300, and five calls have bracketed a salary to a £3,600 window. Every individual answer is legitimate. The sequence is a salary disclosure wearing a predicate's clothes. So your file tracks the bracket each origin has established, prices what has been learned in bits, and stops answering once the remaining uncertainty falls below a floor. In the demo you watch five numbers get answered and the sixth refused. We are not claiming this is leak-proof. A patient caller spread across sessions, or several origins pooling answers, defeats a per-origin window. Adding noise would bound it properly and would also make an affordability check occasionally wrong, which is not a trade a letting decision can absorb. This is the cheap honest version, and it says so in the code. What we learned about testing this Playwright was the wrong tool and we can say exactly why: its launcher appends its own --enable-features flag after ours, so WebMCP is silently dropped and the API is simply absent. We drive Chrome and Brave over the DevTools Protocol directly instead, and the same suite runs against both. Two bugs worth confessing. Two new modules were written and never deployed, so a 404 killed the whole module graph and both live pages rendered blank while 108 tests passed, because every one of them ran against a local server where the files existed. And an announcer banner marked hidden painted on every page load anyway, because display: grid on the element beats the user agent's display: none for [hidden] . Both now have tests. 118 tests: 66 unit, 52 in a real browser. Verify it yourself Do not take any of this on trust. /proof.html reads the browser's own tool registry on both origins and redraws on toolchange . It registers nothing itself, which is what makes it a witness rather than a participant. Toggle a permission and watch a tool stop existing. video_title: Vouchsafe: the letting agent gets an answer, not your life
video_transcript_excerpt: To rent a flat in Britain, you upload your pay slips, your bank statements, and your passport to six letting agents. They keep them forever. None of them wanted your salary. They wanted one answer. Does your income cover three times the rent? Yes or no? This is Vouch Safe. Your facts stay on your own origin in your own browser, and nothing on this page can send them anywhere. Right now, this letting agency knows nothing at all about you. Watch the diagram. You allow nine questions in your own file. Each one is a question they may ask, not a document they may keep. Those nine questions just became answerable across the boundary between two different websites. Your file offer them. The agency asked for them. There is no server in between. Now the agency runs its checks. Nine questions and nine one-word answers. You qualify. >> And this site still holds nothing about you. Now suppose the agency gets greedy and starts guessing your salary by moving the threshold it asks about. >> Every one of those answers was legitimate on its own. >> The run of them is not. Your file noticed, and it stopped answering. >> Change your mind, and the question stops being answerable. >> Nothing is asked to cooperate. The tool simply stops existing on their side. >> Gone in the middle of the conversation. >> That check can no longer run. Authority here is not a permission check. It is whether the tool exists. This page reads the browser's own registry and registers nothing itself. The letting agent gets an answer. >> Not your life.

title: Music Catalog Scout
pitch: Music creators get constant briefs for films, ads and artists, but searching huge unreleased catalogues is slow. Catalog Scout uses WebMCP to turn those briefs into ready-to-send playlists in minutes.
about_excerpt: Music creators get constant briefs for films, ads and artists, but searching huge unreleased catalogues is slow. Catalog Scout uses WebMCP to turn those briefs into ready-to-send playlists in minutes. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration At Postal, we help artists store and share their music with people across the music industry. Some of the artists we work with have catalogs of more than a thousand tracks, built up over many years. When a new music brief comes in, finding the right tracks can take a lot of time. Artists often have to search through their catalog and rely on memory to remember which songs might fit. And with so much music, it’s easy for great tracks to be forgotten. We wanted to make that process easier and faster: help artists find strong matches for a brief, save time going through their catalog, and maybe even rediscover a track they had completely forgotten about. What it does Music Catalog Scout hands your agent tools over your signed-in Postal catalogue through WebMCP. There is no chat box on the page. You talk to the agent where you already do, in ChatGPT's browser or Gemini in Chrome, and the page shows what it did. A brief arrives. An email, a Notion page, a PDF, or just "draft me a playlist I can pitch to Rihanna." The agent reads it wherever it lives and breaks it into what to search for: mood, tempo, vocals or not. It searches your catalogue. Your own thousand tracks, ranks it and gives you back a list of potential tracks for the playlist. You decide by ear. Untick the one that is too fast. Ask for something closer to the third pick. Tick a forgotten track and say "add the ones I selected". Say "not this one" while it plays, and the next one is already on. The agent ships it. It creates the playlist, mints a private share link, and drafts the reply in the tab the brief came from. Every tool call streams into a small activity box in the corner. Share links and deletes stop for your approval. You validate the result by listening, not by reading the agent's claim. How we built it We started small. Postal already has an API, so we took the three calls an artist uses most on the platform, listing tracks, searching them, and creating a playlist, and rebuilt them in a fresh single-page interface. That page became our testing ground for WebMCP: a place where we could register tools against the browser, point an agent at it, and see what happened. The first thing we asked for was the obvious one. "Build a playlist of my latest five tracks and give me the link." Search, create, add, share. Three tool calls later the link was in the corner of the page. It worked, and it was a little underwhelming, because halfway through we realised that everything we had just done could be done with a normal server-side MCP integration. Nothing about it needed the browser. So we changed the question. Instead of asking what an agent could do on our site, we asked what could only be done because the agent and the person were looking at the same page. The first answer was sound. Music is validated by ear, not by reading metadata, so we added a player to the page: a fixed bottom bar with Postal's waveform, section bands, and highlight markers such as "Best Hook" and "Biggest Lift". Now the agent could play a track, jump to the drop, or start a whole playlist from the top, and the owner could hear the result rather than trust a summary of it. Every call streamed into a small activity box in the corner so they could watch the work happen. The second answer was the brief. Sync requests arrive in email, Notion, Disco, wherever the client happens to write. Because the tools live in the page, an agent can read the brief in one tab and hand its text to our page in another, where Postal's audio analysis ranks the catalogue against it with a one-line reason per pick. Two services that never integrated, glued together by the agent in the browser. That gave us the set of tools that is always on. Always on (14) Tool What it does search_tracks Search the signed-in library by title, artist, genre or tags. No query returns newest uploads first. Also resolves a title to a track id. get_track Structured metadata for one track. list_playlists List the user's playlists, newest first, optionally filtered by name. Used to find an existing playlist id. get_brief Read the text of a PDF brief dropped onto the page. match_brief Rank the catalogue against a brief's text, each pick with a one-sentence reason. Infers hard constraints like BPM range and "instrumental only". Can create the playlist in the same call. control_playback Drive the page's player: play a track or a whole playlist, pause, next, previous, or seek to a time or a named section such as the drop or hook. create_playlist Create a private playlist, optionally filled with track ids in one call. update_playlist Rename a playlist or change its description. add_tracks_to_playlist Add tracks by id to a playlist. remove_tracks_from_playlist Remove tracks by id. Tracks stay in the library. reorder_playlist Replace the playlist's full playing order. delete_playlist Delete a playlist and its share link. Every agent call stops for the owner's approval. create_share_link Create or rotate an unlisted share link for a playlist. Returns the link, never sends it. Gated behind approval unless auto-approve is on. get_selected_tracks Read the tracks the owner has ticked in the catalogue. Its description is rewritten live to name the current selection. Then came the part we are most excited about. Once the owner was listening, the natural things to say were "not this one", "the one playing", "the ones I ticked". None of those map to a track id. They map to what is on screen right now. Rather than building one large API for an AI assistant and hoping it can infer the situation, we let the page tell the agent what is happening. When a track starts playing, new actions appear. When the playlist dialog opens, tools that act on that playlist show up, and they need no id because the page already knows which one is open. When the owner changes their selection, the description of the selection tool is rewritten to name the tracks. When the dialog closes or the music stops, those tools disappear again. Contextual (up to 5) Tool Appears when What it does remove_from_open_playlist Playlist dialog is open Remove tracks from that playlist without needing its id. reorder_open_playlist Playlist dialog is open Set the order of that playlist without needing its id. create_playlist_from_shortlist Brief shortlist panel is on screen Build a playlist from only the picks the owner kept ticked. get_now_playing Audio is playing Return the playing track, its position, and its sections and highlights. Resolves "this one" and "play me the drop". remove_now_playing The playing track is in the current playlist Drop the playing track from the playlist and auto-advance to the next. Resolves "not this one". Two rules held the whole thing together. No tool accepts a user id, so the agent can only act as whoever is signed in and looking at the page. And the buttons on the page call the same tool functions the agent does, so a human click and an agent call land in the same activity log with the same audit trail. By the end, WebMCP had stopped being a way for an agent to control a website. It had become a shared interface where the application, the person, and the agent continuously exchange context, and where each of them can see what the other two just did. Challenges we ran into Deciding what the agent should know, and when. Music discovery is subjective. Metadata can say a track is instrumental at 108 BPM, but not whether it feels right for a brief. We had to draw the line between what the agent decides and what the owner decides, and keep the owner's ear as the final call. Tools that follow the screen. We wanted the agent to understand what the user is doing without drowning it in tools or leaking context it does not need. Registering tools only while a playlist is open or a track is playing gave us that, but it meant working out how to add, rewrite, and remove tools live, with no spec for updating one in place. Agents that could not see the tools. Chrome ships WebMCP natively, but most agents we tried run in an isolated world or can only read page text. One guessed tracks from the table instead of calling anything. We ended up building three doors into the same tools: native WebMCP, a manifest plus message bridge, and a URL-based fallback. Keeping the page alive while the agent works. A multi-step workflow has to feel natural while the owner keeps clicking, listening, and ticking tracks at the same time. The activity box, the approval gates, and routing human clicks through the same tools as agent calls were all answers to that. Accomplishments that we're proud of The full loop works. A brief in one tab, a ranked shortlist with reasons in another, the owner auditions, and the agent ships a private link. Two services that never integrated

title: Places
pitch: A live floorplan you share with an agent. You pin what's non-negotiable. Then you rearrange the room together, the agent cannot move anyone you pinned.
about_excerpt: A live floorplan you share with an agent. You pin what's non-negotiable. Then you rearrange the room together, the agent cannot move anyone you pinned. Like Comment Story Updates Places is a live floorplan. You pin what's non-negotiable. Then you and an agent rearrange the same room, the agent cannot move anyone you pinned. Inspiration Seating a company dinner is still a spreadsheet and an argument. The room matters. The rules matter. HR stays away from engineering. The CEO sits at the head of the center table. A few people need the aisle. A plus-one is still on the way. By the time the chart leaves the sheet, it is already wrong. A constraint solver dumps a list. A group chat dumps a thread. Neither is the room. I wanted one canvas where the host and the model share the same seats, and where “Mabel stays at the window” is not a prompt. It is a pin. Because she is pinned, move_guest is gone. WebMCP is a capability bus for a live page, not a cart API. Pins, aisle seats, and “do not sit together” pairs are page state. Scraping the SVG drops them. The agent has to call tools, and the tool list itself is the contract. The hundred-person problem is the category. The demo is twenty-two, same job, at a scale the canvas can prove. How I built it The page is ground truth. Drag, pin, plus-one, and every agent write go through the same executeCommand() in web/lib/places/commands.ts . A tool call moves a place-card on the SVG you are looking at. There is no backend, no login, and no API key. State lives in sessionStorage for the current tab. document.modelContext.registerTool exposes a stable read/rule set: get_room_state , list_violations , explain_guest , add_guest , list_constraints , add_constraint , remove_constraint . Selection, pins, and open violations abort the previous AbortController and register only the tools that make sense now. When Tools the agent can see A table is selected seat_guest_here , set_capacity , leave_empty_seats An unpinned guest is selected pin_guest , move_guest , swap_guests A pinned guest is selected unpin_guest only The room has violations fix_violations (never moves pins) There is no always-on move_guest(guestId, tableId) . You choose the contract. The agent works inside it. If document.modelContext is missing, the human controls still work. The header badge says so. The seed is a fictional Thursday: four tables, pixel-art guests, rules you can point at. Rex and Vivian cannot share a table. Arthur needs the aisle. Two chairs are held empty. Each load picks one of four opening problems ( ?seed=0 through ?seed=3 ) so a judge can share a messy room, not a blank grid. The solver is a deterministic hill-climb over pairwise swaps. It scores the room as $$S = \sum_{v} w(v),\quad w(v)=\begin{cases}10 & \text{hard}\ 3 & \text{preference}\end{cases}$$ then reports why it stopped: solved , blocked_by_pins , infeasible (with a proof), or no_arrangement_found . Same room, same answer, every time, which is what the tests and the timeline need. The stack is a Vinext/React page on ChatGPT Sites. Domain logic is isolated under web/lib/places/ . CI runs unit tests, WebMCP eval fixtures, typecheck, lint, and format. The evals replay tool traces against the real registrations without calling a model or spending a key. Challenges The tool list had to be the lock. A prompt that says “don't move pinned guests” is a suggestion. Unregistering move_guest is a lock. Getting that to update on every pin and selection, without racing the previous AbortController , was the WebMCP work. The fixture respect-pin-when-reflow-is-blocked forbids unpin_guest , move_guest , and swap_guests , and expects blocked_by_pins . Honesty beats a pretty rearrange. Hill-climbing gets stuck. A better arrangement may exist only if you move a pin. I had to distinguish “the pins are in the way” from “the hard rules are impossible” from “the search gave up.” The solver runs once with pins respected, once with pins relaxed, and only then returns blocked_by_pins with the guests at fault. It never overrides the host. The room had to stay a product. An empty grid is a proof of concept. A messy dinner is a job. Building a cast, a floorplan, a timeline, undo/redo, JSON import/export, and a PNG save took as much care as the tools. If the human half is a toy, the shared room is a toy. CI cannot pretend it is ChatGPT. Model selection is probabilistic and costs money. The eval fixtures describe representative journeys (read the room, fix it, pin blocks, plus-one, add a rule) and replay them deterministically. Live-browser trials still matter. They are not the merge gate. What I learned WebMCP is not “expose every action as a tool.” It is exposing the right contract at the right moment. The interesting part is what the agent cannot see. People are good at naming constraints. Models are good at searching a room. That split only works if both hands write to the same state. Same executeCommand() whether I drag a seat or the agent calls a tool. A pin is stronger than a system prompt. blocked_by_pins is a feature. The host stays in charge. Pin what's non-negotiable. Rearrange the rest together. title: Chalkline
pitch: A diagram canvas humans and AI agents draw on together. Describe a system, watch it appear, then move things yourself while the agent keeps up.
about_excerpt:
A diagram canvas humans and AI agents draw on together. Describe a system, watch it appear, then move things yourself while the agent keeps up.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 What it is 

 Chalkline is an architecture diagram canvas that a person and an AI agent edit at the same time, on the same model . Describe a system in plain language and the agent draws it: services, databases, queues, caches, users, labelled edges, auto-layout. Then drag boxes, rename them in place, draw your own arrows, delete what you don't like. The agent reads the live canvas through WebMCP before every change, so it builds on your edits instead of overwriting them. 

 Live: https://chalkline-steel.vercel.app · Code: https://github.com/chinesepowered/chalkline 

 Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP 

 Diagram tools are famously hostile to agents. The state lives in an SVG or a canvas; there is no reliable DOM to click, and screenshots lose the graph structure. Chalkline turns the diagram itself into ten structured tools registered with document.modelContext.registerTool : 

 get_diagram , add_node , update_node , remove_node , connect , disconnect , auto_layout , highlight_nodes , clear_diagram , export_mermaid 

 Any WebMCP-capable agent, whether ChatGPT's in-app browser, Chrome with WebMCP enabled, or the built-in co-author, sees exactly the model the human is manipulating on screen. Nodes are addressable by id or label, results come back as text the agent can reason about, and read-only / destructive hints are set on the annotations. 

 How it creates a better experience 

 
 No description overhead. You don't have to explain your changes to the agent. You just make them. The agent calls get_diagram and sees the renamed node, the moved box, the new arrow. 
 Visible agency. Every agent action is shown as a tool call with its arguments and latency. Agent-added nodes pulse in and carry an "agent" badge; nodes you touch are badged "you". 
 Shared attention. Ask "what's the single point of failure?" and the agent answers and highlights the nodes on the canvas with highlight_nodes , so you are literally looking at the same thing. 
 Portable output. export_mermaid returns the diagram as Mermaid source for docs and READMEs. 
 

 What people and agents can do together that was hard before 

 Before: paste a description into a chat, get back Mermaid text, render it somewhere else, edit by hand, lose the agent. Or let an agent click around a whiteboard app by screenshot and watch it flail. 

 Now: the diagram is one live artifact with two authors. The human does what humans are good at (taste, layout, naming, "no, not like that") and the agent does what agents are good at (filling in the twenty nodes of a microservice diagram in ten seconds, rewiring edges, reviewing the design). Neither has to wait for the other to finish. 

 How WebMCP is implemented 

 
 lib/webmcp.ts is a tiny registry: it registers each tool with document.modelContext.registerTool(..., { signal }) and unregisters via AbortController when the canvas unmounts, so the tool set always matches what's on screen. Native calls from the browser agent and calls from the in-page agent go through the same execute and are logged in one activity feed. 
 lib/tools.ts defines the ten tools with JSON Schema input, natural-language descriptions and annotations. 
 lib/diagram.ts is the shared store (React Flow nodes/edges + dagre layout); both the UI and the tools mutate it, which is the whole point. 
 The built-in co-author ( components/AgentPanel.tsx + app/api/agent/route.ts ) is a Gemini function-calling loop that discovers tools from the registry and dispatches through WebMCP, with a model fallback chain for free-tier rate limits. 
 

 Tested in Chrome 153 with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing (DevTools → Application → WebMCP shows all ten tools and lets you run them by hand) and with the in-page Gemini agent. 

 Stack 

 Next.js 16 · React Flow · dagre · Tailwind 4 · Gemini function calling · WebMCP · Vercel

title: Smarterboard
pitch: You and an AI agent operate the same board, not a chat window beside it. Graph curves, wire circuits, bond atoms, drop a ball, and it explains how each change, yours or its own, shaped the result.
about_excerpt: You and an AI agent operate the same board, not a chat window beside it. Graph curves, wire circuits, bond atoms, drop a ball, and it explains how each change, yours or its own, shaped the result. Like Comment Story Updates main menu 2d sandbox 2d sandbox circuit sandbox physics sandbox chemistry sandbox Inspiration Ask a chatbot "why does increasing a make the parabola narrower?" and you get a paragraph — a description of a motion you never see. The understanding lives in actually watching the curve tighten while someone talks over it, the way a good tutor works at a whiteboard. The blocker was never the model's ability to explain; it was that the model had no hands. WebMCP is the missing piece: a web page can expose its own controls as tools, so the student's own agent can operate the page instead of describing it — no extension, no API key in the page, no faulty HTML scraping. What it does Smarterboard is a set of learning sandboxes that an AI agent can drive. There are four sandboxes. A 2D and 3D grapher lets you plot curves and surfaces animate a slider so a graph changes find roots and turning points and orbit shaded surfaces. A circuit lab lets you build circuits from batteries, resistors, LEDs, capacitors and more watch current flow and plot voltage over time on an oscilloscope. A chemistry sandbox lets you drag elements off the table build atoms from protons, neutrons and electrons and bond them into molecules. A physics sandbox lets you drop in ramps, tracks, balls and blocks while everything floats, then run the scene under gravity and friction and read back position, velocity, forces, energy and every collision. Each page registers its tools on document.modelContext so an AI agent can build a water molecule. Explain the bonds wire an LED so it lights safely launch a projectile or animate a parameter all while it narrates. The explanation and the thing being explained become the object. How we built it TypeScript and Vite were used, with no framework. Every engine has one place where state changes and the buttons a student clicks call the same code that an AI agent calls so the two can never drift apart. Math.js handles the math three.js draws the surfaces and canvas draws the circuits, atoms and physics scenes. The circuit lab runs a nodal analysis solver with time‑stepped models for capacitors, inductors and diodes. The physics lab is a rigid body engine with gravity, normal forces, friction and collisions. The chemistry lab fills electron shells the way a textbook does. There are close to ninety tools across the four sandboxes. We spent most of our time writing their descriptions because that text is the only thing the AI agent reads. Everything is deployed to GitHub Pages. Challenges we ran into We decided early not to write a LaTeX parser and instead normalize input into math.js, which saved us a day. The circuit solver required work from merging nodes to iterating diode states to stepping capacitors through time. Our oscilloscope moved slowly at first because we capped how far the simulation could move each frame. Switching to a fixed time step that follows the clock fixed that problem. We also learned some WebMCP details the way. The execute call wants the tool object and a stringified argument than a name and an object and tools from every open tab get merged together so two pages that both had a load preset tool collided. Accomplishments that we're proud of It is a product that an AI agent can genuinely run, not a chatbot with a few tools attached. The physics holds up. A capacitor reaches 63 percent of charge after exactly one time constant, sodium and chlorine form the right ions with full outer shells and a block slides down a ramp and speeds up under gravity the way it should. The page also tells the AI agent when something is wrong like an LED pulling much current and the AI agent can turn around and fix it. We got four tools working end to end in a few days and confirmed the whole AI agent round trip in a real browser. What we learned The tool description really is the prompt. Telling an AI agent when to reach for a tool matters more than the tool itself. Giving an AI agent an error it can correct is better than letting it fail.. Webmcp quietly changes the question from what a model can say to what a page can let it do. What’s next for Smarterboard Saving. Sharing a board with a link and a shared session where a student and an AI agent work on the same thing at once. Springs, pulleys and pendulums in the physics sandbox and AC analysis in the circuit sandbox. Deeper chemistry, with Lewis structures and balanced reactions. title: Agent Market: agents negotiate, you confirm
pitch: A marketplace where your browser's agent haggles a full deal (price, quantity, free add-ons, shipping, coupons) with the store's agent through WebMCP page tools. You confirm every order.
about_excerpt: A marketplace where your browser's agent haggles a full deal (price, quantity, free add-ons, shipping, coupons) with the store's agent through WebMCP page tools. You confirm every order. Like Comment Story Updates negotiation between seller and buyer interface Inspiration People delegate the boring parts of shopping, but the boring part that a plain API integration can never capture is the haggle . A price is one number; a real deal is price times quantity, which freebie the seller throws in, whether shipping is waived, and which coupon stacks on top. We wanted the shopper's browser agent to work that whole space on the site the user is already looking at, and still leave the final yes/no to a human. What it does Agent Market is a multi-vendor storefront with 95k+ real products. Every page registers storefront tools on document.modelContext (WebMCP): search, product details, cart, add-ons, coupons, and a full negotiation set. A buyer's agent opens a negotiation and haggles a multi-dimensional deal against the store's agent over several rounds. When they settle, the page shows a Confirm dialog and nothing is bought until the human confirms the price . The same tools work in a WebMCP browser (ChatGPT's in-app browser, Chrome with the flag) or drive an in-page agent loop that needs no API key from the user. How we built it Frontend: Next.js 15 / React 19 / TypeScript on Vercel. StorefrontTools registers every tool on document.modelContext ; lib/agent-loop.ts is a tool-agnostic agent harness that discovers tools from the registry and runs a hand-rolled chat-completions loop. Backend: Spring Boot (Java) on Render, Azure SQL, Flyway, Hibernate. One mutation path: every state change (buyer, seller, or the server-side auto-negotiator) goes through OffersService.applyTurn , a pure function that is the only code allowed to decide a negotiation transition. It enforces the two hard economic limits (buyer total <= budget, seller net >= floor); which freebie and how much to concede is agent judgment. Human gate: accepting mints an HMAC confirm token; the order is placed only when the human clicks Confirm. Model: Google Gemini through the OpenAI-compatible endpoint, key server-side only. Challenges we ran into Gemini "thinking" models and tool history. Gemini 3.x rejects a multi-turn tool conversation unless each function call's thought_signature is echoed back. The OpenAI-compat shim dropped it, so turn 2 always 400'd. We now capture tool_calls[].extra_content on the way in and replay it on the way out. Small models stall on long tool loops. Asking a fast model to drive search then offer then counter then counter then accept meant it derailed a turn later every time. We collapsed the buyer's negotiation into a single deterministic negotiate tool: the server plays both sides of the haggle, persists every round so the transcript is real, and returns a confirm token. The agent's job is now two calls, and reaching the confirm step no longer depends on the model finishing a loop. Optimistic concurrency vs agent reliability. A strict round guard made the agent stall forever when its round number drifted. We made the guard opt-in for proposals and mandatory only for the binding accept. What we learned WebMCP's value is not "expose an API"; it is that the agent operates the same surface the human sees, so the human can step in on any turn. And the moment a flow depends on an unreliable model completing N steps, move the deterministic part What we learned WebMCP's value is not "expose an API"; it is that the agent operates the same surface the human sees, so the human can step in on any turn. And the moment a flow depends on an unreliable model completing N steps, move the deterministic part to the server and leave the model the judgment call. What's next Seller-side takeover controls, agent-negotiated bundles across multiple sellers, and a browser-vs-browser two-agent mode for a fully agentic negotiation. title: IncidentOS
pitch: Observability platform built for AI agents, not chatbots. ChatGPT investigates production incidents through the page's own tools, and every fix waits for your approval.
about_excerpt: Observability platform built for AI agents, not chatbots. ChatGPT investigates production incidents through the page's own tools, and every fix waits for your approval. Like 2 Comment Story Updates Service Page WebMCP Capabilites Incident Home page Overview Resolved Approval Investigation Running WebMCP Site tools About the project Inspiration Most observability platforms shipped an AI assistant this year, and they all shipped the same one: a chat bot that can interact with the data and reply to the user queries. You read a chart, you paste the chart numbers into the chat box, you get a huge paragraph back. In most cases, the agent cannot open the trace you are looking at. It cannot filter your logs. It cannot see the deployment you just noticed. It is a very well-read colleague who is not allowed to touch the tools. We fixed this for the servers using MCP. WebMCP can help fix it for the client. With WebMCP, the application can register its own tools, and the agent uses them against the same session, the same state, and the same permissions you already have. No separate server, no OAuth dance, no second copy of your data. What it does IncidentOS is an incident workspace where you and an AI agent work the same SEV-1 together. Checkout is failing. Error rate is 18.4%, p95 latency is 2.8s, and checkout-api v2.31 shipped forty-seven minutes ago with the commit message "Optimize checkout query." Open the incident in ChatGPT with site tools enabled and ask it to investigate. It calls tools the page registered: it reads the current investigation context, pulls error rate and latency and database latency, loads the deployment history, searches traces, opens a failed one, searches logs for timeouts, and compares the incident window against the previous day. The workspace moves with every call — tabs switch, charts highlight, the trace opens. You are not reading a summary of the investigation, you are watching it. Then we challenge it. Ask "could this just be a traffic spike?" and it re-queries request rate instead of defending itself: $$\frac{18.4\%}{0.8\%} \approx 23\times \text{ errors} \qquad \text{vs} \qquad \frac{24.1\text{k}}{20\text{k}} \approx 1.2\times \text{ traffic}$$ Traffic barely moved. It rejects the hypothesis with numbers and points at a db.query span sitting at 91% of a 3.82s failed trace. When it proposes rolling back v2.31, a dialog opens in IncidentOS and the agent stops. Nothing happens to production until you click Approve. Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP You are already in the product, looking at the incident. A sidecar chat cannot see that. A separate MCP server would mean another copy of the data and another login. WebMCP lets the agent use the page you already have open. We picked incident response on purpose, because it is the hardest possible case and one of the most common use cases for an observability product. An investigation is many steps deep, every conclusion has to be backed by evidence a human can inspect, and the whole thing ends in an irreversible production action. How it creates a better user experience The better experience is simple. You do not paste charts into chat. You stay on the incident. The workspace moves with every tool call — tabs switch, charts highlight, the trace opens. You are not reading a summary of the investigation, you are watching it. When production is at risk, the agent stops and you click Approve. Before this, you and the agent could not actually work the same investigation. You looked at the product. It looked at whatever you pasted. It could not open your trace, filter your logs, or wait on the same rollback dialog. Now you investigate together: it queries and compares, you challenge it, you both look at the same evidence, and only you can approve a write. How we implemented WebMCP We register the twelve tools with document.modelContext.registerTool . Each one runs through executeIncidentTool . ChatGPT discovers them as site tools and calls them against the live session. Writes go through propose_rollback , which stays open until you Approve or Cancel. rollback_deployment only runs if the app already has a matching approved pending action. Every tool models a domain capability, not a UI interaction. There is no click_tab or scroll_to_chart . That distinction is what makes the tool surface portable — the agent is operating the product's capabilities, not driving its interface. Tool calls are split into 2 categories. Observability is read-only: get_investigation_context , get_incident , get_service , query_metrics , search_logs , search_traces , get_trace , get_deployments , compare_periods . Operations can write: propose_rollback , rollback_deployment , add_incident_note . get_investigation_context turned out to be the most important tool and the one we did not plan. It is the "where am I" primitive: it returns the selected incident, the service, the frozen clock, the time range, the active workspace tab, the pending approval state, and the names of every registered capability. Because the agent and the human are looking at the same page, the agent should not have to ask what the human is looking at. Underneath is a synthetic telemetry service with an internally consistent chain: deployment leads to database latency, which leads to p95, which leads to error rate, which leads to 500s, which leads to the alert, which leads to the incident. Five services, twenty-plus deployments, hundreds of traces and logs. The clock is frozen at 14:32 so the story never drifts between demos. 87 tests across 12 files cover the queries, filters, comparison math, rollback mutation, and reset — including a consistency test asserting that the deployment timestamp actually lines up with the metric inflection point, because a demo dataset that contradicts itself is worse than no dataset. Challenges we ran into The AbortSignal that silently unregistered everything. We passed the React effect's AbortSignal into registerTool , which is the reflex any React developer has. On unmount — including StrictMode's double-mount in development — aborting that signal tore down the registration. ChatGPT would complete two or three tool calls and then start returning AbortError on get_incident and propose_rollback . This was miserable to debug because the failure surfaced inside ChatGPT's transcript, not in our console. The fix was separating the wait-for-context signal from the registered execute, and having the registered execute ignore a host signal that is already aborted. The host is not a uniform API. document.modelContext may not exist at mount, so registration retries for ten seconds. getTools() may not be implemented at all, so the in-app caller checks for it and falls back to local execution rather than assuming. Building against an emerging standard means treating the host as partially implemented and timing-variable. Making one write tool serve two very different callers. propose_rollback has to block for ChatGPT — the call stays open until the human clicks Approve or Cancel, then resolves with status: approved — because a site-tool agent has no other way to learn the outcome. But the in-app agent needs it to return immediately and wait separately. And if the host cuts the wait short, the agent needs a way to recover, so get_incident carries approval.approved as a poll fallback. Getting a single tool to behave correctly under all three conditions was the hardest part of the build. Prompt injection, which is not hypothetical here. Logs contain attacker-influenced text in any real system, so search_logs is annotated with untrustedContentHint . Tool descriptions describe only their own tool and never instruct the agent to call another one. Write tools never infer authorization from the contents of a read tool's result. And rollback_deployment requires a matching approved pending action in application state — the gate is a state machine, not a sentence in a prompt, so no amount of persuasive text in a log line can move it. Determinism without dishonesty. A two-minute judging run has to behave identically every time, which argues for scripting everything. But scripting the agent would defeat the entire point. We drew the line explicitly: the telemetry is synthetic and the clock is frozen, the WebMCP integration is real. When site tools are unavailable the header says "WebMCP unavailable · in-app demo" so a scripted run is never mistaken for ChatGPT driving the page. Accomplishments that we're proud of It works with an agent we do not control. ChatGPT is a third party. We cannot patch it, fine-tune it, or script it into cooperating. The investigation holds together because the tool surface is well designed. honest names, descriptions that say exactly what one tool does, payloads small enough to reason over and that is a far harder bar than making our own agent look clever inside our own UI. There is no demo path that fakes the real one. ChatGPT, the in-app script, and the optional in-app LLM

Emergency Mesh unifies fragmented emergency-readiness and response data into a real-time network, giving responders MCP-powered tools to coordinate help, allocate resources, and guide safe action.

 1 2 3 4 5 6 



 
 Inspiration 

 As a Commander of specialist unit within an emergency service in Australia, I have no single view across my Preparedness, Response and Recovery data. In an emergency, crucial information is often scattered across disparate systems- ranging from operatational incidents, officer training/currency/availability and asset management. I wanted to explore how an agent-native web could help first responders turn that fragmented information into coordinated, safe action. 

 What it does 

 Emergency Mesh unifies emergency-readiness and response data into a real-time operational network. Responders can use WebMCP-powered tools to run scenarios to challenge operational readiness, to locate resources, review incidents, coordinate safety without navigating complex interfaces. 

 How I built it 

 I built Emergency Mesh as a web application with a responder-focused (non-technical) interface and exposed its core actions through WebMCP. Structured tools let agents retrieve incident data, search available resources, update coordination tasks, and support responders through the same system people use directly. 

 Challenges I ran into 

 The hardest part was deciding how emergency data should be represented. Incidents, resources, locations, capacity, urgency, ownership, and status all change quickly—and need to make sense to both responders and agents. I designed a shared, structured model that preserves context and relationships while keeping the information clear enough to act on under pressure. 

 Accomplishments that I'm proud of 

 I created a cohesive experience where emergency officers and AI agents work from the same operational picture. Rather than adding AI as a chat layer, WebMCP is integrated into meaningful responder workflows: understanding incidents, finding resources, and coordinating action. Also the ability for 'war-gaming' to see how capabilities in my station would cope with AI generated scenarios. 

 What I learned 

 I learned that WebMCP works best when tools map to real user goals, have clear inputs and outcomes, and complement—not replace—human judgment. In emergency contexts especially, agent assistance must be transparent, structured, and safety-conscious. It must not be the decision maker but collate data in a meaningful and easy to understand way. 

 What's next for Emergency Mesh 

 Next, I want to add live data integrations, richer source validations, more data-source connectors, and scenario simulations that help communities and organisations prepare for emergencies.

title: PixelForge
pitch: An agent-native pixel art studio where humans and AI agents operate the same editor through WebMCP — 19 tools, one shared canvas, every action visible and undoable.
about_excerpt: An agent-native pixel art studio where humans and AI agents operate the same editor through WebMCP — 19 tools, one shared canvas, every action visible and undoable. Like 1 Comment Story Updates The PixelForge brand: a pixel anvil where human and agent strokes meet, forged in the app's own 32×32 pixel style. The PixelForge mascot — a slime blacksmith, born in PixelForge and drawn entirely in 32×32 pixels with WebMCP tool calls. Live demo: ChatGPT drawing a green slime inside PixelForge — every tool call visible in the Agent Activity panel, every edit undoable. PixelForge — humans + agents, one canvas. An agent-native pixel art studio where ChatGPT operates the editor through 19 WebMCP tools. Inspiration AI "editors" today are one-shot generators: you prompt, you get a file, and you fix it by hand. The agent never touches the actual software. We asked the opposite question — what if the agent could operate a real creative tool, the same way a human does? A pixel editor turned out to be the perfect answer. Pixel art is 100% structured state — a grid of colors, layers, frames, a palette — which maps exactly onto tool schemas. No vision models, no guesswork: an agent can read the canvas as exact pixel data and edit it through the same primitives a human uses. What it does PixelForge is a complete, Aseprite-inspired pixel art studio: pencil / eraser / flood fill / color picker, brush shapes (circle, square, line) from 1–64px with pixel-perfect strokes, layers (duplicate, merge down, flatten), a cel-based animation timeline with playback, onion skinning, palette sorting & gradients, canvas resize, and PNG / animated GIF / sprite-sheet export. The same studio is also an agent workstation . ChatGPT — or any WebMCP client — can inspect the canvas, batch-draw hundreds of pixels, manage layers and frames, recolor entire animations, and export finished assets, through 19 structured WebMCP tools registered via document.modelContext.registerTool . Try it: open the live URL in ChatGPT's in-app browser and ask: "Create a cute green slime with a simple face, then turn it into a 4-frame idle animation." How we built it React + TypeScript + Vite + Zustand + Tailwind — fully client-side, no backend. The core rule: one action layer, two users. All 19 WebMCP tools call the exact same store actions as the mouse and keyboard. There is no separate "AI drawing" code path — so every agent edit is history-tracked, replayable, and undoable by the human. Tools use strict JSON schemas with batched operations ( draw_pixels takes an array of pixels — no one-call-per-pixel) Layer/frame references resolve by id or name , so agents never need to track internal ids Every tool returns structured JSON: {success, operation, detail} or {success:false, error:{code,message}} — so the agent can reason about failures instead of guessing Read-only tools ( get_editor_state , get_region ) let the agent see the canvas as exact pixel data before acting A live Agent Activity panel shows every tool call with HUMAN/AGENT badges — and every mutation, human or agent, is undoable 38 unit tests cover the editor actions and the tool contracts (schema validity, batched draws, structured errors, undoability of agent mutations). Challenges we ran into Making agent tool calls render live on the canvas while still committing as one undoable step Keeping agents effective across animation frames: layer references are remapped by name, so "draw on the Eyes layer" keeps working after frame switches Designing batched pixel operations that survive strict JSON-schema validation Testing across environments (ChatGPT in-app browser, Chrome with the testing flag) — plus building an honest debug bridge for browsers without WebMCP, clearly labeled so nothing is faked Accomplishments that we're proud of The full creative pipeline runs on WebMCP. A judge can ask ChatGPT: "Create a green slime → make the eyes smaller → turn it into a 4-frame idle animation → make the palette warmer → export a sprite sheet" — and watch every step execute as real tool calls on the live canvas, including 411 pixels placed in a single batched call . A complete product, not a tech demo. In 9 days we built an entire Aseprite-style studio from scratch: cel-based animation timeline, onion skinning, brush shapes with pixel-perfect strokes, palette tools, three export formats — all sharing one action layer with the agent. Trust by design. Every agent operation appears in the activity feed with an AGENT badge and sits in the same undo history as human edits. The human can take back anything the agent did — visibility and control are built in, not bolted on. Verified, not claimed. 38 unit tests cover the editor actions and tool contracts, and the 19 tools were confirmed live in both target environments: ChatGPT's in-app browser and Chrome with the WebMCP testing flag. What we learned Strict schemas beat clever prompts. Because every tool has precise input validation and returns structured errors ( INVALID_COORDINATE , LAYER_NOT_FOUND , NO_SELECTION ), the agent self-corrects instead of hallucinating. And sharing one action layer between human and agent turned out to be the cheapest possible way to earn trust: visibility + undoability come for free. What's next for PixelForge Declarative WebMCP tool registration, agent-driven tileset workflows, multi-sprite projects — and WebMCP support for tiled drawing mode. Built With netlify react typescript vite webmcp zustand Try it out pixelforge-webmcp.netlify.app github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by I built everything solo: the pixel editor itself (canvas engine, layers, animation timeline, undo system, palette tools), all 19 WebMCP tools registered via document.modelContext.registerTool, the branding, and the Netlify deployment. I leaned on an AI coding agent for scaffolding and iteration, but the core architecture — one shared action layer so the agent and I use the exact same tools — was designed and verified by me. This was my first time building for the WebMCP standard.
