title: ReturnReady
pitch: ReturnReady turns scattered receipts and work records into an evidence-linked, review-ready Australian tax return draft, using WebMCP to prepare, verify, and resolve gaps.
about_excerpt: ReturnReady turns scattered receipts and work records into an evidence-linked, review-ready Australian tax return draft, using WebMCP to prepare, verify, and resolve gaps. Like Comment Story Updates Start with a sparse FY2025-26 evidence draft, then complete it manually or let Codex populate structured facts through WebMCP. Codex records 3 disposals while preserving AAPL’s user attestation and BTC’s warning. Generated Review Pack with unresolved warning Inspiration This started with my own tax return. Most of it was prefilled, but my foreign shares and crypto weren't - so I was the one who had to get all of it in. That meant logging into each broker, exporting my holdings (every platform in its own format), and then typing each position in by hand. It's tedious, easy to get wrong, and it's the same job every year. The hard part was never the tax treatment. It was moving structured facts out of a pile of exports and into one draft I could actually review, without losing track of where each number came from or which ones the paperwork couldn't answer. That's the gap ReturnReady goes after. ReturnReady is a small WebMCP experiment: I attach synthetic evidence to Codex, Codex pulls the structured facts out (outside the page), and the app exposes a few narrow tools for recording and checking those facts. I still review everything and fill in anything the evidence can't prove. What it does ReturnReady opens on a sparse FY2025–26 draft with a bit of prefilled PAYG context. From there you can add deductions and disposals yourself, or ask Codex to do it through WebMCP. The demo walks through: 40 hours of work-from-home, at the prototype's fixed rate, giving a visible $28 deduction MSFT and AAPL foreign-share disposals a BTC disposal with the transaction fee left out on purpose The evidence doesn't contain AAPL's acquisition details, so validation raises a blocker instead of making the numbers up. You supply those facts yourself as a user attestation, which stays visibly separate from anything backed by a document. Once the blocker is cleared, ReturnReady builds a review pack, keeping the unresolved BTC warning and logging every action along the way. One thing worth being clear about: ReturnReady organizes evidence. It doesn't lodge returns, give tax advice, work out the authoritative tax, or claim your return is complete. The gains and losses are amounts I worked out myself and entered; the app records and checks them, it doesn't calculate them. Why WebMCP Normal browser automation has to read the DOM, guess what each control does, and poke at fields from the outside. ReturnReady skips all of that. It exposes six tools with tight JSON Schemas: get_return_draft record_deductions record_disposals record_acquisition_details validate_review_pack generate_review_pack Both the agent and the manual UI go through the same controller and the same domain logic. So WebMCP speeds up data entry without getting around validation, provenance, idempotency, or the audit trail and if WebMCP isn't available, the manual workflow still works on its own. How I built it ReturnReady is a static React app in strict TypeScript, built with Vite, no backend. It registers its tools imperatively with document.modelContext.registerTool() . Every tool checks its input against an allow-list at the schema boundary, then checks it again inside the handler. The page never sees the attached files or the raw document text. No tool takes a file path, a URL, a selector, executable content, or arbitrary JavaScript. All the bundled evidence and values are synthetic. For tests, Vitest and Testing Library cover the domain rules, the security boundaries, tool annotations, bounded outputs, idempotency, and making sure a human and the agent get the same result. Playwright runs the whole manual workflow end to end for accessibility. Challenges I ran into The main one was keeping a single trustworthy workflow across two ways in. Early on, validation triggered by the agent could look different from validation triggered by a human. I fixed it by deriving the modal and the review pack from shared controller state, and added a regression test that runs the real WebMCP handler against the rendered UI. The other challenge was one I felt as a builder: the page deliberately never touches the raw files. Part of me wanted to just let the app accept an upload and parse it, that's the obvious and easy path. But that's exactly the boundary that makes this trustworthy, so keeping all the file handling outside the page stayed non-negotiable, even when it made the build feel more restrictive than it had to be. I also kept the scope tight on purpose. ReturnReady shows the recorded facts and a fixed-rate deduction result, but it doesn't try to calculate capital gains or guess at missing acquisition data. Accomplishments that I am proud of 6 small WebMCP tools instead of handing over the whole browser one shared domain layer behind both the manual and agent paths provenance that clearly separates documentary evidence from user attestation invalid or conflicting calls get rejected cleanly, with no change to state repeat calls are idempotent, they don't pile up duplicate records a review pack that carries unresolved warnings through instead of hiding them a fully synthetic demo anyone can reproduce What I learned WebMCP earns its keep when it exposes what things mean, not when it turns every button into a tool. A small, semantic surface lets the agent move fast while the app keeps hold of the parts that matter: validation, state changes, and deciding what the person actually needs to review. What's next for ReturnReady More evidence categories, better review exports for an accountant, and a few real calculation methods so the amounts don't all have to be worked out by hand first, all while keeping raw-file interpretation outside the page and the same trust boundary intact. title: Evidence Workspace
pitch: A fail-closed release desk where browser agents check claims and humans control publication.
about_excerpt: A fail-closed release desk where browser agents check claims and humans control publication. Like 3 Comment Story Updates The problem Editors and analysts publish reports that combine claims, source excerpts, calculations, and approval decisions. A report can confidently say that weekly reviews increased by 40% even though the cited source says output rose from 50 to 60 — a 20% increase. Finding the mismatch is only part of the job. Someone still needs to decide whether a correction is appropriate and control what can be released. The product Evidence Workspace is a privacy-first, browser-local release desk for evidence-backed reports. It keeps the claim, the evidence, the calculation, the review history, and the final release decision in one revisioned workspace. The authored walkthrough starts with the 40% claim and the linked source showing 50 → 60 = 20%. The compiler exposes the disagreement beside the exact source passage and keeps export locked. What people and agents do together The human reviewer chooses which evidence a browser agent may use. The agent can then: discover the current claims and review state; inspect only shared evidence; run deterministic consistency checks; link or unlink evidence; record a review finding; and stage corrected wording with a compiler preview. The reviewer keeps every consequential action. The agent cannot change evidence-sharing permissions, approve its own proposal, confirm a finding, download a packet, or publish a report. When the agent stages a correction, the reviewer sees the proposed wording, the reason, and whether the corrected version would pass before deciding what to apply. Why WebMCP is necessary This is not a chat wrapper or screen-automation demo. WebMCP provides a typed, contextual interface over the same domain logic used by the React application. The agent does not need to infer button locations or scrape hidden application state. The tool surface is also state-dependent: While the report is unresolved, the browser client discovers ten review tools and export is unavailable. After every claim passes its deterministic checks and receives current human confirmation, an eleventh tool, review_export_packet , is registered. If a linked source becomes private again, the affected review is invalidated, release is locked, and the export capability disappears. Every write includes the expected workspace revision, so stale agent actions fail without mutation. Deterministic verification The compiler checks: evidence sharing and coverage; visible claim, metric, unit, and scope binding; exact excerpt binding; linked-source relevance and conflicts; source fact shape; percentage, before/after, and scalar values; and human confirmation as a separate release condition. It checks internal consistency against typed evidence. It does not claim to determine objective truth. Implementation and verification The React interface and WebMCP handlers call the same typed domain functions. The public-origin Chrome 150 path was tested with WebMCP testing enabled, including reads, evidence linking, deterministic checks, staged correction, stale/private/duplicate denials, dynamic export, invalidation, recovery, and export re-registration. The observed capability lifecycle was 10 → 11 → 10 → 11 → 10. The repository includes 73 automated contract tests, TypeScript checks, a production build, browser-local persistence and import validation, accessibility-related checks, and failure-path coverage. Boundaries The bundled walkthrough uses clearly labeled authored material, not customer data. Imported workspaces must contain validated typed facts and exact excerpts; arbitrary Markdown and PDF extraction are not implemented. Reviews and exported packets remain in the browser. There is no hosted database, account system, automatic upload, or multi-user collaboration. The live application and public source repository are available above. title: PersonalWebMCP
pitch: Teach a website workflow once. Reuse it as a personal WebMCP tool.
about_excerpt: Teach a website workflow once. Reuse it as a personal WebMCP tool. Like Comment Story Updates extension overview Teaching workflow Tools overview Project Story Inspiration WebMCP gives websites a reliable way to expose named, typed capabilities to agents. But the web will not become fully agent-ready at once. Many sites expose no tools, some expose only part of what a user needs, and even a well-designed site cannot anticipate every personal routine or preference. That led me to a simple question: why should only website developers be able to define capabilities for agents? I wanted to explore a user-owned layer for WebMCP. Instead of repeatedly asking an agent to rediscover the same buttons and fields, a person could demonstrate a workflow once, decide what should vary, and save the result as a semantic tool. On a WebMCP-enabled site, that same layer could personalize and combine the site's native tools rather than replacing them. What it does PersonalWebMCP is a Chromium extension that lets users create their own WebMCP tools on the websites they use. The extension works in three main ways: Teach a missing capability. The user performs a normal browser workflow, reviews the captured actions, and chooses which values become typed agent inputs and which remain remembered preferences. Personalize and compose existing capabilities. PersonalWebMCP discovers tools already exposed by the website and can combine them with taught actions as one higher-level personal tool. Keep capabilities understandable and repairable. Every saved tool has a name, description, JSON Schema input contract, origin and path scope, provenance, workflow graph, health state, and revision history. The saved capability is registered into the visible page through document.modelContext.registerTool() . A compatible agent discovers it beside the website's native tools and invokes it with structured input. The two central demonstrations show both sides of the idea: A legacy supplier portal exposes zero WebMCP tools. I teach an invoice-search workflow, expose vendor and min_amount as inputs, and an agent later invokes personal_open_latest_unpaid_invoice from another section of the portal. A furniture configurator already exposes five native WebMCP tools, but it lacks an Add to project action. I teach only that missing action, combine it with the native tools, remember my preferred configuration, and expose only quantity to the agent through personal_prepare_my_studio_workspace . How we built it I built PersonalWebMCP as a TypeScript and pnpm monorepo. The product is a WXT Manifest V3 extension with a React side panel, a service worker, an isolated content script, and a small MAIN-world runtime. That separation matters because WebMCP is page-scoped: document.modelContext belongs to the webpage, while extension content scripts normally run in an isolated JavaScript world. The MAIN-world runtime performs WebMCP discovery, registration, invocation, and tool lifecycle management. The content script carries validated messages across the page boundary, while the service worker owns compilation, execution, local persistence, scope, receipts, confirmation state, and repair history. The extension uses the WebMCP API directly: document.modelContext.getTools() discovers website-owned and registered personal tools. document.modelContext.registerTool() registers personal_ping and every saved personal capability. document.modelContext.executeTool() invokes native dependencies inside composite tools. abort signals and tool-change events manage registration and invocation lifetimes. The compiler converts a raw interaction trace into a reusable capability contract and workflow graph. It retains semantic evidence such as accessible names, roles, labels, landmarks, routes, and form relationships while excluding sensitive controls. Personal tools are stored locally and registered only when their origin, path, health, and prerequisites match the visible page. The companion demo site is built with Next.js and React. It supplies deterministic environments for testing a site with no WebMCP, a site with native tools, and a hybrid workflow. The extension remains the product; the hosted pages are controlled evaluation surfaces. Challenges we ran into The first challenge was the browser execution boundary. Registering a tool from an extension is not the same as registering one in ordinary page code, because the service worker and isolated content script cannot directly use the page's document.modelContext . Building a small, validated bridge between those worlds was necessary for genuine WebMCP registration. The second challenge was ensuring the result was more than a macro recorder. A literal recording tends to preserve unstable details such as a result row, changing price, or generated record ID. The compiler had to separate task intent from recorded outcome, let the user choose parameters versus preferences, restore the correct starting context, and expose a typed semantic contract to the agent. Navigation and lifecycle behavior were also difficult. Personal tools must appear on the correct origin and path, follow the active browser tab, refresh after saving, and withdraw or re-register as the page changes. Experimental browser behavior made real Chrome testing essential; a successful TypeScript build alone could not prove the WebMCP lifecycle. Finally, repair requires restraint. Automatically selecting a vaguely similar element may be worse than stopping. The implementation uses semantic evidence, visible outcome checks, versioned revisions, and guided approval when a replacement is ambiguous. Accomplishments that we're proud of A user-created tool is genuinely registered through WebMCP, discovered by an agent, invoked with structured arguments, and produces a visible result. The legacy demonstration goes from zero native tools to a reusable personal capability without requiring the user to write JavaScript or JSON Schema. The configurator demonstrates that PersonalWebMCP remains useful after WebMCP adoption: it combines five website-owned tools with one user-taught action as a single personalized capability. Personal tools retain provenance, local scope, typed contracts, execution receipts, health, and repair history instead of becoming opaque browser scripts. The same extension interface supports inspection, teaching, composition, execution, and repair while keeping the agent's actions visible to the user. What we learned The most important lesson was that WebMCP is not merely a cleaner way to automate clicks. Its value is the contract between a page and an agent: a stable name, a useful description, typed inputs, execution semantics, and a meaningful result. I also learned that native and personal capabilities are complementary. Website developers are best positioned to expose safe, general primitives. Users are best positioned to describe the higher-level routines and preferences that matter specifically to them. A personal capability layer can connect those two levels. Building the extension also made the WebMCP lifecycle very concrete. Registration context, abort signals, navigation, tool discovery, schema quality, scope, and error messages all directly affect whether an agent can use a capability reliably. What's next for PersonalWebMCP The next priority is making the compiler and semantic execution engine reliable across a broader range of real websites, beyond the controlled fixtures. I would also like to add intent-first teaching, where the user describes the desired capability before demonstrating it, and PersonalWebMCP asks only for the missing actions or choices. Other directions include portable tool export and synchronization, richer repair learning, multi-site compositions, stronger review controls for consequential actions, and support for more WebMCP-compatible browsers and agents. Longer term, frequently created personal tools could also help website teams understand which native capabilities their users actually want. title: Cyfix
pitch: Fix web security with humans and agents together - passive-only scans an agent can run, but only a human can authorize.
about_excerpt: Fix web security with humans and agents together - passive-only scans an agent can run, but only a human can authorize. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Every website has a short list of security basics that are cheap to check and cheap to fix: is HTTPS enforced, is HSTS set, does a CSP exist, are cookies flagged HttpOnly, is /.env sitting there in public. Almost nobody checks them, because the work is tedious, the output is jargon, and the tools are built for security engineers rather than for the person who actually owns the site. This is exactly the shape of work an agent should do. But "scan this domain" is not a neutral action — it touches someone else's server, and it carries legal and ethical weight. It has to stay a human decision. Most agent security tooling resolves that tension by removing the human. We wanted to keep them, visibly, in the loop. What it does Cyfix runs a passive-only security scan of a domain you're authorized to test, scores what it finds by severity, explains each issue in plain language, and gives you a copy-pasteable fix. An AI agent in the browser can drive that entire workflow itself through WebMCP — propose a domain, run the scan once you approve, triage findings, draft the CSP header, verify the fix, export the report. Every action, human or agent, lands in a shared audit log. What it will never do: exploit anything, brute force anything, scan ports, or send a single state-changing request. How we built it Next.js 15 (App Router), React, TypeScript, Tailwind, Zustand, deployed on Vercel. Seven tools are registered with document.modelContext.registerTool() from the root layout, so they're discoverable on every page — an agent landing anywhere on the site finds them immediately. Where a browser doesn't implement document.modelContext yet, Cyfix installs a same-shape polyfill, so the tools always exist and stay testable from the on-page Agent Console. Every tool resolves to an MCP-compatible envelope (content blocks, isError, structuredContent). The gate lives in the human's UI, not in a prompt: scan_domain reads the state of a checkbox the human can see and untick — a precondition the tool evaluates, not an instruction an agent could argue past. prepare_scan is the agent's way of asking: it proposes a domain but deliberately leaves the approval box untouched. Approval is scoped to one domain and revoked the instant the target changes. The dashboard is laid out as an application: a persistent left rail carries the sections, tracks the one you're reading, and pins the current target and score. The top bar shows a live count of the WebMCP tools currently registered on document.modelContext and whether that landed on the browser's native implementation or our polyfill. The seven tools prepare_scan — proposes a domain to the human. Cannot approve it. scan_domain — runs the passive scan. Refuses without human approval for that exact domain. list_findings — compact findings, filterable by severity or failures only. explain_finding — plain-language impact of one finding. generate_fix — copy-pasteable remediation snippet. verify_fix — re-scans the live site and confirms the fix actually landed. Human-gated like any scan. export_report — JSON or Markdown report, downloaded for the human. verify_fix is the one we'd point at. Most agent tooling stops at "here's the fix" and declares victory. Cyfix goes back to the live site and checks — and because verifying means re-scanning Cyfix scores 100/100 on itself The first thing anyone does with a security scanner is point it at the scanner. So we did — it scored 61. We fixed everything it found: a nonce-based CSP with no unsafe-inline for scripts, HSTS, nosniff, X-Frame-Options: DENY, a referrer policy, a permissions policy, no framework banner, and a real /.well-known/security.txt. It now scores 100/100. Scan cyfix.vercel.app from the dashboard and check for yourself. Challenges we ran into Designing a gate an agent can't route around while still leaving it something useful to do. Our first version refused unauthorized scans correctly but left the agent at a dead end with no way to ask. Splitting "propose" from "approve" into two tools, and moving the target into shared state both actors read, is what made the collaboration real instead of theatrical. The second was our own CSP. The first policy we shipped used 'strict-dynamic', which silently voids the 'self' allowance — every script chunk was blocked and the dashboard rendered a blank page. The build was perfectly happy; only loading the page in a real browser caught it. A fitting lesson for a project about security headers. What's next Scheduled re-scans with diffing, a broader passive check set (TLS configuration, DNS hygiene, SPF/DMARC), and a shareable report link so the person who has to apply the fix doesn't need the dashboard open. title: CueMend
pitch: A WebMCP rehearsal room where humans protect dramatic beats, agents exhaustively repair caption timing, and every committed WebVTT track is revision-bound and verifiable.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP rehearsal room where humans protect dramatic beats, agents exhaustively repair caption timing, and every committed WebVTT track is revision-bound and verifiable. Like Comment Story Updates Icon MCP demo Inspiration Caption timing is both mechanical and artistic. Software can detect overlapping captions, reading-rate problems, missing speakers, and visual collisions, but it cannot decide whether an audience laugh, lighting reveal, silence, or actor's breath carries artistic meaning. CueMend explores a better division of responsibility: let the computer perform exhaustive, inspectable checking while the stage manager retains artistic judgment and final authority. It is designed around small theatres, school productions, and live-event teams that need systematic caption checks without handing the meaning of a performance to an optimizer. What it does CueMend opens a fictional 32-second rehearsal containing ten caption cues and seven independently reproducible timing issues. Through WebMCP, a compatible browser agent can: inspect the exact rehearsal state and revision; audit caption overlap, minimum gaps, duration, reading rate, speakers, protected beats, and reserved screen regions; ask CueMend's deterministic browser engine to evaluate all 3^8 = 6,561 bounded candidate tracks; stage up to three zero-conflict alternatives without changing the active captions; preview or discard an exact proposal; commit only the plan explicitly selected and approved by a human; run a post-commit deterministic re-audit; export editable WebVTT plus a SHA-256-bound evidence certificate. The 6,561 figure is the exact search space of this demo: eight adjustable cues, each with three authored repair variants. It is not a universal theatre number, and the engine never invents or rewrites dialogue. The signature interaction begins when the cheapest proposal crosses Jon's optional final breath. The stage manager decides that the breath matters and protects it in the visible UI. CueMend increments the workspace revision, reports an additional conflict, and makes the old proposal stale. An attempt to use the old revision receives a structured STALE_REVISION refusal. The agent must inspect the new state and replan under the human's updated constraint. After the human selects and approves one exact plan, a temporary commit capability appears. The commit is bound to the approved plan, current revision, protected beats, profile, and digest. After it is used, mutation tools retire. The finished rehearsal reaches revision 3 with zero conflicts under the named demo profile. Why WebMCP matters CueMend remains usable as an ordinary web application, but WebMCP turns it into a shared, state-aware collaboration surface for humans and agents. Without WebMCP, a browser agent would otherwise have to infer domain state from the DOM, automate brittle coordinates, or depend on a CueMend-specific integration. With WebMCP, the page exposes domain-level tools over the same live state the person sees: exact cue IDs, locks, revisions, alternatives, structured errors, and safe next actions. Tool availability follows the real authority state: a fresh workspace exposes inspect, audit, and stage tools; a current proposal adds preview and discard; a stale proposal cannot be previewed or committed; the commit tool appears only after a person approves the exact artifact; after commit, mutation capabilities disappear and verification becomes available. This means the human does not merely click a cosmetic approval button. A human decision changes the optimization problem, invalidates previous agent work, and changes which capabilities the page exposes to the agent. Without WebMCP, CueMend is a caption-checking and repair application. With WebMCP, it becomes a standardized, tab-bound workspace where repetitive work can be delegated to a compatible browser agent without surrendering artistic decisions. How we built it CueMend is a dependency-free static application built with semantic HTML, responsive CSS, and native JavaScript ES modules. A deterministic engine audits interval, duration, reading-rate, speaker, protected-beat, and reserved-region constraints. It enumerates the exact 6,561-candidate demo search space and ranks valid tracks by: number of changed cues; total timing movement; semantic changes such as speaker or position; a stable lexical key for deterministic output. A shared command layer owns revision validation, proposal and plan digests, human-only operations, idempotent request IDs, session-bound commit receipts, and structured error recovery. The ordinary UI and WebMCP handlers call this same command layer and update the same visible artifact. The page registers tools with document.modelContext.registerTool . Registrations are retired with AbortSignal when the capability inventory changes. Every consequential handler repeats runtime validation because schemas and annotations are not treated as security boundaries. Web Crypto produces SHA-256 digests, and Node's built-in test runner verifies the engine, authority model, and dynamic tool lifecycle without third-party packages. Challenges we ran into The hardest design problem was making human approval substantive instead of decorative. The person needed to change the actual optimization problem by protecting an artistic beat, while the system needed to invalidate an in-flight proposal reliably and explain the recovery path clearly. The evolving WebMCP API also required a careful distinction between registration-lifetime cancellation and execution cancellation. CueMend registers or retires tools only when the available capability set changes, while revalidating all important state immediately before mutation. Another challenge was keeping every numerical and accessibility-related claim auditable. CueMend names its exact demo profile, reports the number of candidates evaluated, preserves dialogue, and displays its limitations instead of implying universal caption compliance. Accomplishments that we're proud of A human decision causes a real agent replan, not a cosmetic approval step. The deterministic engine evaluates every candidate in its disclosed finite search space. A stale proposal cannot be previewed, approved, or committed after a human changes a protected beat. Commit is bound to the selected plan, current locks, profile, revision, and SHA-256 digest. One request ID can apply a change at most once and returns the same receipt if replayed. The final artifact is editable WebVTT rather than a result trapped inside a chat. The visible application remains fully usable when WebMCP is unavailable. The complete native WebMCP journey was repeated three times from a clean reset in Chrome 151, with ten native calls per run and a genuine stale-revision refusal each time. What we learned The most useful WebMCP tools are small domain verbs over live, visible state. Tool count matters less than clear preconditions, explicit postconditions, recoverable errors, and meaningful authority boundaries. Dynamic tool registration becomes especially valuable when it mirrors real authority: the agent should not even receive a commit capability until a person has approved the exact artifact. We also learned that a strong agent experience does not require hiding the application behind chat. Human and agent interfaces can operate on the same state, with every transition remaining visible, reversible before approval, and verifiable afterward. What's next Future versions could add real WebVTT import, user-authored production profiles, venue-specific safe areas, rehearsal-note exchange, and integration with existing caption playback systems. Those extensions would preserve the same principle: automation proposes and proves mechanical changes, while production teams retain control over artistic intent. Important limitations All dialogue and production details in the built-in rehearsal are fictional and rights-safe. The CueMend Demo Theatre Profile v1 is a transparent demonstration profile, not a universal WCAG, broadcast, venue, legal, accessibility, or artistic standard. CueMend does not claim to certify accessibility or replace professional caption review. No generative model runs inside the submitted application; its repair engine is deterministic and local to the browser. title: Zingposts
pitch: Interesting things, organized together: a WebMCP-native marketplace where people work with the outside agents they already trust.
about_excerpt: Interesting things, organized together: a WebMCP-native marketplace where people work with the outside agents they already trust. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Browsing old cars, boats, campers, motorcycles, and machinery is fun. Managing the hunt is not. Good finds get lost across tabs, marketplace search misses obvious matches, alerts are rigid, research lives in scattered notes, and negotiations have no shared memory. A three-way trade is almost impossible to reason about cleanly. Zingposts starts from a different premise: the marketplace should be equally legible to people and their agents without embedding a model in the product. The site owns its native listings and structured deal workflow, while outside listings can be tracked as clearly labeled snapshots. What it does Zingposts is a complete peer-to-peer marketplace and durable workspace for interesting things. People can browse realistic native inventory, create and publish listings, upload photos, save finds, build boards, set alerts, keep research notebooks, message sellers, prepare offers, and create structured multi-party trade rooms. Outside finds can be tracked without confusing them with Zingposts-owned inventory. A connected outside agent receives a compact persistent core plus one focused pack drawn from 121 structured WebMCP tools. It can search with compound criteria, compare candidates, organize boards, tag and rank finds, record cited research and inspection risks, monitor price changes, draft communications and offers, calculate acquisition cost, propose trade scenarios, and coordinate the shared gallery, focus, or thumbnail canvas. The human uses the same structure through a canvas-first interface. Zingposts itself contains no LLM. The centerpiece is the shared canvas: an outside agent opens a durable session, places a shortlist, recommendation, or focused question beside the marketplace objects, and pauses only when human judgment matters. The person can inspect the exact listings and rationale, choose an option or add context, and return structured guidance. The agent reads that durable response on its next tool call and continues. This is turn-taking over shared marketplace objects, not a chatbot transcript. The loop now extends across visits. get_workspace_resume returns the last acknowledged checkpoint, everything that changed since, structured blockers, human responses, proposal status, and safe next actions. An agent can acknowledge the checkpoint only after processing it, so “come back later” is an explicit protocol rather than a hope that conversation context survived. For broad edits, the agent can prepare a sourced, versioned change set instead of making a trail of one-off mutations. Zingposts previews each proposed change in plain language, checks the expected object versions, and lets the person selectively accept only the changes they want. Agents cannot approve their own change sets. Completed deals can be recorded as private outcomes, and transparent aggregate patterns report counts, prices, and reasons without inventing a model-generated score. Either side can arrive first. A person can explore immediately in a prototype workspace, then replace a test email and verify the real address through Supabase only when work reaches the marketplace boundary. One Bring my agent click copies the canonical guide URL. Or an unauthenticated agent can inspect five setup-only tools and open a prototype handoff for the person. Once the person signs in, safe private tools appear automatically to an outside agent operating that browser document. Independent 12-hour revocable sessions remain available through one-use invites or codes for separate-browser or unattended work. The human remains in control. Publishing, enabling notifications, sending a message, submitting or responding to an offer, and inviting a trade participant stop at a visible confirmation gate. Every human and agent action is attributed, and reversible work can be undone. Why WebMCP is essential Without WebMCP, an agent has to infer intent from buttons and screen position. That is brittle for a marketplace with dozens of interdependent objects: listings, boards, research, alerts, conversations, offers, people, assets, and constraints. WebMCP gives Zingposts a stable collaboration language. “Find pre-1980 boats under $15,000, put the best four on a board, record the title risks, and draft a message to the strongest seller” becomes a sequence of typed, attributable actions. The human can watch the same state change, refine it directly, and approve the parts that cross a consequential boundary. That makes the product meaningfully better with an agent—not merely automatable. How we built it Zingposts uses React 19 and Next.js on Netlify. Supabase Auth provides verified human sessions, Supabase Postgres holds marketplace, identity, agent-session, and workflow state, and Supabase Storage holds listing photos. Versioned SQL migrations keep direct browser access locked behind row-level security. The browser client exposes 121 declarative tools through the WebMCP modelContext surface, but only five setup tools while signed out. After the person signs in, AbortSignal-managed registration keeps a compact persistent core plus one replaceable focused capability pack, so navigation never accumulates an oversized registry or silently unlocks business actions. get_agent_bootstrap returns setup guidance while signed out, then canonical browser-delegated identity, workspace, attention, active collaboration, capability index, and guide version after sign-in. activate_capability switches the focused pack without moving the person; open_for_human_review is optional. The action layer derives canonical human and agent identity on the server, prevents duplicate profiles, enforces ownership and state-transition enums, creates reviewable drafts, writes attributed activity, stores inverse operations for undo, supports idempotency keys and optimistic versions, returns stable deep links and WebMCP-native structured errors, and converts consequential operations into pending confirmations. Isolated QA runs register only their own artifacts, provide an exact cleanup preview, and require human approval before deletion. The marketplace is seeded with original project-owned imagery and realistic records so the full human-agent workflow is understandable immediately. WebMCP registration is document-scoped, while Zingposts durably stores connection profiles, scopes, alerts, boards, research, drafts, versions, and audit history. The public /for-agents guide and /api/agent-guide contract show agents how to reconnect safely without storing an invite, code, or stale catalog. Challenges The main design challenge was not adding more agent power; it was deciding where that power should stop. We separated preparation from commitment. Research, organization, comparison, and drafting can proceed quickly. Communication, publication, notifications, invitations, and financial commitments pause for the human. We also designed external-listing tracking so provenance stays honest. Zingposts can organize an outside find, but it never claims that its cached price, availability, or seller statements are authoritative. Accomplishments A coherent marketplace, not a WebMCP proof of concept 121 tools spanning authentication, onboarding, resumable work sessions, versioned proposals, outcomes, canvas views, discovery, organization, negotiation, and multi-party trade Agent-first and person-first onboarding with a five-tool setup surface before human sign-in Durable agent-to-human-to-agent turn-taking with a unified attention queue Explicit resume checkpoints and structured blockers for work that continues across agent runs Sourced, versioned change sets with semantic previews and selective human acceptance Private outcome recording with transparent, non-AI aggregate patterns Live agent activity, exact-payload approval, idempotency, dry runs, structured errors, and stable deep links No built-in AI or model dependency Supabase human authentication plus opaque invite URLs, code fallback, and single-use, expiring, revocable agent sessions—without password or session sharing Persistent bootstrap plus navigation-independent focused capability activation Structured errors, strict workflow transitions, optimistic concurrency, and namespaced QA cleanup Durable attribution, confirmations, and undo Native seller photo upload and publishing workflow Clear separation between owned listings and outside tracked snapshots Production build, automated API smoke tests, desktop browser testing, and mobile verification What we learned Human-agent collaboration works best when both sides operate on the same durable objects. A board is better than a chat-only list. A research notebook is better than an ephemeral summary. A pending confirmation is better than asking the model to remember which action is sensitive. We also learned to separate document-scoped WebMCP

video_transcript_excerpt: What if a marketplace did not contain its own AI? What if it simply gave people and any outside agent a beautiful shared place to work? This is Zing Posts, peer-to-peer commerce designed for Web MCP. The first visit is deliberately small. While signed out, the browser exposes only five setup tools. An agent can inspect the bootstrap guide, prepare a handoff for the person, or accept a one-use credential. After sign-in, it re-discovers the real workspace. Now, human and agent share the same durable canvas. The person can browse visually, flip through finds, drag items onto colored boards, and set preferences. The agent can search the same listings, compare candidates, rank a board, tag discoveries, and leave its reasoning beside the work. Web MCP is not hidden behind one giant prompt. Zing Posts keeps a persistent core, then activates the focus capability for the page. Here, the marketplace pack includes search, view control, comparison, board organization, and the option to open exactly the item a person should review. On a listing, the collaboration gets deeper. An outside agent can build a cited research notebook, record comparable sales, calculate a price range, and draft an offer plan with repair, transport, tax, contingency, and budget assumptions. The evidence stays visible. The private target stays private. The workbench is the shared memory: agent findings, human notes, decisions, undo history, alerts, conversations, offers, and even multi-party trade rooms persist as structured marketplace state. The agent does not own the experience. It helps move evidence toward a decision, while the person stays in control. That control becomes explicit at the verification boundary. Browsing, organizing, research, and drafting stay fluid. Publishing a listing, enabling an alert, contacting a seller, sending an offer, or advancing a trade creates a pending approval. Only the human can cross that line, and every outcome is recorded. The result is a web MCP native marketplace with no built-in model and no agent lock-in. Five tools for setup, 34 focused tools on this marketplace canvas, and 121 across the complete signed-in catalog. zingpost.com Bring your agent and find something worth saving.

title: TrialBridge
pitch: A WebMCP powered ChatGPT and Chrome enabled agent that matches cancer patients to clinical trials in minutes - no filling forms, no endless clicks and no gatekeeping - for early therapy access.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP powered ChatGPT and Chrome enabled agent that matches cancer patients to clinical trials in minutes - no filling forms, no endless clicks and no gatekeeping - for early therapy access. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I (Vilay) started my career as a Clinical Research Coordinator at Stanford Cancer Center. Still the most formative experience working with patients at the end of their lives. I have since built award winning Palliative programs, but keep coming back to the same problem - how do we meet needs of patients who have exhausted all available FDA approved therapies. At that point, what most patients want is not survival for its sake, but to make it to an important life event - son's graduation, daughter's quincenera, or an anniversary. For these patients, clinical trials can be the only pathway that might increase their lifespan through a therapy that won't be on the market for years. Yet, the access is gatekept - geographically limited around academic medical centers who run the trials, or knowledge and bandwidth of community oncologists - all buried in CT.gov, a clunky government database that is difficult to navigate. Meanwhile clinical trials regularly shut down due to low enrollment. Patients who could have qualified never find a trial, and trials that can help many never fill and reach their endpoints. We built TrialBridge to close the gap on both directions. This is also the first project built together by us three brothers working across three different time zones and bringing experience from three very different fields: I, Vilay , am a healthcare executive with background in population health, high risk patient management and healthcare strategy and operations. He lived and breathed clinical trials for good portion of his career and brought the vision. Shobhit , based in India, conceived and created the application, designed the patient-facing workflow and built the WebMCP tools that connect an AI agent with TrialBridge. Harshit , based in New York and the most deeply technical member of the team, helped shape the application’s technical architecture, implementation and engineering reliability. TrialBridge emerged from the intersection of healthcare, technology and patient advocacy—and from three brothers wanting to build something useful together. What it does TrialBridge helps patients and caregivers discover clinical trials that may be worth discussing with their doctors. A patient can describe their situation to an AI agent in ordinary language—for example: “I have stage IV neuroendocrine cancer. I’m 58, live in Chicago, can travel 150 miles, and previously received Afinitor.” Through WebMCP, the agent can then interact with TrialBridge using structured tools registered directly by the webpage. The patient does not need to manually complete every field or navigate multiple filtering menus. However, the profile remains visible and editable, allowing the patient to inspect and correct what the agent entered. TrialBridge can: Convert a patient’s plain-language description into a structured search profile; Resolve supported medication brand names to their generic equivalents, such as Afinitor to everolimus; Search currently recruiting studies using the live ClinicalTrials.gov API; Distinguish the number of registry records checked from the number of trials eventually shown; Explain which records were filtered out and why; Show whether the search reached the end of the available registry results or stopped at an application limit; Compare age, location and supported prior-treatment information against published study details; Display what appears consistent, what appears inconsistent and what remains unknown; Allow the agent to shortlist potentially relevant studies with factual reasons; Open a full side-by-side comparison of shortlisted trials; and Support preliminary pre-screening against published inclusion and exclusion criteria. Importantly, TrialBridge preserves uncertainty. If a patient does not know their ECOG performance status or cannot answer another medical question, the application records that information as unresolved . It does not silently convert an unknown answer into a pass or a failure. TrialBridge does not determine eligibility, diagnose a condition, recommend treatment or provide medical advice. Only a clinical-trial study team can determine eligibility after medical screening. How we built it We began by developing the domain layer required to understand cancer terminology, treatment names and clinical-trial records. This included a curated cancer and treatment catalogue built from publicly available clinical sources and open clinical terminology, supported medication mappings, and brand-to-generic drug-name resolution. ClinicalTrials.gov API v2 provides the live public trial data used by the search. We then built TrialBridge using: Next.js React TypeScript ClinicalTrials.gov API v2 WebMCP Declared tool schemas and application-level input validation Browser-stored patient profile and pre-screening state Replit deployment The webpage registers ten structured tools using the current WebMCP imperative API: document.modelContext.registerTool() Each tool has: A defined name and description; A declared input schema; Structured parameters; Application-level validation before state changes are applied; A specific application action; and A visible result in the same interface used by a human. This means an AI agent does not have to scrape the page, interpret screenshots or guess which element to click. Instead, the webpage acts as an in-page tool server, allowing the agent to invoke capabilities that the application has explicitly exposed. Different tools handle different parts of the workflow, including: Reading and updating the patient profile; Searching conditions and trials; Retrieving trial details; Managing the shortlist; Opening comparisons; Starting pre-screening; and Recording preliminary criterion responses. Search and trial-data operations use the live ClinicalTrials.gov API. Patient profile, shortlist and pre-screening information are maintained within the browser so the patient can see and control the state being used. The agent and the patient share the same screen: when the agent changes something, the patient can see it immediately. Challenges we ran into Working with an emerging browser proposal WebMCP is still an emerging proposal, and its API, browser support and testing workflows continue to evolve. We had to ensure that TrialBridge could register its tools using the current API, expose understandable schemas and produce visible changes that both the agent and the user could verify. ClinicalTrials.gov API and browser restrictions Direct browser requests introduced CORS and preflight limitations. We addressed this through a server-side proxy while preserving live ClinicalTrials.gov data and transparent source attribution. Separating records checked from trials shown Registry metadata can be misleading if the application presents only the final number of displayed trials. We implemented explicit accounting for: Records returned and checked; Trials shown; Trials filtered out; Reasons for filtering; Pages retrieved; and Whether pagination reached the end. Translating complex eligibility language Clinical-trial inclusion and exclusion criteria are often long, inconsistent and written differently across studies. We needed to present them without pretending that TrialBridge could replace clinical judgment. Our solution was to treat the comparison as preliminary and preserve three distinct outcomes: Appears consistent; Apparent mismatch; and Still unknown. Preventing AI-generated certainty One of our most important challenges was ensuring that an agent could not guess an answer when medical information was unavailable. Unknown information remains unresolved, and malformed or unsupported responses are rejected rather than being forced into a pass-or-fail result. Protecting patient privacy We designed the demonstration so that it does not require a patient’s name, email address or date of birth. Search details and pre-screening responses remain visible and controllable in the browser. Accomplishments that we’re proud of Building our first project together as three brothers across three time zones and three industries: healthcare, technology and law; Creating a working clinical-trial discovery engine—not merely a static prototype; Compressing a process that can require hours of manual searching into a structured conversational workflow; Successfully connecting the application to an AI agent through ten WebMCP tools; Allowing the agent to operate the same visible interface that a patient can inspect and correct; Searching live, currently recruiting studies from ClinicalTrials.gov; Distinguishing records checked from trials shown and explaining why records were filtered; Supporting brand-to-generic medication resolution; Building a real preliminary comparison workflow for publis

title: AgentReady
pitch: Your site works for humans. Can an agent finish the job? The WebMCP app that helps devs quickly find out if their site/app is agent ready. If you aren't agent ready, you ain't gonna make it.
about_excerpt: Your site works for humans. Can an agent finish the job? The WebMCP app that helps devs quickly find out if their site/app is agent ready. If you aren't agent ready, you ain't gonna make it. Like Comment Story Updates The WebMCP vision: From Page Chaos to an Agentic Open-door Inspiration Recent discussions online about agentic traffic exceeding human traffic alerted me to the concept that if your site/app isn't agent ready, you ain't gonna make it. I also realized that what's needed during development is a lightweight web app to provide quick check with easy to understand results, and, in line with being agent ready, this app needed to be readily available to one's coding agent. Why WebMCP is the right fit for this use case WebMCP's hardest problem isn't technical — it's adoption. Almost every page an agent visits today declares zero tools. AgentReady attacks that directly, twice over. First, it is a WebMCP app: open it in ChatGPT's browser and the agent discovers audit_site , a declared-and-registered tool that audits any public URL and returns the score, grade, coverage and top finding — human and agent reading the same report on the same page. Second, its output creates more WebMCP : for every audited page, it generates a working tool from that page's own first form — the declarative toolname / tooldescription / toolparamdescription attributes and the document.modelContext.registerTool code with a correct JSON schema — ready to paste. Every WebMCP app improves one site; AgentReady is built to recruit the rest of the web. How it improves the user experience For a site owner, an invisible problem becomes a number in ten seconds, and the number comes with the fix: six evidence-backed checks (discovery, structure, renderability, forms, actionability, WebMCP), a "Do this first" list, copy-paste remediations, and a computed "+N with WebMCP" showing exactly what declaring one tool is worth. For an agent, the site is a first-class user: the audit works as a WebMCP tool call, a plain GET /report?url= (fully server-rendered — the entire report works with JavaScript disabled), or POST /api/audit described by /openapi.json . The report is honest by construction — unobserved evidence never counts against a site, coverage and confidence are always visible, and a blocked fetch yields "no score", never a fake grade. Novel collaborative capabilities The human pastes a URL; the agent calls the same action as a tool; both land on one shared report. In ChatGPT's browser you can ask the agent to audit a site, then expand the findings it summarised and copy the generated stub yourself — a genuine division of labour on a single page. The demo bistro ( /demo ) completes the loop: a reservation form an agent can book through, next to a deliberately gorgeous-but-broken page ( /fixtures/soup , 28/F) that shows what agents face everywhere else. And the tool teaches: what helps agents (labels, landmarks, real buttons, schemas) is what helps assistive technology, so every fix serves both user bases. How it was built Next.js 16 App Router on Vercel, TypeScript, zero database — URL in, report out. A hardened safe-fetch (SSRF-proof: pinned DNS, per-hop robots.txt enforcement, streaming caps) acquires one page plus its discovery sidecars; six pure check modules score it against a published rubric (weights in one file, methodology in /docs and docs/INVARIANTS.md ); a stub generator turns the page's own form into spec-correct WebMCP code ( document.modelContext , plain-value execute returns, the @mcp-b/webmcp-polyfill@5.1.0 pinned with a verified SRI hash). 348 tests, including an SSRF bypass corpus and a runtime test that executes generated tool code against a real DOM. Built entirely within the submission window — the git history is the timeline — by a human directing a multi-agent AI team with adversarial cross-review on every merge. AgentReady audits itself at 96/A , and the one point category it drops is documented as "we don't run an MCP server, and won't pretend to for points." Accomplishments that I'm proud of This whole thing was done in an afternoon, which is the first time I've essentially one-shot a finished, useful, deployed app in a single day. What I learned Just how crazy easy it is to incorporate WebMCP. Now I'll be making sure to go back into other apps I'm working on and add it. What's next for AgentReady Circulate v1 in some communities I'm part of & get any feedback. Next version should include detection of dynamic WebMCP. An agent-ready local maintenance concierge that uses WebMCP to find services, retrieve grounded details, and build practical property maintenance plans.

 1 2 3 4 5 6 



 
 Inspiration 

 AskJosh began as a Forward Ever Foundation digital initiative to explore a simple but practical problem: how can people more easily find the right local service for a property-maintenance need? 

 For the WebMCP Challenge, I wanted to explore what happens when that experience becomes agent-accessible. Rather than requiring a user to manually navigate a directory, an AI agent can interact directly with AskJosh's structured service data and help turn a real-world maintenance problem into an actionable plan. 

 This challenge edition is focused on La Brea, Trinidad and Tobago, and uses a deliberately small illustrative demo catalogue. The goal is to demonstrate an architecture that could later expand to verified providers, additional communities and more service categories. 

 What it does 

 AskJosh is an agent-ready local maintenance concierge. 

 Through WebMCP, the challenge edition exposes three read-only tools: 

 
 find_maintenance_services — finds relevant maintenance services from the AskJosh demo catalogue. 
 get_maintenance_service_details — retrieves grounded information about a specific service using its exact service ID. 
 build_property_maintenance_plan — combines selected services into a structured draft maintenance plan with deterministic sequencing and illustrative cost ranges. 
 

 For example, a user can ask for help preparing a community centre that needs AC servicing, electrical checks, pressure washing and lawn care. 

 The agent can discover the relevant AskJosh services, work with their exact service IDs and create a combined maintenance plan without inventing providers, prices or availability. 

 AskJosh also works as a normal website, allowing people to search the same demo catalogue without using an AI agent. 

 How I built it 

 AskJosh is built with Next.js, React and TypeScript and deployed on Vercel. 

 For the challenge edition, I created a deliberately small deterministic catalogue containing illustrative maintenance services for La Brea, Trinidad and Tobago. 

 The underlying service logic is shared by both the normal website experience and the WebMCP tools. 

 The WebMCP integration uses the browser's Site Tools / WebMCP interface to register structured tools directly from the AskJosh web application. 

 The architecture is intentionally simple: 

 AskJosh illustrative demo catalogue 
→ deterministic shared service logic 
→ WebMCP tools 
→ AI agent 
→ structured grounded response 

 The WebMCP tools are read-only. They do not submit bookings, contact providers, send emails, write personal information to a database or expose private administrative functionality. 

 AskJosh also detects whether WebMCP is available so the normal website remains usable in unsupported environments. 

 Challenges I ran into 

 One of the biggest challenges was making the agent experience useful without allowing the system to invent local service information. 

 Rather than asking an AI model inside AskJosh to generate providers, prices or service information, I designed the WebMCP tools around deterministic catalogue data and stable service IDs. 

 I also separated discovery and planning from consequential actions. The current WebMCP implementation can search, retrieve details and prepare maintenance plans, but it cannot silently contact providers or submit requests on a user's behalf. 

 Another challenge was maintaining a normal human-facing website while introducing an agent-facing WebMCP capability. WebMCP support is feature-detected so unsupported browsers continue to receive the conventional AskJosh experience. 

 Accomplishments that I'm proud of 

 
 Three working read-only WebMCP tools that can be discovered and called by an agent. 
 A multi-tool workflow from service discovery to detailed retrieval to maintenance planning. 
 Exact service-ID grounding to reduce hallucination and incorrect matches. 
 Deterministic illustrative cost aggregation using catalogue values rather than AI-generated estimates. 
 Safe handling of unsupported locations and invalid service IDs. 
 A read-only architecture with no hidden consequential actions. 
 A normal website experience that continues to work independently of WebMCP. 
 Automated tests covering the WebMCP service-search, detail and planning functionality. 
 A separate sanitized public challenge edition that demonstrates the WebMCP architecture without exposing the broader AskJosh project. 
 

 What I learned 

 WebMCP changes the role of a website. 

 Instead of an AI assistant only reading visible page content, a site can expose carefully designed capabilities that allow an agent to interact with the product in a structured way. 

 I also learned that more tools are not necessarily better. A small set of well-scoped, grounded tools can create a useful agent workflow while remaining predictable, deterministic and safe. 

 What's next for AskJosh 

 The challenge edition intentionally uses a small illustrative maintenance catalogue. 

 The longer-term opportunity is to expand AskJosh to verified local providers, additional service categories and more communities while preserving the same agent-access architecture. 

 Future possibilities include broader geographic coverage, provider onboarding and verification, richer service discovery, and carefully reviewed user-authorized request workflows. 

 The goal is to evolve AskJosh from a focused maintenance concierge into a practical AI-accessible community services platform.

about_excerpt: An electronics store whose own filter vocabulary is the agent's tool schema - it ranks, explains what it hid, and can never un-veto a product you rejected. Like Comment Story Updates The catalog: filters generated from real inventory Tool console: describe_catalog called live via WebMCP WebMCP surface: the tool's JSON Schema is generated live from the real catalog and filter vocabulary - the agent's tool surface and the store's own UI share one source of truth. Inspiration Every electronics store hides the answer behind its own vocabulary. A customer knows their need in plain language; the site offers RAM, sRGB percentage, and a price slider - the need turned into a quiz only the store understands. What it does Vidyut Electronics hands its own filter vocabulary to the agent as a tool. search_catalog 's JSON Schema is generated from the real catalog at boot - category, spec, and brand are enums of what the store actually sells - so the translation from need to constraints happens on the store page, visibly, not inside a black box. Every ranked result says what it satisfies and what it misses, with the actual value; near-misses say what would have to give; hidden listings say why. The human vetoes with one click, and no tool can ever bring a vetoed product back. How we built it One file, vanilla JavaScript, a fifteen-product seeded catalog with a deliberate trap (the strongest editor is a 2.3kg desk machine) and a deliberate near-miss. A single pure rank(query) function backs both the page's own render and every tool call, so the rail always shows exactly what the last tool call would return. Challenges we ran into Making the veto boundary airtight against a determined agent: add_to_shortlist has to refuse a vetoed id unconditionally and explain why, every time, including immediately after the agent re-searches and might plausibly try to re-add it thinking the veto was a UI-only state. Accomplishments that we're proud of A tool schema that's generated from real inventory data instead of hand-written - so the agent learns the store's actual vocabulary from the schema itself, and learns any gap in its guess from the error message, not from documentation. What we learned Wrapping every registerTool call in its own try/catch mattered in practice - one schema Chrome's validator disliked should cost one tool, never the whole surface. What's next The optional cross-origin stretch goal - exposing search_catalog to a separate origin via exposedTo / fromOrigins , so a comparison-shopping agent on another site could query Vidyut's catalog directly. Part of a seven-app portfolio Each entry proves a different WebMCP capability: Tablemap (dynamic tool registration), Signoff (a tool that only exists once a human approves it), Paperwork (structurally human-only fields), Jhola (genuinely cancellable long-running tools), Almari (quarantined untrusted content), Dhwani (declarative, no-JavaScript tools).  Inspiration 

 RoboBuddy began in November 2025 when I helped my daughter with an elementary-school project: we 3D-printed and built an Arduino-based 6 DOF robotic arm, then controlled it from a web interface ( RoboBuddy ). That project sparked my own interest in robotics. I later built and operated an SO-101 follower arm using its 3D mesh rigs ( RoboBuddy AI ). 

 For the WebMCP Challenge, I wanted to make robotics exploration more approachable: one browser workspace that humans and agents can use side by side, without a separate project-specific API-key workflow. My original idea was to program robotic arms for scientific lab operations. Then MicroDuck arrived and offered a playful, immediately understandable way to demonstrate agent-accessible web capabilities. 

 What I built 

 RoboBuddy IDE is a browser-based robotics workspace with a code editor, simulation controls, and a 3D MicroDuck policy simulation. Through a bounded WebMCP tool surface, agents can inspect the modeled state and make focused, visible changes—such as moving the duck, interacting with the ball and scene, or adding temporary measurement cues. 

 The experience is designed to be understandable and reversible. Actions stay inside the browser demo, and temporary visual cues disappear on refresh. RoboBuddy IDE does not claim physical hardware control through this WebMCP demo. 

 How I built it 

 I used GPT-5.6-Sol in Codex as a development collaborator to build the IDE interface, integrate the MicroDuck model, and develop WebMCP functions for the duck, related objects, and 3D environment. 
RoboBuddy IDE was built during the submission period. It builds on lessons from earlier RoboBuddy robotics experiments, but the submitted browser IDE, WebMCP collaboration surface, and MicroDuck experience are new work created for this challenge.
The goal was to build useful, comprehensible, expandable capabilities that a human can observe alongside the agent. 

 What I learned 

 WebMCP made the application feel less like a page to automate and more like a set of intentional shared capabilities. Pairing each agent action with visible state makes it easier to see what changed, why it matters, and how to reset the experiment. That makes the experience easier to trust, teach with, and extend. 

 Challenges 

 The main constraints were time and the weekly limits on my Pro account. Technically, GPT-5.6-Sol enabled very fast iteration. The careful challenge was maintaining honest boundaries between a browser simulation and physical robotics while keeping the demo inviting for a broad audience. 

 What comes next (current) 

 This experience inspired me to explore WebMCP in my other learning and science projects, including Lab Studio , AssayLens , and RoboStudio Circuits . Even if I cannot submit them all, they show how human-visible, bounded agent capabilities can extend across robotics, science, and education.

 Inspiration 

 Incident response is still highly fragmented. Engineers investigating an outage often jump between logs, deployment history, configuration changes, dashboards, runbooks, and communication tools while trying to determine what actually went wrong. 

 TraceDesk explores what incident response could look like when a web application is designed for both humans and AI agents from the beginning. 

 What it does 

 TraceDesk is an AI-powered incident response workspace where humans and agents investigate software outages together. 

 The workspace combines incident details, service health, logs, recent deployments, configuration changes, evidence, hypotheses, and remediation plans in one interface. 

 Using WebMCP, an AI agent can directly access structured TraceDesk capabilities such as searching logs, inspecting deployments, reviewing configuration changes, adding evidence, updating hypotheses, and preparing remediation plans. 

 The human remains in control of consequential actions. 

 Why WebMCP 

 Without WebMCP, an AI agent would need to interpret the visual interface, find buttons, navigate panels, and infer how to interact with the application. 

 TraceDesk instead exposes meaningful application capabilities directly as structured WebMCP tools. 

 This allows the agent to focus on investigating the incident rather than figuring out how to operate the website. 

 Humans use the visual workspace while agents use structured tools, but both collaborate on the same incident state. 

 Human + agent collaboration 

 A human can ask an agent to investigate an outage and determine the most likely root cause. 

 The agent can then use TraceDesk's WebMCP tools to gather evidence from logs, deployments, service health, and configuration changes before adding its findings back into the shared workspace. 

 The human can review the evidence, confidence, and proposed remediation before approving any high-risk action. 

 How we built it 

 TraceDesk is built with TypeScript, Next.js, React, Tailwind CSS, WebMCP, and the OpenAI API. 

 WebMCP tools are registered by the application and mapped to real TraceDesk functionality. The OpenAI API provides incident analysis and structured reasoning over technical evidence. 

 The application is deployed on Vercel and the source code is publicly available on GitHub. 

 Challenges 

 The main challenge was designing WebMCP tools that represent meaningful product capabilities rather than simply exposing UI controls. 

 We also focused on separating autonomous investigation from actions that should require human approval. 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP changes the way a web product can be designed. Instead of treating AI as a chatbot added on top of an existing application, the application itself can expose structured capabilities that agents understand and use directly. 

 What's next 

 TraceDesk could eventually connect to real observability platforms, deployment systems, incident-management tools, and infrastructure providers, allowing agents to investigate real production incidents while preserving human oversight.

title: The Last Signal
pitch: The Last Signal is an escape room game where a human and an AI agent must save a failing space station together. Using WebMCP, the agent operates discovered tools while the human interprets clues.
about_excerpt: The Last Signal is an escape room game where a human and an AI agent must save a failing space station together. Using WebMCP, the agent operates discovered tools while the human interprets clues. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most agent-enabled websites treat the agent as an invisible automation layer: it clicks through an interface while the human waits for a result. We wanted to explore something more native to the web—an experience intentionally designed around the different strengths of a person and an agent. The Last Signal is a cooperative escape room for one human and one browser agent. The player is trapped aboard a failing orbital communications station with twelve minutes to restore its systems and release an evacuation airlock. The human interprets the environment, makes judgment calls, and controls physical authorization points. The agent inspects and operates station machinery using structured WebMCP tools. Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP Escape rooms are built from stateful objects, constrained actions, hidden dependencies, and consequences. Those concepts map naturally to WebMCP tools. Instead of scraping a visual control panel or guessing which DOM element represents a relay, the agent can discover an inspect_power_grid tool, read its JSON Schema, test a proposed configuration, and then call route_power with validated relay identifiers. The page's available capabilities change with the state of the game. Restoring power reveals communications tools. Decoding the transmission reveals vault tools. Opening the vault reveals the final evacuation tool. This makes WebMCP discovery part of the game mechanic rather than a thin API wrapper around buttons. The final puzzle demonstrates the human-in-the-loop model directly: engage_emergency_release cannot succeed until the human activates a physical override in the visible interface. That override lasts ten seconds and is checked against live page state. The agent has structured actuation, but the person retains meaningful control. How it creates a better user experience Every agent action updates the same interface the player is watching. When the agent routes power, panels illuminate. When it analyzes a frequency, the decoded fragment appears in the receiver. When it combines inventory items, the new authorization token appears in the player's inventory. A shared chronological mission log attributes every action to the human, agent, or station. This gives the player situational awareness and makes agent behavior legible. The agent receives precise, recoverable error messages instead of silently failing against a visual interface. The player can understand what happened, why it happened, and what capabilities became available next. The experience also progressively enhances. In a WebMCP-capable client, the agent operates structured tools. In an ordinary browser, the complete game remains playable through equivalent manual controls, making the project easy to evaluate and accessible outside experimental environments. What people and agents can now do together The Last Signal creates a shared interactive world rather than dividing the experience into "chat" and "website." The human and agent can inspect the same evidence, manipulate the same state, recover from each other's mistakes, and perform a synchronized final action. Previously, recreating this experience would require brittle screen-coordinate automation, custom browser integrations, or a separate MCP server disconnected from the current visual page. The agent would need to infer the meaning of relays, signal fragments, inventory objects, and locked controls from presentation markup. WebMCP lets the website declare those capabilities and their valid inputs directly while keeping execution visible in the page. Neither participant can deliver the intended finale alone. The agent needs the human's time-limited physical authorization; the human benefits from the agent's structured inspection and rapid operation of linked systems. That complementary relationship is the core of the project. How WebMCP was implemented The application registers 16 imperative WebMCP tools with document.modelContext.registerTool() . Every tool has a focused description, a constrained JSON Schema, structured success and error results, and annotations identifying read-only versus mutating behavior. Tools and human controls call the same command layer. Each command validates preconditions, updates the central game state, records an attributed timeline entry, rerenders the visible room, and returns structured context to the agent. This prevents the manual and agent experiences from diverging. Tool lifetimes are state-dependent. Each registration receives an AbortSignal ; when the mission resets or a capability is not yet available, its controller is aborted. Communications, vault, and evacuation tools are registered only after their prerequisite systems have been unlocked. The deployed site also sends Origin-Agent-Cluster: ?1 and Permissions-Policy: tools=(self) headers.
