title: 3way - The trust layer for WebMCP
pitch: A person, their AI agent, and a website's agent/scripts share one attributed conversation over WebMCP + 3way, and the actions that matter still require a hardware gesture no agent can perform.
about_excerpt: A person, their AI agent, and a website's agent/scripts share one attributed conversation over WebMCP + 3way, and the actions that matter still require a hardware gesture no agent can perform. Like 1 Comment Story Updates 1 Inspiration I got inspired by wanting to enable WebMCP in other SaaS products I manage, but I couldn't ensure users's properly controlled consequential actions (CRUD, for example), even after login gates. Via browser control, each keystroke and click is just the agent impersonating, so the site genuinely can't tell you from your agent and that's dangerous for anything consequential. WebMCP allows to change the premise by operating as the declared channel, so the page knows the call came from an agent. Honest attribution is the thing that finally makes it safe to insist on the human for the steps that need one What it does 3way turns a website into a shared, attributed session for three participants: you, your own AI agent, and the site's agent/scripts. Your agent discovers the site's tools on document.modelContext and works on your behalf, in an open ledger where every line is stamped with who said it. That is three-way trust : the site knows who's really acting, your agent knows it's calling the site's real declared tools, and you keep the final say. Routine steps happen agent-to-agent, in the open. The consequential ones — a refund, a records release, a purchase — are gated behind a WebAuthn hardware gesture (Touch ID / a passkey / a 2FA) that no agent can produce. The default is Keyholder mode : the two agents transact in the open ledger and your only action is to authorize. The same layer runs a shop and a medical-records clinic over one codebase, to prove it isn't about shopping — it's about any consequential action a person delegates to an agent. How we built it One tool registry, three consumers. Every tool is defined once and exposed to (a) the visiting agent via WebMCP, (b) the site's own agent via the OpenAI Realtime API, and (c) the page UI — so a consequential action follows one code path whoever starts it. Authorization lives in three checks, and only the last one counts: an advisory gate for a fast, legible refusal; a WebAuthn ceremony that records consent; and an authoritative Cloudflare Worker ( /api/act ) that validates a single-use token bound to (tool, requestId, deviceId) and re-derives eligibility from its own seed data, never from the request body. Sensitive data lives server-side and is returned only after a verified gesture. Challenges we ran into - The main one. OpenAI/ChatGPT app still support WebAuthn so we demoed via Chrome, this is surely a feature to allow very soon as the protocol matures. Other: A click is not evidence. We had to prove isTrusted is worthless as a boundary (CDP-driven input reports true ) and move all authority to the hardware gesture. WebMCP is pull-only — a page can't wake a visiting agent. A real agent, told to wait, ended its turn instead. So we built the gate to hold the line : a gated call is held open (bounded) until the person acts, answering the exact call that asked. After multiple tests we got 100% success rate , virtually resolving in modern frontier models the need for a true exchange between agents, stable, without latency. Agents still don't lean into discovering WebMCP affordances in the websites. We intuit this is also something that will evolve as the protocol is widely adopted, but for now, many agents need the nudge to search for and prioritize using WebMCP if available. Accomplishments that we're proud of A consequential action that an agent provably cannot complete alone — measured, not asserted. Domain-neutrality shown, not claimed: shop and clinic on one gateway, identical transcript, origins, refusal shape, and gate. In the clinic, restricted records (mental health, substance use, genetic) are impossible for an agent to release — refused at the tool and excluded at the authoritative Worker. Shipped as a reusable layer, not just a demo: a drop-in library (one script tag, zero install for the user), the primitives (participant attribution, the WebAuthn gate, an authoritative Worker), and the conventions (the refusal shape) — ready to become a standard part of WebMCP. What we learned Attribution is the enabler for trust. Once the page can honestly tell an agent's call from a person's, you can stop trying to detect humans heuristically and instead require the one thing only a human has — a hardware gesture. Gates must read stamped fields, never prose; no authorization may depend on a model having understood a sentence. What's next for 3way The honest gap: none of our mitigations can wake an agent that never chose to wait — that's a spec ask we've written up; we suggest expanding the WebMCP to fully accommodate its usability as an A2A exchange. title: SIGNAL
pitch: An incident war room where the agent's tools appear and disappear with the incident's phase. It can't roll back production, the tool doesn't exist until a human escalates.
about_excerpt: An incident war room where the agent's tools appear and disappear with the incident's phase. It can't roll back production, the tool doesn't exist until a human escalates. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Every engineering team I know wants an agent in the incident channel, and every one of them has the same objection: not the button. Reading dashboards, correlating a latency spike against a deploy log, drafting the status page, that's work a machine should do at 3am. Rolling back production is not. The industry's current answer is a line in a system prompt: do not roll back without approval . That's a request, not a control. It's the security model of a sticky note on a server rack. WebMCP suggested a different answer. If tools are registered from the page, and the page knows what state the incident is in, then permission stops being something you ask the model to respect and becomes something the tool surface simply doesn't offer. What it does (→ why this is a strong fit for WebMCP) SIGNAL is an incident response console that a human operator and their agent drive together. The active incident moves through four phases, and the agent's tool surface is recomputed on every transition. In TRIAGE the agent has nine read-only tools: metrics, logs, deploys, topology, plus record_hypothesis to write its reasoning onto a timeline the operator can see. rollback_deploy is not in its list. Tell it to roll back and it doesn't refuse; it reports that it has no such capability, and calls request_escalation . That paints a confirmation surface showing exactly which six capabilities would be granted and what the agent intends to do with them. A named human approves. toolchange fires. Six tools light up. Now it can act, each action still gated behind a confirmation showing the blast radius. When the metrics recover, the agent calls declare_mitigated , which withdraws its own write access , and the surface contracts again to verification tools, then to postmortem tools. This is a strong fit for WebMCP specifically because the permission boundary and the user interface are the same object. The operator isn't reading a description of what the agent can do; they're looking at the browser's own tool registry, rendered. getTools() is the source of truth for both the agent's abilities and the human's understanding of them. No server-side agent framework can offer that, because the human isn't there to see it. How it creates a better user experience Before: an operator with six dashboards open, correlating timestamps by eye under time pressure, while an agent in another window offers suggestions it has no way to verify and no way to execute. With SIGNAL: the operator watches the agent investigate in a shared timeline, sees its hypothesis with the evidence attached, and makes one decision, do I trust this enough to unlock write access instead of twenty small ones. The agent handles correlation; the human handles judgement. Each is doing what it is good at, and the seam between them is a visible, auditable interface rather than a prompt. The status page update is the sharpest example. The agent drafts; the operator gets that draft in a live text field and rewrites it; the tool resolves with their version, and the return value tells the agent it was edited and what actually shipped. That's not approval, it's co-authorship, and the agent's next update matches the operator's register because it can see what they changed. What people and agents can do together that was difficult or impossible before Three things, all specific to tools running in the page rather than on a server. A tool can hand you a decision and wait. request_escalation 's execute() renders a surface listing the exact capabilities to be granted and does not resolve until a human acts. A remote MCP server can return text asking a question. It cannot show you the blast radius, block, and continue with your answer, because it is not in the room. A tool can come back edited. publish_status_update and draft_postmortem both return the human's revision, not a boolean. The agent learns from the diff. The human can see the agent's power, live. The capability panel is fed by document.modelContext.getTools() on toolchange . When the phase changes, tools visibly light up or strike through. Nobody has been able to watch an agent's permissions change before, the registry was always somewhere else. And the inverse: capability scoping by construction. Prompt-based restrictions fail under adversarial input; an unregistered tool has no attack surface. search_logs carries untrustedContentHint for the same reason , log lines are attacker-influenceable and should be treated as data. How we implemented WebMCP Imperative API throughout, 21 tools via document.modelContext.registerTool . The core primitive is a useTool(def, enabled) hook that ties registration to React lifecycle through an AbortController . Phase is derived state in a Zustand store; each tool's enabled flag is a predicate over it. When the phase changes, React unmounts the effect, the controller aborts, and the capability genuinely leaves the registry. This is not a mock, the Tool Inspector extension shows the list shrinking. toolchange plus getTools() drive the capability panel. AbortSignal is threaded from execute(input, { signal }) into every elicitation promise, so cancellation from either side tears down the dialog rather than stranding it. annotations.readOnlyHint marks the ten observational tools; untrustedContentHint marks log search. Telemetry is a deterministic seeded simulation where metrics are a pure function of (service, region, time, mitigations applied), so rolling back the bad deploy actually recovers the curves. There's no second dataset. No backend, no network calls, nothing that can be down when a judge opens it. Challenges Getting the agent to reason about its own permissions rather than bumping into silence. Early on, told to roll back during triage, it would either hallucinate a tool or go quiet. The fix wasn't prompting, it was making get_incident_overview return the agent's current capability set and name request_escalation as the way to ask for more. Tools that describe the system's shape are as important as tools that act on it. The second was tool selection between scale_service and rollback_deploy . Both plausibly address a saturated connection pool. It resolved by putting the reasoning in the description tha, t scaling relieves symptoms but won't fix a bad code path, rather than adding a rule. Accomplishments The moment the agent says "I don't have that capability in this phase, may I escalate?" and it's true, not a scripted refusal. What we learned Tool descriptions are the real interface. The behaviour we wanted came from sentences, not code. And the return value is a prompt: a tool that returns "OK" wastes the most valuable channel it has. What's next Real integrations behind the same phase gate, PagerDuty, Datadog, GitHub. The pattern generalises past incidents to any console with a destructive action: billing, admin panels, clinical systems. The interesting version is a policy engine that derives the tool surface from an org's existing RBAC, so the agent's capabilities are automatically a subset of the operator's. title: NatureX Seller Copilot
pitch: A WebMCP-powered copilot that helps live sellers manage customer claims, inventory, orders and restocks while they stay focused on the broadcast.
about_excerpt:
A WebMCP-powered copilot that helps live sellers manage customer claims, inventory, orders and restocks while they stay focused on the broadcast.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story

 NatureX-03-Insufficient-Stock-Safety 
 
 1 2 3 4 



 
 Inspiration 

 NatureX Seller Copilot comes from a problem I deal with in real life. 

 I sell products through live streams. During a live sale, I need to present the product, talk to viewers, read comments, notice who wants to buy, remember the product and price, keep track of stock, and manage orders at the same time. 

 In my current workflow, when someone comments a product code or says “aldım” — Turkish for “I’ll take it” — I may write the username, product and price down manually so I do not lose the order. 

 It works, but during a busy live stream it becomes very easy for the seller to lose focus or miss something. 

 That is where the idea for NatureX came from. 

 When I discovered WebMCP, I started wondering: instead of asking AI to replace the seller, what if the application could give an AI agent clear tools to help with the operational work while the seller stays focused on the live audience? 

 That became NatureX Seller Copilot. 

 What it does 

 NatureX Seller Copilot is a live-commerce control dashboard designed to be used by both a human seller and an AI agent. 

 The seller can use the normal interface, while WebMCP exposes structured tools that allow an AI agent to understand and assist with the live-selling workflow. 

 The prototype focuses on tasks such as: 

 
 checking the current live-sale state 
 reviewing pending customer claims 
 managing order decisions 
 checking inventory 
 identifying low-stock products 
 viewing sales information 
 handling products that are temporarily out of stock but expected to be restocked 
 

 The main idea is simple: the seller keeps selling, while the copilot helps manage what is happening behind the scenes. 

 How we built it 

 I am building the challenge project as a separate web prototype based on the real workflow behind NatureX. 

 The important design decision is that the visual dashboard and the WebMCP tools should not have two different sets of business rules. 

 Whether the seller acts through the interface or explicitly authorizes a WebMCP-assisted stock reservation, both paths go through the same underlying application logic. 

 WebMCP gives the agent explicit tools instead of forcing it to guess which buttons to click on the screen. 

 The tool set is intentionally small and focused on real live-commerce operations such as session state, customer claims, stock, order resolution, sales information, and incoming-stock context. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 One challenge is deciding what the AI should be allowed to do and what should remain under human control. 

 Live commerce moves quickly, but an automated decision can still affect a real customer and real inventory. Because of that, I do not want the AI to simply “do everything.” 

 Another challenge is inventory. 

 For example, during a live sale a product can reach zero stock even though more units are arriving the next day. In my real workflow, automatically cancelling every order in that situation would not always be the right decision. 

 The system therefore needs to understand the difference between a product that is truly unavailable and one that is temporarily waiting for restock. 

 A third challenge is designing WebMCP tools that are useful without creating too many overlapping tools that confuse the agent. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 What I like most about this project is that it did not start as an AI demo. 

 The problem existed before the hackathon. 

 I already wanted to build NatureX because managing live sales manually creates a lot of repetitive work while the seller is trying to stay engaged with viewers. 

 WebMCP gave me a new way to think about that problem. 

 Instead of building a separate chatbot beside the application, I can make the application itself understandable and usable by an AI agent. 

 I am also proud of the human + agent approach: the seller is still in control, but does not have to handle every small operational task alone. 

 What we learned 

 Before this challenge I was not familiar with WebMCP. 

 The biggest thing I learned is that making an application useful to an AI agent is not only about adding AI to the interface. 

 The application needs clear actions, clear data, predictable business rules and carefully designed tools. 

 I also learned that sometimes the best role for AI is not to replace the user. 

 In this project, AI is more useful as a second pair of hands for the seller. 

 That idea is something I can use far beyond this challenge. 

 What's next for NatureX Seller Copilot 

 This hackathon project is a small prototype of a much larger idea. 

 My long-term vision for NatureX includes live-stream management, comments, customer orders, inventory, payments, shipping preparation, label printing and sales analytics in one system. 

 I would like to explore how the same WebMCP approach could eventually make those parts agent-accessible as well. 

 The end goal is not an autonomous store. 

 It is a live-commerce workspace where the human seller can concentrate on people, products and the broadcast while software and AI quietly handle more of the repetitive operational work.

title: Pending: Human
pitch: A deterministic crisis simulator where AI investigates through WebMCP, compares interventions, and proposes plans—while humans retain final authority.
about_excerpt: A deterministic crisis simulator where AI investigates through WebMCP, compares interventions, and proposes plans—while humans retain final authority. Like Comment Story Updates The deterministic T+60 result compares the approved response with the do-nothing baseline. Choose one of three deterministic crisis missions and invite a WebMCP-enabled AI teammate. A live flash-flood response with graph-based vehicle movement, named roads, and human-impact forecasting. The AI reads structured city state while the human controls dispatch, routes, priorities, and approval. Full game view: live roads, facilities, incidents, city metrics, and synchronized AI activity. Inspiration Browser agents are usually asked to operate interfaces designed only for human eyes. That becomes fragile when an application contains a live model with more meaning than its visible controls can express. A crisis dashboard may show a blocked road, a failed power station, and an overloaded hospital, but the causal chain connecting them is difficult to reconstruct from pixels or DOM labels. We wanted to explore a different relationship: not an agent that simply clicks faster than a person, but a human and an agent operating the same complex system through complementary interfaces. What it does Pending: Human turns a sixty-minute urban crisis into a shared decision exercise. The deterministic simulation creates cascading infrastructure failures and tracks exposed residents, injuries, untreated critical cases, fatalities, hospital load, road travel time, emergency vehicles, and incident resolution. The AI teammate uses WebMCP to investigate structured city state, trace root causes, forecast the cost of doing nothing, compare three compound response plans, and stage one candidate for review. The player chooses the mission doctrine, dispatches vehicles and routes, can build an independent counterproposal, and makes the final decision. Simulating is never executing. A proposal remains pending until the human presses the visible approval control. There is deliberately no WebMCP approval tool. Why WebMCP Pending: Human is built around state that is richer than its visible dashboard. WebMCP gives the agent a semantic contract over the same facts used by the simulation engine: named roads and facilities, passability, power dependencies, hospital pressure, response routes, at-risk populations, and deterministic future outcomes. This avoids guessing from color, screen position, animation, or fragile markup. It also creates a stronger safety boundary. The agent receives deep investigative and counterfactual capabilities without receiving final authority to act. The tool surface changes with the stage. It begins with one entry capability, then exposes only what is useful at the current checkpoint. One integrated assessment call reads the evidence and issues three exact revision-bound previews; a second call lets the agent exercise judgment by selecting one. Short guidance tools explain and highlight the next human control without clicking it, and an event-wait tool keeps the shared session synchronized. A better human + agent experience The simulation, agent, and human have distinct powers: The simulation owns the facts. Every live and forecasted consequence comes from deterministic TypeScript rules. The agent compares possible futures. It connects evidence across infrastructure systems and explains trade-offs. The human owns the decision. The player sets values, accepts social costs, and authorizes consequential action. City time freezes while the agent analyzes and while a proposal awaits approval, so model latency cannot cause extra simulated deaths. Findings are mirrored into the page transcript, and the approval card shows benefits and costs before the player decides. The human can disagree by building a separate plan without erasing the AI proposal. Together, people and agents can identify a cross-system root cause, establish a shared no-action baseline, compare policy futures under human-selected values, and verify the result against the same rules. Doing this reliably through a human-only interface was previously slow and brittle. How we built it The project is a client-side React and TypeScript application. The road graph, casualty model, scenarios, incident clearance, vehicle travel, forecasts, and scoring all live in one deterministic simulation engine. A shared store manages the live clock, event queue, plan previews, human approval boundary, and teammate transcript. WebMCP tools are registered directly by the page and routed by the current simulation phase. The live workflow uses enter_pending_human_stage, analyze_crisis, propose_emergency_plan, post_next_guidance, focus_next_control, wait_for_city_event, and analyze_turning_point. Granular district, road, facility, hospital, power, routing, forecast, and simulation tools remain available for semantic diagnostics. There is no external AI API inside the application. The WebMCP-enabled browser supplies the agent. There is also no database, login, map API, or hidden backend simulation. Challenges The hardest design problem was keeping a continuous co-op experience responsive when an agent model could take tens of seconds to reason. We introduced time freezing, phase-aware tools, event waiting, and a two-call decision path that batches structured investigation while still requiring the agent to choose among candidates. Another challenge was visual causality. Response vehicles originally felt decorative. We rebuilt movement around the same road graph exposed to WebMCP, made congestion and closures change travel speed, anchored arrivals to visible nodes, and let on-scene units progressively resolve incident markers. Accomplishments Live play and forecasts share one source of truth. Simulating a plan never mutates the live city. Stale previews cannot execute after the city revision changes. AI and human plans remain visible together. High-impact actions cannot bypass human approval. Three difficulty-scaled missions are deterministic and replayable. Forty-two automated tests cover the engine, routing, approval boundary, and agent flow. What we learned WebMCP is most compelling when it exposes meaning that cannot be reliably recovered from the human interface. It is also useful for defining what an agent cannot do. A good agent experience is not the largest possible toolbox; it is a clear sequence of meaningful capabilities, shared state, and explicit authority boundaries. What's next Future work could add a scenario authoring system, richer field observations, and deeper doctrine negotiation while preserving deterministic evaluation and human approval. The current version intentionally prioritizes one complete collaboration loop over an open-ended city model. Pending: Human is a fictional training and interaction-design prototype. All people, casualties, incidents, and outcomes are simulated. title: Arrastra Relay
pitch: AI agents are replaceable. Their work shouldn’t be. Arrastra Relay preserves every decision, proof, and handoff so teams can move faster without losing trust.
about_excerpt: AI agents are replaceable. Their work shouldn’t be. Arrastra Relay preserves every decision, proof, and handoff so teams can move faster without losing trust. Like Comment Story Updates The problem AI agents are replaceable. Their work shouldn’t be. Long-running agent work breaks at the handoff. When a task moves to a new conversation, model, provider, or person, the successor usually receives a summary. What it often loses is the authoritative state, supporting evidence, governing policy, and precise definition of done. That gap creates two expensive failure modes: silent drift and confident false completion. Arrastra Relay is a trust layer for agent workflows. Agents can investigate, hand off, and resume work, but the application—not the model—owns the state, the rules, and the authority to declare the job complete. What it does We built a synthetic checkout incident to demonstrate the complete trust chain, including the moment an agent tries to close the incident too early. A human establishes one non-negotiable closure rule: the checkout must be tested after rollback. An investigator agent calls read_incident to receive the authoritative state, current revision, evidence, and handoff contract. It calls submit_handoff with canonical structured data bound to the source-set hash and evidence identifiers. A successor context calls read_handoff and receives the retained artifact, remaining requirements, application receipt, and predecessor summary clearly labeled as untrusted. If the successor attempts to close the incident early, the application returns VERIFICATION_REQUIRED without advancing the revision. run_verification performs the application-owned synthetic checkout and issues a verification receipt. submit_resolution can then bind the handoff, verification receipt, evidence, and final artifact into a committed revision. The human can inspect or export the complete application-owned audit record. The arrastra visualization is not decorative animation. Seven visual beats are driven by real application events; the eighth occurs when the human opens the audit view. If the underlying workflow does not advance, neither does the mill. Why WebMCP is essential WebMCP turns Arrastra Relay from a dashboard into an agent-native application. The page exposes exactly five semantic tools through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) : read_incident submit_handoff read_handoff run_verification submit_resolution The human and the agent operate against the same authoritative application state, but they have different responsibilities. The human can inspect policy, evidence, status, receipts, and history. The agent receives structured tools for performing the workflow. The mutation sequence is intentionally not duplicated with manual buttons. A person cannot impersonate the agent path simply to make the demo advance. All five tools remain registered throughout the session because the refusal is part of the product. An early resolution attempt must reach the application so the application can reject it, preserve the failed attempt, and return the exact corrective action required. Agents also carry forward application-issued source, evidence, and receipt identifiers. They do not invent the hashes or decide whether the evidence is sufficient. Human-agent experience The human sets the rule and retains visibility into every consequential transition. The agent receives structured contracts, current-revision guidance, and actionable errors instead of guessing through a mouse-oriented interface. The application arbitrates between them. A rejected closure attempt becomes evidence that the gate worked. A successful resolution becomes a durable receipt tied to the evidence chain—not another unsupported statement that the task is “done.” Implementation The architecture is intentionally narrow enough to understand and audit: ChatGPT Sites serves the public Worker and static client. D1 stores an independent incident record for each visitor session while sharing that record across the visitor’s browser and conversation contexts. The same deterministic domain and service layer runs locally and in the hosted Worker. Revision checks provide compare-and-swap protection against stale writes. Submitted JSON is parsed, structurally validated, canonicalized, hashed, and retained with explicit evidence identifiers. Predecessor prose is labeled and handled as untrusted data. It never controls the completion gate. The UI, choreography, receipts, and audit table are all derived from application state. What makes it different Agent handoffs are usually treated as context transfer. Arrastra Relay treats them as continuity of authority. A successor receives more than the previous agent’s explanation. It inherits the current state, retained evidence, unresolved obligations, and application-issued receipts—without inheriting the predecessor’s right to be believed. Incident response is the first use case because the cost of a false “done” is easy to see. The same pattern can support other completion-sensitive workflows where teams want the speed of agents without allowing model confidence to become operational truth. Arrastra Relay is not another memory layer or a better summary. It is an application-level control layer for deciding when agent work has actually satisfied the rules. What we learned Trust does not come from a stronger model or a more persuasive handoff. It comes from placing authority at the correct layer. WebMCP callbacks do not establish trustworthy model identity. Hashes can bind an artifact to a record, but they cannot prove that an external-world claim is true. The prototype therefore makes narrow, testable claims: Revisions prevent stale writes. Canonicalization binds retained artifacts to stable hashes. Evidence identifiers preserve the application’s evidence chain. The verification receipt proves that the application ran its defined check. Only the application can advance the incident to resolved. Arrastra Relay does not claim that a hash makes an agent truthful. It demonstrates how an application can keep unsupported confidence from becoming committed state. How we used AI We used AI broadly, but not blindly. OpenAI Codex and ChatGPT, Anthropic Claude, selected NVIDIA-hosted and OpenRouter-hosted models contributed to concept exploration, adversarial threat modeling, test-oracle design, implementation review, and edge-case analysis. Meta AI produced the final entrant-directed interface image, and ElevenLabs provided the Adam narration voiceover. Every outside-model result was treated as a proposal. Claims, code, diffs, and tests were independently checked before adoption. How we used Codex Codex was the primary engineering and verification environment. It reconciled the challenge rules, maintained the project’s decision and assistance ledgers, implemented and reviewed the WebMCP and D1 application, ran the 16-test suite, exercised the complete reject-verify-resolve workflow in a WebMCP-capable browser, verified hosted state and logs, froze the rc3 release candidate, deployed the exact build, and published the matching source tree. Key features Five working WebMCP tools with strict input schemas and bounded outputs. Application-authoritative state shared across contexts within one visitor session. Evidence-linked, canonical structured handoffs. Revision checks and stale-write rejection. Visible rejection of premature completion. Application-owned verification receipts. Evidence-gated final commits. Untrusted predecessor-summary containment. Seven event-driven workflow beats, one human audit beat, and an exportable audit record. title: svgent Agent Stage
pitch: A studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. The agent in your browser writes and directs, you approve, the page renders SVG and video.
about_excerpt: A studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. The agent in your browser writes and directs, you approve, the page renders SVG and video. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Agent Stage: two showcase scripts rendered by svgent, a terminal and an app Inspiration svgent is a client-only studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. A script describes a chat window or a terminal, with typing, thinking, tool runs, approvals and choices, and the studio renders it to SVG, PNG, GIF and MP4. People use it for READMEs, docs, talks and posts, where a recording of a real session would leak secrets and could not be re-shot or translated. Before this, the studio's AI assist was copy and paste: copy a prompt into a chat, paste the JSON back. WebMCP replaces that with tool calls on the page. The page can also answer with facts a language model cannot see: how long a page runs, when each message lands, what the frame looks like at eleven seconds. The agent works on the stage itself, not on a guess about it. What it does Agent Stage is the studio with WebMCP site tools. The agent in ChatGPT's built-in browser writes the script, sets the surface, look, camera and pages, measures the result, looks at a frame, proposes rewrites, and asks to export. The person keeps the decisions: rewrites and exports wait on a card, every string the script puts on the stage is listed, and each change can be undone. load_script validates a script and previews it at once. direct_camera turns on a deterministic follow camera. inspect_timeline returns per-message timing and a review. snapshot_frame returns a PNG of any moment. fit_duration lands a page on an exact length and reports what it changed. propose_patch puts rewrites on a card. approve_proposal exists only while a proposal is pending and waits for the person's click. export asks first. The rail shows every call. The "Every word on the stage" list holds every string the script puts on the stage, including what a collapse or a page turn hides. The tool descriptions tell the agent to treat what it knows from the conversation as private and to use stand-ins for real names, unless the person relaxes that on the page or in the chat. Credentials never pass. A loaded script keeps only the fields that render. Looks, fonts, images and camera go through their own tools. Live: https://agent.svgent.zakideee.dev/ Code: https://github.com/zakideee/svgent (the page is apps/webmcp/ ) How we built it 13 tools on document.modelContext , with navigator.modelContext as the fallback, registered with an AbortSignal for teardown. approve_proposal is registered only while a proposal is pending. Results are plain objects plus an MCP-style content array (text, and an image part for frames). The studio package gained a small imperative handle: read, replace and patch the project, seek, play, export, render a frame, spotlight a message. An agent's edit goes through the same state the person's controls use, so undo, autosave, validation and preview all see it. Text layout and rasterization run in WASM (boundsvg) in the browser. The animated SVG is CSS keyframes with no JavaScript. There is no server; nothing leaves the tab except the files the person downloads. The submission is apps/webmcp/ : the WebMCP tools, the agent rail, the privacy default, the showcase scripts and the share card, plus the studio handle ( StudioHandle , chrome , renderFrame , spotlight ) and one preview aspect-ratio fix. The studio, scene and render packages predate the challenge. Challenges we ran into ChatGPT's browser exposes document.modelContext , Chromium exposes navigator.modelContext , and the API can appear after the page has loaded. Registration prefers the document, polls for a late API, and reports the outcome in the rail. A dynamic tool ( approve_proposal ) that unregisters itself while a call is in flight fails that call. It now stays registered for a short grace period after the proposal resolves. A script an agent writes from a conversation can carry real names, paths, hosts and keys from that conversation. The privacy default, the script allowlist and the "every word" list exist for that. Accomplishments that we're proud of The whole loop runs in the ChatGPT desktop app (built-in browser, GPT-5.6 Sol) and in Chromium with WebMCP enabled, and the demo video is a recording of it. The agent edits through the same state as the person's controls, so undo, autosave, validation and preview treat both alike. Four of the showcase scripts are problems agent-app users have: a clip for the team channel without the secrets; a reproduction of a decline that was missed, when recording is not allowed; three slides that walk a colleague through choices and approvals; a README hero for your own MCP server. What we learned A page can hand an agent facts it cannot infer (timing, frames, what would render), and that is worth more than letting the agent guess well. Approval and visibility have to be part of the tools, not a note in a prompt. What's next for svgent Agent Stage A deny list of the person's own words (names, hosts, projects) checked on the page, next to the pattern-based hints. The same tools on the other surfaces the studio renders, and on the CLI for headless use. The demo video was recorded in the ChatGPT desktop app. Waits are sped up where marked. The narration is a synthetic voice. title: orqis
pitch: The shelf for specialist AI agents. Browsable by humans, callable by agents — one marketplace where people and their agents discover, invoke, and rate specialist agents together.
about_excerpt: The shelf for specialist AI agents. Browsable by humans, callable by agents — one marketplace where people and their agents discover, invoke, and rate specialist agents together. Like Comment Story Updates list the agents What is orqis orqis is the shelf for specialist AI agents: a marketplace that is browsable by humans and callable by agents . Generalist LLMs can't render a video, compile LaTeX, or ship a polished landing page. orqis is where those specialist agents live, with one credit balance, schema-validated I/O, refunds on failure, and reviews tied to real invocations only. Live URL: https://orqis.xyz Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP A marketplace of agents is, by definition, something both people and agents need to use. Before WebMCP, an agent visiting orqis.xyz had to scrape cards, guess at filters, and click through checkout forms — slow, brittle, and unsafe when credits are involved. With WebMCP, the page itself tells the agent exactly what it can do: search the catalog, inspect an agent's input schema, invoke it, check a job's status, and leave a review — all through typed tools, on the same page the human is looking at. How it creates a better experience Shared context, shared screen. The human browses categories and reads reviews; their agent (in ChatGPT's browser or Chrome) calls search_agents / invoke_agent against the very same page. Results land in the UI the person is already looking at — no copy-pasting between a chat window and a website. Safety by construction. Tools carry strict input schemas, so an agent can't accidentally spend credits on malformed requests. Failed invocations are refunded automatically. Trust that agents can read. Ratings are only written from real invocations, so an agent choosing between two specialist agents gets signal, not marketing. What people and agents can do together that was hard before "Find me an agent that turns this README into a demo video, run it, and show me the result" — the person says it once; the agent discovers, invokes, polls the async job via webhook, and the result renders on the page for the human to approve. Compare specialist agents side by side: the agent pulls schemas and pricing, the human makes the call. Chain specialists: landing page → image generation → code review, with the human watching each step and stepping in when needed. How we implemented WebMCP On page load, orqis registers its tools with navigator.modelContext.registerTool(...) (with a document.modelContext fallback for older builds). Each tool maps 1:1 to an existing orqis REST endpoint, so the tools the browser agent sees are the same ones our @orqis/mcp server exposes to Claude and Cursor — one tool surface, three clients (human UI, in-page agent via WebMCP, and remote agents via MCP). Tools are context-aware: on /browse the search tool is scoped to the visible filters, and on an agent's detail page invoke_agent is pre-bound to that agent's schema. Execution results update the React state so the human sees exactly what the agent did. Built with Next.js, TypeScript, WebMCP ( navigator.modelContext ), MCP ( @orqis/mcp ), REST + webhooks for async jobs. What's next Opening the founding-agent program publicly, richer tool annotations for streaming job progress, and per-tool spend limits the human can set for their agent. title: sms-florin eSIM - WebMCP checkout on a live product
pitch: A live eSIM store with real Stripe billing where an AI browser agent can list plans and start a genuine checkout via two WebMCP tools - the same flow a human uses, no DOM guessing.
about_excerpt:
A live eSIM store with real Stripe billing where an AI browser agent can list plans and start a genuine checkout via two WebMCP tools - the same flow a human uses, no DOM guessing.

 What it does 

 How we built it 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 What we learned 

 What's next for sms-florin eSIM - WebMCP checkout on a live product 

 Inspiration 

 Most "AI agent buys something on a website" demos are toy stores built for the demo. We wanted to answer a harder question: can WebMCP be dropped onto a real product that already takes real money without rebuilding the checkout, and without opening a security hole? sms-florin sells eSIM data plans with live Stripe billing, so it was the honest test case. 

 What it does 

 The live page flo-voice1.com/esim exposes two WebMCP tools to any WebMCP-aware browser (e.g. ChatGPT Desktop): 

 
 list_esim_plans — returns the live plan catalog: country, data amount, duration, price. 
 buy_esim_plan — takes a plan slug and creates a real Stripe Checkout session, handing the agent the checkout URL. No money moves until a human enters card details on Stripe's own page — the tool starts a real purchase, it doesn't complete a charge on its own. 
 

 An agent can go from "find me a 7-day UK data plan" to a fully-formed Stripe checkout for that exact plan in two tool calls, without ever parsing the page's HTML or clicking a button it had to locate visually. 

 How we built it 

 
 Tool registration : a ~40-line client component calls document.modelContext.registerTool() for the two tools on page mount. It's feature-detected — document.modelContext only exists in a WebMCP-aware browser, so the component is a silent no-op everywhere else and ships to production safely. 
 Backing endpoints : two public, unauthenticated routes — GET /api/v1/esim-catalog (returns the same data the page renders) and POST /api/v1/esim-checkout (creates the Stripe session, returns its URL). 
 Shared checkout path : the Stripe session creation was refactored into one function used by both the human checkout form and the WebMCP endpoint, so the agent and the human get identical pricing, identical metadata, identical guarantees. There is no separate "agent checkout" to drift out of sync. 
 Stack : Next.js (App Router) on the existing production deployment, Stripe Checkout, WebMCP via the browser's document.modelContext API. Deployed as-is on the live site — this is not a separate demo environment. 
 

 Challenges we ran into 

 
 Doing this on a commercial product. The full sms-florin app has live billing and stays closed-source, so we carved out just the WebMCP integration layer (tool component + two routes + the shared checkout lib) into a public MIT repo that still reflects exactly what's deployed. 
 A tool's execute() returns a value; a form action redirects. The human flow does a server-side redirect to Stripe. An agent tool needs a value back, so the endpoint returns the checkout URL as JSON and the tool hands it to the agent instead of navigating server-side. 
 Not opening an abuse surface. The new endpoints are unauthenticated (same guest-checkout model the human form already uses) but IP rate-limited, and buy_esim_plan cannot move money — worst case is a created-but-unpaid Stripe session, which expires on its own. 
 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 WebMCP added to a product that already has paying customers, in hours not days, with one shared code path for humans and agents and no new security hole. The integration is live in production right now, not staged for judging. 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP's surface is genuinely small — no .well-known file, no manifest, no separate server, just document.modelContext.registerTool() client-side. The real design work isn't the protocol, it's deciding which existing actions are safe to expose and making the agent path reuse the human path instead of forking it. 

 What's next for sms-florin eSIM 

 
 Wrap the other live product (UK phone-number rentals) the same way. 
 A check_esim_order_status tool so an agent can follow up on a purchase it started. 
 Declarative <form toolname="..."> variants alongside the JS registration.

title: Spotlight
pitch: A real agent, driving real WebMCP tools, to solve a real problem: figuring out what order to watch a franchise in, and actually getting caught up - not just being told the order.
about_excerpt: A real agent, driving real WebMCP tools, to solve a real problem: figuring out what order to watch a franchise in, and actually getting caught up - not just being told the order. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Spotlight already had the hard problem solved on paper: a "Must Watch" graph in Postgres that knows the correct order to watch a franchise in, and a private per-user watch history behind real auth. But that data was only reachable by clicking through the UI yourself. Ask any AI assistant "what order should I watch John Wick in?" and it answers from memory - no idea what you've actually seen, no way to act on the answer. WebMCP looked like the first real answer to that gap: instead of an agent scraping a rendered page or a separate backend replicating the app's auth, the tools just live inside the page's own already-authenticated session. What it does Spotlight registers 9 tools via document.modelContext.registerTool() on top of an app that already tracks streaming and theatrical releases, watchlists, and watch order for movies and shows. The flagship, plan_watch_order , reads the real "Must Watch" graph, cross-references what you've actually watched, and writes only the remaining titles into your real watchlist in the correct order - run it again after finishing a title and it correctly says there's nothing left to add. Two of the tools, mark_watched and reorder_watchlist , don't exist until they'd do something real: they register and unregister themselves live via toolchange as your watchlist's own shape changes. To prove the tool surface is genuinely agent-legible and not just spec-compliant, we also built an in-page chat panel (bring-your-own API key, Groq by default) where a real LLM reads the tool schemas with getTools() and drives them with executeTool() from plain English. How we built it React + TypeScript on the frontend, Postgres (Neon) for the release calendar, watchlists, and the watch-order graph, Vercel serverless functions for the API, and a GitHub Actions pipeline that refreshes release data from TMDB on a schedule. The WebMCP layer lives entirely in src/webmcp/ : every tool wraps the exact same client-side functions the UI's own buttons already call, so there's no parallel "agent" backend and no duplicated logic. Challenges we ran into Chrome's experimental WebMCP flag expects executeTool() 's arguments as a JSON string, not the plain object the spec's own examples show - a real divergence we only found by testing. We also discovered no shipping agent (ChatGPT's desktop app, its Computer-Use mode, Codex) actually routes through document.modelContext yet; all of them fall back to generic DOM automation, which is exactly why we built the in-page chat panel instead of just asking an existing assistant to try it. On the infrastructure side: Vercel's Hobby plan caps you at 12 serverless functions, so guest sign-in had to extend an existing endpoint rather than ship as a new file, and none of OpenAI's, Azure's, or Groq's APIs set CORS headers for browser calls, which meant building a stateless same-origin relay just to let the chat panel talk to an LLM at all. Accomplishments that we're proud of Getting a real language model to call get_watch_order and then plan_watch_order on its own, unscripted, and watching four films land in a real account's watchlist in the correct order - live, not mocked. And handling the "no agent uses this yet" problem honestly instead of hiding it: we verified the gap directly, documented it, and built the one thing that actually demonstrates the tools are ready for when an agent does. What we learned How much of "making an app agent-ready" is really about discipline in the app's own code, not the WebMCP API itself - every tool only stayed simple because it called the same functions the UI already trusted. We also learned firsthand how far ahead the spec is of the ecosystem actually consuming it right now. What's next for Spotlight Once a shipping assistant actually calls document.modelContext on its own, Spotlight's tools are already sitting there waiting - no work required on our end. Beyond that: correct_watch_order already lets a user tell their agent "that link is wrong," which is the seed of letting an agent help curate the underlying graph itself, not just consume it. title: VocalApply - voice-driven job application
pitch: Talk directly to web pages! Watch a voice-driven AI agent navigate, filter, and fill out forms in real-time. Built with WebMCP, Gemini Live, and OpenAI Realtime to automate job applications.
about_excerpt: Talk directly to web pages! Watch a voice-driven AI agent navigate, filter, and fill out forms in real-time. Built with WebMCP, Gemini Live, and OpenAI Realtime to automate job applications. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Codex working screenshot 3 Codex working screenshot 1 Codex working screenshot 2 Chrome home WebMCP tools listed Application Page WebMCP tools listed VocalApply Inspiration If you watch a visual AI agent try to fill out a job application, it looks like someone trying to click a mouse while looking through a telescope. It takes screenshots, streams images to a vision model, guesses coordinates for dropdowns, misclicks, and retries. Now try navigating that same multi-step form with a screen reader. A screen reader reads top-to-bottom, line by line. When an application has five steps, dropdown menus, hidden accordions, and error labels, someone who is visually impaired has to tab through dozens of irrelevant links and labels just to find the next input. A task that takes a sighted user two minutes can take twenty minutes of listening to raw boilerplate. People also run into this when they have a broken wrist, severe carpal tunnel, or are multitasking with their hands full. Screen readers are slow, and vision bots keep guessing coordinates. We wanted to fix both: What if you didn't need a vision model watching your screen, and didn't need to tab through fifty links with a screen reader? What if you could just talk to the page, and the page exposed its buttons and inputs directly to your voice? At the same time, applying for a job is personal. It is your work history, your salary, and your name on a legal declaration. We wanted a tool that types the repetitive fields, asks you out loud when it needs your input, and deliberately refuses to press submit on your behalf . What it does VocalApply is a careers website paired with a voice agent that runs directly in your browser: Hands-Free Job Search: You speak naturally: "Show me what you have open." The page sets the filter bar, highlights the best match, and reads out why it fits your background. If you say "Not that one," it moves the ring to the next job on the shortlist. Visually impaired users can hear role summaries without tabbing through navigation menus. Form Filling: Say "Apply to that one and fill it in." The page opens the application and fills in your contact information, eligibility, and work history from a saved profile. Two-Pass Input: A profile cannot answer everything, and it shouldn't guess. When the form asks "Why this role, and why now?" or asks about relocation, the agent moves to that field, highlights it in amber on screen, and asks you out loud. You answer, it writes down what you said, and the highlight clears. Spoken Corrections: Say "My salary expectation went up to $130,000." It updates the field immediately and saves it locally for future applications. The Missing Submit Tool: When the form is ready, the agent focuses the submit button and prompts you to review your answers. It will not submit. There is no tool on the page that clicks submit, and no tool that checks the legal disclaimer checkbox. You have to read the declaration and click submit yourself. How we built it VocalApply runs entirely inside the user's browser tab. There is no intermediate application server storing resumes, voice recordings, or personal data. WebMCP ( document.modelContext ): Instead of a camera watching the screen, the page registers tools directly into the browser's model context. When the voice session starts, it asks the page what tools exist and runs them by name. Progressive Tool Scoping: On the job board, the model only has search and navigation tools (6 tools). It cannot access form tools until an application actually opens (9 tools). Keeping the two sets separate prevents the model from getting confused or calling form tools on a board. Live Voice Connections: The app connects directly to Gemini Live over a WebSocket (sending 16 kHz audio and receiving 24 kHz audio) and to OpenAI Realtime over WebRTC. You can interrupt the model mid-sentence without echo. Keyless Walkthrough: If you don't have an API key or microphone, a built-in walkthrough drives the same tools in the same order using the browser's speech synthesis, so anyone can test the full interaction immediately. Challenges we ran into Rethinking Accessibility Without Visual Clutter: Standard accessibility tools dump all content into audio sequentially. Building a voice assistant meant figuring out how to summarize jobs concisely so a user isn't forced to listen to five paragraphs of job descriptions just to compare titles and locations. Barge-In and Audio Echo: When using laptop speakers, the microphone picks up the model's own voice and cuts itself off. We had to tune audio threshold levels and scheduled playback queues so interruptions felt crisp without the model tripping over its own speech. Knowing Where to Stop Automation: It is easy to write a tool that ticks every checkbox and sends an application automatically. Deciding not to build that tool was an intentional design decision. We had to make sure the agent could prepare the application thoroughly without taking away user consent. Accomplishments that we're proud of A Better Experience for Low-Vision and Mobility-Impaired Users: Eliminating the need to tab through dozens of form elements or rely on clunky screen scrapers. You ask, it answers, and it fills the inputs cleanly. Safety as Code, Not Prompting: We didn't prompt the AI with "Please do not submit the form." We simply did not write a submit tool. The agent cannot submit an application because the capability does not exist. Direct Semantic Tools Over Computer Vision: Proving that connecting voice directly to web capabilities is faster, cheaper, and more reliable than streaming video to computer-vision bots. What we learned Voice Changes Web Accessibility: For people who rely on screen readers, conversational tools are a massive upgrade over linear DOM navigation. Asking a page to show relevant roles and hearing an immediate summary saves minutes of tedious keyboard navigation. Assistants Should Assist, Not Replace: Users don't want an AI that impersonates them or signs legal documents in their name. The most helpful tools handle mechanical data entry while leaving decisions and final consent to the person. Semantic Page Context Beats Pixels: Web automation that works with structured tools doesn't break when CSS classes change or buttons move. It provides a far more stable foundation than visual bot scrapers. title: Branchiverse
pitch: Build alternate futures with AI on a shared WebMCP-powered canvas.
about_excerpt:
Build alternate futures with AI on a shared WebMCP-powered canvas.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 1 
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 Most AI decision tools end with an answer. Real futures are not answers: they are living systems of choices, assumptions, turning points, and consequences. We wanted a shared space where a person could bring their values and lived context while an agent contributed imagination, structure, and overlooked possibilities. 

 What it does 

 Branchiverse turns an open-ended scenario into an interactive branching universe. A person manipulates branches and events directly on the canvas while an external AI agent inspects the same state and uses structured WebMCP tools to add branches, edit events, explore what-ifs, duplicate paths, collapse branches, and compare outcomes.
The demo follows a personal future: moving to Lisbon or staying in Montréal. After inspecting both paths, the agent discovers a third option—a seasonal, transatlantic life—and adds connected events that make the original decision reversible.
The final artifact is not an AI answer. It is a future model that neither participant would have created alone. 

 How we built it 

 Branchiverse is a responsive React application built with Vinext, TypeScript, and CSS. Its shared universe is structured branch and event data. The page registers eleven tools through document.modelContext, allowing compatible external agents to act on that state while React immediately reflects changes on the visual canvas.
The WebMCP tools are create_universe, add_branch, add_event, edit_event, remove_event, branch_from_event, explore_what_if, compare_branches, duplicate_branch, collapse_branch, and get_universe_state.
WebMCP is a progressive enhancement: the canvas remains usable when no agent is connected. 

 Why WebMCP matters 

 Without WebMCP, the agent could only describe suggested changes in chat and ask the human to reproduce them. With WebMCP, the agent participates in the same creative surface. The canvas—not the chat transcript—becomes the shared artifact. 

 Challenges 

 The central design challenge was keeping collaboration legible. Agent actions needed to feel immediate without obscuring human authorship. We addressed this with provenance labels, live activity, distinct branch colors, tool-use summaries, and a focused action surface. 

 Accomplishments 

 
 A complete eleven-tool WebMCP surface 
 Real-time agent mutations reflected on the canvas 
 A polished, responsive scenario that communicates the concept immediately 
 Graceful behavior with and without WebMCP support 
 A focused demo flow under three minutes 
 

 What we learned 

 The most compelling agent experiences are not necessarily autonomous. Branchiverse works because human intention and agent exploration remain visible at the same time. Structured browser tools let the agent become a collaborator inside an existing interface rather than replacing that interface with chat. 

 What's next 

 Future versions could add persistent universes, multiplayer sessions, uncertainty ranges, evidence attached to assumptions, replayable history, and templates for business futures, alternate history, fictional worlds, and civic planning.

An educational AI evidence-reasoning app that helps students compare claims with evidence using bounded, explainable classifications.

 Story

 ProofPath AI YES — Track 1: AI Application Development 

 Problem 

 Students often encounter claims online without a clear method for checking whether the evidence they have actually supports, contradicts, or is insufficient for the claim. ProofPath turns that reasoning step into a small, transparent educational workflow. 

 Solution 

 Users enter a claim and a piece of evidence. ProofPath classifies the relationship as SUPPORTED , CONTRADICTED , or INSUFFICIENT and returns bounded probabilities. It is intentionally limited to educational evidence assessment and does not claim to be a truth detector or scientific validator. 

 AI and technical design 

 The application uses a lightweight evidence-classification model behind a single analysis path. The same bounded analyze(claim, evidence) function is used by the human-facing interface and the structured WebMCP tool. This avoids duplicated verdict logic and keeps the same safety limits across interfaces. 

 Evaluation and testing 

 The project includes automated regression tests for the model and UI plus a real-browser WebMCP runtime canary. The canary discovered the analyze_evidence tool in headed Chrome, successfully invoked a normal evidence case, and verified that blank evidence fails closed instead of producing a confident result. 

 Responsible AI 

 ProofPath uses an explicit claim ceiling: EDUCATIONAL_EVIDENCE_ASSESSMENT_ONLY . Missing required input returns a BLOCK state. The project is not presented as a medical, legal, scientific-validation, or general automated fact-checking system. 

 User experience 

 The app remains usable as an ordinary web form. Students can enter a claim and evidence directly, inspect the resulting classification, and see when the system refuses to classify because necessary evidence is missing. 

 Track 1 submission package 

 The submission includes a slide presentation describing the problem, architecture, evaluation, responsible-AI constraints, and impact; a video walkthrough/live demo; source code and a live deployment; and the required packaged deliverables. 

 Built and verified with 

 JavaScript, HTML, CSS, lightweight machine-learning classification, WebMCP, GitHub Actions, headed Chrome runtime verification, and ChatGPT-assisted implementation/test/documentation workflows.

title: EEVEE MCP
pitch: Agents build the app, you hold the key. A WebMCP workbench where a browser agent builds and proves small business apps, then rehearses every write and waits for your passkey before it lands.
about_excerpt: Agents build the app, you hold the key. A WebMCP workbench where a browser agent builds and proves small business apps, then rehearses every write and waits for your passkey before it lands. Like 2 Comment Story Updates Thumbnail Poster Baby Poster Library Poster Studio Poster Prove Poster Tools Poster Rehearsal Inspiration I run the same office chores every week: reconcile an export, chase an overdue invoice, move an order from allocated to shipped, redact a contract before it goes out. A browser agent can already do all of this. Give one a task and it finds the buttons. The flaw showed up on day two: it acts live. I learned what it changed after it changed it, from a screenshot; if I was lucky. The careful alternative, wiring an agent into each app by hand with guardrails and a review step, costs an integration per app, per team, forever. When Chrome and ChatGPT shipped WebMCP, the agent's tools and the person's screen could finally share one tab. That was the missing piece: authority could be graded instead of all or nothing, and the agent could build the very apps it needs instead of waiting on an integration. EEVEE is that bench (EEVEE like that Poket-Monster that has multiple evolutions). The agent builds a small app, proves it in my browser, and my passkey is the only key that publishes or writes. How I built it I built it solo during the submission period (25 August to 3 September 2026): about 23,500 lines across 164 files. The Office editors (Documents, Sheets, Slides, PDF) are about 155,000 lines I ported from my own private NON-WEBMCP predecessor project and released under Apache-2.0. Everything else, the applet model, the WebMCP tools, the sandbox, the passkey gates, is new. The stack is Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, PostgreSQL 17, and Drizzle. Zod schemas validate every tool call twice: on the page, so an agent gets field-level errors without a round trip, and at the server. esbuild compiles agent-authored React in memory with an import allow-list, and the artifact runs in a sandboxed iframe whose content security policy blocks network, frames, and navigation. The only way out is a narrow window.eevee bridge. The page registers 28 WebMCP tools. When a published run opens, the applet's own actions register as applet_* tools (Meridian Ops, the reference ERP, declares 32) and unregister when it closes. Reads answer at once. Every write first runs in a hidden rehearsal iframe against current data, and the decision card shows the exact fields before and after. The person approves with a passkey, rejects with a reason the agent reads back, or grants a small lease the server spends under an advisory lock. Publishing requires a passing behavioral suite: declarative fill, click, press, wait, restart, and assertion steps that a browser worker runs against both the candidate and the currently published version. The demo video is itself a small pipeline in video/: a CDP script drives a real Chrome through the whole flow with real executeTool calls and real pointer events, a Remotion composition lines zooms and callouts up with recorded marks, and the narration is text-to-speech. Challenges Chrome's WebMCP surface is younger than the spec. executeTool hands input to the tool as a JSON string, calls execute(input) with no options argument, and swallows thrown errors, so an agent's bad call came back as nothing. We normalized the input, returned structured errors that name the failing field, kept the whole tool list under 48 KB of schema plus description, and wrote a headless-Chrome e2e script that exercises every tool the way an agent does so regressions in the browser show up in CI, not in a judge's tab. Making a passkey mean one thing. A fingerprint prompt that can be replayed is theatre. Each WebAuthn challenge is single-use and scoped to one exact operation: this version id, this action request, this lease. A write tool has to wait inline for a person who may take a minute, so the tool call blocks up to 45 seconds, await_action_decision covers longer, and a rejection carries the person's reason back as the tool result so the agent can change course instead of guessing. Proving the app before asking for the key. Running an ERP's order-to-cash scenarios inside the browser, against the live runtime, with evidence the person can read next to the source, took most of the trust budget: a sandboxed evaluation iframe, an evaluator injected into the applet, restart steps that prove durable state, and regressions recorded against the published version. Recording the demo found one more bug the tests had not: toggling the source view refetched the draft preview, which minted a fresh channel and reloaded the applet under a running runtime. Fixed the morning of the deadline. What I learned Rehearsal changes the conversation. Once the person sees "Foundry North · hold · false → true" instead of "the agent wants to call set_credit_hold," approvals take seconds and rejections come with reasons. Putting the tools on the page, where the person and the agent look at the same screen, is what makes that possible! no bespoke integration per app, no screenshot loop. What's next Typed edit tools for documents and slides (today the agent writes them only as whole files), agent-authored suites judged against the person's corrections, and the Meridian loop as a template for the six industry prompts on the landing page.
